# Credentials and Cracking Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) | [Full procedure](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Recover and use authentication material](../notes/methods/credentials.md) ```text source -> format -> identity/context -> compatible use -> authentication -> authorization -> new access -> re-enumerate ``` ## Classify > **Run/context:** classify and process recovered artifacts on the testing workstation; authentication checks contact the explicitly selected service. **Decide:** an NT hash, Net-NTLMv2 response and Kerberos cache are different capabilities. Follow the matching format section below; use [one known credential validation](#validate-one-known-credential) before choosing [remote access](active-directory.md#lateral-movement-chooser). Offline recovery alone does not establish service access. ```bash hashid HASH_OR_FILE john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat --example-hashes | less ``` | Material | Do not confuse it with | Next action | | --- | --- | --- | | NT hash | Net-NTLMv2 response | Crack mode 1000 or compatible NTLM PtH | | Net-NTLMv2 | Reusable NT hash | Crack mode 5600 or authorized relay conditions | | DCC2/MSCache v2 | NT hash | Offline recovery with username; not ordinary PtH | | `.kirbi`/ccache | Password/hash | Validate ticket, SPN, time and service | | SSH key | Password | Fix permissions; crack only its passphrase if protected | | KeePass/ZIP/PDF/Office | Raw password | Convert with matching `*2john` tool | ## Validate one known credential ```bash ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ``` > Login accepted proves authentication to that service. Shares, sessions, execution and administrator rights are separate authorization claims. ## Authorized online dictionary/spray ```bash # one known user, candidate passwords hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET # one password, candidate users hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET ``` HTTP form after capturing the real request and failure marker: ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' ``` > Check lockout/rate controls first and manually confirm tool hits. Dynamic CSRF/cookies and weak condition strings require manual handling. ## Hashcat ```bash hashcat -b -m MODE hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head ``` ```bash # known pattern hashcat -a 3 -m MODE hashes.txt '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session mask-job # word plus three digits hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session hybrid-job # resume hashcat --session job --restore ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode; `-a 3` expects a mask, not a wordlist. Measure the actual mode before attempting a large keyspace. ```bash # confirm modes locally hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH|Kerberos' ``` Common current mappings: NTLM `1000`, Net-NTLMv2 `5600`, KeePass `13400`, AS-REP etype 23 `18200`, TGS etype 23 `13100`. Installed help/example hashes win. ## John ```bash john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=job ``` ## Convert protected files ```bash zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash 7z2john archive.7z > 7z.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash ``` ## SSH key ```bash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` ```bash # protected key recovery ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash ``` > Key unlock and server authorization are separate. `Permission denied (publickey)` can occur after the passphrase was correct. ## Linux password records ```bash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo linux.hash john --show linux.hash ``` ## Pass-the-hash ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore ``` > Authentication ≠ remote authorization. Re-enumerate every service/share/right after a successful identity transition. Responder spoofing is prohibited on the OSCP+ exam; keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs. ## Net-NTLMv2 and DCC2 ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash ``` > Neither is a reusable NT hash. Net-NTLMv2 relay is a separate live exchange; DCC2 preserves username-dependent context. ## Kerberos ticket/cache ```bash klist KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN' ``` Check principal, realm, TGT/TGS type, SPN, validity, clock, DNS/FQDN, route and service rights. ## Failure router | Symptom | Next action | | --- | --- | | Timeout/refused | Fix route/service before judging material | | Local/domain login fails | Recheck identity context and supported auth method | | Parser/token error | Recheck complete format, converter, mode and tool version | | Auth succeeds, access denied | Preserve valid identity; enumerate authorization | | SSH key unlocks, server rejects | Recheck user/server/authorized key/policy | | Ticket loads, service rejects | Check expiry, SPN, realm, clock and DNS | | PtH authenticates, execution fails | Check admin rights, UAC restrictions and method prerequisites | ## Re-enumerate ```text identity -> groups/roles -> services -> shares/files -> application features -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> next block ``` ## Use a known password from a Windows foothold Run a reviewed RunasCs build on the current Windows host with the intended account scope. It accepts a plaintext password, not an NT hash. ```cmd REM Domain account: inspect the resulting token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN REM Local account on this host RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" REM Network-only: local identity stays unchanged; inspect the remote result RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 ``` With logon type 9, whoami does not validate the outbound password. An authentication success is separate from resource authorization or an elevated token. [Full credential-use procedure](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md). ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Recover and use authentication material
Find: Classify the artifact and its identity context Return to the file, database row, capture or session that produced the artifact; inspect structure and account labels before choosing a tool mode. ```bash file FILE head -c 160 FILE ``` > **Recognize:** Headers and producing context distinguish a private key, challenge response and stored NT verifier. > **Validate next:** Record the exact source, user/domain and complete format; identify compatible recovery/authentication operations. [Classify the artifact and its identity context](../notes/methods/credentials.md#credential-classify).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol ```text SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY -> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION -> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION ``` Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together. | Material | Recognition | Compatible use | | --- | --- | --- | | Cleartext password | Text tied to an identity/source | Normal protocol/application login | | SSH private key | OpenSSH/PEM private-key block | SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected | | Linux password record | `USER:$id$salt$digest:...` | Offline recovery with complete record/format | | Application/file verifier | Tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | Offline recovery with matching mode/parser | | NT hash | Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context | Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it | | Net-NTLMv2 response | `USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob` | Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material | | DCC2/MSCache v2 | Username-dependent cached-domain verifier | Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material | | Kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN, validity, clock and route | | Kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode | | Session/API token | Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token | Issuing application and authorization context only | Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format: ```bash hashid HASH_OR_FILE john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat --example-hashes | less ``` > **Failure cue:** `No hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password. | Output | Type | Immediate compatible possibilities | Not valid as | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Cleartext password | Reusable secret | Password authentication, key derivation, DPAPI where applicable | Proof of authorization | | NT hash | NTLM key | Offline crack; PTH where NTLM/service policy allows; Kerberos RC4 transition where supported | Net-NTLM response or DCC2 | | AES128/AES256 key | Kerberos long-term key | Request Kerberos material using compatible tooling | Direct NTLM authentication | | `.kirbi` / ccache | Kerberos ticket container | Use while valid for its client/realm/SPN scope | Password/hash | | DCC2/MSCache v2 | Offline verifier | Offline cracking | PTH | | DPAPI key/blob | Protected-data material | Decrypt only with matching context/keys | General logon credential | | Machine-account key | Computer identity | Map the computer account's rights and Kerberos/NTLM paths | Human/domain-admin identity | ##### Net-NTLMv2 relay is a live authentication path, not hash reuse A captured Net-NTLMv2 response is suitable for offline recovery, but cannot be passed as an NT hash. A relay path instead needs a fresh inbound NTLM authentication event, a different reachable target that accepts the relayed protocol, target protections that permit the exchange, and useful authorization for the relayed identity. For an explicitly selected SMB destination, inspect signing behavior before considering it a relay receiver: ```bash nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode TARGET ``` > **Interpret:** signing required closes the ordinary SMB-to-SMB relay receiver path. Signing enabled but not required is only one prerequisite; it does not supply an authentication source, bypass EPA/channel binding on another protocol, or grant the relayed identity useful rights. The current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits poisoning/spoofing. Do not use Responder-style name-resolution poisoning in the exam workflow. A direct, already-existing authentication source still needs a separately reviewed, scope-compliant relay procedure and an action-specific verification; the incomplete procedure is tracked as `RW09`. Every newly usable identity returns to Block 10 before movement: ```text VERIFY MATERIAL -> AUTHENTICATE SAFELY -> CONFIRM IDENTITY -> MAP GROUPS/RIGHTS/SHARES/HOSTS/ROUTES ``` > **Verify:** Identify artifact type, source, account/domain and compatible next operation; record unknowns instead of guessing. > **If it fails:** A 32-character hexadecimal value is not enough to identify its algorithm. Use application/source evidence and converters.
Find: Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse Use the account label from the producing source and the observed service inventory to choose one compatible, correctly qualified validation. ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' ``` > **Recognize:** Accepted authentication proves one service/account pairing; it does not establish shares, administration, RDP or WinRM. > **Validate next:** Qualify local/domain/application identity explicitly, test a compatible reachable service and record the accepted identity. Then test the specific share/logon/execution right; successful authentication is not administrative authorization. [Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse](../notes/methods/credentials.md#credential-use).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state Use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ``` Local Windows account: ```bash nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares ``` > **Decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET ``` Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client.
Variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success ``` One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' ``` Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives.
RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell Use a reviewed, compatible build on the current Windows host with a known plaintext password. This creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an NT hash into a password. ```cmd REM Domain account: verify the new process token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN REM Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" REM Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 ``` > **Read:** in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. With logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. Logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. An accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. [RunasCs upstream](https://github.com/antonioCoco/RunasCs). Native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. Neither tool guarantees an elevated token.
```text accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs ``` Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. ```cmd net accounts /domain ``` ```powershell Get-DomainPolicyData | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SystemAccess ``` Password validation belongs to the existing [credential procedure](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md). Do not spray by default. If explicitly required, account for lockout threshold, duration, observation window and prior failures; use one justified candidate, stop on lockout/rate-limit evidence and preserve successful identities separately. > **Verify:** Record exact identity, service and tested read/write/session effect; classify authentication and authorization separately. > **If it fails:** Account disabled, expired password, wrong domain and denied logon require different responses. Avoid repeating a known-valid password against a denied action.
Find: Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks Identify a supported verifier/converter and build candidate structure from relevant names/policy/context rather than selecting an arbitrary hash mode. ```bash hashcat --example-hashes john --list=formats ``` > **Recognize:** A verified format and feasible candidate model enable offline recovery; a hash-shaped string alone does not. > **Validate next:** Check complete salt/context, conversion correctness, tool backend and whether all required factors are present. [Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks](../notes/methods/credentials.md#offline-recovery).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct format/mode, complete salt/context, justified candidates and an available offline tool/backend ```bash hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" ``` Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: ```text exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible ``` Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: ```bash hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 ``` ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode. Do not use `-a 3` with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. Common source examples identify NTLM as mode `1000`, Net-NTLMv2 as `5600` and KeePass as `13400`, but confirm against the installed version: ```bash hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH' ```
Mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time.
Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.
```bash john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt ``` ```bash john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job ``` File-to-hash converters: ```bash zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash ``` Converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: ```bash command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null ``` > Preserve the complete converter output. Some formats include a filename label before `:` that John accepts but Hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy. > **Verify:** Use the tool's show/result output and then validate the recovered credential in its correct context. > **If it fails:** Token/separator errors imply wrong or incomplete input; no recovery means only the tested candidate space was exhausted.
Find: Recover a protected KeePass database password Look for a vault in readable backups/shares/application data, then inspect file identity and nearby factor/configuration references. ```bash file FILE keepass2john FILE > keepass.hash ``` > **Recognize:** A supported database gives a recovery target, but a referenced key file indicates a separate factor. > **Validate next:** Confirm vault version, required key/account factors and a feasible password search. [Recover a protected KeePass database password](../notes/methods/credentials.md#keepass-recovery).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Complete database, compatible converter, and every required factor; a feasible password candidate strategy ```bash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash john --show keepass.hash ``` Hashcat alternative after confirming KDBX/KDF and input format: ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show ``` > Mode `13400` covers common KeePass 1/2 AES formats. Installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. A recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault. > **Verify:** Open the database with all factors and distinguish vault credentials from target account credentials. > **If it fails:** Missing factors, unsupported versions or malformed conversion require fixing the input, not endless password guessing.
Find: Inspect and recover SSH private-key access Trace readable key files from home/configuration/backups to a specific username; inspect the key parser's response before testing the server. ```bash file KEY ssh-keygen -y -f KEY ``` > **Recognize:** The artifact is a private key protected by a local passphrase; this is separate from the SSH account password. > **Validate next:** Determine the protecting passphrase, associated remote user, accepted algorithm and server key authorization. [Inspect and recover SSH private-key access](../notes/methods/credentials.md#ssh-key).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct key format, passphrase if encrypted, matching server account/key authorization and accepted algorithm/policy ```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > Cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'OpenSSH\|Private Key' hashcat -a 0 -m MODE ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r RULE_FILE ``` Choose `MODE` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. Token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.
> **Verify:** Verify the key parses and an SSH authentication/session succeeds under the correct target identity. > **If it fails:** Invalid format, line endings, wrong passphrase and server rejection are separate layers.
Find: Recover Linux account passwords from matched records Inspect permission-backed account backups or privileged read results; associate shadow verifiers with the matching passwd metadata. ```bash file passwd.txt shadow.txt head -n 3 passwd.txt head -n 3 shadow.txt ``` > **Recognize:** The matching account name and verifier prefix identify an offline password-recovery candidate. > **Validate next:** Confirm snapshots, hash format and account state; a locked field or absent salt is not a normal usable verifier. [Recover Linux account passwords from matched records](../notes/methods/credentials.md#linux-hashes).
Find: Recover or reuse an NT password hash Inspect the output schema of a justified local/domain credential source, keeping RID, machine and domain labels. ```bash head -n 3 hashes.txt ``` > **Recognize:** The source and record fields identify an NT verifier for that local account, not a captured challenge response. > **Validate next:** Verify the actual NT field, account scope and an accepting service/client with the required destination right. [Recover or reuse an NT password hash](../notes/methods/credentials.md#nt-hash).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct account/domain and actual NT hash; recovery mode or an accepting NTLM service with required destination rights Offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` Compatible SMB validation: ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH ``` > NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material.
Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore ``` WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.
> **Verify:** Verify source/type, identity context and the exact permitted service action. > **If it fails:** Local/domain confusion, remote UAC and denied NTLM are different from an invalid hash. Use tickets only when their own prerequisites exist.
Find: Recover a password from a captured NTLM response Use the saved authorized capture's structure and source context; inspect username/domain/challenge/response fields before selecting recovery. ```bash head -n 2 responses.txt ``` > **Recognize:** A challenge-bound response supports its appropriate offline verification workflow; it is not the long-term NT hash. > **Validate next:** Check complete capture format, account mapping and feasible candidates; acquisition/relay policy is a separate issue. [Recover a password from a captured NTLM response](../notes/methods/credentials.md#netntlm-recovery).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct challenge/response formatting and feasible candidates; acquisition method must fit the allowed context ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash ``` > A Net-NTLMv2 response is not an NT hash and cannot be supplied to `-H` or `-hashes`. Relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights. The OSCP+ exam prohibits spoofing, including NBNS. Do not use Responder poisoning on the exam. Keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide. > **Verify:** Retain response provenance and recovered account/password mapping; confirm relevant login rights separately. > **If it fails:** Incomplete captures or wrong separators break recovery. Prohibited spoofing/poisoning workflows are not an operational exam acquisition method.
Find: Recover a password from cached domain logon verifiers Inspect SECURITY/SYSTEM parser output and distinguish cached-domain logon verifiers from local SAM hashes and service secrets. ```bash head -n 3 dcc2.txt ``` > **Recognize:** The DCC2 structure and username-associated derivation identify offline cached-logon material. > **Validate next:** Verify iteration/username context, source consistency and current online account state after any recovery. [Recover a password from cached domain logon verifiers](../notes/methods/credentials.md#dcc2-recovery).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct username/salt/iteration context and feasible offline candidates ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'Domain Cached' john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash ``` > Preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. DCC2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary PtH material. > **Verify:** Confirm artifact format, account mapping and current password acceptance. > **If it fails:** No recovery does not disprove account existence; stale cached credentials may fail current online authentication.
Find: Classify tickets and use a compatible cache Inspect an existing ticket/cache before collecting new material; identify its client, service, realm and validity. ```bash klist -c FILE ``` > **Recognize:** This is service-scoped CIFS material, not a TGT for requesting arbitrary services. > **Validate next:** Check lifetime, cache format, exact SPN/name, route and destination object authorization. [Classify tickets and use a compatible cache](../notes/methods/credentials.md#ticket-use).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context. Correct principal/realm, valid lifetime, service scope, compatible cache format and naming/KDC route Inspect before use: ```bash klist KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache ``` Compatible client example: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN' ``` > Verify client principal, realm, TGT versus service ticket, SPN, start/end time, clock, DNS/FQDN and routes. A readable cache does not prove authorization. Roasting, forging and detailed PtT/overpass belong to the AD procedures. > **Verify:** Inspect principal, ticket service, realm and lifetime, then verify the actual service action. > **If it fails:** Expired tickets, wrong hostname/SPN, cache format and time skew require different fixes; an IP-only connection can break correct Kerberos naming.

# Discovery and Scanning Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) · [Complete procedures](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/README.md) · [Next: service opportunities](service-opportunities.md) · [Mechanics](../notes/Master_Notes.md#finding-attack-surfaces) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Use when:** an assigned IP/list must become a defensible queue of reachable applications. Replace every placeholder and stay inside explicit scope. ## Fast baseline: one directly reachable host ```bash mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET sudo nmap -sS -n -p- --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET ``` > **Read:** initial TCP gives quick leads; `-p-` covers TCP 1-65535; `-sV -sC` acts only on the discovered PORTS; UDP is a separate 20-port sample. Start service enumeration while wider coverage runs. Build one line per useful endpoint: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST ``` Carry that line into the [service opportunity sheet](service-opportunities.md) and append access context, namespace/object, effective right, result and next action. New hosts/routes/listeners return here; a new credential normally triggers authenticated service re-enumeration instead of an automatic complete rescan. ## Command chooser ### Check source and route ```bash ip -br addr ip route get TARGET ``` Decisive output: the intended interface and source address. A route does not prove two-way reachability. ### Discover an assigned host, list or subnet ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET ``` Choose `SUBNET` only when the whole CIDR is assigned. No response is not proof that a host is off. ### Initial/common TCP selection ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET ``` Coverage: Nmap's 1,000 common TCP ports, not ports 1-1000. ### Full TCP coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET ``` Coverage: TCP 1-65535. This says nothing about UDP. ### No raw-packet privileges ```bash nmap -sT -n -p- --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET ``` Choose connect scanning for ordinary OS connections. A SYN scan normally requires elevated raw-packet access. ### Known-running target skipped by discovery ```bash sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET ``` `-Pn` skips liveness proof; it does not fix a bad route. Read actual port responses, not only a host-up label. ### Selected ports across an assigned list ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` Useful for locating one service family. It is not a full port map. ### TCP through an established SOCKS route ```bash proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET ``` Only ordinary TCP connect calls traverse this route. SYN and UDP probes do not become proxy-compatible. Record the 100-port limit. ### Identify applications on discovered TCP ports ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Use the first for application probes; add default scripts only when their interactions answer a useful question. A version match is an exploit candidate, not proof. ### Inspect and run one named NSE script ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Decisive output: behavior or metadata relevant to the chosen question. Read script help before use. The example performs an HTTP HEAD request for `/`. ### UDP common sample, focused detail and full coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET ``` Choose a bounded sample first, a protocol-aware focused probe when a candidate matters, and full UDP only when the objective/time justifies it. Silence can remain `open|filtered`; full coverage can be slow. ### Verify one TCP endpoint ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET ``` Use one port for the Netcat check. Success confirms connection acceptance; refusal is explicit rejection; timeout is unresolved. `--reason` shows what drove Nmap's classification. ### Windows source position ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("TARGET", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` Use one port with `Test-NetConnection`. The loop prints successful ordinary TCP connections and hides errors; no line does not classify a port as closed. Results belong to the Windows host's route and filtering context. ## State decisions > **Run/context:** interpret saved output from the actual scanning source and route. **Decide:** an open listener needs [application-specific enumeration](service-opportunities.md#decision-loop); filtered or silent results do not establish absence. Use [failure repair](#failure-repair) for a coverage gap and [rescan triggers](#rescan-triggers) when access or routing changes. | State | What it establishes | Next action | | --- | --- | --- | | `open` | An endpoint accepted the selected connection/probe from this source | Identify and enumerate the application | | `closed` | Explicit rejection in this context | Move on unless target/source state later changes | | `filtered` | Filtering, loss or path behavior prevented a decision | Diagnose only when the endpoint matters | | `unfiltered` | Reachable by the chosen probe; open versus closed unresolved | Use a scan type that answers that distinction | | `open|filtered` | Either listening silently or filtered | Try a protocol-aware probe; preserve ambiguity if silent | | `closed|filtered` | Either rejected or filtered | Resolve only if it changes the next action | A port-number service label is a clue. `-sV`, protocol behavior and configuration evidence raise confidence. None of them alone proves exploitability. ## Prioritization Prefer the cheapest test likely to produce one of these: 1. direct anonymous or supplied-credential access; 2. exposed files, configuration, backups or useful metadata; 3. a clear application/product/configuration prerequisite for a public exploit; 4. credentials, names, shares or routes that expand another surface; 5. a decisive disproof that lets you leave a path. Investigate applications, not port stereotypes. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete full TCP, UDP or application coverage. ## Rescan triggers - New route, source host or tunnel: repeat the relevant network checks from that position. - Target restart or changed assignment: confirm the IP and refresh affected results. - New credential or identity: re-enumerate authentication-dependent service behavior; a complete port rescan is not automatically necessary. - Foothold: inspect local and internally bound listeners, then map how to reach them. - Higher privilege: re-enumerate protected configuration, credentials, services and routes. - Lossy or inconsistent evidence: repeat only the decisive focused test with the same tuple and clearer diagnostics. Do not repeat an unchanged disproven scan merely because an exploit failed. ## Failure repair | Symptom | Check | | --- | --- | | Every host appears down | Portal/target state, current IP, interface and route; then one assigned known endpoint | | SYN scan lacks privileges | Use `sudo` or switch to `-sT` | | Discovery omits a known-running target | Focused `-Pn` scan and actual response reasons | | Only filtered results | Route/source, loss and one known/relevant endpoint | | Kali and Windows disagree | Hold target, transport, port and time constant before blaming source filtering | | Scan is slow | UDP silence, service probes, retries, loss and selected coverage; use progress output | | Few results | Confirm default/common versus selected/range/full port coverage | | `tcpwrapped` or early close | Treat as an early-close observation, not a product or vulnerability; probe further only if identity matters | ## Evidence minimum Save commands and output with different prefixes. Record source, target, transport, selected ports, discovery mode, scan type, time, state, application confidence, uncertainty and the next action. `-oA PREFIX` writes normal, grepable and XML output; keep the readable `.nmap` and the raw formats. Sources: supplied PEN-200 2025 edition, sections 6.4.2-6.4.3, pp142-156; [Nmap port states](https://nmap.org/book/man-port-scanning-basics.html), [scan techniques](https://nmap.org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques.html), [version detection](https://nmap.org/book/man-version-detection.html), [NSE usage](https://nmap.org/book/nse-usage.html), [timing](https://nmap.org/book/man-performance.html), and [output](https://nmap.org/book/man-output.html). Supplemental source: [Hexdump live enumeration cheatsheet](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/blob/main/cheatsheet.org#enumeration). ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Discover attack surfaces
Find: Validate the source path and discover hosts From the assessment host inspect the assigned interface and the route to the exact target before interpreting silence. ```bash ip addr ip route get TARGET nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery ``` > **Recognize:** The route names the intended interface/source; a responder is evidence from that source, not a global reachability claim. > **Validate next:** Check scope, target state and whether host-discovery probes are permitted by this path. [Validate the source path and discover hosts](../notes/methods/discovery.md#path-hosts).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path > **Purpose:** Confirm the source path and discover explicitly assigned hosts before spending time on port coverage. ##### 1. Check the path From the target's working folder: ```bash mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET ``` > **Read:** selected interface/source address. A route lookup does not prove reachability.
Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet ##### Host discovery **One host:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET ``` **Assigned list:** put IPs in `targets.txt`, one per line. ```bash nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts ``` **Explicitly assigned subnet:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET ``` No response does not establish that a host is offline. A list of assigned hosts does not imply the surrounding subnet is in scope.
> **Verify:** Record source address/interface, route and the exact responding endpoint; a missing ping response does not prove a host is down. > **If it fails:** No route or wrong VPN interface is an environment failure. If only discovery is blocked, use the known-host TCP method; a SOCKS path requires a compatible connect-based client.
Find: Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans After path validation, compare a first TCP pass with explicit full-port coverage; record skipped discovery or privilege limitations. ```bash nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full ``` > **Recognize:** The high listener exists outside the first selection; its application label remains provisional. > **Validate next:** Confirm scan completion, source, errors and application behavior on each interesting port. [Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans](../notes/methods/discovery.md#tcp-coverage).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage > **Purpose:** Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. ##### 2. Get initial TCP results ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** 1,000 common TCP ports. Review `scans/tcp-initial.nmap` in a text editor.
Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports ##### Initial view: 1,000 common ports **Assigned host list, SYN scan:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list ``` **One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET ``` Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. ##### Selected ports or a range **One host:** replace PORTS with, for example, `25,43` or `1-1024`. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET ``` **Find relevant services across assigned hosts:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` A focused service sweep is not a full port map.
##### 3. Complete TCP coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs.
Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress ##### All TCP ports: 1-65535 **Connect scan:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET ``` Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. ##### Discovery skips a running target **Recheck relevant ports with response reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET ``` **Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET ``` `-Pn` assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use `-sT` without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. ##### Timing and progress **Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET ``` **Faster timing on a stable path:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET ``` `-T3` is normal timing; `-T4` is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. ##### TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: ```bash proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET ``` `proxychains` cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. `-Pn` avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.
> **Verify:** Retain the selected port set, source context, completion/errors and raw output; follow open ports with focused application evidence. > **If it fails:** Filtered is not closed. Through SOCKS use supported TCP-connect behavior and skip unsupported raw discovery/UDP; if results conflict, compare from the actual source.
Find: Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks Take the discovered open-port list and request protocol/version evidence rather than choosing attacks from conventional port numbers. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services ``` > **Recognize:** An HTTP response on a nonstandard port routes investigation to application mapping; a product string is still only fingerprint evidence. > **Validate next:** Verify normal requests, hostname/TLS requirements and exact build/configuration before selecting an exploit. [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](../notes/methods/discovery.md#identify-app).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior > **Purpose:** Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ##### 4. Identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET ``` > **Next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability.
Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints ##### Identify applications on discovered ports **Version probing plus the default NSE script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET ``` Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ##### Select a named script **Inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ##### OS fingerprinting and bundled probing **Estimate OS from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET ``` **Request more tentative OS guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET ``` **Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET ``` OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; `-A` does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.
> **Verify:** Preserve the responding product/version evidence and distinguish an inferred fingerprint from a confirmed vulnerable build. > **If it fails:** A timeout, generic banner or scanner label leaves identity inconclusive; use native protocol clients or the unknown-port method.
Find: Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence Inspect discovery results and DNS/SNMP/RPC clues, then probe a separate bounded UDP selection from the same source. ```bash sudo nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 20 --reason TARGET -oA udp-initial ``` > **Recognize:** A DNS response confirms a UDP application; open|filtered SNMP silence is a candidate requiring a correctly formatted request. > **Validate next:** Check accepted service parameters, response identity and possible ICMP rate limiting. [Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence](../notes/methods/discovery.md#udp-coverage).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit > **Purpose:** Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. ##### 5. Check UDP separately ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET ``` > **Limit:** this is a sample. `open|filtered` remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it.
Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP ##### Common-port samples **Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET ``` These are samples. `open|filtered` is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. ##### Selected ports **Check a relevant UDP port/list:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET ``` **Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET ``` A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add `-Pn` with the same limitations as TCP. ##### Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET ``` This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. ##### Combined TCP/UDP selection **Example selection:** change the TCP (`T:`) and UDP (`U:`) lists for the actual question. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET ``` The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan.
> **Verify:** Use an application response for a confirmed service; document unresolved silence, coverage and ICMP rate-limit effects. > **If it fails:** Do not translate UDP silence into a closed service. Retry a focused application-aware probe or a different permitted vantage point.
Find: Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue Compare saved scan results with one direct connection and a service-native request for the endpoint that changes your next decision. ```bash nc -nvz TARGET PORT nmap -Pn -sT -p PORT --reason TARGET ``` > **Recognize:** Independent TCP reachability supports an endpoint candidate, not credentials, read permission or execution. > **Validate next:** Identify the application and validate the particular next-layer action. [Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue](../notes/methods/discovery.md#result-validation).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. A selected endpoint and a test that can resolve the decision-changing uncertainty > **Purpose:** Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. ##### 6. Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access.
Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output ##### Netcat connection check **One TCP port:** replace PORTS with one number. ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` **Short port range:** replace PORTS with a range such as `3388-3390`. ```bash nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. ##### Output and diagnostics **Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET ``` Open saved `.nmap` or `.txt` output in a text editor. `-oA` writes `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml`; `-oN` writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run.
##### 7. Build the service queue Open the saved `.nmap` files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST ``` > **Next:** carry the complete endpoint tuple into [Stage 02 service enumeration](../reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md) and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage.
Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established - `open` establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. - `closed` records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. - `filtered` leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. - `unfiltered` means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. - UDP `open|filtered` is inconclusive. A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. - `closed|filtered` is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. - A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. - Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position.
##### 8. Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed. > **Verify:** Record which layer was demonstrated: transport, application, authentication, read/write or execution. > **If it fails:** Connection success with no useful response needs a protocol-aware test; repeated identical failures without new evidence do not justify repeating the same path.
Find: Enumerate reachable endpoints from a Windows source From the Windows foothold inspect interfaces/routes, then check an assigned internal host's selected service ports. ```powershell Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 ``` > **Recognize:** The service is reachable from this Windows source; this can reveal a useful vantage point unavailable from Kali. > **Validate next:** Confirm application/authentication and whether a forward or a native client can use that route. [Enumerate reachable endpoints from a Windows source](../notes/methods/discovery.md#windows-discovery).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. A permitted Windows shell, explicit target list and built-in networking support > **Purpose:** Test TCP reachability from a Windows host when source position or available tooling matters. Test one TCP port from the Windows source host: ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS ``` > **Read:** `TcpTestSucceeded`, source and destination addresses. Use one number for PORTS. Failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem.
Variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list ##### Scan a low-port range ```powershell 1..1024 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("DC_IP", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` ##### Check a selected port list The example list can be changed to the endpoints of interest. ```powershell 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("TARGET", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` `$_` is the current port; errors are hidden. No printed result does not prove every port is closed. Results reflect the Windows host's access and the stated port selection.
> **Verify:** Associate each result with the actual Windows source and selected port; do not claim UDP or full-port coverage. > **If it fails:** A false result may be routing, filtering or service absence; use route and listener evidence before deciding the service is down.
Find: Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives Select an unexplained listener from the saved queue, compare native connection behavior, then use focused version/TLS probes. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` > **Recognize:** TLS and an HTTP redirect suggest a hostname-selected web application rather than an attack tied to the port number. > **Validate next:** Reproduce the hostname/TLS request and confirm exact software/configuration. [Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives](../notes/methods/discovery.md#unknown-port).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates > **Use when:** Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. ##### RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation > **Prerequisite:** RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. **Coverage:** only the explicit TCP range. **Decisive output:** a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup ``` If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap.
Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 ``` > Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection.
##### Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation > **Prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **Choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **Failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. ```bash sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt ``` Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: ```bash PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified ``` Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. ##### Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Next action:** route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. ##### NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db ``` Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt ``` The broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt ``` Avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization. ##### Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation > **Prerequisite:** an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. **Choose it:** after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. **Decisive output:** a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. ```bash nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt ```
HTTPS, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect `nikto -H` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.
Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. > **Verify:** Confirm the endpoint through independent application behavior and preserve the rate/scope used for discovery. > **If it fails:** No response may require TLS or a protocol-first request. Avoid treating speed-oriented results as complete, and keep prohibited mass vulnerability scanners outside the exam path.
