# Service Opportunity Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) · [Previous: discovery and scanning](discovery-scanning.md) · [Complete procedures](../reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md) · [Mechanics](../notes/Master_Notes.md#extracting-opportunities-from-services) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Extract opportunities from services](../notes/methods/services.md) Use this after application identification. Commands are examples for explicitly authorized targets; replace every placeholder. Enter with the discovery tuple and extend it: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | TRANSPORT/PORT | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | ACCESS CONTEXT | NAMESPACE/OBJECT | ACTION | RESULT | NEXT ``` ## Decision loop ```text CONFIRM APPLICATION -> TEST LEAST-PRIVILEGED CONTEXT (anonymous/null/known credential) -> LIST NAMESPACE BEFORE COPYING/QUERYING -> MEASURE READ / WRITE / ADMIN / EXECUTE RIGHTS SEPARATELY -> EXTRACT NAMES, FILES, CONFIGURATION, CREDENTIAL CLUES -> VALIDATE THE CHEAPEST DECISIVE HYPOTHESIS -> RE-ENUMERATE AFTER NEW IDENTITY, HOST, ROUTE OR ACCESS ``` | Output | Safe conclusion | Next action | | --- | --- | --- | | Authentication accepted | Identity/method works for this protocol | Enumerate authorization; do not assume session/admin rights | | Read succeeds | This identity can read that object | Inspect locally; map disclosed names/credentials | | Write succeeds | This identity can alter that object/path | Find consumer, execution identity and trigger before claiming execution | | Access denied | This object/action denied in this context | Try a legitimately acquired identity or a different allowed object | | Timeout/silence | Cause unresolved | Check route, transport, version and a protocol-aware probe | ## FTP ```bash ftp TARGET # anonymous / email-like password; then: status, pwd, ls -la, binary, get FILE nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt ``` > `230` accepts login; `530` rejects that login. Upload proves write only. [Full FTP procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/01-ftp.md). ## SSH ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET ``` > Separate route, host-key, method, credential and shell-policy failures. Spraying/cracking is a later block. [Full SSH procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/02-ssh.md). ## SMTP ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT # EHLO example.invalid # HELP # VRFY USER # EXPN postmaster # QUIT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT ``` > `252` is inconclusive, not a confirmed user. Compare response codes and final multiline reply. [Full SMTP procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/03-smtp.md). ## DNS ```bash dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET ``` ```powershell nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET ``` > AXFR refusal disproves only that transfer attempt. `NXDOMAIN` differs from `NOERROR` with no answer. Check wildcard results. [Full DNS procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/04-dns.md). ## NFS and Unix RPC ```bash rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs TARGET sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit # Only when a harmless write check is required: sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` > NFSv4-only servers may not answer `showmount`. Interpret numeric UID/GID, `root_squash`, write rights and privileged consumption separately. [Full Unix file-services procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md).
Rsync daemon — list modules, then retrieve selected artifacts ```bash nmap -sV -p 873 --script rsync-list-modules TARGET rsync rsync://TARGET/ rsync --list-only rsync://TARGET/MODULE/ rsync -av rsync://TARGET/MODULE/path/FILE ./FILE ``` > A module listing proves namespace visibility, not read/write/execute. Retrieve only selected material; never use remote `--delete` during enumeration. [Interpretation and variants](../reference/02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md#rsync-daemon--list-modules-before-copying).
TFTP — retrieve an evidence-backed filename ```text tftp TARGET tftp> binary tftp> get FILE tftp> quit ``` > TFTP has no directory listing or login step. A timeout does not distinguish a missing name, blocked UDP or transfer-policy failure. Upload only when the objective requires a write check and a cleanup route exists. [Interpretation and write boundary](../reference/02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md#tftp--known-name-retrieval-only).
## SMB and MS-RPC > **Run/context:** SMB/RPC clients run on the testing workstation against the named server, using an explicit anonymous, local or domain identity. **Decide:** share listing does not establish file read, write or execution. Validate the exact object with the [complete SMB procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/06-smb-rpc.md); send a recovered secret to [credential classification](credentials-cracking.md#classify), and record a denied object as denied in this context. ```bash smbclient -N -L //TARGET smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' # pwd, ls, allinfo FILE, get FILE rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET # srvinfo, enumdomains, enumdomusers, enumdomgroups, queryuser RID, netshareenumall nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET ``` ```powershell net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE ``` > Null, guest and authenticated sessions can expose different namespaces. Confirm useful results manually. [Full SMB/RPC procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/06-smb-rpc.md). ## SNMP ```bash onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 # users, processes, installed software, TCP listeners snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` > No response can be community, version, OID, loss or filtering. A write community is not permission to alter state during enumeration. [Full SNMP procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/07-snmp.md). ## LDAP and Kerberos ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -s base -b '' defaultNamingContext dnsHostName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName ``` ```bash getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u ``` > RootDSE may work when anonymous directory search does not. Kerberos failures often come from DNS/hostname/SPN/time/route rather than the password. [Full LDAP/Kerberos procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/11-ldap-kerberos.md). ## Databases ### MySQL / MariaDB ```bash mysql -h TARGET -P PORT -u USER -p ``` ```sql SELECT VERSION(), USER(), CURRENT_USER(); SHOW DATABASES; SHOW GRANTS; USE DATABASE; SHOW TABLES; SELECT * FROM TABLE LIMIT 20; SELECT @@secure_file_priv; ``` ### MSSQL ```bash impacket-mssqlclient 'USER@TARGET' impacket-mssqlclient 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' -windows-auth ``` ```sql SELECT @@VERSION; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); SELECT name FROM sys.databases; ``` ### PostgreSQL ```bash psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres # \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* ``` ```sql SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); ``` > DB admin is not OS admin. Server file/program functions act as the DB service identity and require explicit grants. [Full database procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/08-databases.md). ## Windows remote access ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 ``` ```powershell $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred ``` > Valid credentials may still lack RDP logon or WinRM endpoint rights. Check the installed FreeRDP/Evil-WinRM help for version-specific spelling. [Full Windows remote-access procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/09-windows-remote-access.md).
Host-side RDP decision check — local administrative context ```powershell Get-Service TermService reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v PortNumber reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication qwinsta net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users" $policy = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'rdp-user-rights.inf' secedit /export /mergedpolicy /areas user_rights /cfg $policy /quiet Select-String -Path $policy -Pattern '^SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight','^SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight' ``` > `fDenyTSConnections = 0` permits RDP at the local setting; check applied GPO when policy may override it. `UserAuthentication = 1` requires NLA. The candidate needs an effective `SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight`, and any applicable `SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight` wins. Confirm the configured port from the actual source before testing authentication. [Full interpretation and policy-precedence sequence](../reference/02-service-enumeration/09-windows-remote-access.md#rdp-host-side-inspection-local-administrative-context).
## New-state triggers | New finding | Immediate study/practice action | | --- | --- | | Hostname or IP | Confirm scope, resolve both directions, run discovery/service identification | | Username/domain | Record confidence and source; do not promote ambiguous SMTP output to confirmed | | Credential/key | Identify local/domain context and likely services; perform one controlled validation | | Readable file | Preserve metadata and inspect locally for paths, names, keys and configuration | | Writable path | Identify consumer, execution identity and trigger before testing exploitation | | Remote session | Verify host/identity/IP, then re-enumerate local privileges, files, listeners and routes | ## SMBMap and authenticated SMB/RPC collection Use an accepted account and reachable SMB; inspect one share before downloading a selected file. ```bash smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --no-write-check smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -r 'SHARE' --depth 2 --no-write-check smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --download 'SHARE\PATH\FILE' --no-write-check enum4linux-ng -A -w DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' TARGET ``` A readable config/backup → classify the value and test the matching service. Share-list denial does not rule out a known share path. [Full SMB/RPC procedure](../reference/02-service-enumeration/06-smb-rpc.md). ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Extract opportunities from services
Find: Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access After identifying FTP, test the allowed anonymous context or one known credential and inspect its directory namespace. ```bash curl -v ftp://TARGET/ curl -v --user 'USER:PASSWORD' ftp://TARGET/ ``` > **Recognize:** A listing identifies candidate artifacts; a completed RETR with recognizable bytes establishes read access. > **Validate next:** Validate the account context, file contents, data-channel reachability and any separate write/consumer conditions. [Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access](../notes/methods/services.md#service-ftp).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights > **Recognize:** FTP usually appears on TCP/21, but trust an FTP banner or protocol response on any port. **Goal:** determine authentication, listable/readable content and effective write locations. ##### Baseline: anonymous access ```bash ftp TARGET ``` At the prompts, try user `anonymous` and an email-like password. Then: ```text status pwd ls -la binary get FILE quit ``` If login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's `passive` command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. > **Decisive output:** code `230` accepts the login; directory listings and successful `RETR` establish read access. Inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. Store target artifacts outside this public repository.
Variant — authenticated FTP ```bash ftp TARGET ``` Enter `USER` and the password when prompted. Enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access.
Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test ```bash curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER ftp://TARGET/ curl --user USER -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt ``` Omit `--user` for anonymous access. Let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. Upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the FTP client after the test.
Variant — focused Nmap helpers ```bash nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET ``` `ftp-anon` checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; `ftp-syst` asks for server/system information. Manually confirm useful access with a protocol client.
> **Failure cues:** `530` means that login was rejected, not that FTP has no other usable identity. A listing failure after `230` may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. A successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. > **Next action:** inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block. > **Verify:** Retrieve recognizable bytes or independently verify an uploaded canary; distinguish listing, read and write rights. > **If it fails:** Login succeeds but transfers hang: diagnose the data path. A writable upload directory alone does not establish command execution.
Find: Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access Find SSH in service discovery, then trace a candidate password/key back to its recorded user before a bounded authentication attempt. ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > **Recognize:** Accepted key authentication plus a verified shell identity establishes that specific login, not root or unrestricted forwarding. > **Validate next:** Check actual account/shell/subsystem and separately inspect forwarding policy if a tunnel is needed. [Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access](../notes/methods/services.md#service-ssh).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission > **Recognize:** SSH commonly uses TCP/22. **Prerequisite for access:** an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. ##### Baseline: validate one known identity ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. A shell prompt establishes session access as that identity.
Variant — private key ```bash chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` The key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions.
Variant — discover methods for a known username ```bash nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET ``` This starts an authentication exchange and is logged; Nmap classifies it as intrusive. Use it only when the supported methods change the next decision.
Variant — non-interactive key check ```bash ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET 'id' ``` Batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. It is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively.
> **Failure cues:** timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; `Permission denied` proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. A valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. > **Next action:** after a shell, verify `whoami`, groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. Password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure. > **Verify:** Run hostname and id in the resulting context; retain whether a shell, SFTP or only forwarding was actually granted. > **If it fails:** Permission denied may be username, key, passphrase, policy or method mismatch. A successful banner exchange proves none of these.
Find: Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols Identify mail-related listeners, inspect greeting/capabilities and compare permitted user-discovery replies with a known-invalid control. ```bash nc -nv TARGET 25 ``` Then enter the protocol dialogue: ```text EHLO example.invalid VRFY USER VRFY INVALID_CONTROL QUIT ``` > **Recognize:** A reproducible reply difference can expose a possible mailbox identity. > **Validate next:** Check catch-all policy and account context; recipient acceptance does not prove mailbox credentials or OS access. [Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols](../notes/methods/services.md#service-smtp).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context > **Recognize:** SMTP commonly uses TCP/25, submission uses 587, and implicit TLS commonly uses 465. **Goal:** collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. ##### Baseline: banner and capabilities ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` Then enter: ```text EHLO example.invalid HELP VRFY USER EXPN postmaster QUIT ``` > **Decisive output:** `250-` capability lines reveal extensions such as STARTTLS or AUTH. `250` after `VRFY` may support a valid mailbox; `550` commonly rejects or denies it; `252` explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists.
Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet ``` Run `EHLO example.invalid` after TLS negotiation. Certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism.
Variant — focused automated user checks ```bash smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT ``` `RCPT` testing requires an SMTP transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. Treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses.
Variant — Windows source position ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORT ``` This verifies TCP reachability only. Use an available Netcat/Ncat or OpenSSL client for protocol dialogue.
> **Failure cues:** multiline replies begin with `NNN-` and finish with `NNN `; read the final line. `503` often means the command sequence is wrong. Uniform `252` or `550` responses make enumeration inconclusive. A visible AUTH method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. > **Next action:** add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. Do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. ##### POP3 and IMAP handoff Mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995 -crlf -quiet # POP3S openssl s_client -connect TARGET:993 -crlf -quiet # IMAPS ``` POP3 dialogue: ```text CAPA USER USER PASS PASSWORD STAT LIST QUIT ``` IMAP dialogue: ```text a1 CAPABILITY a2 LOGIN USER PASSWORD a3 LIST "" "*" a4 LOGOUT ``` > Test one legitimately acquired credential. Capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force NSE scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap mail blocks. > **Verify:** Record response/control differences and separate inferred account existence from successful mailbox authentication. > **If it fails:** Uniform replies, disabled VRFY or a catch-all make username enumeration inconclusive; investigate other identity sources.
Find: Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers Use DNS-server evidence and discovered domain names to query authority and specific records before considering a transfer. ```bash dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR ``` > **Recognize:** An authoritative zone and returned records can expose hostnames, aliases and applications needing separate enumeration. > **Validate next:** Check each new name's scope/address and verify host/virtual-host behavior. [Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers](../notes/methods/services.md#service-dns).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer > **Recognize:** DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries and TCP/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. **Prerequisite:** a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. ##### Baseline: query the target DNS server directly ```bash dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN A dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT ``` > **Decisive output:** `ANSWER` records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. The `aa` flag supports an authoritative answer. Record `status` separately from the answer count.
Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer ```bash dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR ``` A successful AXFR returns the zone records and closing SOA. `Transfer failed`, `REFUSED` or `NOTAUTH` only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries.
Variant — name guessing after the domain is known ```bash dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN ``` Check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. Every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input.
Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range ```bash dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET ``` Use this only when the entire `SUBNET` is assigned. PTR names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results.
Variant — host and Windows nslookup ```bash host -t mx DOMAIN TARGET host -t txt DOMAIN TARGET ``` ```powershell nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=MX DOMAIN TARGET ```
> **Failure cues:** `NXDOMAIN` means that queried name does not exist in that view; `NOERROR` with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. Timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. A recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. > **Next action:** add new hostnames/IPs to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints. > **Verify:** Identify responding server, record type, answer and zone authority; transfer refusal disproves only that transfer/context. > **If it fails:** No answer may mean wrong server, recursion policy, transport or zone. Resolve authoritative context before retrying AXFR.
Find: Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity Follow RPC/NFS discovery with export inspection, then examine actual ownership/mapping on an allowed mount. ```bash rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET ``` > **Recognize:** An export lists a filesystem candidate and client policy; it does not establish file access or trusted UID 0. > **Validate next:** Use the owning procedure to verify NFS version, allowed client, numeric identity mapping, read/write and squash/mount policy. [Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity](../notes/methods/services.md#service-nfs).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access > **Recognize:** rpcbind commonly appears on TCP/UDP 111 and NFS on TCP/UDP 2049, with additional dynamically assigned RPC ports. **Goal:** find exports, allowed client ranges and effective UID/GID-based permissions. ##### Baseline: list RPC services and exports ```bash rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** `rpcinfo` maps RPC programs to versions/transports/ports. `showmount -e` returns exports and apparent allowed clients, but NFSv4-only servers may not expose the mount service and `showmount` completeness varies by implementation.
Variant — Nmap without mounting ```bash nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs TARGET ``` The scripts can list exports, file attributes and access flags. Confirm access manually when a finding matters.
Variant — mount read-only first ```bash sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` If version 3 fails and version 4 is advertised, retry with `-o ro,vers=4`. NFSv4 may present a pseudo-filesystem whose export path differs from `showmount` output.
Variant — inspect numeric ownership ```bash ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable -ls ``` NFS commonly authorizes Unix identities by numeric UID/GID. A matching local username is irrelevant if its number differs. `root_squash` usually maps remote UID 0 to an unprivileged identity; `no_root_squash` is dangerous but still requires a useful writable object and privileged consumption path.
Variant — bounded write verification ```bash sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` Use a unique harmless name only when write validation is needed and authorized. Record the resulting numeric owner/group. Success proves write in that directory, not execution or privileged ownership.
> **Failure cues:** `showmount` failure does not rule out NFSv4. `access denied by server` can mean export client restrictions or wrong path/version. `permission denied` after mounting is file authorization, not network failure. Do not change local UIDs or write to an export during concept study. > **Next action:** inspect readable backups, home data, keys and configuration; record numeric ownership and actual write boundaries; send a writable/privileged-consumer hypothesis to the escalation block. ##### Rsync daemon — list modules before copying > **Recognize:** an rsync daemon normally listens on TCP/873, although the application can use another port. The daemon namespace uses `HOST::MODULE` or `rsync://HOST/MODULE`; a single colon is SSH/remote-shell syntax and is a different access path. ```bash nmap -sV -p 873 --script rsync-list-modules TARGET rsync rsync://TARGET/ rsync --list-only rsync://TARGET/MODULE/ ``` > **Decisive output:** a named module and a file listing establish only that the current anonymous or supplied account can enumerate that namespace. Read access is proven by retrieving selected bytes, not by the module name.
Variant — retrieve a selected file or a reviewed module ```bash # One selected artifact rsync -av rsync://TARGET/MODULE/path/FILE ./FILE # A reviewed module into a dedicated local evidence directory mkdir -p ./rsync-MODULE rsync -av --safe-links rsync://TARGET/MODULE/ ./rsync-MODULE/ ``` `--safe-links` ignores symbolic links that point outside the copied tree. Review module size and content first; do not mirror a large tree by default. If authentication is required, let rsync prompt or use a protected `--password-file` rather than putting a password on the command line.
> **Failure cues:** no listed modules can mean the daemon hides its module list; `@ERROR: auth failed` is an authentication boundary; `@ERROR: Unknown module` is a namespace error; a listed module can still deny individual reads or writes. > > **Next action:** inspect selected readable backups, keys, source and configuration locally. Treat a writable module as file placement only until a specific consumer, destination identity and trigger are proven. Do not use `--delete` against a remote module during enumeration. ##### TFTP — known-name retrieval only > **Recognize:** TFTP normally uses UDP/69 for the initial request and has no directory-listing or login model. It is useful only when configuration, source, boot metadata or another service gives a plausible filename. ```text tftp TARGET tftp> binary tftp> get FILE tftp> quit ``` > **Decisive output:** a completed transfer plus recognizable local bytes establishes read access to that exact name. A timeout is ambiguous because the UDP request, server policy, transfer port or filename can fail without a useful error.
Variant — bounded write check only when the objective requires it ```bash printf '%s\n' 'TFTP_WRITE_CANARY' > tftp-probe.txt ``` ```text tftp TARGET tftp> binary tftp> put tftp-probe.txt tftp> quit ``` Use a unique harmless filename and only when write capability changes the next decision. TFTP normally offers no remote delete operation; do not create a probe unless you already have an authorized cleanup route.
> **Next action:** inspect a retrieved artifact and follow only evidence-backed filenames. A successful upload is not execution; prove the server-side path and consumer separately. > **Verify:** Verify the export, mapped identity, actual bytes and any created file's server-side ownership. > **If it fails:** An empty showmount response does not rule out NFSv4. Mount failure may be transport/export/client-policy rather than absence of files.
Find: Inspect rsync modules and retrieve selected artifacts After application identification shows an rsync daemon, list visible modules and inspect one selected namespace before copying data. ```bash nmap -sV -p 873 --script rsync-list-modules TARGET rsync rsync://TARGET/ rsync --list-only rsync://TARGET/MODULE/ ``` > **Recognize:** A visible module and file listing identify an rsync namespace; they do not establish write or execution. > **Validate next:** Retrieve one selected file and verify its bytes; record anonymous or supplied-account context. [Inspect rsync modules and retrieve selected artifacts](../notes/methods/services.md#service-rsync).
Find: Retrieve an evidence-backed file over TFTP Use TFTP only after another artifact or boot/configuration clue supplies a plausible exact filename. ```text tftp TARGET tftp> binary tftp> get FILE tftp> quit ``` > **Recognize:** The exact known filename is retrievable; TFTP still exposes no general directory namespace. > **Validate next:** Verify recognizable bytes and provenance; distinguish read from any separately required write test. [Retrieve an evidence-backed file over TFTP](../notes/methods/services.md#service-tftp).
Find: Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities Start from confirmed SMB and explicitly compare anonymous versus a known authenticated context, then open a relevant named share. ```bash smbclient -L //TARGET -N smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' ``` > **Recognize:** A share name supplies a filesystem investigation target; listing it does not prove read, write or service creation. > **Validate next:** Connect to the named share under the identity that listed it, then ls/get the exact object. Listing a share does not prove read or write. For a write candidate, verify the path operation and identify a separate execution consumer before treating it as access. [Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities](../notes/methods/services.md#service-smb).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter > **Recognize:** direct-hosted SMB commonly uses TCP/445; NetBIOS session service commonly uses TCP/139; MS-RPC endpoint mapping commonly uses TCP/135. They are related Windows surfaces but not interchangeable. **Goal:** distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. ##### Baseline: list shares without credentials ```bash smbclient -N -L //TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. It does not prove access to share contents. `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential.
Variant — authenticated share listing and connection ```bash smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' ``` The first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. Let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. Inside the share: ```text pwd ls allinfo FILE get FILE mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit ``` Use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. A successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution.
Variant — recursive retrieval ```bash smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON;prompt OFF;mget *' ``` Run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. Search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data.
Variant — RPC null or authenticated session ```bash rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET ``` Useful interactive queries: ```text srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser RID netshareenumall quit ``` Null-session denial is common on modern systems. Authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it.
Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates ```bash nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET ``` NetExec (`nxc`) is the current command name on recent Kali releases; older material may use `crackmapexec`. These tools consolidate candidates. Confirm useful shares and files with `smbclient` or native access.
Variant — protocol, signing and time clues ```bash nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET ``` Signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. The older `smb-os-discovery` script depends on SMBv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably.
Variant — Windows built-ins ```powershell net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE ``` These use the current Windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. An existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors.
SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file Use from Kali when SMB is reachable. Choose the same domain/local identity that worked with smbclient. Suppress write probes when inventorying reads; this means a writable label is not being tested here. ```bash # Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --no-write-check # Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -r 'SHARE' --depth 2 --no-write-check # Download the specific file found above smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --download 'SHARE\PATH\FILE' --no-write-check ``` > **Read:** a listed file must still be readable under this identity. A downloaded config/backup → classify its credential material, then test only the relevant account/service. A denied share → try another listed share or a newly obtained identity; do not infer a host-wide denial. [SMBMap upstream](https://github.com/ShawnDEvans/smbmap). For broader SMB/RPC collection, use the existing enum4linux-ng baseline; authenticate explicitly when credentials exist: ```bash # No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates enum4linux-ng -A TARGET # Known identity: domain objects visible to this account enum4linux-ng -A -w DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' TARGET ``` > **Next:** validate returned users/groups/shares with rpcclient or smbclient. A collector can return partial data despite a successful login.
> **Failure cues:** distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. A share named `IPC$` is not a general file share. Guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. A share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. > **Next action:** inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. Move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/AD blocks. ##### NetBIOS names before SMB enumeration Use when UDP/137 or SMB suggests Windows names but DNS/domain identity is unclear. ```bash # Ask the assigned host for its NetBIOS names nbtscan TARGET nmblookup -A TARGET ``` Read: a machine name and group/domain label are leads. A workgroup label does not prove AD membership. Resolve the returned name and use the SMB/LDAP checks with the accepted identity. No reply can mean filtering or disabled NetBIOS while TCP/445 still works. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.kali.org/tools/nbtscan/). ##### SMB/RPC RID lookups when a normal user listing is denied Use when the accepted identity can translate SIDs but cannot list the directory directly. Keep the queried host/domain and a bounded RID range explicit. ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --rid-brute 4000 ``` Read: classify returned SID types—users, groups and machine accounts are different objects. The upper bound is coverage, not proof that higher RIDs contain nothing. A resolved name is not a password, service authorization or successful logon. Prefer the existing native directory/RPC listing when it is available; do not infer no accounts from a single denied enumeration method. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.netexec.wiki/smb-protocol/enumeration/enumerate-users-by-bruteforcing-rid). > **Verify:** Prove the specific share/object action; a successful login or administrative indicator does not establish every remote-execution route. > **If it fails:** Access denied after login usually means authorization/context. Test local/domain qualification and the exact object rather than repeating passwords.
Find: Extract configuration and process information through SNMP Take UDP/161 evidence and a justified management credential/community, then request a small known OID branch before a broad walk. ```bash snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 ``` > **Recognize:** A real OID response confirms the accepted read context and supplies software/name clues. > **Validate next:** Determine which useful views/branches are actually readable; process data and write rights are separate. [Extract configuration and process information through SNMP](../notes/methods/services.md#service-snmp).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions > **Recognize:** SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. **Goal:** turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. ##### Baseline: find a read community, then walk ```bash onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Use `-v1` instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. > **Decisive output:** returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path.
Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
Variant — high-value Windows OIDs ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view.
Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. `authNoPriv` authenticates without encryption; `noAuthNoPriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
Variant — focused UDP verification ```bash sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **Failure cues:** UDP silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `Timeout: No Response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. `No Such Object` means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **Next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage. > **Verify:** Preserve the OID, accepted security context and returned value; empty branches can reflect view restrictions. > **If it fails:** Silence can mean UDP filtering, wrong community/version or denied view; change only the condition supported by evidence.
Find: Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives Use a known application/database login and inspect identity, grants and file-operation constraints before choosing an OS transition. ```sql SELECT USER(),CURRENT_USER(),VERSION(); SHOW GRANTS; SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv'; ``` > **Recognize:** SELECT permits data investigation; absent FILE/admin rights and the restricted directory constrain file/OS hypotheses. > **Validate next:** Check exact grants, useful tables, destination OS permissions and an execution consumer before escalating a file operation. [Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives](../notes/methods/services.md#service-mysql).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Database authentication and exact schema/file privileges; secure_file_priv and server filesystem identity constrain file actions ```bash mysql -h TARGET -P PORT -u USER -p ``` ```sql SELECT VERSION(), USER(), CURRENT_USER(); SHOW DATABASES; SHOW GRANTS; USE DATABASE; SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE TABLE; SELECT * FROM TABLE LIMIT 20; SELECT @@secure_file_priv; ``` > **Interpret:** `USER()` shows the presented client identity; `CURRENT_USER()` shows the account used for privilege checking. `secure_file_priv` restricts server-side import/export: a directory constrains it, an empty value is unrestricted by that variable, and `NULL` disables these operations. The `FILE` privilege is still required.
MySQL variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites ```sql SELECT LOAD_FILE('/path/on/database/server'); SELECT 'probe' INTO OUTFILE '/allowed/server/path/probe.txt'; ``` Use only an authorized harmless path. `LOAD_FILE` returning `NULL` is ambiguous among missing file, permissions, size, FILE privilege and `secure_file_priv`. `INTO OUTFILE` will not overwrite an existing file. A written file becomes execution only if another privileged component consumes it.
> **Verify:** Check current database identity, grants and actual returned data or written file through an independent observation. > **If it fails:** Permission denied or a restricted file directory changes the available primitive; pivot to data/credential use or a different entry point.
Find: Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities Once SQL Server authentication works, inspect actual login/server role and supported impersonation context. ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); ``` > **Recognize:** A valid login with sysadmin=0 is data/rights evidence, not permission to enable xp_cmdshell. > **Validate next:** Enumerate actual database/server grants and useful impersonation; independently verify any OS facility and its identity. [Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities](../notes/methods/services.md#service-mssql).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Correct SQL versus Windows authentication; database role and configuration must permit the requested operation ```bash impacket-mssqlclient 'USER@TARGET' impacket-mssqlclient 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' -windows-auth ``` Let the tool prompt for the password. At the SQL prompt: ```sql SELECT @@VERSION; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); SELECT name FROM sys.databases; USE DATABASE; SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES; SELECT TOP 20 * FROM SCHEMA.TABLE; ``` > **Interpret:** `IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')` returns `1`, `0` or `NULL`; `NULL` is not success. Impacket also exposes helpers such as `enum_impersonate` and `xp_cmdshell` depending on version and rights.
MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary ```sql EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; ``` `xp_cmdshell` is disabled by default on new installations. Enabling it generally requires high privilege and changes server configuration; do not enable it merely to enumerate. When available, a sysadmin's child process normally runs as the SQL Server service account; an authorized non-sysadmin may use a configured proxy. Verify returned identity before choosing the next action.
##### MSSQL linked-server and login-context mapping Treat a linked server as another authentication and authorization boundary. The local SQL login, its mapped remote login, remote SQL role and RPC/data-access settings can all differ. ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS current_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS original_login, SUSER_SNAME() AS effective_login, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') AS is_sysadmin; SELECT name, product, provider, data_source, is_linked FROM sys.servers WHERE is_linked = 1; EXEC master.dbo.sp_helplinkedsrvlogin; ``` > **Interpret:** `sys.servers` proves configuration, not remote access. `sp_helplinkedsrvlogin` shows local-to-remote mappings; a `NULL` local login can represent a mapping that applies to all local logins. Preserve the local and remote identities separately. After selecting one named link, test the smallest remote query supported by its configuration: ```sql EXEC ('SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS remote_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS remote_original_login, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER(''sysadmin'') AS remote_is_sysadmin') AT [LINKED_SERVER]; ``` If RPC execution is disabled but data access is allowed, use a read-only pass-through query instead: ```sql SELECT * FROM OPENQUERY([LINKED_SERVER], 'SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS remote_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS remote_original_login'); ``` > **Decide:** a returned remote identity enables only the operations granted to that mapped login. `RPC OUT is disabled`, login-mapping failures and data-access failures rule out different mechanisms; they do not prove the server is unreachable. If `enum_impersonate` identifies a specific permitted login, test only that login and always return to the original context: ```sql EXECUTE AS LOGIN = 'LOGIN'; SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), SUSER_SNAME(), IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); REVERT; ``` Do not enable RPC, create mappings or change server configuration merely to enumerate. A remote SQL query is not OS execution; independently validate any file or command facility and the operating-system identity behind it. Sources: [Microsoft `sys.servers`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-catalog-views/sys-servers-transact-sql), [`sp_helplinkedsrvlogin`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-stored-procedures/sp-helplinkedsrvlogin-transact-sql), [`EXECUTE AS`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/statements/execute-as-transact-sql), and [`OPENQUERY`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/functions/openquery-transact-sql). > **Verify:** Verify SQL identity and any OS effect with hostname/whoami; record service/proxy execution identity. > **If it fails:** Login success with denied configuration changes is a rights boundary. Do not repeatedly enable an unavailable facility.
Find: Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution Authenticate to the observed database and inspect current/session identity and role attributes before program/file functions. ```sql SELECT current_user,session_user,version(); SELECT rolname,rolsuper FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname=current_user; ``` > **Recognize:** An ordinary database role does not automatically have COPY PROGRAM or server-file access. > **Validate next:** Inspect effective role memberships and exact operation rights, then the database service's OS context. [Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution](../notes/methods/services.md#service-postgres).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Accepted connection/database role; COPY PROGRAM needs the corresponding server privilege and an executable OS context ```bash psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres ``` ```text \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* ``` ```sql SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb FROM pg_roles; ```
PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary ```sql SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); ``` Server-side `COPY ... FROM/TO 'file'` uses the PostgreSQL server's filesystem and service identity. `COPY ... PROGRAM` executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. Client-side `\copy` reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive.
> **Failure cues:** connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization. Query only bounded rows first. Never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies OS execution. > **Next action:** identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change. > **Verify:** Separate returned rows, file operations and command execution; prove the actual operating-system identity for the latter. > **If it fails:** Role or OS permission failures require another allowed primitive, not a different spelling of the same denied operation.
Find: Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries Identify Redis and use its authentication context to distinguish accepted commands from denied administrative facilities. ```bash redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING ``` > **Recognize:** The connection is usable but command ACLs can remove persistence/configuration methods. > **Validate next:** Inspect allowed operations, data visibility and actual persistence/destination/consumer conditions. [Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries](../notes/methods/services.md#service-redis).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script redis-info -p PORT TARGET redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT INFO redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL WHOAMI redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL LIST ``` Authenticated when a password is legitimately known: ```bash redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT --askpass ``` > `PONG` proves an accessible Redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. Check ACLs, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. Do not run `CONFIG SET`, write keys or load modules during enumeration. > **Verify:** Verify authentication context, allowed commands and actual key/file effects without assuming old Redis exploit defaults. > **If it fails:** NOAUTH and NOPERM identify different boundaries. Investigate credentials or permitted data rather than assuming unauthenticated execution.
Find: Triage Oracle listener and database identity Use service discovery and an application's connection descriptor to distinguish listener identification from a valid database session. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p 1521 TARGET ``` > **Recognize:** Listener/product evidence and a service name establish a connection candidate, not database credentials or DBA rights. > **Validate next:** Validate the exact descriptor/account and inspect its permitted database action. [Triage Oracle listener and database identity](../notes/methods/services.md#service-oracle).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Correct service/SID, reachable database transport and valid database credentials for authenticated work ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script oracle-tns-version -p 1521 TARGET nmap -Pn --script oracle-sid-brute -p 1521 TARGET ``` > A discovered SID/service name is a namespace clue, not credentials. Continue with an installed Oracle client only when a legitimate identity is available; preserve listener/version/SID evidence and do not treat a conventional port as Oracle proof. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap Oracle block. > **Verify:** Distinguish listener identification, database login and a permitted SQL action. > **If it fails:** An invalid service descriptor is different from an invalid password; resolve it before further credential decisions.
Find: Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts Take remote-access listeners from discovery and validate one known identity against the specific endpoint/logon type. ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 ``` > **Recognize:** Transport offers an RDP candidate from this source; it does not establish remote-interactive rights. > **Validate next:** Check actual protocol, local/domain context, accepted authentication and endpoint/logon authorization. [Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts](../notes/methods/services.md#service-remote).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights > **Recognize:** RDP commonly uses TCP/3389; WinRM commonly uses 5985/HTTP and 5986/HTTPS. **Goal:** determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. ##### RDP baseline: authentication-only check ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` Some distributions expose the binary as `xfreerdp`. Omit `/d:DOMAIN` for the intended local-account context; use `/u:TARGET\\USER` if needed to make that context explicit. > **Decisive output:** successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition.
Variant — open an RDP desktop ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. `/cert:ignore` suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection.
Variant — identify RDP security requirements ```bash nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET ``` This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential.
##### RDP host-side inspection: local administrative context Use this read-only sequence after obtaining an authorized local administrative session on the destination, or when the exercise explicitly supplies equivalent remote-management access. It answers four different questions: is RDP enabled, is a listener actually present, what security layer/NLA policy applies, and does the candidate identity have an effective remote-interactive logon right? Do not change registry values or policy merely to make a credential work. ##### 1. Listener, service and configured port ```powershell Get-Service TermService reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v PortNumber qwinsta ``` ```cmd netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING | findstr ":3389" ``` > **Read:** `fDenyTSConnections = 0` permits RDP at the local setting; `1` denies new RDP connections. `PortNumber` is displayed as a registry DWORD, commonly hexadecimal `0xD3D` for 3389. A running `TermService` plus an `RDP-Tcp` listener in `qwinsta` and a listening socket establishes host-side listener state. A missing `:3389` socket is not decisive if `PortNumber` is nondefault. Policy can override the local value, so inspect resultant policy before treating this as effective configuration. ##### 2. NLA, transport security and policy precedence ```cmd reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v SecurityLayer reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v MinEncryptionLevel reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v fDenyTSConnections reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v UserAuthentication reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v SecurityLayer ``` ```cmd gpresult /scope computer /v ``` > **Read:** `UserAuthentication = 1` requires Network Level Authentication. For `SecurityLayer`, `0` is native RDP security, `1` negotiates, and `2` requires TLS. `MinEncryptionLevel` further constrains client compatibility. A missing policy value means “not configured at this policy path,” not that the feature is absent. Use `gpresult` to identify the winning computer policy when local and policy-backed values conflict or revert after refresh. These settings explain negotiation failures; they do not grant a user logon rights. ##### 3. Candidate membership and effective logon rights ```cmd net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users" whoami /groups ``` From an elevated PowerShell or Command Prompt, export the currently applied user-right assignments and inspect only the RDP entries: ```powershell $policy = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'rdp-user-rights.inf' secedit /export /mergedpolicy /areas user_rights /cfg $policy /quiet Select-String -Path $policy -Pattern '^SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight','^SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight' ``` > **Read:** the candidate must be covered by `SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight`; membership in local **Administrators** or **Remote Desktop Users** commonly supplies that right, but the actual applied policy is decisive. `SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight` overrides the allow right. Exported entries can be names or SIDs, so resolve unfamiliar SIDs before deciding. `whoami /groups` proves only the current process token; use it for the candidate only when you are actually running in that candidate's context. A group listing alone does not prove an effective right when domain policy or nested membership changes the result. ##### 4. Source-relative validation and decision ```bash nmap -Pn -n -p 3389 --reason TARGET xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` > **Ready for an interactive attempt:** the actual source reaches the configured RDP port; the listener is enabled; the client can meet the NLA/security requirements; the credential is accepted in the intended local/domain context; and the identity has the effective allow right without an applicable deny right. **Ruled out in this context:** a decisive required condition is absent, such as an effective deny assignment or no listener on the configured port. **Inconclusive:** access to policy data is denied, group/SID expansion is unresolved, GPO precedence is unclear, or network filtering prevents source-relative validation. Do not turn an inconclusive result into “bad password” or “RDP disabled.” > **Security baseline:** on a normally secured host, RDP may be disabled when not needed; when enabled, NLA is normally retained, access is limited to intended administrative/remote-user principals, deny assignments override broad membership, and the firewall limits exposure. The state machine records deviations and capabilities; it does not recommend weakening these controls. ##### WinRM baseline: interactive session ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER ``` ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' ``` Omitting `-p` makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. > **Decisive output:** an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization. Immediately verify identity and host context with `whoami`, `hostname` and `Get-NetIPAddress`.
Variant — WinRM over HTTPS ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 ``` Check `evil-winrm -h` because the established Ruby client and newer `evil-winrm-py` use different long-option spelling. Do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation.
Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting ```powershell $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred ``` PowerShell remoting uses the configured WinRM endpoint. Local trusted-host, Kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity.
> **Failure cues:** certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. RDP errors can reflect NLA, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. WinRM `401` supports authentication/authorization failure; `WinRM cannot process the request` can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. Valid SMB credentials do not guarantee RDP or WinRM rights. > **Next action:** after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. Password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/AD blocks. Host-inspection sources: [Microsoft RDP troubleshooting](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/remote/rdp-error-general-troubleshooting) · [Microsoft `secedit /export`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/secedit-export) · [Microsoft account-right constants](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/account-rights-constants) · [Microsoft `qwinsta`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/qwinsta) · [Microsoft Remote Desktop Services policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/mdm/policy-csp-remotedesktopservices) ##### VNC ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vnc-info -p PORT TARGET vncviewer TARGET:PORT ``` > VNC may expose a desktop without Windows logon semantics; the VNC server's authentication and the resulting OS session identity are separate. Use `realvnc-auth-bypass` or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. ##### Telnet ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT telnet TARGET PORT ``` > Telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. Validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make `telnet-brute` a baseline. After login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an OS shell. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap VNC/Telnet blocks. ##### GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check Use only after identifying the affected GNU Inetutils telnetd/login chain and its patch status. CVE-2026-24061 concerns how a supplied USER value reaches login; it does not apply to every Telnet server. Distribution backports matter. ```bash # Client supports sending the autologin USER environment value USER='-f root' telnet -a TARGET PORT ``` Read: if a shell is obtained, verify hostname and id. A prompt or echoed username is not root access. A different daemon, fixed build, client negotiation mismatch or a rejected USER value → return to service identification. The affected upstream range and distribution fixes must be checked against the advisory rather than inferred from port 23. Sources: [upstream 1](https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/CVE-2026-24061). > **Verify:** Verify destination hostname, represented identity and usable effect in the resulting session. > **If it fails:** A valid password is not proof of RDP/WinRM rights. Diagnose TLS, transport, account qualification and logon policy separately.
Find: Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search Identify the directory endpoint and query RootDSE before a subtree search under a known bind identity. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP -s base -b '' defaultNamingContext namingContexts ``` > **Recognize:** RootDSE supplies the search base; it does not grant arbitrary anonymous subtree access. > **Validate next:** Check bind identity, transport/signing requirements and read visibility on the selected objects. [Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search](../notes/methods/services.md#service-ldap).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context > **Recognition:** LDAP commonly appears on TCP/389 or TCP/636; Global Catalog on TCP/3268 or 3269; Kerberos on TCP/UDP 88. Applications may listen elsewhere, so follow protocol evidence rather than port labels. ##### Baseline: discover naming contexts > **Prerequisite:** LDAP reachability. **Coverage:** RootDSE only; this can work even when directory searches require authentication. **Decisive output:** `defaultNamingContext` and `dnsHostName`. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://TARGET:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext configurationNamingContext dnsHostName ``` Convert `DC=corp,DC=example` into `corp.example` for DNS/Kerberos work. Preserve the server's exact hostname because Kerberos is name-sensitive.
LDAPS and certificate-name inspection ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:636 -servername DC_HOST A certificate can disclose domain/DC names. A TLS validation error is a client trust/name issue, not proof that LDAP is unavailable.
##### Anonymous directory search > **Prerequisite:** known base DN and server permitting anonymous search. **Failure cue:** `Inappropriate authentication` or `Insufficient access` closes only the anonymous path. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description ``` ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectClass=group)' cn member description ``` ##### Authenticated search > **Prerequisite:** a valid directory identity. **Decisive output:** objects/attributes unavailable anonymously. Avoid placing a real password in shell history when an interactive prompt is available. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 \ -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName userAccountControl ```
Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=computer)' \ dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=group)' cn member ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf ```
##### Kerberos prerequisites before an attack Kerberos failures are often name/time/route failures rather than credential failures. Establish: ```bash getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u nmap -Pn -sV -p 88,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 DC_IP -oN dc-services.txt ``` > **Interpretation:** resolve `DOMAIN` and `DC_HOST` consistently, keep clock skew within Kerberos tolerance, and ensure the KDC is reached through the selected route. `KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN` points to identity/domain naming; `KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW` points to time; `KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED` normally points to authentication material. ##### Handoff - New users, groups, computers, SPNs or domain names → [domain mapping](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md). - A user confirmed without preauthentication → [Kerberos and identity transitions](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md). - Valid credentials → rerun authenticated LDAP plus SMB/share/remote-access enumeration. - Certificate templates/AD CS clues → [AD CS and object-control abuse](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md). > **Verify:** Record DC, base DN, bind identity and actual returned attributes; RootDSE alone is not a complete directory dump. > **If it fails:** Stronger-auth-required may mean TLS/signing policy; invalid credentials or an empty base require different fixes.
Find: Investigate SIP/IRC identity and configuration clues Classify the unusual listener, then use its normal greeting/registration behavior and the owning procedure's bounded protocol checks. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` > **Recognize:** The real protocol and registration state determine the next client operation; the expected port label is insufficient. > **Validate next:** Verify application/version, accepted interaction and exact exploit/access conditions. [Investigate SIP/IRC identity and configuration clues](../notes/methods/services.md#service-sip-irc).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Application-specific request format; permitted registration/channel/configuration access These source-site topics contain only first-pass reconnaissance. Treat them as application-identification branches, not default exploitation paths. ##### SIP > Commonly UDP/TCP 5060 or TLS 5061; follow protocol evidence. ```bash nmap -Pn -sU -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET nmap -Pn -sT -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** a SIP response and supported methods. `open|filtered` without application response remains ambiguous. Do not run `sip-brute` until the exact registrar, known test identities, lockout policy and explicit authorization are established. ##### IRC ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script irc-info -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` Minimal registration for an authorized test client: ```text NICK testnick USER testuser 0 * :Test User QUIT ``` > **Decisive output:** IRC numeric replies, server/network name, version/capabilities or authentication requirement. Do not use `irc-brute` as identification; authenticate only with legitimately acquired credentials. > **Verify:** Retain protocol responses and distinguish product clues from confirmed vulnerabilities. > **If it fails:** A generic banner or denied registration leaves access unproven; return to version/configuration matching.

If `enum_impersonate` identifies a specific permitted login, test only that login and always return to the original context: ```sql EXECUTE AS LOGIN = 'LOGIN'; SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), SUSER_SNAME(), IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); REVERT; ``` Do not enable RPC, create mappings or change server configuration merely to enumerate. A remote SQL query is not OS execution; independently validate any file or command facility and the operating-system identity behind it. Sources: [Microsoft `sys.servers`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-catalog-views/sys-servers-transact-sql), [`sp_helplinkedsrvlogin`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-stored-procedures/sp-helplinkedsrvlogin-transact-sql), [`EXECUTE AS`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/statements/execute-as-transact-sql), and [`OPENQUERY`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/functions/openquery-transact-sql).
[Notes and interpretation](../notes/Attack_Surface_Supplements.md#surface-S15).
