## Follow the result into the next method

| Observed result | What must still be proved | Next objective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New hostname, interface, listener or subnet | Scope, source position and reachability | Discovery and service enumeration |
| Readable configuration, repository history or file | Artifact type, account context and whether its value is current | Credential classification and compatible reuse |
| File write or upload | Executing consumer, file interpretation, permissions and trigger | Web execution or local escalation |
| Command execution | Host, identity, output channel and connection direction | Session establishment and transfer |
| Higher local privilege | Effective token/UID and additional readable credential sources | Credential access and re-enumeration |
| New domain identity or directory right | Effective right on the exact object and the resulting service authorization | AD identity transitions or lateral movement |
| Successful authentication | Destination-specific execution/logon rights | Compatible remote service method |
| New route or proxy | Destination service reachability, name resolution and callback path | Re-enumerate from the new vantage point |

### Paper-based chain rehearsal

- **Linux standalone:** [Validate the source path and discover hosts](methods/discovery.md#path-hosts) → [Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans](methods/discovery.md#tcp-coverage) → [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](methods/web-mapping.md#web-identity) → [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](methods/web-mapping.md#web-behavior) → [Read files through directory traversal](methods/web-exploitation.md#web-traversal) → [Classify the artifact and its identity context](methods/credentials.md#credential-classify) → [Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse](methods/credentials.md#credential-use) → [Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access](methods/services.md#service-ssh) → [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](methods/linux-privesc.md#linux-state) → [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](methods/linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo) → [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](methods/linux-privesc.md#linux-state).

- **Windows standalone:** [Validate the source path and discover hosts](methods/discovery.md#path-hosts) → [Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans](methods/discovery.md#tcp-coverage) → [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](methods/web-mapping.md#web-identity) → [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](methods/web-mapping.md#web-behavior) → [Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval](methods/web-exploitation.md#web-upload) → [Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler](methods/web-exploitation.md#web-upload-exec) → [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](methods/sessions-transfers.md#session-proof) → [Establish Windows token, host and process context](methods/windows-privesc.md#windows-state) → [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](methods/windows-privesc.md#windows-service-config) → [Establish Windows token, host and process context](methods/windows-privesc.md#windows-state).

- **AD roast and movement:** [Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-state) → [Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-directory) → [Request a selected service ticket for offline service-account recovery](methods/ad-identities.md#kerberos-roast) → [Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks](methods/credentials.md#offline-recovery) → [Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse](methods/credentials.md#credential-use) → [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight) → [Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting](methods/lateral-movement.md#move-winrm) → [Establish Windows token, host and process context](methods/windows-privesc.md#windows-state) → [Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route](methods/windows-privesc.md#windows-token) → [Obtain accessible live logon-session credential material](methods/ad-identities.md#ad-lsass) → [Recover or reuse an NT password hash](methods/credentials.md#nt-hash) → [Select password, NT hash, key-to-ticket or ticket authentication](methods/lateral-movement.md#move-auth-material) → [Execute through uploaded service creation using PsExec](methods/lateral-movement.md#move-services).

- **AD replication and evidence:** [Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-state) → [Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-directory) → [Validate effective directory-object control](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-acl) → [Use validated directory replication rights for bounded credential proof](methods/ad-identities.md#ad-dcsync) → [Capture state-transition, proof and exploit-adaptation evidence](methods/integration.md#attack-evidence) → [Build and validate the report and submission artifacts](methods/integration.md#attack-report).

- **Pivoted domain access:** [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](methods/pivoting.md#pivot-state) → [Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng](methods/pivoting.md#ligolo-route) → [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](methods/pivoting.md#pivot-dns) → [Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-state) → [Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-directory) → [Collect focused BloodHound data and validate an attack path](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-graph) → [Validate effective directory-object control](methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-acl) → [Add a controlled identity to a group through effective membership rights](methods/ad-identities.md#ad-group-control) → [Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting](methods/lateral-movement.md#move-winrm).

- **Execution and callback repair:** [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](methods/sessions-transfers.md#session-proof) → [Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter](methods/sessions-transfers.md#session-reverse) → [Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order](methods/execution.md#execution-callback) → [Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle](methods/execution.md#execution-handler) → [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](methods/sessions-transfers.md#session-proof).

At every arrow identify the produced capability and the next method's missing prerequisite. An expected result in these examples is hypothetical, not recorded lab evidence.

## Study order and boundaries

Use Units 1–8 in the [speedrun study sequence](Speedrun_Breakdown.md#grouped-study-sequence): Blocks 1+2; 3+4; 5; 6+7; 8 then 9; 13 fundamentals then 10→11→12; remaining 14; and 15. Relevant execution diagnostics recur throughout.

Core methods follow the established OSCP preparation route. AD CS, delegation/RBCD, broader GPO/ticket-forging branches and less-common service/tunnel options retain their explicit conditional context. Their prerequisites must be verified before selecting them.

Dedicated buffer-overflow and shellcode development remain excluded by learner choice; selecting, compiling and adapting an existing memory-corruption PoC remains covered. Commercial/mass vulnerability scanners, automatic exploitation and prohibited spoofing workflows are not operational exam paths. Some course topics therefore have recognition-only or conditional treatment. Read the current [official exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) before choosing restricted framework features; the [Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) describes competencies separately from tool permission.

Concept study includes the worked commands and reasoning here. Practical exploitation and independent retests follow the learner's explicit closure of the concept phase. Study coverage is separate from practical competence.

pages.title: Conditional attack-surface notes
pages.markdown: # Conditional attack-surface notes [Surface map index](Attack_Surface_Maps.md) | [Cheatsheets](../cheatsheets/README.md) Use these additional surfaces when the observation fits. Each entry preserves its discovery, prerequisite and verification boundary. ## Inspect host-side RDP enablement and logon policy [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/windows-privesc.md#surface-S01). - **Enter:** you have authorized local administrative or equivalent management access to a Windows destination, and RDP access is relevant or failing. - **Discover:** inspect `TermService`, `fDenyTSConnections`, configured `PortNumber`, `qwinsta` listener state and the actual source-to-port path. - **Validate:** inspect NLA/security-layer policy, applied GPO, local Remote Desktop Users membership, and the effective `SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight` / `SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight` assignments. Deny overrides allow. - **Execute:** [RDP host-side inspection](../reference/02-service-enumeration/09-windows-remote-access.md#rdp-host-side-inspection-local-administrative-context); then use the [RDP access procedure](../reference/03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) only when its conditions are satisfied. - **Verify:** a usable desktop followed by `whoami`, `hostname` and `ipconfig` establishes the new host/identity/source position. Authentication-only success is not an interactive session. - **Outcomes:** listener/right/client conditions satisfied → [remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight) then [session verification](../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); decisive deny/no listener → ruled out here; policy, SID expansion or filtering unresolved → inconclusive. ## Read a classic LAPS password for one computer [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S02). - **Enter:** a specific computer object is relevant and the current directory principal may read `ms-Mcs-AdmPwd`. - **Discover:** identify the computer object and test the attribute read; merely enumerating the object is not enough. - **Validate:** the returned value is present, current and scoped to that computer's managed local account; identify the intended local username and destination service separately. - **Execute:** [Delegated LAPS/gMSA reads](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#delegated-reads--laps-and-gmsa-material). - **Verify:** validate the password on one compatible service using explicit local-account context, then prove the specific permitted operation. Password acceptance does not prove local administration or remote execution. - **Outcomes:** readable current value → [credential classification](../notes/methods/credentials.md#credential-classify)/[remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); attribute denied/absent for this principal/object → ruled out here; schema, replication freshness or object identity unresolved → inconclusive. ## Read or decrypt a Windows LAPS password [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S03). - **Enter:** a relevant computer uses Windows LAPS and the principal may read `msLAPS-Password` or decrypt the protected value. - **Discover:** query the exact computer attribute and record whether the result is plaintext JSON, encrypted content, empty or denied. - **Validate:** plaintext/decryption rights, password age, managed account name and host scope. An encrypted blob without the permitted decryption context is not a password. - **Execute:** [Delegated LAPS/gMSA reads](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#delegated-reads--laps-and-gmsa-material). - **Verify:** validate only against the named host and intended local account, then establish the actual service capability. - **Outcomes:** usable current password → [credential classification](../notes/methods/credentials.md#credential-classify)/[remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); no read/decrypt right → ruled out here; returned protected data but decryption context unknown → inconclusive. ## Recover and classify gMSA material [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S04). - **Enter:** a specific gMSA is used by a relevant service and the current identity may read `msDS-ManagedPassword`. - **Discover:** inspect the gMSA object and allowed managed-password readers; distinguish a raw blob from a decoded NT hash. - **Validate:** exact account name including `$`, managed-password read permission, working LDAPS/tool path, decoded representation and intended service/host. - **Execute:** [Raw and decoded gMSA checks](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#gmsa--obtain-a-decoded-hash-only-with-managed-password-read-rights). - **Verify:** test one service compatible with the decoded material and record the exact accepted identity and operation. Authentication is not administrative execution. - **Outcomes:** decoded material accepted for the intended identity → [credential classification](../notes/methods/credentials.md#credential-classify)/[remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); read denied or wrong object type → ruled out here; raw blob, TLS failure or empty output → inconclusive. ## Use a validated shadow-credential path [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S05). - **Enter:** the effective principal can write the target object's `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`, and the assigned lab permits the object change. - **Discover:** list existing key credentials before mutation and preserve their identifiers. - **Validate:** target identity, exact effective write right, DC PKINIT/key-trust support, DNS/time/KDC route, certificate tooling and a cleanup route. - **Execute:** [Shadow credentials — add, authenticate and remove only the added DeviceID](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#shadow-credentials--object-key-write-pkinit-then-cleanup). - **Verify:** establish the cached target principal and one intended service action; then confirm that only the newly added key credential was removed. - **Outcomes:** target TGT/service capability established → [ticket and key context](../notes/methods/credentials.md#ticket-use)/[remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); effective write or PKINIT prerequisite disproved → ruled out here; write succeeds but certificate/KDC mapping is unresolved → [failed-boundary diagnosis](../notes/methods/execution.md#execution-format)/inconclusive. ## Authenticate to LDAP with a mapped certificate [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S06). - **Enter:** you possess a certificate and private key plausibly mapped to an AD identity, and LDAP over TLS is reachable. - **Discover:** identify certificate subject/SAN/EKU, trust chain, private-key availability and the DC TLS path. - **Validate:** the certificate maps to the intended principal, the private key matches, Schannel authentication is accepted and the mapped identity has the exact object right required by the intended LDAP operation. - **Execute:** [PassTheCert identity check and LDAP shell](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#passthecert--schannelldap-when-the-certificate-is-usable-there). - **Verify:** `whoami`/bind establishes only the mapped LDAP identity; separately verify the selected LDAP read or write and its object state. - **Outcomes:** mapped identity and permitted object operation confirmed → [directory-right validation](../notes/methods/ad-mapping.md#domain-acl); mapping/trust/private key disproved → ruled out here; PKINIT fails while Schannel remains untested, or TLS errors mask mapping → inconclusive. ## Create a controlled machine account only for a selected AD path [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S07). - **Enter:** a validated RBCD/delegation path needs a service principal or machine key you control. - **Discover:** inspect machine-account quota, target OU/container ACL, existing names and whether the current identity can create the account in the intended location. - **Validate:** the downstream path actually needs this principal, the resulting SPNs/key will be usable, target-object rights are independently present, and cleanup/deletion rights are understood. - **Execute:** [Powermad machine-account creation](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#powermad--create-an-account-only-when-the-chosen-ad-path-needs-it). - **Verify:** confirm the created object, its SPNs and controlled key; do not record RBCD or target access until the separate delegation operation and service ticket succeed. - **Outcomes:** controlled principal created for an already validated receiver path → [conditional AD paths](../notes/methods/ad-identities.md#ad-delegation); quota/ACL/name condition fails → ruled out here; object exists but downstream target right is missing → retain only the machine-account capability. ## Evaluate DNSAdmins without assuming immediate execution [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S08). - **Enter:** the controlled principal is a direct/effective DNSAdmins member or has equivalent DNS-server configuration rights. - **Discover:** identify the actual DNS server, DNS service state/identity and service ACL from the current authorized source. - **Validate:** effective configuration permission, product/build behavior, a usable plugin/configuration operation, payload delivery path and a separately authorized restart trigger. A restart on a DC is disruptive and is never a discovery probe. - **Execute:** [DNSAdmins condition checks](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/06-conditional-infrastructure-and-trusts.md#dnsadmins-distinguish-dns-configuration-from-a-service-trigger). - **Verify:** current content supports only membership/service/trigger investigation. A complete plugin execution and cleanup procedure is not registered; see the pending action procedure. - **Outcomes:** all prerequisites identified → ready for a separately reviewed procedure; membership absent/effective right denied → ruled out here; group present but configuration or trigger unknown → inconclusive. ## Map WSUS client policy to a server-side authorization question [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S09). - **Enter:** host policy or traffic indicates the machine uses WSUS. - **Discover:** read `WUServer`, `WUStatusServer` and `UseWUServer`; record URL, port, TLS and actual source reachability. - **Validate:** authenticated access to the identified server, update-approval/content/signing/deployment rights, target group scope and the privileged client consumer. Client configuration alone supplies none of those rights. - **Execute:** [WSUS client authority discovery](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/06-conditional-infrastructure-and-trusts.md#wsus-identify-the-update-authority-from-the-current-client). - **Verify:** this state produces a named update authority and a missing-rights checklist, not code execution. A complete update-deployment procedure is not registered; see the pending action procedure. - **Outcomes:** authority plus exact server-side control established → ready for a separately reviewed procedure; server rights denied → ruled out here; registry values absent or server role unknown → inconclusive. ## Recognize SCCM client context and locate the management boundary [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S10). - **Enter:** `CcmExec`, `SMS_Client` or readable client configuration indicates Configuration Manager. - **Discover:** identify client state, assigned site, management point and reachable authenticated interfaces. - **Validate:** SMS Provider/site-server authorization, deployment or CMPivot rights, relevant collection scope and any specifically readable credential source. Client presence does not imply server rights. - **Execute:** [SCCM client recognition checks](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/06-conditional-infrastructure-and-trusts.md#configuration-manager--sccm-recognize-the-client-before-choosing-a-server-side-path). - **Verify:** this state establishes product/site context only. A complete SCCM rights-to-action procedure is not registered; see the pending action procedure. - **Outcomes:** exact management interface and relevant permission found → ready for a separately reviewed procedure; no applicable server permission → ruled out here; namespace access denied or site/role unresolved → inconclusive. ## Interpret an AD trust as a boundary, not a privilege transition [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S11). - **Enter:** directory or native trust enumeration identifies another domain/forest relationship. - **Discover:** record source and destination domain, direction, trust type/transitivity, same-forest versus cross-forest context, selective authentication and SID filtering. - **Validate:** destination DNS/KDC/service reachability, accepted identity, target SPN, allowed-to-authenticate/resource rights and the exact capability sought. A trust object or child-domain administration is not automatically forest compromise. - **Execute:** [Trust-boundary inspection](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/06-conditional-infrastructure-and-trusts.md#trusts-inspect-the-boundary-before-treating-another-domain-as-reachable-privilege), then [movement preflight](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#2-preflight-from-the-actual-source). - **Verify:** establish one destination service action under the named identity. Trust-key/SID-history forgery and coercion chains are not registered complete procedures; see the pending action procedure. - **Outcomes:** destination service accepts the identity and action → [remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); filtering/selective-auth/resource authorization decisively denies it → ruled out here; direction/filtering/identity or route unresolved → inconclusive. ## Map an authentication, session or multistep web flow [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md#surface-S12). - **Enter:** the application exposes login, registration, recovery, role change, state-changing business action, authenticated API or another session-dependent flow. - **Discover:** capture a working anonymous and/or authenticated request, then record method, scheme/host/path, headers, cookies/tokens, body fields, hidden values, redirects, role and each step required to complete the action. Include non-GET/POST methods, JSON/XML bodies and WebSocket/API messages when the application actually uses them. - **Validate:** replay the unchanged request first; then change one identity, object, property or session boundary at a time. Confirm freshness, CSRF/token coupling, object ownership and whether the result is server-side rather than a browser-only presentation change. - **Execute:** [HTTP and web mapping](../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md), then route only the demonstrated effect to the existing parameter, authorization, IDOR, mass-assignment, XSS, parser or command/SQL method. - **Verify:** preserve one reproducible request/response pair and the exact role/session/object delta. Mapping a field or flow is not itself exploitation. - **Outcomes:** controlled unauthorized effect → [application authorization](../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md#web-authz) or the matching primitive; invariant authorization/ownership enforcement → ruled out for that transition; token expiry, cache, redirect or client-side behavior masks the result → inconclusive/[failed-boundary diagnosis](../notes/methods/execution.md#execution-format). - **Source:** [OWASP WSTG entry-point mapping](https://wstg.owasp.org/stable/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/01-Information_Gathering/06-Identify_Application_Entry_Points/). ## Inspect a Java RMI registry before selecting an exploit [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#surface-S13). - **Enter:** service detection or an application response identifies Java RMI on a selected port. - **Discover:** enumerate bound names, classes, remote endpoints and codebase annotations without assuming the registry is exploitable: ```bash nmap -sV -p PORT --script rmi-dumpregistry TARGET ``` - **Validate:** confirm the selected endpoint is the actual registry/service, its class-loading/serialization behavior, Java/version prerequisites and whether any proposed test is intrusive. The Nmap class-loader probe is categorized intrusive and must not be the baseline: ```bash nmap -p PORT --script rmi-vuln-classloader TARGET ``` - **Execute:** no generic RMI/serialization execution procedure is registered. Route a matched component/version/condition to [exploit prerequisite matching](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-select) only after the required behavior is established; see the pending action procedure. - **Verify:** registry names or a vulnerable class-loader result are component evidence, not a session. A complete action must separately verify the executed identity and resulting capability. - **Outcomes:** matching component and vulnerable behavior → candidate for reviewed [exploit prerequisite matching](../notes/methods/public-exploits.md#exploit-select) procedure; no registry or prerequisite decisively absent → ruled out here; filtered/incomplete registry or ambiguous class loading → inconclusive. - **Sources:** [Nmap `rmi-dumpregistry`](https://nmap.org/nsedoc/scripts/rmi-dumpregistry.html) and [`rmi-vuln-classloader`](https://nmap.org/nsedoc/scripts/rmi-vuln-classloader.html). ## Classify a Tomcat Manager interface and accepted role [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#surface-S14). - **Enter:** the application is confirmed as Apache Tomcat and a `/manager/*` interface responds. - **Discover:** inspect the selected interface and authentication boundary without spraying credentials: ```bash curl -sk -D - "https://TARGET:PORT/manager/html" -o /dev/null curl -sk -D - "https://TARGET:PORT/manager/text/list" -o /dev/null ``` - **Validate:** identify the accepted account and manager role: `manager-gui`, `manager-script`, `manager-jmx` or `manager-status`. GUI access and text-script access are intentionally separate; a `401`, `403` and application `404` have different meanings. - **Execute:** current notes do not yet own a version-scoped deployment, verification and cleanup procedure. Preserve the authenticated management capability and see the pending action procedure. JBoss/Jenkins and other managers remain separate product branches under the pending action procedure. - **Verify:** a manager listing proves the interface/role only. A deployable application, reachable context path and server-side execution identity require separate proof. - **Outcomes:** accepted deployment-capable role → ready for a reviewed product procedure; role/interface denies the required operation → ruled out for that role; proxy rewriting, wrong scheme/path or ambiguous realm → inconclusive. - **Source:** [Apache Tomcat Manager App HOW-TO](https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-11.0-doc/manager-howto.html). ## Follow an MSSQL linked server as a new SQL identity boundary [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md#surface-S15). - **Enter:** a working MSSQL login reveals one linked server or login mapping. - **Discover:** enumerate `sys.servers` and `sp_helplinkedsrvlogin`, preserving local login, remote server, provider/data source and mapping. - **Validate:** test one read-only remote identity query through the supported RPC or data-access mechanism. Do not enable RPC, create mappings or change configuration for enumeration. - **Execute:** [MSSQL linked-server and login-context mapping](../reference/02-service-enumeration/08-databases.md#mssql-linked-server-and-login-context-mapping). - **Verify:** record returned `SYSTEM_USER`, `ORIGINAL_LOGIN()` and the remote role result. A remote SQL query is not OS command execution. - **Outcomes:** mapped remote query succeeds → re-enter [database identity](../notes/methods/services.md#service-mssql) for that server/identity; link exists but RPC/data access is decisively unavailable → ruled out for that mechanism; mapping/authentication/provider failure is unresolved → inconclusive/[failed-boundary diagnosis](../notes/methods/execution.md#execution-format). ## Inspect VSS/shadow-copy credential-source conditions [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S16). - **Enter:** you control a Windows Server/DC context where offline credential material is relevant and the token may hold administrative or backup rights. - **Discover:** inspect `whoami /priv`, `vssadmin list shadows`, then `diskshadow` → `list shadows all`. - **Validate:** establish platform, exact volume, existing-versus-new snapshot, read rights, matched `NTDS.dit` and SYSTEM-hive requirement, output destination and cleanup authority. - **Execute:** [shadow-copy boundary checks](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/02-credential-access.md#shadow-copy-boundary-inspect-before-creating-anything). Creating/exposing/deleting a shadow and acquiring the matched files remain unavailable until the pending action procedure is complete. - **Verify:** listing proves only snapshot metadata. Credential acquisition requires readable, point-in-time-compatible NTDS/SYSTEM material and successful offline parsing. - **Outcomes:** suitable existing snapshot and read path identified → ready for the pending action procedure procedure; platform/rights/volume/source decisively incompatible → ruled out here; snapshot listed but access/freshness/matching hive unresolved → inconclusive. - **Source:** [Microsoft DiskShadow](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/diskshadow). ## Evaluate a direct Net-NTLMv2 relay path without spoofing [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S17). - **Enter:** an explicitly authorized, live NTLM authentication source is already present and a different receiver target is relevant. A saved Net-NTLMv2 response alone does not enter this state. - **Discover:** identify source protocol/event, relayed principal, receiver protocol/host and source-to-target reachability. For a selected SMB receiver, inspect signing with `nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode TARGET`. - **Validate:** receiver accepts NTLM, signing/EPA/channel binding/reflection protections permit the exchange, and the relayed principal has one useful target operation. Current exam rules prohibit poisoning/spoofing; Responder name-resolution poisoning is never the source in the exam workflow. - **Execute:** the existing [tool reference](../cheatsheets/tool-command-reference.md#responder-and-ntlm-relay) is not a complete action-specific procedure. Keep execution unavailable pending the pending action procedure. - **Verify:** define success as the chosen receiver operation under the relayed identity, not merely an inbound connection or captured challenge-response. - **Outcomes:** source + compatible receiver + useful authorization established → ready for the pending action procedure procedure; signing/protocol/authorization decisively blocks it → ruled out for that receiver; protection or source-event behavior unresolved → inconclusive. ## Inspect AD-integrated DNS record control [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S18). - **Enter:** AD-integrated DNS is present and a selected zone or record object may be writable by the current principal. - **Discover:** enumerate the zone container and record objects from a domain Windows context: ```powershell $Root = (Get-ADRootDSE).defaultNamingContext $DnsBase = "CN=MicrosoftDNS,DC=DomainDnsZones,$Root" Get-ADObject -SearchBase $DnsBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=dnsNode)' -Properties dnsRecord -ResultSetSize 50 ``` - **Validate:** identify one exact `dnsNode` distinguished name, effective create/write-child or record-property right, zone replication scope, resolver path, intended record/value, TTL and cleanup/restore plan. Zone visibility is not write permission. - **Execute:** no record-add/modify/delete procedure is registered; keep mutation unavailable under the pending action procedure. - **Verify:** a future write must resolve through the intended client path and cleanup must restore only the changed record. LDAP success alone is insufficient. - **Outcomes:** exact writable object/zone and resolver path established → ready for the pending action procedure; effective right denied or non-AD-integrated zone → ruled out here; object visible but ACL/replication/client resolver unresolved → inconclusive. ## Separate an unconstrained-delegation flag from tickets actually present [Quick commands](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md#surface-S19). - **Enter:** a computer/service account has `TrustedForDelegation`/unconstrained delegation and the selected host/session context is accessible. - **Discover:** confirm the account/SPNs and inspect the actual selected ticket cache with `klist` or `Rubeus.exe triage` in the permitted context. - **Validate:** ticket owner, realm, service/TGT type, validity, logon-session/LUID access, export/cache compatibility and the exact receiving service. A delegation flag without a cached client ticket is only configuration. - **Execute:** when a relevant ticket already exists, use the [ticket classification and cache procedure](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md) and [movement preflight](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#2-preflight-from-the-actual-source). Forced/coerced authentication remains unavailable under the pending action procedure. - **Verify:** prove one named service action under the ticket principal, then preserve the host/LUID/cache scope. Do not record a password, hash or domain-wide privilege. - **Outcomes:** usable cached ticket accepted by the named service → [ticket and key context](../notes/methods/credentials.md#ticket-use)/[remote operation preflight](../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); no relevant ticket in the inspectable context → current cached-ticket path ruled out; inaccessible LUID, stale ticket or ambiguous principal → inconclusive.

pages.title: Choose an enumeration toolkit
pages.markdown:
# Choose an enumeration toolkit

[Main index](../README.md) · [Tools by task](../cheatsheets/tools-and-scripts.md) · [Attack Strategy Map](Attack_Strategy_Map.md)

Build on established collectors: **AutoRecon for network/service orchestration, PEASS for local hosts, and SharpHound/BloodHound Community Edition for AD relationships**. Keep the existing procedures beside their output to interpret findings and validate prerequisites. A collector completing does not establish a complete attack surface or practical competence.

## 1. Select by current access

| Starting position | Collector | Combined coverage | Missing decision to validate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Explicit host/IP scope before a foothold | [AutoRecon](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon) | Port/service discovery, service-specific plugins, saved commands/results and reports | Selected plugins, scan coverage, virtual-host/session context and exploitation prerequisites |
| SMB/RPC with anonymous or known identity | [enum4linux-ng](https://github.com/cddmp/enum4linux-ng) | Users/groups, domain/OS context, shares, policy and supported SMB/RPC reads; JSON/YAML | Identity context, denied reads, file contents and effective authorization |
| Linux shell | [linPEAS](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng/tree/master/linPEAS) | Host, permission, service, scheduled-execution and credential-location checks | Exact permission, privileged consumer, trigger and resulting identity |
| Linux shell with a suspected recurring consumer | [pspy](https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy) | Process observation, including command lines and periodic privileged consumers, without requiring root | Sufficient observation time, controllable path and usable trigger |
| Windows shell | [winPEAS](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng/tree/master/winPEAS) | Host/user context, services, tasks, permissions and credential-location clues; optional domain checks | Correct build/platform and manually verified conditions in the current token |
| Windows shell needing another configuration/permission view | [PrivescCheck](https://github.com/itm4n/PrivescCheck) | Privilege-escalation/configuration checks with TXT/HTML reports | Baseline versus extended/audit/risky behavior; validate the decisive condition |
| Domain identity with a working collection context | [SharpHound + BloodHound CE](https://github.com/SpecterOps/SharpHound) | Objects, groups, ACLs, delegation/trusts and selected host/session relationships | Compatible collector/CE versions, target scope, volatile sessions and each useful graph edge |
| Domain identity from Kali, needing readable LDAP inventory | [ldapdomaindump](https://github.com/dirkjanm/ldapdomaindump) | Users/groups/computers/trusts in HTML/JSON/greppable output | Attribute visibility, effective permissions, credentials and reachable authorized services |
| Newly found credentials and selected reachable hosts/services | [NetExec](https://www.netexec.wiki/) | Protocol-specific authentication and selected share/user/group/session inventory | Domain versus local identity, service authorization and rights required by each enumeration; no automatic dumping/execution modules |

These are **on-demand CLIs**, supplementing existing manual Nmap/SMB/LDAP/host checks, with **zero persistent MCP definitions**. Less typing and fewer context switches are expected benefits, not measured speed/coverage guarantees. This guide installs nothing and executes no target commands.

## 2. Preferred orchestration base: AutoRecon

AutoRecon exposes plugin selection and preserves the underlying commands/results. Keep its orchestration/report structure and configure reviewed plugins rather than rewriting its scanner. The current repository is `AutoRecon/AutoRecon`; older Tib3rius links redirect there.

Review automatic run methods separately from generated manual suggestions. In the inspected source, SMB brute-force and ODAT suggestions are manual commands. Conversely, the optional SMB vulnerability plugin actually runs `smb-vuln-*` with `unsafe=1`. Do not enable it wholesale. HTTP/MSSQL Nmap plugins use broad script expressions, and directory discovery can follow redirects; inspect concrete behavior and scope. A `safe` tag is an author label, not exam approval.

Source checks: [SMB vulnerability plugin](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon/blob/bf40763dcc58f547680645616b1ee4155baf2e7a/autorecon/default-plugins/smb-vuln.py), [HTTP Nmap plugin](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon/blob/bf40763dcc58f547680645616b1ee4155baf2e7a/autorecon/default-plugins/nmap-http.py), [MSSQL Nmap plugin](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon/blob/bf40763dcc58f547680645616b1ee4155baf2e7a/autorecon/default-plugins/nmap-mssql.py), [manual SMB suggestions](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon/blob/bf40763dcc58f547680645616b1ee4155baf2e7a/autorecon/default-plugins/bruteforce-smb.py).

Use the [plugin controls](https://github.com/AutoRecon/AutoRecon/wiki/Usage) to allowlist reviewed behavior and retain expanded commands. Keep full TCP discovery distinct from service detection and top-100 UDP coverage, which is partial. Review redirects/discovered names before more connections. The [discovery](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/README.md) and [service procedures](../reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md) remain the validation baseline.

**Runnable profiles:** The [toolkit launchers](../scripts/enum-toolkit/README.md) now provide an explicit AutoRecon plugin profile and focused web/SMB/LDAP/host/AD entry points. They use existing tools, stage fingerprint-matching plugins and retain raw output; they do not install dependencies or automate an exploitation chain. The selected plugin set is pinned, while the installed framework, NSE library and other dependencies still need trusted matching versions. No all-default invocation or full upstream feature set is designated exam-approved.

## 3. Host and AD collectors

The linPEAS builder can select checks; release builds contain broad coverage. Retain the output and validate highlighted leads with the [Linux escalation procedure](../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/01-linux-privilege-escalation.md). Use pspy when the missing evidence is a recurring privileged consumer, rather than repeatedly rerunning static checks.

winPEAS distinguishes normal checks, optional domain collection and extra features. Its optional `-vulnpackages` sends package names/versions to an online lookup: exclude that from an offline exam-evidence workflow. Optional WSL/linPEAS download execution and external lookups need separate review. PrivescCheck provides readable reports and separate extended/audit/risky categories; an EDR/noise label is not itself an exam-permission category. Validate with the [Windows escalation procedure](../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/02-windows-privilege-escalation.md).

For AD, use the SharpHound version supported by the deployed **Community Edition**. Begin with appropriate directory collection, then use focused host/session collection only where scope and evidence justify it. The [domain-mapping procedure](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md) owns these variants. enum4linux-ng supplies the SMB/RPC view; ldapdomaindump supplies a readable LDAP inventory. The latter's `--minimal` reduces retained attributes, while optional hostname resolution needs scope review. Its old BloodHound conversion targets obsolete 1.x formats, not a current CE graph.

Our [native helper](../scripts/ad-map/README.md) stays a fallback and interpretation bridge. Expand upstream configuration and links before expanding it into another PEASS. Check the actual upstream licenses before redistributing a combined package; PEASS includes GPL-based terms and integration clarifications. Do not bulk-copy scanners into a new bundle.

## 4. Other bases assessed

| Candidate | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| [yaldobaoth/OSCP-Scripts](https://github.com/yaldobaoth/OSCP-Scripts) | Useful convenience wrappers and workflow ideas, not a broad enumeration engine. Its AD wrapper also performs roasting; its psexec wrapper generates/executes a shell. The installer changes shell PATH and sudo secure_path. No LICENSE file was found in the inspected tree; review reuse permissions and each script before adopting the collection. |
| [nmapAutomator](https://github.com/21y4d/nmapAutomator) | A smaller Bash alternative for staged scans and recon suggestions. Its vulnerability modes use broad `vuln`/`vulners` selections; do not adopt All as an exam profile. Inspected source is older than current AutoRecon, which alone does not prove breakage. |
| [linWinPwn](https://github.com/lefayjey/linWinPwn) | Broad AD wrapper with enumeration and explicit attack operations. It documents an enumeration-only automatic mode, but discovery can still span servers and active checks. Keep it as an optional, separately audited configuration rather than an unattended default. |

The example repository uses an ordinary `windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp` payload, not Meterpreter. msfvenom alone does not imply the restricted Metasploit/Meterpreter target allowance was consumed; the complete wrapper still needs feature-specific review. Function names and OSCP branding do not establish permission.

## 5. Policy and use boundaries

After new credentials, repeat the relevant directory/group/host-access collection using the new identity. After a new route, use the same network/service collectors against explicit reachable scope through the verified transport; do not assume raw SYN/UDP behavior works through every SOCKS proxy. The [lateral-movement](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md) and [pivoting procedures](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/README.md) own the access and route checks. No automatic collector chooses the exploitation path or replaces the evidence/reporting workflow.

The [exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) and [FAQ](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/4412170923924-OSCP-Exam-FAQ) control restricted actions. Automated enumeration is distinct from automatic exploitation; wrappers inherit the restrictions of the features they actually run. No named OffSec approval or live-lab validation is claimed here.

Use explicit scope, controlled local evidence, compatible versions and manually verified leads. During concept study, inspect saved/synthetic output and the owning procedures; target-based execution remains for the later practice phase.

# getSH Source Coverage

[Back to the index](../README.md) | [Master Notes](Master_Notes.md) | [Cheatsheets](../cheatsheets/README.md)

This page records how the public [getSH OSCP notes](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/home) were incorporated into this repository. It is a coverage and provenance map, not a substitute for the task-oriented procedures.

## Source boundary

- Source repository: [lizaJose/getSH](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH)
- Reviewed snapshot: [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98), dated 2026-10-19
- Reviewed routes: Home, Scan, Common Services, Web, Password Cracking, Privilege Escalation, Active Directory, Useful Stuff and Tool Cheatsheet
- Treatment: ideas and commands were reorganized into original explanations, procedures and quick-reference sheets. The application source was not copied wholesale.

The source is a community reference, not an official OffSec control and not evidence that a technique has been independently executed. Current OffSec rules, supplied PEN-200 material, official tool documentation and the Hexdump modules take precedence where claims or syntax conflict.

## Route-to-note map

| getSH route | Source topics accounted for | Canonical destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scan | Nmap service probes/NSE, banner checks, unknown ports, RustScan, Masscan, Nikto and saved output | [Discovery and scanning](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/README.md), [scanner alternatives](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/07-scanner-alternatives.md), [discovery cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/discovery-scanning.md) |
| Common Services | SSH, FTP, SMB, HTTP, SMTP, SNMP, LDAP, RDP, MySQL, MSSQL and PostgreSQL | [Service enumeration](../reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md), [LDAP/Kerberos](../reference/02-service-enumeration/11-ldap-kerberos.md), [service cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) |
| Web | Recon, technology/headers, Gobuster/Feroxbuster/ffuf/wfuzz, WordPress, authentication/sessions, SQLi, command injection, XSS, upload, traversal/LFI/RFI, wrappers/log poisoning, SSRF and API testing | [HTTP mapping](../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md), [web initial access](../reference/03-initial-access/README.md), [WordPress and SSRF](../reference/03-initial-access/05-wordpress-and-ssrf.md), [web sheets](../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) |
| Password Cracking | Feasibility/keyspace, mutation rules, John, KeePass, SSH keys, NTLM/Net-NTLMv2, pass-the-hash/relay and Credential Guard | [Credential use and cracking](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md), [credential cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/credentials-cracking.md) |
| Privilege Escalation | Linux and Windows enumeration, credentials, sudo/SUID/capabilities, cron/services/tasks, PATH/DLL/wildcards, containers, tokens, Backup Operators, kernel/software candidates and automated-enumerator validation | [Local privilege escalation](../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/README.md), [Linux sheet](../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md), [Windows sheet](../cheatsheets/windows-privesc.md) |
| Active Directory | Native/PowerView enumeration, SPNs, ACLs, shares/GPP, BloodHound, credential access, Kerberos, password attacks, AD CS, DCOM, GPO, DCSync, post-compromise checks, Linux/Windows flows and a worked multi-host chain | [AD and lateral movement](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/README.md), [AD cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) |
| Useful Stuff | File transfer, Git/file hunting, database references, tunneling/forwarding, payload formats, Python environments and RDP | [Stage 04](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/README.md), [pivoting](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/README.md) and their quick sheets |
| Tool Cheatsheet | Nmap, RustScan/Masscan, ffuf/Gobuster, Nikto, PowerView, Mimikatz, Rubeus, NetExec/CME, Impacket, BloodHound/SharpHound, Certipy, ldapsearch, SMB tools, Hydra, Responder/relay, Hashcat, John, SQLmap, WPScan, msfvenom/Netcat, Chisel/Ligolo/SSH and FreeRDP | Task-specific procedures, [tool selection matrix](../cheatsheets/tool-selection.md) and [tool command reference](../cheatsheets/tool-command-reference.md) |
| Home | Workflow ordering and route descriptions | [Speedrun breakdown](Speedrun_Breakdown.md) and the repository [main index](../README.md) |

## Topic-level accounting

The following source blocks are deliberately consolidated rather than duplicated:

- Repeated Nmap service scripts live beside the relevant service procedure; Nmap coverage and state interpretation remain in Stage 01.
- Repeated file-transfer commands have one canonical home in Stage 04 and are linked from privilege-escalation and AD pages.
- Repeated password/hash/ticket commands are split by state: extraction in the producing technique, classification/cracking in Stage 04, and compatible reuse in the relevant access or AD page.
- Repeated web-discovery invocations live in the HTTP mapping procedure; exploit-specific syntax remains in Stage 03.
- The source's three-host AD narrative was converted into a generic worked reasoning chain. Machine names, credentials and exact solutions are not retained.
- Tool-card duplicates are represented in the task procedure and selection matrix instead of separate copies of every command.

## Corrections and scope decisions

- SQLmap is retained only as a recognition/research reference. The current [OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide#h_01HQ6G5QXV1B3C5H5XG3K5M4P6) prohibits automatic exploitation tools such as SQLmap; the operational exam path remains manual SQL injection.
- Metasploit/Meterpreter restrictions are called out wherever relevant. `msfvenom` and `multi/handler` are treated separately because the official guide explicitly permits them across targets subject to the Meterpreter limitation.
- Responder poisoning and NTLM relay are retained as lab concepts, but spoofing is prohibited on the exam. Do not translate a lab workflow into an exam action without rechecking current rules.
- Dedicated buffer-overflow development is excluded by learner choice. Public memory-corruption exploit reading, prerequisite checking, compilation and parameter/payload adaptation remain in scope.
- The getSH navigation contains a disabled future privilege-escalation item under the AD route. It has no content to migrate; the populated standalone privilege-escalation route is fully mapped.
- The source includes commands whose flags, package names or behavior may vary by distribution and version. Procedures identify version-sensitive areas and prefer current upstream names; unverified host availability is not claimed.

## Coverage limits

The source is broad but not complete enough to replace the speedrun map. It is comparatively light on public-exploit adaptation, shell reliability/failure isolation, evidence/report construction, detailed NFS/DNS mechanics, some lateral-movement authorization distinctions and systematic dead-end recovery. Those subjects remain explicit Blocks 6, 7, 14 and 15 and are supplemented from PEN-200, current official guidance and relevant [Hexdump modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules).

This import establishes **studied reference coverage**, not practical competence. Live-target work, capstones, cold re-solves and mastery evidence remain deferred until the concept phase is complete.

# Master Notes

[Back to the index](../README.md) | [Attack Strategy Map](Attack_Strategy_Map.md)

Use these notes to understand why an attack works, recognize its prerequisites, interpret results and decide what to try next. Open the linked operational procedures for commands. Source section/page references identify topics in the supplied 2025 PEN-200 edition; the explanations here are original summaries.

Use the [method guides](Attack_Strategy_Map.md#all-objectives-and-methods) for complete study entries: outcome, recognition, prerequisites, prerequisite discovery, mechanics, baseline/variants, worked example, verification, failure and next transitions. This page keeps the shared concepts that connect those entries: evidence and access claims, effective permissions, identity/material types, privileged consumers, authentication versus authorization and network reachability. Method-specific commands remain synchronized with their owning operational procedures.

## Contents

- [Discovering and recognizing attack opportunities](#discovering-and-recognizing-attack-opportunities)
- [Finding attack surfaces](#finding-attack-surfaces)
- [Enumeration and attack selection](#enumeration-and-attack-selection)
- [Extracting opportunities from services](#extracting-opportunities-from-services)
- [Scan coverage and uncertain results](#scan-coverage-and-uncertain-results)
- [Credentials and changing access](#credentials-and-changing-access)
- [Web behavior to access](#web-behavior-to-access)
- [Public exploit selection and adaptation](#public-exploit-selection-and-adaptation)
- [Shells and file transfer](#shells-and-file-transfer)
- [Payload delivery and execution controls](#payload-delivery-execution-controls-and-framework-boundaries)
- [Privilege escalation](#privilege-escalation)
- [Active Directory attack reasoning](#active-directory-attack-reasoning)
- [Tunnels and network reachability](#tunnels-and-network-reachability)
- [Integrated attack control, stagnation and recovery](#integrated-attack-control-stagnation-and-recovery)
- [Evidence and reproducibility](#evidence-and-reproducibility)

## Discovering and recognizing attack opportunities

A useful recognition clue is not just a fact worth memorizing. It is an observation obtained from a particular access position through a reproducible investigation. Start with the capability you actually have, choose a relevant location or interface, perform a scoped discovery action, and identify the exact output detail that makes a method worth considering.

Use this sequence: starting access → investigation location → discovery action → observation → candidate method → missing-condition check → selection. Each [topic workflow](Attack_Strategy_Map.md#discover-the-clue-before-choosing-a-method) supplies a first pass; each method's recognition section shows how a clue can emerge, what synthetic evidence might resemble, and what it does not prove.

Keep the scope of the observation attached to the conclusion. A query of the current host does not enumerate a remote destination. A valid password does not establish authorization to execute commands. A writable script does not establish that a privileged consumer will execute it. A banner does not establish the affected configuration. A truncated directory query does not establish absence.

Separate discovery from confirmation. “An unquoted service path exists” can justify investigating writable earlier path components; it cannot replace that permission check. “An account has a directory flag” can justify investigating an identity transition; enabled state, KDC behavior, credential requirements and connectivity still constrain the result.

Classify the decision as enabled after the relevant validation, ruled out in the tested context, or inconclusive because decisive evidence is missing. A timeout, incomplete query or inaccessible setting normally leaves uncertainty; it is not automatically a negative result. A disproven condition rules out this route from this context, not every other attack against the host.

The guide examples are synthetic teaching evidence, not transcripts or lab validation. Some combine abbreviated command-style fields with explicitly labelled observations from preceding investigation; do not expect an exact tool-format match. Attempt the [unanswered recognition cases](Recognition_Practice.md) before consulting the guides, and explain the missing check as well as the attack name.

### Put collection early, then follow the finding

After a foothold, confirm identity and runtime, then use a reviewed collector such as LinPEAS or winPEAS early to find leads. Manual competence means understanding and verifying the selected finding, not postponing useful collection until every manual technique has been exhausted. A useful sudo rule or readable credential can be followed immediately; finishing every collector is not a prerequisite.

Use the named object to choose the next test: sudo -l for an allowed operation; namei/stat/getfacl for a Linux path; sc qc/sc sdshow and icacls for a Windows service; pspy or task/unit inspection for a transient privileged consumer. A color, graph edge or writable file does not substitute for that check. Follow the linked procedure when its conditions hold; otherwise choose another observed lead.

See the [Linux first pass](methods/linux-privesc.md#first-pass-tools-and-findings) and [Windows first pass](methods/windows-privesc.md#first-pass-tools-and-findings). Supplements: [PEASS-ng](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng), [pspy](https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy), [Hexdump Linux](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/linux) and [Hexdump Windows](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/windows).

### Tool lookup follows the task

Use the [tools/scripts index](../cheatsheets/tools-and-scripts.md) to reach a complete procedure by tool name. The command-first organization is informed by [0xsyr0/OSCP](https://github.com/0xsyr0/OSCP); our recognition examples and permission/context explanations remain alongside the procedures. Verify syntax against the owning tool: a community sheet can describe an older release. For example, current PrivescCheck uses -Report for formats, whereas older examples can use a separate -Format option.

A credential transition also has a context: RunasCs can create a process with another account, while logon type 9 supplies outbound credentials without changing the local identity. Therefore local whoami is useful for the former and insufficient to validate the latter. Application-store recovery similarly depends on the profile and decryption context available to LaZagne; a recovered value must still be matched to an identity and service.

## Finding attack surfaces

An attack surface is the set of reachable behaviors an attacker can interact with from a particular source position. For the first network pass, represent every candidate as:

```text
SOURCE -> TARGET | TRANSPORT/PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | ACCESS CONTEXT | COVERAGE LIMIT
```

This prevents several common reasoning errors. A TCP and UDP endpoint with the same number are different surfaces. A service reachable from an internal host may be filtered from Kali. A port-based name is not application proof. A listening application is not automatically vulnerable, and a vulnerable build may still lack the configuration or access prerequisite needed by an exploit.

### The four questions are separate

| Question | Evidence that answers it | What remains unknown |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is the host observable from this source? | Host-discovery response or another direct response | Untested hosts may suppress discovery; ports remain unknown |
| Which endpoints respond? | Port-scan states for the stated transport and selection | Untested ports/transport and exact applications |
| What application is present? | Version probes, banners or protocol behavior | Configuration, permissions and vulnerability prerequisites |
| Which path deserves the next test? | Application evidence plus a cheap prerequisite test | Exploitability until the required conditions are confirmed |

Treat a scan as a measurement, not a verdict. Its conclusion is bounded by source, destination, time, transport, ports, discovery mode, scan type and network conditions. Record those dimensions whenever a result changes the investigation.

### Why the states occur

TCP supplies explicit connection signals. In a SYN scan, SYN/ACK normally supports `open`, RST normally supports `closed`, and silence or selected ICMP errors can lead to `filtered`. A connect scan asks the operating system to complete an ordinary connection; it is the practical choice when raw packets are unavailable or the path is a TCP proxy. Neither technique is invisible, and neither proves a vulnerability.

UDP has no handshake. A UDP reply supports `open`; ICMP port-unreachable supports `closed`; other unreachable errors can support `filtered`. Silence cannot distinguish a listening application that ignores the probe from a device that drops it, so Nmap may report `open|filtered`. A protocol-aware probe can resolve that ambiguity only if it elicits a response.

Nmap has six states. `open`, `closed` and `filtered` are the usual first-pass results. `unfiltered` means a port is reachable by the chosen probe but that probe cannot decide whether it is open or closed. `open|filtered` and `closed|filtered` explicitly preserve two unresolved possibilities. These states describe Nmap's observation from one source; they are not permanent properties of the target.

### A complete first pass

1. Confirm authorization, the exact target/list, source host, interface and route. Do not expand an assigned list into a surrounding subnet.
2. Use discovery for prioritization, but scan an assigned known-running host with discovery bypass when the discovery stage is the only blocker.
3. Get a quick TCP view, then cover TCP ports 1-65535. The default selection is 1,000 common ports, not the contiguous range 1-1000.
4. Probe discovered ports for application identity. Follow application evidence even when it contradicts the conventional port label.
5. Check UDP separately. Begin with a bounded common-port sample, then test protocol-relevant or objective-relevant ports. Record sample size and ambiguity.
6. Verify only uncertainties that change a decision. Use a focused response-reason check, a simple TCP connection, or the same endpoint from another source position.
7. Build a queue of service-specific tests. Preserve incomplete TCP, UDP and application-identification work as explicit return items.

Prioritize by expected information or access gained per unit of effort. High-value early tests commonly include anonymous or supplied-credential access, exposed files/configuration, directly browsable web applications, informative unauthenticated protocol queries and exact product/configuration checks for plausible public exploits. A surprising high port can outrank a familiar low port when its application behavior is more actionable.

Re-run network discovery when the route, source host, tunnel or target availability changes. Re-enumerate application behavior when credentials, identity or privilege changes. After a foothold, inspect local listeners because loopback-only and internally bound services cannot appear in the original external scan. Do not repeat a disproven scan unchanged merely because exploitation stalled.

### Worked interpretation: from results to a queue

Assume a common TCP scan of the documentation address `192.0.2.25` reports open TCP/22 and TCP/80 plus filtered TCP/445. A later full TCP scan also finds TCP/8000. Version probes suggest OpenSSH on 22, Apache HTTP on 80 and a Werkzeug/Python HTTP application on 8000. A top-20 UDP sample identifies responsive DNS on UDP/53 and reports UDP/161 as `open|filtered`.

The defensible conclusions are:

- Full TCP closed a coverage gap by finding port 8000; the common selection never established that all other TCP ports were closed.
- Version probes strengthened application identity but did not prove vulnerability, configuration or usable authentication.
- Responsive UDP/53 is an observed endpoint. UDP/161 remains inconclusive, and the UDP scan still covers only its stated sample.
- Filtered TCP/445 establishes neither an open SMB listener nor Windows/domain identity.
- A reasonable first queue places the custom-looking high-port web application and responsive DNS ahead of credential-gated SSH, while preserving UDP/161 and TCP/445 as conditional return items. Supplied credentials, objectives or a new route can change that order.

Block 1's reference boundary stops at the queue, but Study Unit 1 continues immediately into service enumeration. DNS records, SMB shares, FTP/NFS files, SNMP objects, database rights and remote-access authorization belong to Block 2; web paths/behavior, credential attacks and public-exploit adaptation retain their later boundaries.

Sources: supplied PEN-200 2025 edition, sections 6.4.2-6.4.3, pp142-156; [Nmap port-scanning states](https://nmap.org/book/man-port-scanning-basics.html), [service/version detection](https://nmap.org/book/man-version-detection.html), and [output controls](https://nmap.org/book/man-output.html). The [Hexdump live enumeration cheatsheet](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/blob/main/cheatsheet.org#enumeration) supplies concise Nmap, Windows and proxied-connect examples; the workflow above adds the necessary coverage and interpretation boundaries. Procedures: [Stage 01](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/README.md) and [discovery/scanning cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/discovery-scanning.md).

## Enumeration and attack selection

An open port establishes a reachable endpoint. It does not establish a vulnerability. A service name may be a conventional port label rather than the result of an application probe. A banner supplies a candidate identity; application behavior, configuration and access conditions decide which attacks are plausible.

Work through **observation -> hypothesis -> prerequisite -> discriminating test -> interpretation -> next action**. For each candidate path, ask:

- What observation supports it?
- What permission, feature, access or configuration must exist?
- What is the cheapest useful test of that prerequisite?
- Which result would disprove the hypothesis?
- What new access or information would success provide?

Choose tests that change a decision. Increasing the amount of output is useful only when it closes a meaningful coverage or interpretation gap.

Keep evidence labels distinct:

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Observed | Direct output or behavior |
| Inferred | An explanation supported by observations |
| Possible | A candidate with unverified prerequisites |
| Confirmed | A claim validated in its relevant context |
| Disproven | A stated hypothesis contradicted by a useful test |
| Inconclusive | A result that does not distinguish the alternatives |

For example, SMB exposure alone establishes neither Windows nor domain membership nor a domain-controller role. Those are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

Source route: PEN-200 Ch 6, particularly sections 6.4.3-6.4.4. See [service identification](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/03-service-identification.md) and [results and next actions](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/05-results-and-next-actions.md).

## Extracting opportunities from services

Service enumeration asks what a confirmed application will disclose or permit in the current access context. The reusable model is:

```text
SERVICE -> AUTHENTICATION CONTEXT -> NAMESPACE -> OBJECT -> EFFECTIVE RIGHT -> OPPORTUNITY
```

The namespace is what the protocol organizes: SMB shares, FTP directories, DNS records, SNMP OIDs, database schemas, or remote-session endpoints. Listing that namespace before grabbing individual objects reduces blind guessing and exposes authorization boundaries.

### Keep the four privilege claims separate

| Claim | Evidence required | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authentication works | Service accepts an identity/method | Read, write, session or administrative rights |
| Read works | A named object can be listed/retrieved/queried | Ability to change it or execute code |
| Write works | A harmless object can be created/changed in the exact path | A privileged process will consume it |
| Execution works | Observable command effect under a verified identity | Higher privilege than that execution identity |

A common failed attack path jumps from *writable* to *code execution*. The missing questions are: which component consumes the object, from what exact path, under which identity, with what syntax, and what triggers it? A writable FTP directory, SMB share, NFS export or database file path is only an input primitive until those conditions are proven.

### Authentication context is part of the result

Anonymous, null, guest, local-account and domain-account access are different experiments. A service may accept the connection while silently mapping the caller to guest. Record both the identity supplied and the identity/effective permissions observed. Re-enumerate after obtaining a new legitimate identity because authenticated views often expose new shares, records, tables or remote-session rights.

Failures also occur at different layers:

1. route or listener failure;
2. protocol negotiation/version failure;
3. authentication failure;
4. authorization or object-level denial;
5. client-side TLS, host-key, name-resolution or format failure.

Changing passwords cannot repair a route failure, and changing tools cannot grant a denied permission. Diagnose the layer before choosing the fallback.

### What each service is good at revealing

| Service | High-value output | Critical boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FTP | Anonymous/authenticated files, backups, upload locations | Write is not execution |
| SSH | Accepted method/identity and a shell | Valid key/password may still be barred by account policy |
| SMTP | Banner, capabilities, domain and possible user clues | `252` and normalized replies are inconclusive |
| DNS | Hostnames, roles, addresses, mail servers, TXT data, zone contents | Transfer refusal does not end ordinary enumeration |
| NFS/RPC | Exports, numeric ownership, readable/writable files | UID/GID and squash behavior govern access |
| SMB/MS-RPC | Shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup and signing clues | Null, guest and authenticated views differ |
| SNMP | Host, interface, route, user, process, software and listener data | UDP silence and MIB-view limits preserve uncertainty |
| Databases | Application data, credentials, grants, server file/program primitives | Database and OS identities are separate |
| RDP/WinRM | Valid authentication and interactive Windows access | Valid credentials still require logon/endpoint rights |

### DNS and SNMP are graph expanders

DNS records and SNMP management objects often reveal endpoints that the original scan did not name or could not see. Their main value is not a direct shell: it is transforming an IP-only map into a host/service/role graph. Each in-scope hostname, address, interface, route or local listener becomes a new hypothesis and may require a new source position. Preserve whether it was directly observed, inferred from naming, or merely possible.

For DNS, distinguish authoritative data from recursive answers and `NXDOMAIN` from `NOERROR` with no answer. A successful AXFR is a bulk disclosure; refusal only closes that route. For SNMP, a returned OID proves a working version/community and exposed MIB view. No response can still be filtering, loss, version mismatch, community mismatch or an unavailable OID.

### Remote services are identity validators, not password oracles

SSH, RDP and WinRM can validate one legitimately acquired credential and may provide a session, but broad guessing belongs to the credential-attack block. Separate the local/domain identity, authentication mechanism and service-specific right. An SMB login can succeed while RDP denies interactive logon; a password can be correct while WinRM rejects the account because it lacks endpoint rights.

### Database primitives cross a security boundary

Database queries normally operate inside the database authorization model. Features such as MySQL `LOAD_FILE`/`INTO OUTFILE`, PostgreSQL server-side `COPY`, and MSSQL `xp_cmdshell` cross toward the host only when explicit rights, configuration and filesystem conditions align. Their paths refer to the database server, and their operating-system actions run as the database service account or configured proxy. Database `root`, `sa`, `sysadmin` or superuser is not automatically OS root/SYSTEM.

### Worked attack path: one service produces the next test

Assume a hypothetical assigned host exposes DNS, SMB, MSSQL and RDP:

1. An AXFR is refused, but targeted DNS queries return `files01.example.test` and `sql01.example.test`. **Confirmed:** names and addresses. **Not confirmed:** roles are accurately described by names.
2. Anonymous SMB lists `Public` and reads a deployment backup. **Confirmed:** anonymous read of that object. The backup contains a database username and password; the values remain private evidence.
3. The credential authenticates to MSSQL. `IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')` returns `0`, but the user can read an application table. **Confirmed:** database access and bounded data read. **Disproven:** sysadmin through role membership.
4. The same identity passes an RDP authentication-only check but an interactive session reports missing logon rights. **Confirmed:** credential accepted in the tested RDP context. **Not confirmed:** desktop access.
5. A share is writable, but no privileged consumer or trigger is identified. **Confirmed:** write primitive. **Inconclusive:** code execution.

This is progress even without a shell: the service graph now contains confirmed names, one readable artifact, a database identity, application data, a valid RDP authentication context and an explicit authorization blocker. The next test should target the blocker or a new evidence-backed route, not repeat the same login with another client.

### The complete surface-to-opportunity loop

Study Blocks 1 and 2 as one feedback system while keeping their evidence claims separate:

```text
source/route -> endpoint -> application -> service queue
             -> access context -> namespace/object -> effective right
             -> information/access -> new host/identity/route/listener
             -> re-enter the relevant discovery or authenticated-enumeration step
```

A new hostname, address, interface, route or listener changes the network graph and returns to Block 1 from the relevant source position. A new credential or identity usually keeps the endpoint map but changes the authorization view, so return to Block 2's authenticated enumeration. A web application hands off to the combined web-behavior/weakness unit; a credible product/configuration exploit candidate hands off to public-exploit adaptation; verified execution hands off to session establishment.

## Scan coverage and uncertain results

Discovery asks whether a host appears reachable. Port scanning asks about endpoints. Service probing asks what application responds. A failure at one layer does not automatically answer the others.

Nmap's default common TCP ports differ from a contiguous low-port range. A full TCP port scan covers TCP ports 1-65535; it provides no UDP coverage. Discovery bypass assumes hosts are online and must not be interpreted as evidence that they responded.

A SYN scan interprets SYN/ACK as open, RST as closed, and certain ICMP responses or silence after retries as filtered. A connect scan uses the operating system's connection mechanism. Neither method guarantees invisibility or complete results under all network conditions.

A closed result indicates rejection in that context. A filtered result leaves listener state unresolved. UDP silence may mean filtering or a service that ignores the probe; an application-specific response may resolve the ambiguity. Preserve uncertainty when the test cannot resolve it.

Results depend on the source host, route and filtering. A port reachable from an internal Windows host may be unreachable from Kali. Record where each test originated before comparing results.

Validate further when uncertainty changes the required answer or next action. Do not turn every incidental scanner label into another investigation.
