# Recognition practice

[Strategy map](Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](Master_Notes.md#discovering-and-recognizing-attack-opportunities) | [Study sequence](Speedrun_Breakdown.md#grouped-study-sequence)

These are unanswered paper exercises, not target assignments. All evidence is hypothetical and abbreviated; none records a completed attack or practical competence. Attempt a case before opening the corresponding guide.

For every case, write:

1. Your established access and the facts actually supported by the evidence.
2. The precise recognition clue and candidate method.
3. The missing enabling condition, the exact check you would select, and the decisive evidence you would expect.
4. Your decision: enabled after validation, ruled out in this context, or inconclusive. State how one changed condition would change the next action.

Do not substitute an attack name for prerequisite reasoning.

## Case 01 — Network discovery

Your starting access is a Kali workstation with an assigned target IP. A default TCP scan reports ports 22 and 80 open. Host discovery succeeds. No UDP scan or full TCP scan has been recorded.

A draft note says: “The target has only SSH and HTTP; discovery is complete.”

What investigation produced useful clues, and what coverage claim is unsupported?

## Case 02 — Service access

A supplied domain password authenticates to SMB. You can list a share and its filenames. Opening a configuration file returns access denied. No execution-capable service authorization has been checked.

A draft note says: “We have remote execution and the database credentials.”

Which access boundaries have actually been crossed, and which checks come next?

## Case 03 — Web mapping

An HTTP path-discovery run returns status 200 for many random names. A nonsense path and the home page have matching titles, sizes and body text. One export endpoint returns a different content type and a consistent application-specific response.

How would you separate a useful route clue from soft-404 noise? What would you inspect before selecting an exploit?

## Case 04 — Web exploitation

An authenticated upload accepts a file with a script extension. Its returned URL downloads the exact source text rather than running it. The application stores the file on a separate static-content host.

Does accepted upload establish code execution? Which conditions would have to change, and what alternative capability might still exist?

## Case 05 — Credential material

A capture contains an NTLM challenge-response exchange. A colleague proposes placing the complete captured response into a tool option that expects an NT hash.

How do you classify the material? Which recovery or use paths require different prerequisites?

## Case 06 — Public exploit adaptation

A reviewed public proof of concept exits with a Python import error before sending any request. The product name resembles the target banner, but the target's affected component and exact build have not been established.

A draft note says: “The exploit failed, so the target is patched.”

Which failure boundary was reached? What evidence is needed before making a vulnerability claim?

## Case 07 — Shells and sessions

An application command primitive is confirmed. A staged payload contacts a listening socket, but no usable command session follows. The listener is a plain TCP listener, not a handler for that staged payload.

Which observed result is real, what remains unproved, and how would you distinguish a handler mismatch from a blocked callback?

## Case 08 — Linux privilege escalation

A low-privilege account can modify a backup script. The script contains administrative-looking commands. You have not identified a privileged scheduler, service, executable owner context or manual administrator trigger that consumes it.

Why is this a candidate rather than confirmed escalation? Where would you investigate the consumer and trigger?

## Case 09 — Windows privilege escalation

A service executable path contains spaces and is unquoted. All earlier executable-prefix locations are either protected from your account or occupied by existing files you cannot replace. You have not found a writable loaded dependency or service configuration right.

What does the formatting clue establish? Which effective permission decides whether this particular method is available?

## Case 10 — AD mapping

Your domain account can bind to LDAP. A broad query returns a size-limit warning. No service principal names appear in the returned subset.

A draft note says: “The domain has no service accounts.”

How would you repair enumeration coverage and preserve the distinction between an empty result and an incomplete result?

## Case 11 — AD identity transition

A directory account has userAccountControl value 0x00400202. For this exercise, 0x00400000 means preauthentication is not required, 0x00000200 identifies a normal account, and 0x00000002 means the account is disabled.

A draft note selects the account solely because the preauthentication flag is present.

Which additional flag changes the decision? What identity state and KDC result would you need before claiming a usable path?

## Case 12 — Lateral movement

The same domain password is accepted for an SMB share, but WinRM returns an authorization denial. You have not checked remote-management group membership or endpoint policy.

A draft note says: “The password is wrong.”

Which fact supports authentication, which result concerns authorization, and what other movement routes remain conditional?

## Case 13 — Pivoting

An application inside a private subnet is reachable through your SOCKS proxy. An exploit's reverse connection never arrives. The payload was configured to call a workstation address for which no return route or reverse forward has been established.

Why does successful proxied access not establish a working callback path? Draw the separate paths and choose the missing check.

## Case 14 — Execution troubleshooting

A document reaches the intended host. Office opens it in a restricted state and blocks its macro. No command process or outbound connection is observed.

A draft note recommends changing listener ports repeatedly.

At which boundary did execution stop? What evidence would justify investigating connectivity instead?

## Case 15 — Completion and reporting

Your archive opens successfully and contains the expected screenshots and notes. In the rendered PDF, one reproduction command is clipped, and a privilege screenshot does not show the relevant host identity.

A draft note says: “The archive is valid, so the report is ready.”

Which checks concern file integrity, which concern reproducibility and attribution, and what must be corrected before completion?

## Review after attempting a case

Use the [topic discovery workflows](Attack_Strategy_Map.md#discover-the-clue-before-choosing-a-method) to trace your proposed investigation. Compare the matching entry's discovery action, synthetic evidence, exact clue, missing checks and three decision outcomes with your answer. Record uncertainty rather than treating a plausible attack name as proof.

pages.markdown:
# Attack-first OSCP speedrun breakdown

[Back to the index](../README.md) | [Attack Strategy Map](Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](Master_Notes.md)

Each numbered block is a stable reference unit for notes and exam lookup. Study the blocks through the grouped attack-path units below rather than as fifteen disconnected mini-courses. This map has no time allocations and does not require the earlier chapter/class sequence.

The [Attack Strategy Map](Attack_Strategy_Map.md) is the main content entry point. Its topic guides organize each objective into named methods with recognition clues, access/configuration prerequisites, checks, associated concepts, complete command examples and variants, worked reasoning, verification, failure diagnosis and linked next transitions. Use this breakdown for study order and block definitions.

Teach mechanisms when they help select an attack, execute it, interpret evidence or diagnose failure. Other background is optional. For each task, work through recognition clues -> prerequisites -> method -> execution -> result interpretation -> failure diagnosis -> next action.

Present popular, well-supported approaches first, then less popular but viable methods, manual checks and built-in alternatives. Explain when each is preferable and give complete usable examples. Record taught approaches in the operational procedures and cheatsheets, with necessary explanations in Master Notes. This list describes study coverage, not completed work or demonstrated competence.

## Study phase before practical exploitation

Before selecting a method, use the [discovery workflows](Attack_Strategy_Map.md#discover-the-clue-before-choosing-a-method). All 166 documented methods show where to investigate, a discovery action, synthetic evidence, the precise clue, missing conditions and enabled/ruled-out/inconclusive examples. Use [Recognition Practice](Recognition_Practice.md) to test that reasoning without opening the explanations first.

Finish concept study across all 15 blocks before beginning practical exploitation. This phase includes full command examples, tool selection, attack prerequisites, worked attack chains, sample/saved-output interpretation, failure diagnosis and alternative approaches. Teach the attacks in enough detail to understand their execution while keeping hands-on attack activity for the later phase.

Use hypothetical worked examples, paper-based changed-condition exercises and recall during concept study. Continue building Master Notes, complete procedures and extensive cheatsheets. Command examples are material to study and retain; they are not assignments to execute against a target during this phase.

Defer target-based exploitation, hands-on attack drills, capstones and practical retests. Pending lab work remains recorded for later and does not block the next concept section; no live scan, flag or lab-output submission is required to progress through this document.

When coverage of all grouped units and their numbered blocks has been reviewed and the learner indicates concept study is complete, select scoped labs and validate the methods through practical execution and independent retests. Record concept coverage and practical evidence separately. A request to explain a command or attack does not itself start the practical phase.

## Grouped study sequence

Keep the numbered blocks separate in the reference, but study them in this dependency order:

| Study unit | Blocks and order | Attack chain |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 + 2 | Find a reachable application, then extract names, files, permissions, credentials or access from it |
| 2 | 3 + 4 | Map normal web behavior, validate a weakness, then convert the primitive into useful access |
| 3 | 5 | Classify credentials/keys/hashes/tickets, validate compatible use and re-enumerate after success |
| 4 | 6 + 7, with relevant Block 14 diagnostics | Adapt a public exploit, prove execution and turn it into a reliable verified session |
| 5 | 8, then 9 | Apply the same control -> consumer -> identity -> trigger reasoning separately to Linux and Windows |
| 6 | 13 fundamentals, then 10 -> 11 -> 12, with relevant Block 14 diagnostics | Build the route, map domain rights, gain a better identity and move with the compatible authentication material |
| 7 | Remaining Block 14 | Consolidate delivery, parsing, architecture, security-control, connectivity and session troubleshooting |
| 8 | 15 | Integrate the full attack, recover from dead ends and retain reproducible evidence |

Block 14 is cross-cutting: teach its relevant failure model inside Units 2, 4 and 6 when the failure can first occur, then use Unit 7 as consolidation. Block 5 is also a recurring state transition: study its credential mechanics once, then reapply them whenever another block produces authentication material.

Finishing one numbered block does not mean forgetting its loop. New hostnames, routes or listeners return to Blocks 1-2; a new credential returns to Block 5 and authenticated enumeration; execution moves to Block 7; a new identity or privilege triggers re-enumeration.

## Reference task index

1. [Find attack surfaces](#1-find-attack-surfaces)
2. [Extract opportunities from services](#2-extract-opportunities-from-services)
3. [Find useful web behavior](#3-find-useful-web-behavior)
4. [Turn application weaknesses into access](#4-turn-application-weaknesses-into-access)
5. [Use discovered credentials and keys](#5-use-discovered-credentials-and-keys)
6. [Adapt public exploits](#6-adapt-public-exploits)
7. [Obtain a reliable session](#7-obtain-a-reliable-session)
8. [Escalate on Linux](#8-escalate-on-linux)
9. [Escalate on Windows](#9-escalate-on-windows)
10. [Map AD attack paths](#10-map-ad-attack-paths)
11. [Gain a more useful domain identity](#11-gain-a-more-useful-domain-identity)
12. [Move to another host](#12-move-to-another-host)
13. [Reach internal services](#13-reach-internal-services)
14. [Resolve payload execution obstacles](#14-resolve-payload-execution-obstacles)
15. [Complete and document an unfamiliar attack](#15-complete-and-document-an-unfamiliar-attack)

## 1. Find attack surfaces

**Study unit:** 1 of 8, first half. Continue directly into Block 2; return here whenever service enumeration discloses a new in-scope hostname, address, listener, route or source position.

**Situation:** I have a target IP. Where can I attack?

- Discover exposed services, including coverage missed by limited scans.
- Interpret open, closed, filtered and ambiguous results.
- Establish application identity and select relevant enumeration.
- Rank the first investigations and recognize when to rescan.

**Skill to develop:** turn scan output into decisions.

## 2. Extract opportunities from services

**Study unit:** 1 of 8, second half. Enter with the Block 1 service queue and leave with evidence-labelled information/access plus a route into web behavior, credentials, public exploits or a verified session.

**Situation:** this service is exposed. What can it give me?

- **SMB/RPC:** users, shares, files, domain clues and anonymous/authenticated access.
- **FTP/NFS:** accessible files, writable locations, permissions and credential opportunities.
- **DNS/SNMP/SMTP:** names, users, host details and configuration disclosures.
- **SSH/RDP/WinRM:** usable authentication and remote access.
- **Databases:** useful data, credentials, file access and execution where rights permit.

**Skill to develop:** follow a service finding toward information or access.

## 3. Find useful web behavior

**Study unit:** 2 of 8, first half. Carry observed requests, roles, parameters, files and response differences directly into Block 4.

**Situation:** there is a website. Where is the useful behavior?

- Explore normal functionality, downloads, exports, uploads and account features.
- Discover hidden content, virtual hosts, APIs, backups and exposed configuration.
- Inspect requests, parameters, cookies, authentication and roles.
- Identify technologies and components worth investigating.

**Skill to develop:** recognize clues through application behavior before choosing an exploit.

**Operational pages:** [HTTP and web application mapping](../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) and [web mapping cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md).

## 4. Turn application weaknesses into access

**Study unit:** 2 of 8, second half. Use Block 14's relevant parsing, delivery and execution diagnostics here instead of postponing them.

**Situation:** this application behavior looks exploitable. How do I turn it into access?

- Traversal and file disclosure.
- Local/remote file inclusion and conditions for execution.
- Upload handling, bypasses, storage locations and execution conditions.
- Command injection, including blind cases.
- Manual SQL injection: error, UNION, boolean and time-based methods.
- Authentication/access-control weaknesses and relevant XSS paths.

**Skill to develop:** move from a validated primitive to credentials, privileges, files or execution.

**Operational pages:** [web file handling](../reference/03-initial-access/02-web-file-handling.md), [command and SQL injection](../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md), [access control and XSS](../reference/03-initial-access/04-access-control-and-xss.md), and [web exploitation cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md).

## 5. Use discovered credentials and keys

**Study unit:** 3 of 8 and a recurring transition. Re-enter this block whenever service enumeration, web access, local escalation or AD work produces new authentication material.

**Situation:** I found credentials or a key. What can I do with them?

- Identify the account and its local/domain context.
- Distinguish passwords, keys, stored hashes, captured responses and tickets.
- Crack supported material and build targeted password candidates.
- Test relevant reuse and interpret authentication failures.
- Re-enumerate accessible services and files after success.

**Skill to develop:** distinguish a valid credential from useful access.

**Operational pages:** [credential classification, cracking and reuse](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) and [credentials/cracking cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/credentials-cracking.md). Re-enter this procedure after every new credential artifact.

## 6. Adapt public exploits

**Study unit:** 4 of 8, first half. Treat execution proof, callback assumptions and payload compatibility as the handoff into Block 7.

**Situation:** there is a public exploit. Can I make it work?

- Check the exact software, configuration, architecture, authentication and other prerequisites.
- Read the relevant code and identify its assumptions.
- Adjust parameters, paths, requests, payloads and callbacks.
- Resolve dependencies and compile existing exploits.
- Troubleshoot and verify the actual result.

**Scope:** retain practical use and adaptation of existing memory-corruption PoCs. Skip dedicated overflow development, stack/register/offset drills and shellcode development. Explain the mechanics necessary for the existing exploit alongside its use.

**Skill to develop:** select and adapt a suitable public exploit and explain why it should work.

**Operational pages:** [public exploit selection and adaptation](../reference/03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md) and [public exploit quick sheet](../cheatsheets/public-exploits.md). Leave this block only after the exploit's effect is independently verified.

## 7. Obtain a reliable session

**Study unit:** 4 of 8, second half. Apply Block 14 diagnostics for payload, listener, connectivity and session failures while they are relevant.

**Situation:** I can execute commands. How do I get a reliable session?

- Choose direct execution, reverse/bind shells or authenticated remote access.
- Handle shell syntax, quoting, encoding, architecture and payload compatibility.
- Establish listeners and diagnose missing callbacks.
- Improve limited shells and transfer files.
- Verify the host, identity, privilege and network position.

**Skill to develop:** separate execution failure, connection failure and session instability.

**Operational pages:** [shells, payloads and session repair](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md) and [shell/payload quick sheet](../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md). Apply the callback ladder before replacing a payload blindly.

## 8. Escalate on Linux

**Study unit:** 5 of 8, Linux track. Share the permissions/execution reasoning model with Block 9 but keep the operating-system mechanisms separate.

**Situation:** I have a Linux shell. How do I become root?

- Credentials in files, histories, configuration and processes.
- Sudo, SUID/SGID and capabilities.
- Scheduled jobs, services, writable scripts, binaries and directories.
- PATH/environment dependencies and relevant mounts.
- Software/kernel exploit selection when supported by evidence.
- Manual validation of automated-enumerator findings.

**Skill to develop:** trace your control into privileged execution.

**Operational pages:** [Linux privilege escalation](../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/01-linux-privilege-escalation.md) and [Linux quick sheet](../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md). Leave this block only when every candidate can be expressed as controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → verified effect.

## 9. Escalate on Windows

**Study unit:** 5 of 8, Windows track. Study after Linux using the same control -> consumer -> identity -> trigger model without merging their techniques.

**Situation:** I have a Windows shell. How do I become administrator or SYSTEM?

- Account context, groups, tokens, privileges and effective permissions.
- Stored credentials and useful configuration artifacts.
- Service permissions, writable binaries, unquoted paths and DLL loading.
- Scheduled tasks and other privileged consumers.
- Relevant token and software exploitation.
- Trigger conditions and final privilege verification.

**Skill to develop:** establish both control over an object and a viable privileged trigger.

## 10. Map AD attack paths

**Study unit:** 6 of 8. Study after Block 13's route/proxy fundamentals, then continue through Blocks 11 and 12 as one identity-and-movement chain.

**Situation:** I have domain credentials. Where can this identity take me?

- Identify the domain, DCs, computers, accounts and groups.
- Enumerate shares, service accounts, permissions, sessions and host access.
- Collect and interpret BloodHound relationships.
- Validate promising edges and rank possible paths.

**Skill to develop:** connect identity -> rights -> access -> new opportunities.

## 11. Gain a more useful domain identity

**Study unit:** 6 of 8. Enter with a mapped relationship and leave by re-enumerating what the new identity can read, control or reach.

**Situation:** how do I gain a more useful domain identity?

- AS-REP roasting and Kerberoasting.
- Credential access where current host privileges permit it.
- Account, group and directory-object permission abuse.
- Useful password, hash and ticket transitions.
- Ticket-abuse and DCSync prerequisites.
- Re-enumeration after every identity change.

**Skill to develop:** explain why each transition works and what it unlocks.

**Operational pages:** [credential access](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/02-credential-access.md), [Kerberos and identity transitions](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md), [object control and domain compromise](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md), and the [AD cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md). The active core follows the current BOK: password/roast paths, cached credentials, service-ticket forging and DCSync, plus the directory rights that directly enable those transitions. AD CS, delegation/RBCD and broad GPO abuse remain conditional supplements rather than core Block 11 requirements.

## 12. Move to another host

**Study unit:** 6 of 8. Match password, hash or ticket to a reachable service and its authorization requirements; use the relevant Block 14 failure model immediately.

**Situation:** I have useful credentials. How do I move to another host?

- SMB/service-based execution, WMI, WinRM and RDP.
- Password, hash and ticket authentication.
- Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket and Overpass-the-Hash.
- Authentication versus remote-access authorization.
- Host-specific permissions, service availability and failure diagnosis.

**Skill to develop:** choose a movement method that matches the credential and destination.

**Operational pages:** [lateral movement](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md), [Kerberos and identity transitions](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md), [pivoting/tunneling](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md), and the [AD cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/active-directory.md). Block 12 owns authentication-material-to-service execution; Block 13 owns the route that makes the service reachable.

## 13. Reach internal services

**Study unit:** 6 of 8, studied before Blocks 10-12. Routing is not inherently an AD technique, so retain this as a separate reference block even though it precedes the domain chain during study.

**Situation:** the next service is behind another machine. How do I reach it?

- Discover internal interfaces, routes and services.
- Local/remote forwarding, dynamic forwarding and SOCKS.
- SSH tunnels and suitable alternative tunneling tools.
- DNS, proxy compatibility and callback routing.
- Diagnose each connection in the path.

**Skill to develop:** draw and build the complete route your tools require.

**Operational pages:** [tunneling and port forwarding](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md), [pivoting cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/pivoting.md), [discovery through a SOCKS route](../reference/01-discovery-scanning/02-tcp-scanning.md#tcp-only-access-through-a-socks-proxy), and [lateral movement](../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md). Block 13 owns transport and reachability; Blocks 1, 2, 10 and 12 consume the new vantage point.

## 14. Resolve payload execution obstacles

**Study unit:** cross-cutting during Units 2, 4 and 6; Unit 7 consolidates what remains. Do not wait until this point to diagnose a failure encountered earlier.

**Situation:** the payload will not run. What needs changing?

- Relevant client-side delivery and required user interaction.
- Payload format, architecture, execution environment and dependencies.
- Security-control interference and justified adaptations.
- Metasploit modules, payloads, handlers and sessions.
- Tool-feature restrictions affecting practical choices.

**Skill to develop:** isolate delivery, execution and connectivity problems.

**Operational pages:** [payload execution obstacles](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/06-payload-execution-obstacles.md), [payload-execution cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/payload-execution.md), [shells and session repair](../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md), and [pivoting](../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md). Block 14 owns the first-failed-boundary diagnosis; Blocks 4, 6, 7 and 13 own the original execution primitive, exploit, shell and route.

## 15. Complete and document an unfamiliar attack

**Study unit:** 8 of 8. This is integration and independent selection, not another catalogue of attack techniques.

**Situation:** how do I finish an unfamiliar target without losing the thread?

- Maintain a compact map of hosts, identities, credentials, routes and hypotheses.
- Prioritize tests and recover from dead ends.
- Capture access/privilege transitions and reproducible steps.
- Produce a report from retained evidence.
- Revisit assisted steps and test recognition on different targets.

**Skill to develop:** integrate the techniques into an independent attack.

**Operational pages:** [integrated attack tracking and evidence](../reference/08-evidence-reporting/01-attack-tracking-and-evidence.md), [integrated attack/reporting cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/evidence-reporting.md), the [cross-stage task index](../README.md) and each owning stage procedure selected by the state-change router. Block 15 owns orchestration, evidence and recovery; it does not duplicate the attack mechanics in Blocks 1–14.

## Tooling map

This table identifies tooling to cover. Exact commands, prerequisites, decisive output, failure examples and version checks accompany the individual teaching sections; it is not an installation list or a claim that these tools have been tested in the learner's environment.

| Tasks | Tooling to cover |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery and service investigation | Nmap, service-native clients and relevant built-in utilities |
| Web mapping and exploitation | Browser, Burp Suite Community, curl, a suitable content-discovery tool and database clients |
| Credentials | John/Hashcat, relevant login clients and targeted authentication-testing tools |
| Existing exploits | SearchSploit, source inspection, interpreters, compilers and payload tools |
| Shells and transfers | Netcat, Socat, SSH/SCP, HTTP/SMB transfer methods and PowerShell |
| Local escalation | Native host checks first; LinPEAS/WinPEAS as candidate generators |
| AD and movement | Native enumeration, PowerView, BloodHound/SharpHound and relevant Impacket utilities |
| Pivoting | SSH, Chisel or another suitable tunnel, and proxy-aware clients |

Research the tools needed for the particular section, establish a popular baseline and cover viable alternatives with their selection criteria. Check official tool documentation for syntax and current OffSec guidance before labelling a feature exam-permitted.

## Teaching and reference outputs

Every taught section should produce:

- A hypothetical worked attack with prerequisites, commands, illustrative output and decisions explained.
- A paper-based changed-condition exercise that tests reasoning; hands-on validation follows after concept study is complete.
- Popular approaches first, followed by less popular but viable alternatives and failure-driven fallbacks.
- Master Notes explaining the necessary mechanisms.
- Complete operational procedures and extensive indexed cheatsheets for the approaches taught, usable with this chat closed.

Preserve target-specific commands, actual credentials, flags, transcripts and assistance records in private lab records. Keep reusable public material generic and do not claim mastery or successful execution from a demonstration alone.

## Sources

- [Hexdump OSCP modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules): consult relevant sections as recurring supplements; exclude dedicated overflow development.
- [Official Nmap reference](https://nmap.org/book/man.html): tool syntax and scan interpretation.
- [OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge): published competency scope.
- [OffSec OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide): current format, restrictions and evidence requirements.

This is a tutor-organized study map, not an official exam blueprint or a prediction of particular targets.

pages.title: 6.2.5 Enumerate and validate effective object permissions
pages.markdown:
# 6.2.5 Enumerate and validate effective object permissions [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) A selected directory object and a controlled identity whose direct/nested memberships are known. **Where to look:** Read the target object security descriptor. Resolve the trustee SID, target object type, right, object-specific GUID, inheritance and relevant deny rules. Trace whether your controlled identity actually reaches the trustee. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Delegated administration is legitimate when narrowly scoped to intended trustees. Reading an ACL is usually not controlling its target. A powerful-looking ACE for an unrelated principal grants you nothing. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.2.5.1 Baseline — Windows PowerShell > **Run:** Windows PowerShell with reviewed PowerView. **Requires:** Read access to the selected object security descriptor; controlled trustee membership must be checked separately. **Effect:** Reads candidate ACEs; does not change permissions. ```powershell Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight|WriteProperty|Self' } | Select-Object ObjectDN,SecurityIdentifier,ActiveDirectoryRights,ObjectAceType,AceType,IsInherited,InheritanceType ``` **What this checks:** The filter selects interesting candidate ACEs, not a complete effective-access calculation. Resolve all applicable rules and the specific attribute/extended right before choosing a transition. ## 6.2.5.2 Interpret the output **Raw/view evidence first.** These are synthetic, abbreviated tool or graph-view excerpts. Graph relationship rows are a representative view, not collector console output. Version-specific wording and spacing can differ. The normalized observations below are a separate interpretation. Read [§6.6.1 — SecurityIdentifier](glossary.md#term-securityidentifier) as the trustee field, [§6.6.1 — ObjectAceType](glossary.md#term-objectacetype) as the scoped operation/attribute GUID, and [§6.6.1 — ActiveDirectoryRights](glossary.md#term-activedirectoryrights) as the represented operations. None alone establishes effective access.
6.2.5.2.1 Expected — raw evidence **Command/view:** Filtered Get-DomainObjectAcl projection *The filtered query prints no rows. This sentence is an annotation, not program output.* **Decisive clue:** No rows in this particular projection/filter. **Supported:** No candidate matching this query was displayed. **Still missing:** Read coverage, object scope and filter accuracy must be known before ruling out all control paths. **Next check:** [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1)
6.2.5.2.2 Interesting — raw evidence **Command/view:** Selected ACE projection (abbreviated) ```text ObjectDN : CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test SecurityIdentifier : S-1-5-21-111-222-333-1200 ActiveDirectoryRights : WriteProperty ObjectAceType : member AceType : AccessAllowed IsInherited : False ``` **Decisive clue:** member write is shown for a particular trustee SID. **Supported:** A group-membership write candidate exists; its connection to a controlled principal remains unverified. **Still missing:** Resolve the SID and check controlled direct/nested membership plus applicable deny and scope rules. **Next check:** [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1)
6.2.5.2.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence **Command/view:** A copy that projected the wrong trustee property ```text ObjectDN : CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test IdentityReference : ActiveDirectoryRights : WriteProperty ObjectAceType : member ``` **Decisive clue:** The projected IdentityReference value is blank. **Supported:** This may be a property-selection issue; it does not establish an ownerless ACE or permission denial. **Still missing:** Inspect the returned object before projection. Use SecurityIdentifier when that is the emitted trustee field, then resolve the principal. **Next check:** [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1)
**Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text ObjectDN: CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test IdentityReference: EXAMPLE\Support ActiveDirectoryRights: WriteProperty ObjectAceType: member AceType: AccessAllowed ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Support trustee | A group receives the rule. | Prove your identity belongs directly or through nesting. | [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1) | | member on Helpdesk | A candidate group-membership modification right. | Check applicable scope/deny rules and what membership would enable. | [§6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition](object-change.md#s-6-3-7-1) | | WriteProperty alone | The output may be incomplete or attribute-specific. | Resolve its GUID; it does not mean every property is writable. | [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1) | **Stop when:** Trustee, applicable right, target type and missing effective-access checks are explicit. **Revisit only when:** Membership, object ACL, scope or the controlled identity changes. ## 6.2.5.3 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Effective control reaches a useful target: select a narrow permission-backed transition. | [§6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition](object-change.md#s-6-3-7-1) | | Ruled out in this context | The trustee is uncontrolled or the ACE does not apply: rule out this path. | [§6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships](bloodhound.md#s-6-2-8-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | SID/GUID/inheritance is unresolved: do not perform a speculative modification. | [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1) | ## 6.2.5.4 Tooling and complete procedure Reviewed PowerView provides readable ACE candidates; native/RSAT/LDAP alternatives are in the canonical mapping procedure. Import the correct module and resolve object GUIDs. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md#9-directory-acls-and-effective-control). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-mapping.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.3.3 AS-REP roasting — conditions and output
pages.markdown: # 6.3.3 AS-REP roasting — conditions and output [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) A known username/realm and KDC connectivity. A password is not required for the no-preauthentication branch; authenticated discovery is an alternative. **Where to look:** Inspect the account's preauthentication configuration or perform the selected-account request. Keep username existence, preauthentication setting, returned cipher and recovered password as separate evidence states. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Kerberos preauthentication is normally required. An account configured without it may expose an offline-guessable response. Strong credentials can still make guessing infeasible; receiving a response is not account compromise. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.3.3.1 One known user, no password — Shell > **Run:** Kali / Linux with Impacket. **Requires:** Known target username/realm and KDC route; no password for the selected no-preauth request. **Effect:** Requests AS-REP material; does not recover a password by itself. ```bash impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/TARGET_USER' -no-pass -request \ -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep-TARGET_USER.hashes ``` ## 6.3.3.2 Authenticated directory-backed discovery — Shell > **Run:** Kali / Linux with Impacket. **Requires:** Valid querying identity and directory/KDC route. **Effect:** Authenticated discovery/ticket requests; no directory modification. ```bash impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/USER' -request \ -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep.hashes ``` **What this checks:** GetNPUsers requests AS-REP material for a compatible account. The no-pass form does not submit password guesses. The authenticated form can discover/request eligible material with the supplied identity. ## 6.3.3.3 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text $krb5asrep$23$svc_legacy@example.test:SYNTHETIC_NOT_A_HASH Alternative: User svc_modern does not have UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $krb5asrep$23$ | Typed RC4 AS-REP verifier, if actual complete output. | Use the matching offline format; the displayed example is deliberately invalid. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | Preauthentication required | This account is not eligible for this method now. | Move to another supported clue; do not call the password invalid. | [§6.2.4.1 — Enumerate service accounts and SPNs](spns.md#s-6-2-4-1) | | KDC timeout | The request did not produce account evidence. | Check DC address, realm and KDC connectivity. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | **Stop when:** Eligibility, returned artifact type or the precise failed boundary is known. **Revisit only when:** Account preauthentication, username/realm or KDC connectivity changes. ## 6.3.3.4 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | A complete compatible verifier is returned: assess offline guessing feasibility. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | Ruled out in this context | Preauthentication is required for that account: rule out this branch. | [§6.2.4.1 — Enumerate service accounts and SPNs](spns.md#s-6-2-4-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Timeout or unknown principal: separate transport from spelling/realm and account existence. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | ## 6.3.3.5 Tooling and complete procedure Kali impacket-GetNPUsers is the baseline; Rubeus is a Windows alternative. Names may use upstream .py entry points instead of Kali wrapper names. Hashcat/John applies only after format classification. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md#3-as-rep-roasting). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-identities.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.2.8 Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships
pages.markdown:
# 6.2.8 Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) A supported collector, compatible BloodHound deployment and a known collection identity. Mark only the identities and capabilities actually controlled. **Where to look:** Begin with directory relationships, then inspect the controlled principal's memberships and outbound control. Collect targeted local-group/session facts only where needed. For a chosen path, inspect each edge's object, source, age and missing prerequisite. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** A graph contains potential relationships, including stale, inferred or incompletely collected edges. A missing edge can reflect collection gaps. DCOnly avoids host collection; it is not a complete host/session survey. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.2.8.1 Baseline directory-only collection > **Run:** Windows with compatible SharpHound CE. **Requires:** Domain DNS, authenticated directory context and compatible BloodHound ingestion. **Effect:** Collects directory relationships; DCOnly does not collect live workstation sessions. ```powershell .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName domain-dconly.zip ``` ## 6.2.8.2 Targeted host-group and session collection > **Run:** Windows with compatible SharpHound CE. **Requires:** Explicit candidate-host file; required host connectivity and collection rights. **Effect:** Queries selected hosts; session collection loops and creates network activity. ```powershell .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods LocalGroup --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-localgroups.zip .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --Loop --LoopDuration 00:10:00 --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-sessions.zip ``` **What this checks:** The first command collects directory data. The next commands add selected-host group/session evidence. Choose the source matching the deployment; legacy and current collectors are not interchangeable. ## 6.2.8.3 Interpret the output **Raw/view evidence first.** These are synthetic, abbreviated tool or graph-view excerpts. Graph relationship rows are a representative view, not collector console output. Version-specific wording and spacing can differ. The normalized observations below are a separate interpretation.
6.2.8.3.1 Expected — raw evidence **Command/view:** Directory-only collection choice and graph results ```text CollectionMethods: DCOnly Directory membership/ACL relationships: collected Live workstation sessions: not part of this collection ``` **Decisive clue:** DCOnly collection scope. **Supported:** Directory relationships can be analyzed; no workstation session survey is implied. **Still missing:** A missing HasSession edge is not evidence of no logged-on users. **Next check:** [§6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions](sessions.md#s-6-2-7-1)
6.2.8.3.2 Interesting — raw evidence **Command/view:** Graph relationship inspection, representative exported view ```text analyst --MemberOf--> Support Support --AddMember--> Helpdesk Helpdesk --AdminTo--> APP01 ``` **Decisive clue:** A possible identity-to-group-to-host chain. **Supported:** This is a path hypothesis composed of different relationship types. **Still missing:** Validate current membership, effective group-write permission, resulting host right, route and compatible service. **Next check:** [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1)
6.2.8.3.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence **Command/view:** Host/session collection summary, representative view ```text APP01: session collection denied Session edges returned: 0 Directory import: completed ``` **Decisive clue:** The host-derived session operation was denied. **Supported:** Directory ingestion succeeded while the session evidence is incomplete. **Still missing:** Collection permissions and freshness need validation; importing the ZIP did not repair host-query access. **Next check:** [§6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions](sessions.md#s-6-2-7-1)
**Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text analyst --MemberOf--> Support Support --AddMember--> Helpdesk Helpdesk --AdminTo--> APP01 APP01 --HasSession--> admin_ops ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | MemberOf / AddMember | A possible identity-to-group transition. | Validate current membership and exact effective group right. | [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1) | | AdminTo APP01 | A host-control candidate. | Validate current host rights, reachable service and token context. | [§6.2.6.1 — Validate host-specific access rights](hosts.md#s-6-2-6-1) | | HasSession admin_ops | A volatile lead beyond host control. | Recheck freshness and credential-source prerequisites; no automatic Domain Admin compromise. | [§6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions](sessions.md#s-6-2-7-1) | **Stop when:** One candidate path has each required edge classified and its next manual check chosen. **Revisit only when:** Collection scope, identity, host rights or session freshness changes. ## 6.2.8.4 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The selected directory-object control edge is effective and useful: choose its permission-backed transition. Host and session edges use their interpretation rows above. | [§6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition](object-change.md#s-6-3-7-1) | | Ruled out in this context | One edge is disproven: reject that chain and rank another evidence-backed lead. | [§6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships](bloodhound.md#s-6-2-8-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Host/session data was not collected: collect narrowly or validate manually. | [§6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships](bloodhound.md#s-6-2-8-1) | ## 6.2.8.5 Tooling and complete procedure SharpHound CE plus compatible BloodHound CE. Domain DNS and directory connectivity are required; targeted host collection also needs host connectivity/rights. Use --help for the actual installed collector. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md#12-bloodhound-collect-narrowly-rank-then-validate). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-mapping.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.3.10 Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch
pages.markdown: # 6.3.10 Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) A concrete service, configuration or object-right clue that selects one of these method families. These are conditional branches, not a default catalogue to run blindly. **Where to look:** AD CS: inspect enrollment services/templates, enrollment rights and applicable certificate/authentication conditions. Delegation: inspect exact flags, SPNs, allowed targets and controlled principals. GPO: inspect effective links/scope, writable components, affected objects and refresh/trigger. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Certificates, delegation, trusts and linked policies can all be legitimate. A tool's vulnerable label or an isolated setting is only a candidate. The complete conjunction of effective rights, service configuration and authentication/trigger conditions determines whether a path exists. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.3.10.1 Baseline — Shell > **Run:** Kali / Linux with compatible Certipy. **Requires:** Directory/CA connectivity, explicit credentials and a concrete certificate-service clue. **Effect:** Enumerates configuration; a candidate label is not certificate issuance or account access. ```bash command -v certipy-ad || command -v certipy certipy-ad find -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -enabled -vulnerable -stdout ``` **What this checks:** This command belongs only to the certificate branch after AD CS evidence is found. The full owning procedure separates template/CA enumeration, certificate requests, authentication and cleanup; GPO/delegation have different commands and prerequisites. ## 6.3.10.2 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text Template: WorkstationAuth Enrollment: Domain Users Client Authentication EKU: present Requester-controlled identity/SAN behavior: not established CA policy and effective template ACL: not established ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Enrollment allowed | A principal may be able to request this template. | Confirm effective CA/template rights and issuance policy. | [§6.3.10.1 — Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch](conditional.md#s-6-3-10-1) | | Client Authentication | A relevant certificate use is advertised. | Check identity mapping and all conditions of the selected method. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | Missing SAN/ACL/CA facts | No complete certificate attack path is shown. | Collect the missing configuration; do not label the domain compromised. | [§6.3.10.1 — Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch](conditional.md#s-6-3-10-1) | **Stop when:** A concrete clue selects one extension and its complete missing conditions are listed. **Revisit only when:** New CA/template, delegation, GPO or effective-right evidence appears. ## 6.3.10.3 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | All selected branch prerequisites align: open its complete conditional procedure. | [§6.3.10.4 — Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch](conditional.md#s-6-3-10-4) | | Ruled out in this context | Only a legitimate feature is present: record it and return to stronger evidence. | [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Collector labels lack configuration detail: validate manually before an attack choice. | [§6.3.10.1 — Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch](conditional.md#s-6-3-10-1) | ## 6.3.10.4 Tooling and complete procedure Certipy/Certify for the selected certificate investigation; PowerView/LDAP/RSAT for delegation and GPO facts. Use version-matched documentation from the canonical procedure; no coercion or relay baseline is introduced. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#conditional-ad-cs-enumeration). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-identities.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.1.1 Establish the current identity and domain
pages.markdown: # 6.1.1 Establish the current identity and domain [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) A Windows session, or domain credentials on Kali. A Windows username alone does not establish the identity used for network authentication. **Where to look:** Start in the current Windows token and logon context; then inspect domain/DC discovery, DNS records and time. On Kali, use the explicit domain credentials and resolver context in the complete procedure. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** A member workstation can identify its domain and DC when its DNS and connectivity work. A local account, a /netonly process or a remote session can have different local and network identities. Multiple DCs are normal; the PDC emulator is not the only usable LDAP or Kerberos server. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.1.1.1 Baseline identity, DC and time checks > **Run:** Windows. **Requires:** Current token; domain/DC queries additionally need a usable domain/network context. **Effect:** Reads identity, discovery and time state. ```cmd whoami /all echo %USERDNSDOMAIN% echo %USERDOMAIN% echo %LOGONSERVER% nltest /dsgetdc:DOMAIN nltest /dclist:DOMAIN w32tm /query /status ``` ## 6.1.1.2 PowerShell domain and DNS queries > **Run:** Windows PowerShell. **Requires:** Domain .NET context for the domain query; DNS connectivity for SRV lookups. **Effect:** Reads directory/DNS state. ```powershell [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain() Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN ``` **What this checks:** whoami describes the process token. Domain environment variables are clues, not proof of successful authentication. nltest discovers a DC; SRV lookups test the naming layer. A plausible time source is useful, but does not itself prove the clock agrees with the KDC. ## 6.1.1.3 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text whoami: EXAMPLE\analyst USERDNSDOMAIN: example.test DC: \\DC01.example.test Address: \\192.0.2.10 Domain Name: example.test ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | EXAMPLE\analyst | The current token names a domain-style identity. | Record its SID/groups and how this session was obtained. | [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1) | | DC01.example.test / 192.0.2.10 | A discovered DC name and address. | Check the required service route; do not treat discovery as an LDAP bind. | [§6.1.1.1 — Establish the current identity and domain](context.md#s-6-1-1-1) | | No DC found | Discovery failed in this context. | Check DNS and route; this does not prove the credentials are wrong. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | **Stop when:** The local/network identity, domain/DC and relevant naming/time/route dependencies are recorded. **Revisit only when:** Identity, DC, resolver, clock or source route changes. ## 6.1.1.4 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Domain/DC naming and the required protocol work: enumerate users, groups and shares. | [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1) | | Ruled out in this context | This is a local account with no domain authentication context: obtain or select a supported domain query context first. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Discovery or time checks fail: repair that dependency before judging an account or technique. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | ## 6.1.1.5 Tooling and complete procedure Windows built-ins first; PowerShell DNS/.NET alternatives require Windows domain connectivity. No RSAT prerequisite for the native baseline. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md#2-establish-identity-domain-dc-dns-and-time). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-mapping.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.3.5 Select a credential source on a controlled host
pages.markdown: # 6.3.5 Select a credential source on a controlled host [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) An authorized host/session with known effective token and privileges. Ordinary-user access does not grant access to every credential source. **Where to look:** Start with current-user tickets and application configuration. For elevated contexts, choose among LSASS, matched SAM/SYSTEM, SECURITY/SYSTEM, Credential Manager/DPAPI or DC-specific NTDS/replication according to the exact question. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Protected process access, VBS/Credential Guard and user/machine DPAPI boundaries can prevent collection. Missing registry values do not prove protection is off. Modern Windows does not guarantee plaintext passwords in LSASS. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.3.5.1 Baseline token and protection checks > **Run:** Windows. **Requires:** Current token; registry/process information can be restricted. **Effect:** Reads privilege/protection clues; does not dump LSASS. ```cmd whoami /all tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe" reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LsaCfgFlags reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard /v LsaCfgFlags ``` ## 6.3.5.2 Runtime protection checks using CIM > **Run:** Windows PowerShell. **Requires:** CIM availability and access to the local DeviceGuard class. **Effect:** Reads runtime security-service state. ```powershell Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | Select-Object SecurityServicesConfigured,SecurityServicesRunning,VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus ``` **What this checks:** The commands establish token/process/protection context before choosing a collector. They do not themselves dump credentials. A configured protection value and running security service are different kinds of evidence. ## 6.3.5.3 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text Token: medium integrity; Administrators SID deny-only LSASS process exists RunAsPPL registry query: value not found Memory read: access denied ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Deny-only / medium token | The process is not equivalent to an elevated administrative token. | Inspect usable privileges and the appropriate local escalation path. | [§6.1.1.1 — Establish the current identity and domain](context.md#s-6-1-1-1) | | LSASS exists | Normal Windows process presence. | No secret residency or readable memory is proved. | [§6.3.5.1 — Select a credential source on a controlled host](credential-sources.md#s-6-3-5-1) | | Missing value / denied read | Protection and access remain unresolved. | Use runtime/protection evidence and an alternative authorized source; do not assume an empty store. | [§6.3.5.1 — Select a credential source on a controlled host](credential-sources.md#s-6-3-5-1) | **Stop when:** One source is matched to actual token rights and protection state. **Revisit only when:** Privilege, logon session, protection state or source access changes. ## 6.3.5.4 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Exact source rights and protection conditions are satisfied: use its bounded canonical collection procedure. | [§6.3.5.5 — Select a credential source on a controlled host](credential-sources.md#s-6-3-5-5) | | Ruled out in this context | Only ordinary-user access is available: remain with user-readable sources or escalate first. | [§6.2.3.1 — Interpret scripts, configuration and exposed secrets](files.md#s-6-2-3-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Collection is denied/empty: identify the failed layer and retain uncertainty. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | ## 6.3.5.5 Tooling and complete procedure whoami, tasklist, reg and CIM are baseline state checks. Mimikatz, offline parsers and secretsdump are source-specific later choices, with exact privileges and protections documented in the owning procedure. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/02-credential-access.md#2-establish-privilege-and-protection-state). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-identities.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.5.1 Diagnose the failed boundary
pages.markdown: # 6.5.1 Diagnose the failed boundary [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) The exact command/context, observed output or error, current source host and the last boundary known to work. **Where to look:** Walk inward: invocation/runtime -> route -> listener/protocol/TLS -> identity syntax -> authentication -> authorization -> operation -> output channel. Record whether the command reached each layer. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Read restrictions and incomplete collection are common. Empty data can mean a filter, scope, pagination, permission or freshness issue. A tool crash before network traffic says nothing about the target's vulnerability state. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.5.1.1 Baseline selection Select the prerequisite check indicated by the interpreted result below. This chooser requires no additional tool or state change. **What this checks:** Use the error to choose one discriminating check. Repeating the same command or switching tool names without changing a hypothesis usually adds little evidence. ## 6.5.1.2 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text A: connection timed out B: STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE C: authentication succeeded; ACCESS_DENIED on file read D: collection complete; zero Session edges ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A timeout | No successful protocol exchange was established. | Check source route, listener and relevant transport. | [§6.1.2.1 — Validate routes, naming and pivot connectivity](routes.md#s-6-1-2-1) | | B logon failure | The selected authentication attempt failed. | Check local/domain syntax, material type, account state and protocol support. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | C denied file read | Authentication and object authorization had different outcomes. | Retain valid identity; inspect other permitted objects or rights. | [§6.2.2.1 — Enumerate shares, SYSVOL and NETLOGON](shares.md#s-6-2-2-1) | | D zero Session edges | The collection has no session evidence. | Check whether Session was collected, collection rights and freshness; do not assert no users are logged on. | [§6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships](bloodhound.md#s-6-2-8-1) | **Stop when:** The last successful layer and one discriminating next check are recorded. **Revisit only when:** New evidence changes the failed layer; do not repeat a disproven path unchanged. ## 6.5.1.3 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The failed condition is domain naming, DC selection or time context: repair that dependency before retrying the relevant protocol. | [§6.1.1.1 — Establish the current identity and domain](context.md#s-6-1-1-1) | | Ruled out in this context | The condition is disproven in this context: close that hypothesis and choose another lead. | [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | Evidence is unavailable: label inconclusive and record what would resolve it. | [§6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary](failure.md#s-6-5-1-1) | ## 6.5.1.4 Tooling and complete procedure Use the smallest relevant native or protocol-specific check already linked by the chosen investigation. No additional failure-scanner or universal automation tool is required. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md#14-failure-routing). [Study mechanisms and alternatives](../methods/ad-identities.md). [Shared concepts](../Master_Notes.md). [§6.6.2 — Choose an approach](method-choice.md).

pages.title: 6.2.3 Interpret scripts, configuration and exposed secrets
pages.markdown: # 6.2.3 Interpret scripts, configuration and exposed secrets [AD cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) | [§6 — AD Notes](README.md) | [§6.5.3 — Read output](read-output.md) Read permission to a particular file. Write permission or an execution trigger has not been established. **Where to look:** Read the selected file and its referenced configuration paths. Look for server/database names, service identities, connection strings, deployment secrets and legacy preference XML. For a writable script, identify who consumes it and when before claiming execution. **Expected behavior / secure boundary:** Scripts often contain harmless paths and usernames. Sensitive secrets should not be available to unrelated readers. A writable file becomes an execution opportunity only if a useful consumer actually executes or loads the controlled content. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. ## 6.2.3.1 Baseline — Shell > **Run:** Kali / Linux, working copy. **Requires:** Selected SYSVOL files already retrieved into ./sysvol; matching legacy cpassword artifact. **Effect:** Reads local files and decrypts a candidate offline; no login validation. ```bash grep -Rni 'cpassword' ./sysvol gpp-decrypt 'C_PASSWORD' ``` **What this checks:** This command is the conditional legacy-GPP branch, not a universal SYSVOL step. A cpassword attribute is a specific clue to a recoverable stored value; ordinary policy XML is not. General file inspection and selective retrieval are covered on the shares page. ## 6.2.3.2 Interpret the output **Normalized observations:** the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ```text Another file: \\APP01\Deploy\install.ps1 ``` | Interpreted result | What it establishes | Required next check | Continue at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | userName + cpassword | A legacy preference credential candidate, not a validated login. | Preserve context privately; recover using the source procedure and validate the resulting account/material. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | APP01 path | A newly discovered application/deployment location. | Add it to the map, establish scope and test access. | [§6.2.6.1 — Validate host-specific access rights](hosts.md#s-6-2-6-1) | | A script is writable | Control of a file only. | Identify the consumer, run-as identity and trigger; do not assume logon scripts run as SYSTEM. | [§6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions](acl.md#s-6-2-5-1) | **Stop when:** The selected artifact is classified and its useful references or secret candidates are recorded. **Revisit only when:** A new readable path, decryption context or consuming process appears. ## 6.2.3.3 Decide and continue | Result | Decision | Next numbered section | | --- | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | A recovered candidate authenticates: map its exact identity and useful rights. | [§6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope](material.md#s-6-3-2-1) | | Ruled out in this context | The password is stale/disabled or the consumer never reaches the file: reject that proposed transition. | [§6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups](users.md#s-6-2-1-1) | | Inconclusive / failed check | An attribute/path is missing or permissions prevent inspection: keep that branch inconclusive. | [§6.2.2.1 — Enumerate shares, SYSVOL and NETLOGON](shares.md#s-6-2-2-1) | ## 6.2.3.4 Tooling and complete procedure Existing SMB/native file readers are sufficient for ordinary inspection. gpp-decrypt is only the legacy cpassword branch; do not add a cracking workflow without a matching artifact. The commands above are extracts from the owning procedure; Windows-host and Kali/target tool availability must be checked in that environment. No installation or target execution is implied by this page. [Open the owning procedure, prerequisites and complete variants](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md#gpp-cpassword--recover-a-candidate-from-readable-sysvol-xml).
