# Map useful web behavior [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) Build the request and role map before selecting a weakness. Distinguish scheme, virtual host, route, method, parameter, object and identity; the same path can expose different behavior in another context. **Speedrun blocks:** 3. **Documented methods:** 6. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Capture a real request before fuzzing Use the browser/proxy to capture the real method, host, cookie and input; curl is the replay baseline. ```bash curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` - **If Redirect to a different hostname:** Resolve and replay that hostname before testing paths. → [Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications](web-mapping.md#web-vhosts). - **If A login, upload or object endpoint:** Capture its normal authenticated request and available roles. → [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](web-mapping.md#web-parameters). - **Otherwise:** Every request reaches the wrong/default site: fix the host/scheme/session first. → [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### Discover paths with Gobuster or the documented ffuf variant First request a missing path to learn the false-positive body/status/length. Keep the correct host and session. ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt ``` - **If A backup, config, source or repository path:** Read its content; a 200 response alone does not establish an artifact. → [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](web-mapping.md#web-artifacts). - **If A new application function:** Map its parameters and authorization boundary. → [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](web-mapping.md#web-parameters). - **Otherwise:** All candidates look identical: repair the response controls rather than collecting more false positives. → [Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering](web-mapping.md#web-content). ### Enumerate hostname-selected sites Use this when DNS, certificates, redirects or page content suggest another hostname. ```bash gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt ``` - **If A host has a distinct response:** Browse it with the correct Host header and repeat function/path mapping. → [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). - **Otherwise:** No distinct host: return to real application functions and exposed scripts. → [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior). ## Discovery workflow Start with a reachable URL. A suspicious parameter, hidden administration path or accepted account is not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. 1. Record scheme, hostname, redirects and session state: [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). 2. Browse real functions and capture their requests; inspect source/scripts and exposed artifacts: [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior); [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](web-mapping.md#web-artifacts). 3. Use missing-path/host controls before content or virtual-host discovery: [Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering](web-mapping.md#web-content); [Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications](web-mapping.md#web-vhosts). 4. Map methods, input locations, object ownership and roles before selecting a weakness: [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](web-mapping.md#web-parameters). **Decision rule:** an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive. ## Method families - **Application identity and hosts:** [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](#web-identity), [Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications](#web-vhosts). - **Functions, artifacts and content:** [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](#web-behavior), [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](#web-artifacts), [Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering](#web-content). - **Inputs, objects and APIs:** [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](#web-parameters). ## Choose a method | Method | Recognition clue | Required access | Enabling conditions | Resulting capability | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](#web-identity) | An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons | A reproducible application identity and baseline request | | [Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications](#web-vhosts) | DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing | Additional verified applications on the same address | | [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](#web-behavior) | Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons | An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses | | [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](#web-artifacts) | JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope | Hidden functionality, version clues or typed credential artifacts | | [Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering](#web-content) | An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist | Verified candidate routes and files | | [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](#web-parameters) | An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods | A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state | A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type | A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis | ## Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#baseline-the-application-identity) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A reproducible application identity and baseline request. ### 2. Recognition clues An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Request the assigned HTTP endpoint without following redirects blindly; inspect location, cookies and alternate scheme/hostname behavior. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: https://HOSTNAME/ Set-Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE ``` **Recognize this detail:** The hostname/scheme redirect identifies the application request context to reproduce. **Still missing before method selection:** Confirm the hostname routes to the assigned address and preserve its TLS/Host/session state. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The correct named request reaches a distinct application: map its functions. | | Ruled out in this context | The candidate name produces only the default missing-host response: discard that virtual-host inference. | | Inconclusive | Redirect loops can mean missing cookies/host routing; repair the normal request before testing vulnerabilities. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [this topic's discovery workflow](#discovery-workflow). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` ### 5. Why it works TLS SNI, Host, redirects and cookies can select different applications. A response from the IP URL does not describe every hostname served by that listener. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash curl -skL -D headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Decisive output:** record the scheme, hostname/`Host` header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated.
Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate ```bash curl -sk -H 'Host: CANDIDATE.DOMAIN' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` Compare it with a random hostname. A different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects.
Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects ```bash curl -skL -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Use a separate cookie jar per identity. Do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence.
Variant — replay through Burp Community ```bash curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Confirm the proxy listener is active on `127.0.0.1:8080`. Use `-k` only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the IP URL redirects to a hostname. Test: send the correct Host/SNI while routing to the assigned address. Illustrative output: a distinct application login appears. Interpretation: map that application separately. ### 8. Verify the result Record final URL, host, status, redirects, cookies and authentication context before comparing payload results. ### 9. Failure and fallback A redirect loop or generic default page may indicate a wrong host or missing session rather than a nonexistent application. ### 10. Next transitions [Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications](web-mapping.md#web-vhosts); [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior); [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](web-mapping.md#web-artifacts). ## Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#discover-virtual-hosts) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Additional verified applications on the same address. ### 2. Recognition clues DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Collect hostnames from redirects, certificates, DNS and source; compare named requests against an invalid-host control. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk --resolve HOSTNAME:PORT:TARGET https://HOSTNAME:PORT/ ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Host HOSTNAME: application login page Host INVALID_HOST: default server page ``` **Recognize this detail:** A reproducible hostname-selected application is a new mapping target on the same address. **Still missing before method selection:** Send a random Host header as a negative control, compare the candidate's real response, then browse it with the correct hostname. A different status caused only by redirects or a default site is not a confirmed vhost. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | The named application has distinct verified behavior: give it its own session/function map. | | Ruled out in this context | All candidate hosts receive the same default body: discard the claimed distinct application. | | Inconclusive | TLS routing or local DNS is wrong: fix that context before deciding a vhost is absent. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -sk --resolve HOSTNAME:PORT:TARGET https://HOSTNAME:PORT/ ``` ### 5. Why it works Virtual-host routing uses the requested hostname. DNS resolution, HTTP Host and TLS SNI must be aligned when the server selects behavior at more than one layer. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt ``` Alternative with automatic calibration: ```bash ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.DOMAIN' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json ``` > **Failure cue:** uniform status/length may be the default vhost. Compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a certificate suggests an internal application name. Test: resolve it to the assigned address while preserving SNI. Illustrative output: a separate administration interface. Interpretation: give it its own request and credential map. ### 8. Verify the result Compare candidate and nonexistent-host responses, including content and redirects; resolve to the intended scoped address. ### 9. Failure and fallback A default response for every host or an SNI mismatch makes the result inconclusive; do not treat every guessed hostname as a real application. ### 10. Next transitions [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity); [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior); [Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers](services.md#service-dns). ## Map functions, roles and normal requests manually **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#manual-behavior-map) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses. ### 2. Recognition clues Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Browse the site's normal account, export, upload and download features while recording requests in the browser/proxy. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D response-headers.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Observed browser request: GET /download?file=report.pdf Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE ``` **Recognize this detail:** The normal request exposes a file-selecting input discovered through functionality, not guessed from a payload list. **Still missing before method selection:** Find the actual input semantics, account/role and normal response before file/read/authorization tests. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Controlled comparisons prove a useful primitive: choose its method and remaining checks. | | Ruled out in this context | The parameter only selects an allowlisted public report: discard unrestricted-path inference. | | Inconclusive | Unknown ownership or an expired session prevents interpreting differences; re-establish the baseline. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D response-headers.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` ### 5. Why it works The same functionality can expose different trust boundaries through object IDs, methods and roles. Changing one property while preserving request state makes differences interpretable. ### 6. Execute and choose variants For every visible function, capture one unchanged request in Burp Proxy history, send it to Repeater and record: ```text METHOD PATH | CONTENT-TYPE | ACCESS CONTEXT/ROLE INPUT LOCATION + NAME | BASELINE VALUE STATUS | LENGTH/HASH | REDIRECT | MARKER/ERROR/TIME OBJECT/FUNCTION SELECTED | NEXT ONE-VARIABLE TEST ``` Check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every JavaScript API call. > **Next:** a browser-side restriction is not server authorization. Replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a report download accepts a numeric ID. Test: compare objects owned by two authorized study accounts. Illustrative output: a lower role receives another account's report. Interpretation: proceed to an object-authorization method. ### 8. Verify the result Retain method, route, input location, identity and expected normal behavior; do not infer vulnerability from an interesting parameter name. ### 9. Failure and fallback Expired sessions, CSRF failures and malformed requests can imitate access-control differences; reproduce a valid baseline first. ### 10. Next transitions [Cross an object-ownership boundary](web-exploitation.md#web-idor); [Read files through directory traversal](web-exploitation.md#web-traversal); [Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval](web-exploitation.md#web-upload); [Prove server-side template evaluation and identify its engine](web-exploitation.md#web-ssti); [Use an XML parser's external-entity behavior for bounded file read](web-exploitation.md#web-xxe); [Test structured NoSQL operator injection with identity controls](web-exploitation.md#web-nosql); [Match PHP deserialization gadgets to installed dependencies](web-exploitation.md#web-php-deserialization); [Validate unsafe YAML object construction](web-exploitation.md#web-yaml); [Test Shellshock only through a confirmed CGI-to-Bash chain](web-exploitation.md#web-shellshock); [Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering](web-mapping.md#web-content). ## Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#inspect-exposed-artifacts) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/04-file-and-repository-hunting.md#exposed-git-metadata) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/04-file-and-repository-hunting.md#repository-secrethistory-search) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Hidden functionality, version clues or typed credential artifacts. ### 2. Recognition clues JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Inspect linked JavaScript/source, robots/sitemaps, relevant backups and a bounded Git metadata check from the mapped web application. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text robots.txt: Disallow: /INTERNAL_PATH/ .git/HEAD: ref: refs/heads/main ``` **Recognize this detail:** The path and Git reference are investigation leads; neither proves a working secret or complete repository. **Still missing before method selection:** Compare missing-path controls, retrieve actual permitted artifacts and verify recovered history/account context. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Relevant source/history is recoverable and exposes a typed artifact: inspect it through the credential workflow. | | Ruled out in this context | The same body is returned for arbitrary missing paths: reject the apparent metadata exposure. | | Inconclusive | HEAD without objects leaves repository recovery incomplete; document available content instead of inventing history. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD ``` ### 5. Why it works Client code and repository history can preserve endpoints and removed secrets. An exposed Git HEAD proves metadata exposure; repository completeness and secret validity require separate checks. ### 6. Execute and choose variants ```bash curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/sitemap.xml curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/openapi.json curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/swagger.json ``` Also inspect HTML comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked JavaScript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers. > **Decisive output:** a path, parameter, API schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. Source disclosure is not command execution. ```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/config ``` > A readable `HEAD`/`config` supports exposed repository metadata. A `403`, redirect or generic template is not proof. Preserve the correct host header/base path. If authorized, recover into a new local directory with a purpose-built tool and inspect locally: ```bash git-dumper http://TARGET:PORT/.git/ repo-output git -C repo-output status git -C repo-output log --oneline --all --decorate git -C repo-output log -p --all ``` `git-dumper` is an optional third-party helper; install on demand in an isolated environment only when the exposure has been confirmed. Manual object recovery is possible but slower. ```bash rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' repo-output git -C repo-output log --all -S'password' --oneline git -C repo-output log --all -G'pass(word)?|secret|token' --oneline ``` Inspect candidate commits without dumping all history: ```bash git -C repo-output show COMMIT -- PATH git -C repo-output diff COMMIT^ COMMIT -- PATH ``` Validate freshness, identity and compatible use. Removed historical values are often rotated or environment-specific. ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: Git metadata is exposed. Test: recover only available objects and inspect history. Illustrative output: a removed database connection string. Interpretation: classify the account and validate current database access. ### 8. Verify the result Confirm actual file/history content and distinguish a historical secret from a usable current credential. ### 9. Failure and fallback A 200 soft-404 or incomplete object database is not a recovered repository. Compare known-missing paths and record missing history. ### 10. Next transitions [Classify the artifact and its identity context](credentials.md#credential-classify); [Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration](public-exploits.md#exploit-select); [Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties](web-mapping.md#web-parameters). ## Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#discover-files-and-directories) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result Verified candidate routes and files. ### 2. Recognition clues An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Establish the application's missing-path response, then run a bounded content search with the existing session/host context. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk -D - http://TARGET:PORT/KNOWN_MISSING_PATH ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Missing control: status=200, body=DEFAULT_ERROR Candidate /EXPORT_PATH/: status=200, body=EXPORT_FORM ``` **Recognize this detail:** The candidate's actual function differs from the soft-404 control despite equal status codes. **Still missing before method selection:** Request a known-missing path under the same host/session and compare status, body and length. Open each distinct Gobuster/ffuf result; a uniform login page or soft-404 is a filter problem, not a directory finding. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | Independent retrieval confirms an actual function: add its request to the behavior map. | | Ruled out in this context | The candidate matches the wildcard error body: remove it from the useful queue. | | Inconclusive | Rate limiting or session expiry distorts response size; restore stable controls before filtering. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -sk -D - http://TARGET:PORT/KNOWN_MISSING_PATH ``` ### 5. Why it works Discovery enumerates names; wildcard responses, redirects and soft-404 pages can make every guess appear valid. Confirm candidates through independent retrieval and behavior. ### 6. Execute and choose variants Request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt ``` > **Decisive output:** manually verified routes including useful `200`, redirect, `401`, `403` and `405` responses.
Variant — technology-aware extensions ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt ``` Choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension.
Variant — authenticated discovery ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -c 'SESSION=VALUE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt ``` Use only the cookie or header that applies. An expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect.
Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST --exclude-length NOISE_LENGTH -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt ``` Filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path.
### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: every path returns 200. Test: compare the missing-path body/length before filtering. Illustrative output: one candidate has a distinct export response. Interpretation: inspect that function manually. ### 8. Verify the result Open candidates and record their actual behavior; status/length alone is only a selection clue. ### 9. Failure and fallback Aggressive filters can hide genuine routes and rate limiting can fabricate differences; validate the baseline and reduce the request rate. ### 10. Next transitions [Map functions, roles and normal requests manually](web-mapping.md#web-behavior); [Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts](web-mapping.md#web-artifacts); [Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval](web-exploitation.md#web-upload). ## Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties **Blocks:** 3. [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#discover-parameters-and-object-values) | [Operational procedure](../../reference/02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md#map-api-methods-schema-and-authorization) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-mapping.md) ### 1. Purpose and result A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis. ### 2. Recognition clues An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods. #### Find the clue from your starting access **Where to investigate:** Capture a valid API request, inspect its schema/client code and compare allowed methods and controlled object/role contexts. **Discovery action — reference example:** ```bash curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH ``` **Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated:** The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. ```text Object fields: id, ownerId, role Observed request: PATCH /api/profile Body: {"displayName":"VALUE"} ``` **Recognize this detail:** The actual object, method and writable input are known; returned owner/role fields are only candidate security boundaries. **Still missing before method selection:** Determine field binding, ownership, persistence and server authorization with controlled accounts. | Outcome after checking | Example and next decision | | --- | --- | | Enabled after validation | A protected field/action changes under a lower role and is independently verified: select its authorization method. | | Ruled out in this context | The server ignores the sensitive field and privileges remain unchanged: reject that assignment hypothesis. | | Inconclusive | Malformed JSON or wrong content type makes a failed request inconclusive; reproduce the valid update first. | **If you do not yet have this clue:** start with [Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state](web-mapping.md#web-identity). ### 3. Prerequisites **Starting access:** A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. **Required conditions:** A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type. ### 4. Discover and verify prerequisites ```bash curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH ``` ### 5. Why it works APIs enforce security at route, object and property boundaries. A valid JSON body can be accepted while a sensitive field is ignored; test its persisted effect separately. ### 6. Execute and choose variants GET parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH?FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-get.json ``` POST form parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/PATH -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-post.json ``` Object values with an authenticated API: ```bash ffuf -w NUMBERS -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/FUZZ' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json ``` > **Decisive output:** a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. Tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws.
ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request Save a working raw request from the proxy as request.txt, retain its Host/cookie/body, and put FUZZ at the single parameter name/value or path being tested. Replay it once manually first. The request file does not specify TLS: choose the transport explicitly. ```bash # HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto https -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-https.json # Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto http -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-http.json ``` > **Read:** compare an outlier's status/length/body with a known missing value, then replay that exact request. A login redirect for every value → refresh the session before continuing. A one-time CSRF token → repair token handling; the saved-request flag does not refresh it automatically. [ffuf request configuration](https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf/wiki/Home#request-configuration).
```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/login ``` > **Interpretation:** `405` can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. Validation errors can reveal required fields. A token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request. Build a matrix across anonymous, user A, user B and administrator contexts where available: ```text PATH | METHOD | IDENTITY/ROLE | OBJECT/PROPERTY | RESULT | NEXT ``` ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an API response includes a role property. Test: compare documented writable fields and a controlled update. Illustrative output: the field is ignored and privilege is unchanged. Interpretation: that mass-assignment hypothesis is disproven; investigate other boundaries. ### 8. Verify the result Prove which input is consumed and whether state changes persist in an independent read. ### 9. Failure and fallback HTTP 400/415 may indicate encoding/schema rather than security enforcement. Keep a valid request before changing permissions-related properties. ### 10. Next transitions [Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields](web-exploitation.md#web-mass-assignment); [Cross an object-ownership boundary](web-exploitation.md#web-idor); [Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection](web-exploitation.md#web-command); [Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context](web-exploitation.md#sql-influence); [Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action](web-exploitation.md#web-xss); [Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior](web-exploitation.md#web-ssrf). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8 pp201–244. [OWASP Web Security Testing Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/). Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

# Escalate privileges on Windows [Strategy map](../Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | [Master Notes](../Master_Notes.md) | [Operational index](../../README.md) | [Cheatsheets](../../cheatsheets/README.md) An administrator-group membership, enabled token privilege, writable object and effective privileged execution are different claims. Establish the precise right, consumer identity and available trigger before choosing a route. **Speedrun blocks:** 9. **Documented methods:** 13. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. ## First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. ### Record the token and host context Check the current token before choosing an exploit or collector build. ```cmd hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all ``` - **If SeImpersonatePrivilege:** Check its enabled state and the operation/access needed by that specific technique. → [Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route](windows-privesc.md#windows-token). - **If SeBackupPrivilege:** Inspect the permitted backup operation and the exact source it can read. → [Use backup privilege to obtain protected local credential material](windows-privesc.md#windows-backup). - **If Service/task activity or a useful group membership:** Inspect the actual objects and ACLs. → [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](windows-privesc.md#windows-acl). - **Otherwise:** No immediate token route: run the broad collector, then verify its service/file findings. → [Turn automated Windows findings into manually verified candidates](windows-privesc.md#windows-enumerators). ### Run winPEAS early and save its report Transfer a reviewed binary matching the host architecture. The log option writes out.txt; inspect it before selecting a route. Native checks remain available if execution is blocked. ```cmd winPEASx64.exe log ``` - **If Modifiable service or writable service binary:** Check sc qc/sdshow and the actual binary/parent ACL, service account and restart rights. → [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-config). - **If Unquoted service path:** Check the exact executable prefixes for write access and a privileged restartable consumer. → [Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix](windows-privesc.md#windows-unquoted). - **If A saved credential/config finding:** Read the named source and classify the account/material. → [Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts](windows-privesc.md#windows-secrets). - **Otherwise:** The collector is blocked or reports no useful candidate: continue native ACL/service/task inspection. → [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](windows-privesc.md#windows-acl). ### Verify the specific service/task route Configuration write, binary replacement, unquoted-prefix write and dependency loading require different rights. ```cmd whoami /all icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" icacls "C:\Path\To" sc.exe sdshow SERVICE ``` - **If Service configuration can be changed:** Confirm the service runs as a stronger identity and you can cause a start/restart. → [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-config). - **If Only the binary or its parent is writable:** Check replacement semantics, the consumer identity and a trigger. → [Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-binary). - **If A scheduled task consumes a writable file:** Inspect the task principal, action and schedule. → [Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers](windows-privesc.md#windows-tasks). - **Otherwise:** The highlighted path is not effectively writable: reject that candidate and inspect another actual object. → [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](windows-privesc.md#windows-acl). ## Discovery workflow Start with a Windows foothold. Administrator-group membership, a high-integrity token and a working privileged trigger are separate facts. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. 1. Inspect whoami /all and host/process state before choosing a privilege route: [Establish Windows token, host and process context](windows-privesc.md#windows-state). 2. Inventory real services/tasks and inspect exact object and parent ACLs: [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](windows-privesc.md#windows-acl); [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-config); [Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers](windows-privesc.md#windows-tasks). 3. Separate writable service configuration, replaceable binaries, unquoted prefixes and dependency loads: [Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-binary); [Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix](windows-privesc.md#windows-unquoted); [Control a privileged DLL, helper or configuration load](windows-privesc.md#windows-dll). 4. Follow application/history/saved-credential artifacts and exact token privileges: [Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts](windows-privesc.md#windows-secrets); [Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route](windows-privesc.md#windows-token); [Use backup privilege to obtain protected local credential material](windows-privesc.md#windows-backup). 5. Match software/driver/build evidence only after validating simpler permission routes: [Select a matching application, driver or kernel exploit](windows-privesc.md#windows-kernel). **Decision rule:** an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive. ## Method families - **Token, ACL and credential state:** [Establish Windows token, host and process context](#windows-state), [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](#windows-acl), [Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts](#windows-secrets). - **Services and privileged consumers:** [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](#windows-service-config), [Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file](#windows-service-binary), [Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix](#windows-unquoted), [Control a privileged DLL, helper or configuration load](#windows-dll), [Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers](#windows-tasks). - **Installer and token-backed operations:** [Validate elevated installer policy and AV/script-policy failure is a tooling limitation—use native checks. Convert every highlight into: ```text CANDIDATE | CURRENT TOKEN | CONTROLLED INPUT | EFFECTIVE RIGHT | CONSUMER | RUN-AS | TRIGGER | EXPECTED EFFECT | STATUS ``` ### 7. Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a scanner flags an unquoted path. Test: inspect the earlier path prefixes and trigger. Illustrative output: none is writable. Interpretation: discard the exploit hypothesis and retain the configuration fact. ### 8. Verify the result Read out.txt or the helper report. Use sc.exe qc/sdshow plus icacls for a service, inspect task XML/run-as for a scheduled task, or check whoami /priv for a token finding ### 9. Failure and fallback Binary/script blocked or report empty: check architecture and PowerShell language/policy, then use native service/task/ACL checks. A blocked helper does not disprove the finding ### 10. Next transitions [Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions](windows-privesc.md#windows-acl); [Change a privileged service's executable configuration](windows-privesc.md#windows-service-config); [Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route](windows-privesc.md#windows-token). ## Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 17 pp494–549. [Hexdump Windows modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/windows); Microsoft access-control, service and token sources remain beside the operational procedure. Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

pages.title: Path and Host Discovery
pages.markdown:
# Path and Host Discovery [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Next: TCP scanning](02-tcp-scanning.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Confirm the source path and discover explicitly assigned hosts before spending time on port coverage. ## 1. Check the path From the target's working folder: ```bash mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET ``` > **Read:** selected interface/source address. A route lookup does not prove reachability.
Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet ### Host discovery **One host:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET ``` **Assigned list:** put IPs in `targets.txt`, one per line. ```bash nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts ``` **Explicitly assigned subnet:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET ``` No response does not establish that a host is offline. A list of assigned hosts does not imply the surrounding subnet is in scope.

pages.title: TCP Scanning
pages.markdown:
# TCP Scanning [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: Path and discovery](01-path-and-host-discovery.md) · [Next: Service identification](03-service-identification.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. ## 2. Get initial TCP results ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** 1,000 common TCP ports. Review `scans/tcp-initial.nmap` in a text editor.
Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports ### Initial view: 1,000 common ports **Assigned host list, SYN scan:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list ``` **One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET ``` Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. ### Selected ports or a range **One host:** replace PORTS with, for example, `25,43` or `1-1024`. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET ``` **Find relevant services across assigned hosts:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` A focused service sweep is not a full port map.
## 3. Complete TCP coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs.
Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress ### All TCP ports: 1-65535 **Connect scan:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET ``` Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. ### Discovery skips a running target **Recheck relevant ports with response reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET ``` **Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET ``` `-Pn` assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use `-sT` without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. ### Timing and progress **Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET ``` **Faster timing on a stable path:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET ``` `-T3` is normal timing; `-T4` is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. ### TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: ```bash proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET ``` `proxychains` cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. `-Pn` avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.

pages.title: Service Identification
pages.markdown:
# Service Identification [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: TCP scanning](02-tcp-scanning.md) · [Next: UDP scanning](04-udp-scanning.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ## 4. Identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET ``` > **Next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability.
Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints ### Identify applications on discovered ports **Version probing plus the default NSE script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET ``` Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ### Select a named script **Inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ### OS fingerprinting and bundled probing **Estimate OS from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET ``` **Request more tentative OS guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET ``` **Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET ``` OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; `-A` does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

pages.title: UDP Scanning
pages.markdown:
# UDP Scanning [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: Service identification](03-service-identification.md) · [Next: Results and next actions](05-results-and-next-actions.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. ## 5. Check UDP separately ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET ``` > **Limit:** this is a sample. `open|filtered` remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it.
Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP ### Common-port samples **Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET ``` These are samples. `open|filtered` is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. ### Selected ports **Check a relevant UDP port/list:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET ``` **Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET ``` A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add `-Pn` with the same limitations as TCP. ### Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET ``` This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. ### Combined TCP/UDP selection **Example selection:** change the TCP (`T:`) and UDP (`U:`) lists for the actual question. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET ``` The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan.

pages.title: Scan Results and Next Actions
pages.markdown:
# Scan Results and Next Actions [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: UDP scanning](04-udp-scanning.md) · [Next: Windows network checks](06-windows-network-checks.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. ## 6. Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access.
Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output ### Netcat connection check **One TCP port:** replace PORTS with one number. ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` **Short port range:** replace PORTS with a range such as `3388-3390`. ```bash nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. ### Output and diagnostics **Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET ``` Open saved `.nmap` or `.txt` output in a text editor. `-oA` writes `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml`; `-oN` writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run.
## 7. Build the service queue Open the saved `.nmap` files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST ``` > **Next:** carry the complete endpoint tuple into [Stage 02 service enumeration](../02-service-enumeration/README.md) and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage.
Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established - `open` establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. - `closed` records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. - `filtered` leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. - `unfiltered` means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. - UDP `open|filtered` is inconclusive. A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. - `closed|filtered` is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. - A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. - Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position.
## 8. Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed.

pages.title: Windows Network Checks
pages.markdown:
# Windows Network Checks [← Reference index](../../README.md) · [Previous: Results and next actions](05-results-and-next-actions.md) · [Next: RDP access](../03-initial-access/01-rdp-access.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Purpose:** Test TCP reachability from a Windows host when source position or available tooling matters. Test one TCP port from the Windows source host: ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS ``` > **Read:** `TcpTestSucceeded`, source and destination addresses. Use one number for PORTS. Failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem.
Variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list ### Scan a low-port range ```powershell 1..1024 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("DC_IP", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` ### Check a selected port list The example list can be changed to the endpoints of interest. ```powershell 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("TARGET", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` `$_` is the current port; errors are hidden. No printed result does not prove every port is closed. Results reflect the Windows host's access and the stated port selection.

pages.title: Scanner Alternatives and Web Baseline Checks
pages.markdown:
# Scanner Alternatives and Web Baseline Checks [← Stage index](README.md) | [Discovery cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/discovery-scanning.md) | [Master Notes](../../notes/Master_Notes.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Discover attack surfaces](../../notes/methods/discovery.md) > **Use when:** Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. ## RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation > **Prerequisite:** RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. **Coverage:** only the explicit TCP range. **Decisive output:** a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup ``` If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap.
Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 ``` > Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection.
## Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation > **Prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **Choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **Failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. ```bash sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt ``` Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: ```bash PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified ``` Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. ## Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Next action:** route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. ## NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db ``` Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt ``` The broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt ``` Avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization. ## Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation > **Prerequisite:** an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. **Choose it:** after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. **Decisive output:** a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. ```bash nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt ```
HTTPS, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect `nikto -H` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.
Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. ## Sources - [getSH Scan route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/scan), reviewed at source commit [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [Nmap service/version detection](https://nmap.org/book/man-version-detection.html) - [RustScan usage](https://github.com/bee-san/RustScan) - [Masscan README](https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/masscan) - [Nikto documentation](https://github.com/sullo/nikto/wiki) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide)
