pages.markdown:
# Tunneling and Port Forwarding [← Stage index](README.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/pivoting.md) | [Master Notes](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#tunnels-and-network-reachability) | [Lateral movement](../06-ad-lateral-movement/05-lateral-movement.md) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Reach internal services](../../notes/methods/pivoting.md) > **Selection rule:** required application flow → reachable tunnel transport → pivot egress → client compatibility → return path. > > **Exit:** a protocol-appropriate client reaches the intended internal endpoint through a documented route; DNS/SPN behavior and any callback route are independently verified. ## 1. Draw the route before choosing a command ```text APPLICATION TOOL -> local listener / SOCKS endpoint / TUN route -> tunnel transport endpoint -> pivot exit -> internal destination service CALLBACK TARGET -> pivot listener or routable address -> relay/tunnel -> final listener ``` Record: ```text TOOL_HOST -> ENTRY_SOCKET/ROUTE -> TRANSPORT -> PIVOT -> DESTINATION application protocol | TCP/UDP | initiator | bind address | DNS point credential/SPN name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects ``` Do not use “pivot works” as a single state. Confirm these layers separately: 1. the tunnel process started; 2. its listener/transport connection exists; 3. the pivot can reach the intended destination socket; 4. the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit; 5. the application actually uses that path; 6. name resolution and authentication match the application; 7. a callback, if required, has its own return path. ## 2. Discover the pivot's network position Linux: ```bash id ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf ``` Windows: ```cmd whoami /all ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano ``` PowerShell selected endpoints: ```powershell Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object DestinationPrefix,RouteMetric Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 ``` > An interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. Validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel. ```bash nc -nvz -w 3 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT/ ``` ```powershell Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_HOST -Port INTERNAL_PORT ``` ## 3. Choose the smallest compatible route | Need | Baseline | Choose when | Main limitation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | One TCP service through an SSH pivot | SSH local forward | Kali can initiate SSH to pivot | One destination socket per forward | | Many TCP destinations through SSH pivot | SSH dynamic forward | Kali can initiate SSH to pivot | SOCKS/client compatibility | | Pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked | SSH remote or remote-dynamic forward | Pivot has OpenSSH client and can reach Kali SSH | Kali SSH policy; OpenSSH version for remote dynamic | | SSH hop directly to internal SSH | `ProxyJump` | Both pivot and destination provide SSH | SSH-only path | | Simple Linux TCP relay | Socat | Binary already exists and listener can be exposed | Clear TCP relay; no authentication/encryption | | Transparent selected subnets through SSH | sshuttle | Suitable SSH server with Python; local privileges | TCP/DNS-oriented, local firewall changes | | Windows SSH-based forward | Built-in `ssh.exe` or Plink | Compatible client exists and outbound SSH works | Server policy and credential/host-key handling | | Windows native fixed TCP relay | `netsh interface portproxy` | Elevated token; target modification acceptable | TCP only; firewall/IP Helper/stateful cleanup | | Outbound HTTP/WebSocket-shaped tunnel | Chisel | Pivot can run matching binary and reach server | Client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits | | Routed access for ordinary clients | Ligolo-ng | Agent can reach proxy and TUN/route setup is possible | Userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking | | DNS is the only viable egress | dnscat2 | DNS path plus authoritative/direct server control | Slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required | Prefer one explicit forward for one known service. Use SOCKS when several TCP endpoints must be explored. Use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. Do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient. ## 4. Socat fixed TCP relay On a Linux pivot, expose one internal TCP service: ```bash socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` Loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage: ```bash socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` Verify the listener on the pivot with `ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT`. Run `nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT` from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. These checks run on different machines: ```bash ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT ``` > `fork` handles multiple connections. `reuseaddr` eases rebinding after restart. Socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. A listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails. ## 5. OpenSSH forwarding Add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: ```text -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` `ExitOnForwardFailure` proves requested listening sockets were established. It does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. ### 5.1 Local forward: listener on the SSH client Run on Kali when Kali can SSH to the pivot: ```bash ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` Use the listener as though it were the internal service: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 LOCAL_PORT curl -v http://127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT/ ``` > The SSH server/pivot resolves and connects to `INTERNAL_HOST`. Bind to `127.0.0.1` unless another authorized local host must use the forward; `-g` or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. ### 5.2 Dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH client ```bash ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` OpenSSH acts as a SOCKS4/5 server. The pivot makes destination connections selected by each SOCKS request. ### 5.3 Remote forward: listener on the SSH server Run on a pivot that can initiate an SSH connection back to Kali: ```bash ssh -N \ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` Kali then uses: ```bash nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT ``` > The SSH client/pivot connects to `INTERNAL_HOST`. `AllowTcpForwarding` and server policy must permit the forward. A non-loopback remote bind additionally depends on `GatewayPorts`; do not assume `0.0.0.0` was honored. ### 5.4 Remote dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH server Run on the pivot: ```bash ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ``` The SOCKS listener appears on Kali and destination connections exit through the pivot. Remote dynamic forwarding requires OpenSSH 7.6 or later on the client that issues `-R`. Run `ssh -V` on the pivot (the SSH client). Run `ss -lntp | grep 1080` on Kali (the SSH server hosting the SOCKS listener). These checks run on different machines; do not paste both into one terminal: ```bash ssh -V ss -lntp | grep 1080 ``` ### 5.5 SSH jump and proxy command Direct SSH through an SSH pivot: ```bash ssh -J PIVOT_USER@PIVOT TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ``` SSH through an existing SOCKS5 endpoint with Ncat: ```bash ssh -o ProxyCommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST ``` `%h` and `%p` are replaced with the destination host and port. Prefer this native proxy route when ProxyChains interposition is unreliable.
Use an SSH configuration for repeated access ```sshconfig Host pivot HostName PIVOT User PIVOT_USER Host internal HostName INTERNAL_HOST User TARGET_USER ProxyJump pivot ``` ```bash ssh internal scp FILE internal:DESTINATION_PATH ```
## 6. ProxyChains and SOCKS-aware clients Use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: ```text strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ``` ```bash proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' ``` Constraints: - ProxyChains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. - ProxyChains supports TCP only. It does not proxy UDP, ICMP, SYN scans or pcap-based discovery. - For Nmap use `-sT -Pn -n` with a focused port list. Proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot. - `proxy_dns` moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. `-n` prevents Nmap's local reverse lookups. - Prefer an application's native proxy option when available. Native examples: ```bash curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT ``` ## 7. sshuttle transparent selected-subnet route ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@PIVOT:SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET ANOTHER_SUBNET ``` Through a previously established local forward to the SSH pivot: ```bash sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@127.0.0.1:LOCAL_SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET ``` > sshuttle is useful when many TCP clients need transparent access. It requires privileges and firewall/redirection support on the client; the remote side needs a compatible Python execution path. It is not a general layer-2 VPN and does not make arbitrary raw-packet or UDP behavior equivalent to direct routing. Record the selected subnets so existing VPN routes are not accidentally captured. ## 8. Windows forwarding alternatives ### 8.1 Built-in OpenSSH client ```cmd where ssh.exe ssh.exe -V ssh.exe -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 KALI_USER@LHOST -p KALI_SSH_PORT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 ``` The same `-L`, `-D`, `-R`, `ProxyJump` and `ProxyCommand` concepts apply to current Windows OpenSSH. Remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version. ### 8.2 Plink Remote fixed forward from Windows to Kali: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l KALI_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\kali-password.txt ^ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ^ -P KALI_SSH_PORT LHOST ``` Local dynamic SOCKS on Windows: ```cmd plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l SSH_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\ssh-password.txt ^ -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -P SSH_PORT PIVOT ``` > Current Plink supports `-L`, `-R` and `-D`, but not OpenSSH's remote-dynamic shorthand. `-batch` prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified `-hostkey`. `-pwfile` avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. Prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible. ### 8.3 Netsh portproxy Elevated Windows shell: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT ^ connectaddress=INTERNAL_HOST connectport=INTERNAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy show all netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":LOCAL_PORT" ``` If the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized: ```cmd netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ^ dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=LOCAL_PORT ``` Cleanup: ```cmd netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ``` > `portproxy` requires an elevated token, forwards TCP rather than UDP, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the IP Helper service. A stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. Record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule. ## 9. Chisel HTTP/WebSocket tunnel ### 9.1 Reverse SOCKS: pivot initiates outward On Kali: ```bash chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT ``` Record the server fingerprint. On the pivot: ```bash chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` `R:socks` is the shorter equivalent using the default server-side `127.0.0.1:1080` listener. Traffic sent to Kali's SOCKS listener exits through the Chisel client/pivot. ### 9.2 Reverse fixed TCP forward ```bash # Kali chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT # Pivot: expose an internal service on Kali loopback chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' LHOST:CHISEL_PORT \ R:127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ``` ### 9.3 Forward SOCKS when the client is on the tool side ```bash # Pivot/server side chisel server --socks5 --port CHISEL_PORT # Kali/client side chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' PIVOT:CHISEL_PORT \ 127.0.0.1:1080:socks ``` ### 9.4 Current UDP-aware mode Current upstream Chisel distinguishes: ```text socks / R:socks -> SOCKS5 TCP CONNECT only udpsocks / R:udpsocks -> TCP CONNECT plus SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE ``` ```bash # Requires compatible current peers chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks ``` > This does not make ProxyChains UDP-capable—ProxyChains remains TCP-only. The UDP application must support SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE, or another compatible adapter must be used. Current Chisel peers, TCP and UDP firewall access to the SOCKS listener, and its documented association/fragmentation limits all matter. ### 9.5 Chisel failure cues ```bash chisel --version chisel server --help chisel client --help ss -lntp ``` | Cue | Interpretation | | --- | --- | | No connection at server | Pivot egress, address, listener or WebSocket/proxy path | | HTTP reaches server but upgrade fails | Intermediary may block WebSocket upgrade | | `exec format error` | Wrong OS/architecture | | Missing GLIBC/version symbol | Build/runtime incompatibility; choose a compatible official build | | Fingerprint mismatch | Wrong server or changed key; do not bypass verification blindly | | SOCKS listener exists but endpoint fails | Pivot-to-destination or application/proxy compatibility | | TCP works but UDP fails | Ordinary `socks`, old peer, UDP bind/firewall or unsupported client | ## 10. Ligolo-ng routed pivot ### 10.1 Proxy and agent On Kali: ```bash ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT ``` In the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint: ```text certificate_fingerprint ``` On the pivot: ```bash ./agent -connect LHOST:LIGOLO_PORT -accept-fingerprint CERT_FINGERPRINT ``` `-ignore-cert` is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline. ### 10.2 Current managed interface and route In the Ligolo console: ```text interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route INTERNAL_SUBNET tunnel_start --tun ligolo ``` Manual Linux alternative: ```bash sudo ip tuntap add user "$USER" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add INTERNAL_SUBNET dev ligolo ``` Then use normal clients: ```bash ip route get INTERNAL_HOST nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST curl -v http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ``` > Ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. Ordinary TCP clients generally work without ProxyChains, but raw-packet assumptions, ICMP details and some UDP behavior can differ from direct access. Use connect-based validation first. ### 10.3 Pivot loopback services Ligolo maps its special `240.0.0.0/4` range to the selected agent's loopback. Add one narrow route: ```bash sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS 240.0.0.1 ``` Use this only when the desired service is bound to `127.0.0.1` on the agent. ### 10.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent In the selected Ligolo session: ```text listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT --to 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT --tcp listener_list ``` Kali listener: ```bash ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT ``` An internal target connects to `PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP:PIVOT_PORT`; Ligolo relays it to Kali's loopback listener. Cleanup: ```text listener_stop LISTENER_ID ``` ## 11. DNS and Kerberos across pivots - Decide whether the application resolves the name locally, ProxyChains intercepts it, the SOCKS exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. - Use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. - Kerberos needs an SPN-compatible hostname, realm/KDC route and correct time. A working IP connection does not prove Kerberos naming works. - A temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. ```bash getent hosts INTERNAL_FQDN curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_FQDN:PORT/ klist KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/TARGET_HOST ``` The first command checks Kali's normal resolver. The `curl` form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through SOCKS. Do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by ProxyChains: NSS implementation and process behavior vary. For Impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an IP when the tool supports it: ```bash impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' ``` ## 12. Callback and delivery routing A forward path and callback path are different graphs: ```text Kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> Kali listener # callback path ``` Options: 1. make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; 2. expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to Kali; 3. use a Ligolo agent listener or SSH/Chisel remote forward; 4. choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. Fixed SSH callback relay, run from the pivot: ```bash ssh -N -g -L 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT:127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT \ KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes ``` This creates the listener on the SSH client/pivot and makes the destination connection from Kali's SSH server to Kali loopback. `-g` permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. Verify the actual bind with `ss`; do not infer it from command syntax. Also route payload delivery separately. An internal host may reach the pivot but not Kali's HTTP server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. ## 13. Multi-hop routes For every additional hop, write another complete segment: ```text Kali -> tunnel A -> PIVOT_A -> tunnel B -> PIVOT_B -> INTERNAL_HOST:PORT ``` Rules: - validate one hop before adding the next; - avoid overlapping local/VPN/internal routes; - use unique listener and SOCKS ports; - record which session owns each route; - ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; - re-evaluate DNS and callback direction at every hop; - prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. An upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. Do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. ## 14. DNS tunneling with dnscat2 Use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and DNS is demonstrably permitted. This is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official BOK. Prerequisites: - command execution sufficient to run a compatible client; - either authoritative control/NS delegation for `TUNNEL_DOMAIN` or direct UDP/53 reachability to the server; - a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally; - permission to bind/listen on the required DNS port; - tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous DNS patterns. Authoritative-domain mode: ```bash dnscat2-server --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN ``` Client: ```bash ./dnscat --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN ``` Direct DNS-server mode shown by the server's own usage output: ```bash ./dnscat --dns server=DNS_SERVER,port=53 --secret=SHARED_SECRET ``` Server console: ```text windows window -i SESSION_ID help ``` > A DNS query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. Match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. Cache, recursion, EDNS, TCP fallback, DNS security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. DNS tunneling is not DNS spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide. ## 15. Failure router | Evidence | Failing layer | Next decision | | --- | --- | --- | | Pivot cannot reach destination | Internal route/firewall/service | Fix or choose another pivot before tunneling | | Tunnel client cannot reach server | Transport/egress/listener | Test the exact server address/port from pivot | | SSH says forwarding disabled | Server policy | Use an authorized alternative; do not keep changing client flags | | Local/remote port does not bind | Address in use, privilege or bind policy | Inspect listeners and `ExitOnForwardFailure` output | | Listener exists; simple TCP test fails | Pivot-to-destination or wrong destination | Test from pivot and inspect tunnel logs | | Simple TCP works; application fails | Client/protocol/authentication | Check native proxy support, hostname/SPN and application prerequisites | | ProxyChains shows no hook/connection | Static/incompatible client or config | Use native proxy option, explicit forward or routed pivot | | Nmap through SOCKS finds nothing | Wrong scan type/discovery/DNS/latency | Use focused `-sT -Pn -n`; verify with Ncat/curl | | Kerberos works by IP only for TCP, auth fails | DNS/SPN/KDC/time | Separate route address from service hostname | | Forward access works; callback absent | Reverse path/listener bind | Draw target-to-listener route independently | | Chisel starts but server sees nothing | Egress/URL/WebSocket/binary execution | Capture stderr and inspect transport | | Ligolo session exists; route misses tunnel | OS route/interface/session | Check route selection and selected agent/tunnel | | TCP works, UDP fails | Tool/client transport limitation | Identify a genuine UDP-capable path; do not assume SOCKS/ProxyChains | | DNS queries never reach authority | Delegation/resolver/egress | Prove the DNS path before debugging dnscat2 crypto | | Deep route suddenly fails everywhere | Upstream tunnel/session | Repair from the first hop outward | ## 16. Verification and cleanup Kali/Linux: ```bash ss -lntup ip -brief address ip route ps -ef | grep -E '[s]sh .*-[LDR]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle' ``` Windows: ```cmd netstat -ano tasklist netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ``` Record: - exact process/command and version; - bind address and port; - transport direction and initiator; - pivot and destination; - routes/name mappings/configuration files added; - simple TCP proof and final application proof; - callback proof where applicable; - cleanup command and result. Stop tunnel processes and remove TUN routes, Ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, Netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task. ## Tooling for this section | Tool | Purpose | Required context | Baseline | Decisive output | Failure cue | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `ip`/`route`/`ss`/`netstat` | Discover and verify each hop | Shell on relevant host | Sections 2 and 16 | Correct route and listener | Listener exists on wrong interface | | Ncat/curl/Test-NetConnection | Prove one socket | Route from test source | Sections 2 and 16 | TCP handshake/application response | Complex tool fails before baseline proof | | Socat | Simple fixed TCP relay | Binary and bind permission | Section 4 | Listener plus remote connection | Clear relay exposed too broadly | | OpenSSH | Fixed, dynamic, remote and jump routes | SSH authentication/policy | Section 5 | Requested listener and successful client flow | Forwarding or bind denied | | ProxyChains | Wrap compatible TCP clients | SOCKS endpoint + dynamic linking | Section 6 | Connection log through proxy | UDP/raw/static client unsupported | | sshuttle | Transparent selected-subnet TCP/DNS route | SSH, client privileges, remote Python | Section 7 | Ordinary client reaches selected subnet | Route collision/firewall backend issue | | Windows `ssh.exe`/Plink | SSH forwards from Windows | Client present and server reachable | Section 8 | Kali/Windows listener established | Hidden host-key/password prompt | | Netsh portproxy | Native Windows fixed TCP relay | Elevated token | Section 8 | Stored rule + listener + remote flow | Firewall/IP Helper/destination failure | | Chisel | HTTP/WebSocket reverse SOCKS/forwards | Compatible binary and egress | Section 9 | Session + SOCKS/forward listener | WebSocket, fingerprint or runtime error | | Ligolo-ng | Routed access and agent listeners | Agent/proxy + TUN route | Section 10 | OS route and ordinary client flow | Wrong session/interface/route | | dnscat2 | Conditional DNS channel | Resolver/authority or direct DNS path | Section 14 | Authenticated encrypted session | DNS never reaches server | Package names and command behavior vary. Check local `--help`/versions before use. Do not install tooling or alter host/network configuration without scope and authorization. ## Exam restriction The current OSCP+ exam guide explicitly states that Metasploit cannot be used for pivoting because that would involve more than one target. The current guide does not individually approve every other tool; the learner remains responsible for restrictions and must recheck the guide before a mock or exam. ## Sources - Supplied PEN-200, Chapter 19 pp. 583–629 and Chapter 20 pp. 630–652. - [OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/38543335188756-OSCP-Body-of-knowledge) and [current exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide) - [OpenSSH client manual](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh) - [Socat documentation](http://www.dest-unreach.org/socat/doc/socat.html) - [ProxyChains-NG](https://github.com/rofl0r/proxychains-ng) - [sshuttle](https://github.com/sshuttle/sshuttle) - [PuTTY/Plink manual](https://the.earth.li/~sgtatham/putty/latest/htmldoc/Chapter7.html) - [Microsoft Netsh interface/portproxy](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/netsh-interface) - [Chisel](https://github.com/jpillora/chisel) - [Ligolo-ng quickstart](https://docs.ligolo.ng/Quickstart/), [listeners](https://docs.ligolo.ng/Listeners/) and [agent loopback access](https://docs.ligolo.ng/Localhost/) - [dnscat2](https://github.com/iagox86/dnscat2) - [getSH tunneling route](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/useful-stuff?section=tunneling), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98) - [Hexdump OSCP repository](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP) and [Port Forwarding and Pivoting video index](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/yt-en). The upstream module provides the four SSH-forwarding categories; current syntax and tool behavior above were checked independently.

pages.title: Integrated Attack Tracking and Evidence
pages.markdown:
# Integrated Attack Tracking and Evidence

[← Stage index](README.md) | [Quick sheet](../../cheatsheets/evidence-reporting.md) | [Master Notes](../../notes/Master_Notes.md#evidence-and-reproducibility) | [Strategy map](../../notes/Attack_Strategy_Map.md) | Study methods: [Complete attacks and retain reproducible evidence](../../notes/methods/integration.md)

> **Goal:** finish an unfamiliar scoped target by keeping the current attack state, candidate paths and required evidence synchronized. This is the integration procedure for the earlier stages; it does not replace their service- and technique-specific procedures.

## Establish the operating contract

Before interacting with a target, record:

```text
scope and explicit exclusions
objective and required evidence
starting identity/credential and whether it is local, domain or application scoped
source host, interface, route and DNS context
allowed/restricted tools and the current Metasploit target decision
case directory and note/evidence locations
cleanup or restoration obligations
```

An interesting vulnerability is not automatically the objective. The attack is complete only when the required access or privilege is verified and the reproduction/evidence chain is retained.

Create a private case workspace using target-neutral names until the real scope is known:

```bash
mkdir -p case/{00-admin,01-scans,02-services,03-web,04-exploits,05-loot,06-sessions,07-screenshots,08-report}
touch case/00-admin/{scope.md,state.md,credentials.md,routes.md,hypotheses.md,transitions.md}
```

Do not put exam or private target material in a public repository.

## Maintain a live state map

Keep target-specific values in a private case/lab record, not this public repository.

```text
HOSTS
- host/IP | role | reachable from | open services | evidence file

IDENTITIES
- local/domain identity | credential type | validated services | privilege | source

ROUTES
- source -> listener/tunnel -> pivot -> destination | DNS point | callback path

HYPOTHESES
- observation | hypothesis | prerequisite | next discriminating test | status

TRANSITIONS
- old state -> action -> new access/identity/route | decisive output | evidence

EVIDENCE COVERAGE
- objective | reproduction complete? | identity/IP proof? | screenshot? | panel/task state
```

Label each claim `observed`, `inferred`, `possible`, `confirmed`, `disproven` or `inconclusive`. Close a path only with a test that addressed its prerequisite; do not confuse a tool error with a disproven attack hypothesis.

## Run the attack as a state machine

```text
Observe
→ Enumerate
→ Interpret
→ Hypothesize
→ Validate prerequisite
→ Exploit the confirmed primitive
→ Verify the new state
→ Re-enumerate from that state
→ Escalate, move or pivot
→ Capture evidence and cleanup
```

The sequence is a loop, not a one-time checklist. A state change routes work back to the relevant earlier stage:

| New state | Mandatory re-entry |
| --- | --- |
| Hostname, address, interface, listener or route | Discovery and service identification from the source position that can reach it |
| Credential, key, hash or ticket | Classify identity/material, validate compatible access, then authenticated enumeration |
| Application role/session | Revisit the same application and objects through the new authorization view |
| Command execution or shell | Verify host/identity/network, repair the session, transfer only what is needed, start local enumeration |
| Administrator/root/SYSTEM | Re-enumerate protected files, credentials, services, sessions, routes and domain context |
| Domain identity/group/right | Rebuild reachable host/service/object paths and validate the specific right |
| Pivot or proxy | Repeat discovery from the new vantage point; separately design callback and delivery routes |

### Keep two queues

The **coverage queue** prevents missed surfaces:

```text
host/source position → endpoint → confirmed application → required enumeration → state
```

The **hypothesis queue** prevents random exploitation:

```text
observation → possible transition → prerequisite → cheapest discriminating test
→ decisive success/failure → next action
```

Do not spend the whole assessment deepening one hypothesis while high-value coverage remains unknown. Conversely, do not keep scanning after a confirmed path only to avoid validating it.

## Rank candidate paths

Create one card per distinct mechanism:

```text
Observation:
Desired state transition:
Required prerequisites:
Already confirmed:
Still unknown:
Cheapest discriminating test:
Success means:
Failure means:
Noise/change/cleanup:
Handoff if successful:
Status/evidence:
```

Rank without false numerical precision:

1. **Confirmed prerequisite, direct objective transition.** Test first.
2. **Strong observation, one cheap missing prerequisite.** Validate next.
3. **Useful information path.** Prefer when it can unlock several branches.
4. **Multiple unsupported assumptions or disruptive action.** Defer.
5. **Disproven prerequisite.** Close until new evidence changes it.

Evidence strength overrides technique popularity. Prefer low-cost tests that split plausible explanations and create reusable information. A path that succeeds only after several unverified assumptions is not yet a high-priority path.

## Standalone attack workflow

Use the earlier procedure linked at each transition; the integration layer owns order and state:

1. Record scope, objective, source position and evidence requirements.
2. Establish TCP coverage, bounded UDP coverage and confirmed application identities.
3. Enumerate every confirmed service in its anonymous/current context; map web requests, hosts, parameters, content and roles.
4. Search files, configuration, repositories and application data for identities or prerequisites.
5. Build candidate cards for manual application weaknesses, compatible credentials and exact public-exploit prerequisites.
6. Validate one prerequisite at a time and prove the smallest useful effect.
7. Convert execution into a verified session; record host, identity, privilege, interfaces and routes.
8. Capture the initial-access transition and any required unprivileged objective before changing state.
9. Enumerate local privilege paths as controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → trigger → effect.
10. Verify the elevated identity, capture required evidence, re-enumerate protected context and remove exercise artifacts.
11. Reconstruct the ordered reproduction path while the commands and assumptions are still known.

Failure at a step returns to its owning block. Do not skip service enumeration because one banner suggests a CVE, and do not start privilege escalation before proving which host and identity the shell represents.

## Assumed-breach AD workflow

```text
starting credential
→ local/domain identity + DNS/time/DC context
→ reachable host/service map
→ users/groups/computers/shares/SPNs/ACLs/sessions
→ ranked identity or host transition
→ compatible password/hash/ticket use
→ verified session/new identity
→ re-enumeration
→ route/movement to next host
→ higher domain privilege/objective
```

Keep five variables together for every edge:

```text
controlled identity
effective group/right
target object or host
required protocol/route
resulting identity/access
```

BloodHound and enumerators generate candidate edges. Validate the underlying group membership, ACL, session, service right, route and authentication material before acting. After every new identity or host session, repeat authenticated enumeration rather than continuing from the old authorization view.

For multihop work, maintain a route diagram and a separate callback diagram. A route that permits an operator tool to reach a service does not prove that a payload can return to its handler.

## Capture every state transition

Linux:

```bash
date -Is
hostname
id
ip addr
ip route
```

Windows:

```cmd
echo %DATE% %TIME%
hostname
whoami /all
ipconfig /all
route print
```

For each access or escalation, retain:

1. the observation that selected the path;
2. the exact command/request with secrets redacted in the reusable copy;
3. relevant output or response;
4. host and identity verification;
5. the effect/new capability;
6. cleanup/restoration; and
7. the next re-enumeration result.

Use a compact transition packet:

```text
time/timezone | source host/interface | target host/service | starting identity
observation | prerequisite | exact action | decisive output
new identity/access/route | evidence files | cleanup | next re-enumeration
```

Capture the transition when it happens. Reconstructing it later risks losing a required token, request, route, working directory, listener or source identity.

## Save tool output deliberately

```bash
mkdir -p evidence/nmap evidence/web evidence/loot evidence/screenshots
nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p PORTS TARGET -oA evidence/nmap/TARGET-services
script -q -f evidence/session.txt
```

Run `exit` when finished so the transcript closes and flushes. Do not record unrelated secrets in a broad transcript.

```powershell
Start-Transcript -Path .\evidence\powershell-session.txt
# commands
Stop-Transcript
```

Hash important transferred or generated artifacts:

```bash
sha256sum FILE | tee FILE.sha256
```

Never publish credentials, flags, target IPs, full private transcripts or copyrighted course text to this repository.

## Proof/evidence checkpoint

Current official exam guidance requires proof-file content to be displayed from its original location in an interactive target shell and included in a screenshot with the target IP. The control-panel submission is separate and must occur before the exam ends. Recheck the guide immediately before an exam because these rules can change.

Linux example layout:

```bash
hostname; id; ip addr
cat /root/proof.txt
```

Windows example layout:

```cmd
hostname & whoami & ipconfig
type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt
```

Use the actual objective-provided path and required identity. Do not use AI on actual exam targets, proofs or reports; the current guide prohibits AI chatbots during the exam.

## Public exploit evidence

For an unmodified exploit, retain its source URL rather than pasting pages of code. For a modified exploit, retain:

- original URL and version/commit;
- local modified copy;
- a focused diff/highlight of changes;
- why each change was necessary;
- build/interpreter command and dependencies;
- payload-generation command, if any; and
- exact execution and result verification.

```bash
git diff --no-index original.py modified.py > exploit-changes.diff
sha256sum original.py modified.py
```

## Reproduction-path template

```markdown
### Objective / result

**Starting state:** source host, network position and identity.

1. Observation and evidence.
2. Enumeration command/request and decisive output.
3. Vulnerability/prerequisite validation.
4. Exploitation command/request, including required listener/route.
5. Session verification: host, identity and privilege.
6. Escalation evidence and final verification.
7. Cleanup/restoration.

**Artifacts:** screenshots, saved output, hashes and exploit source/diff.
```

Write steps in execution order. Explain why a command was needed and what the output established; a transcript alone is not a report.

## Dead-end recovery

Treat stagnation as a state problem, not an instruction to try more commands. Warning signs include unchanged evidence, repeated disproven tests, increasingly exotic mechanisms, tool switching without a new hypothesis, and work whose success would not advance the objective.

When progress stalls:

1. Freeze the current host/identity/route/credential map.
2. Mark each path with the last decisive result.
3. Recheck scan/service/application coverage and authenticated views.
4. Separate environment/tool failure from a disproven prerequisite.
5. Choose the cheapest test that can change the decision.
6. Switch paths when the expected information gain is higher.
7. Return only when new evidence changes an assumption.

Use this failure router:

| Symptom | Classification | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool cannot reach any known-good endpoint | Environment/route failure | Repair source interface, proxy, DNS or tool configuration |
| Test did not exercise the claimed prerequisite | Inconclusive | Replace it with a discriminating test |
| Exact prerequisite is absent | Disproven path | Close the card until state changes |
| Authentication works but action is denied | Authorization boundary | Enumerate service/object rights under that identity |
| New credential or route exists but old enumeration is unchanged | Stale state | Re-enumerate from the new identity/vantage point |
| Many weak possibilities, no decisive observation | Coverage gap | Return to surface/service/application enumeration |

## Build the report from transitions

For every achieved objective, the report path should read:

```text
starting state and scope
→ decisive enumeration
→ prerequisite/vulnerability validation
→ exact exploitation action
→ session/identity verification
→ privilege or movement transition
→ final objective evidence
→ cleanup/restoration
```

Include only enough non-decisive enumeration to make the selection understandable. Screenshots need captions and nearby interpretation; they do not replace commands or prose. Raw transcripts are supporting artifacts, not the final narrative.

Current official exam grading follows the target order used in the report. Keep target/objective labels aligned with the control panel and place each target's complete chain together.

## Final PDF and archive validation

Recheck the current guide immediately before a mock or exam. The current baseline is one PDF inside a non-password-protected `.7z`, exact case-sensitive filenames and an archive no larger than 200 MB:

```bash
7z a OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf
7z l OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z
7z t OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z
md5sum OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z
```

Windows hash fallback for a local rehearsal:

```powershell
Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 -LiteralPath '.\OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z'
```

Inspect every exported PDF page before archiving. Confirm that code is not clipped, screenshots remain readable, captions match the correct target and the archive contains only the required PDF. Required scripts and PoCs belong as text inside that PDF, not as extra archive members. The current guide recommends creating/uploading from Kali and warns of a Windows 11 archive compatibility issue. Compare the local MD5 with the upload site's value, click the final submission control and retain the acknowledgement.

The official Word or LibreOffice template is the reliable baseline. A Markdown/Pandoc pipeline, including Hexdump's `report/` generator, is a viable alternative only after a complete dummy export/archive rehearsal; do not install or debug a new report stack during an assessment.

## Final quality checks

- Commands are copyable and placeholders/secrets are resolved in the private report.
- Screenshots are legible and show required identity/IP/proof context.
- Every claim is supported by nearby evidence.
- Target order and objective labels match the control panel.
- Exploit modifications and payload-generation steps are documented.
- The final PDF is visually reviewed after export.
- Archive name/format/size and upload hash match current official requirements.

## Tooling for this section

| Tool or utility | Purpose | Required context | Baseline | Decisive output | Failure cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plain Markdown/editor | Portable live state and reproduction notes | Private case directory | Six ledgers and transition packets above | Current state and next action can be recovered without memory | Notes contain commands but no interpretation/state |
| Nmap `-oA` and client-native output options | Preserve raw enumeration evidence | Authorized scoped target | Save output beside target/service record | Raw and human-readable result exists | Terminal-only output cannot be reconstructed reliably |
| `script` / PowerShell transcript | Record interactive command sequences | Local shell; avoid recording unrelated secrets | `script -q -f evidence/session.txt` / `Start-Transcript` | Timestamped command/output stream | Transcript is not a report and may omit GUI/HTTP state |
| Screenshot utility | Capture required visual proof and decisive GUI/request state | Readable display and private storage | Capture one objective/context per image | Legible proof, IP, identity/context as required | Cropped, unreadable or wrong-host image |
| `sha256sum` / `Get-FileHash` | Integrity for artifacts and evidence | Local files | Hash original/modified/transferred files | Matching expected digest | A hash does not establish exploit success |
| Official Word/LibreOffice template | Baseline report composition/export | Template and tested local editor | Export dummy report to PDF before assessment | Visually correct PDF | Broken code wrapping/images after export |
| `7z` plus `md5sum`/`Get-FileHash` | Package and verify final report | Final reviewed PDF and exact OSID naming | Commands above | One PDF, archive test succeeds, local/upload MD5 match | Wrong name, extra files, password or size over limit |

No new attack tool is required for Block 15. The value comes from disciplined state/evidence handling around the tools already taught.

## Sources

- Supplied PEN-200 Chapter 27 pp. 963–1017, especially pp. 963–968 and 1015–1016; Chapter 5 pp. 94–113.
- [getSH Home and AD flow](https://lizajose.github.io/getSH/home), source snapshot [`e1f62dd`](https://github.com/lizajose/getSH/commit/e1f62dd351bd061b59e2573beea741f6c5bb4f98)
- [Current OSCP+ exam guide](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040165632-OSCP-Exam-Guide)
- [Current OSCP+ reporting requirements](https://help.offsec.com/hc/en-us/articles/360046787731-OSCP-Reporting-Requirements)
- [Hexdump report workflow](https://github.com/LeonardoE95/OSCP/tree/main/report): optional Markdown/Org → Pandoc/LaTeX → PDF/7z path; use only after local rehearsal.
